commits.message: never install against another checkout's database; ask how the app is opened
commits.body:
The first public test install (2026-09-13) wrote its administrator, team
and space into a different checkout's database and ended with a copilot
that could not reach apps/ai. Five defects, all in the setup path:

- .env.example shipped SUPABASE_URL / VITE_SUPABASE_URL / SUPABASE_DB_URL as
  values, so env init saw them as set and never read `supabase status`;
  a stack on another port band kept the default band. The three carry no
  default now, env init always harvests them, refuses a stack whose port is
  not this checkout's supabase/config.toml, and rewrites the block on a
  rerun when the file names another stack's port. doctor has the same row.
- "Optional: run portless:setup?" became "How will you open engenty?":
  localhost (default) or Portless, Portless only when the CLI is installed.
  `engenty dev` warns when the dev-URL block and the start mode disagree.
- env init ran after migrations, so the Mastra schema step never saw
  SUPABASE_DB_URL on a first run and skipped. env init runs first now.
- "Environment ready" printed under "1 need attention"; the verdict and
  the summary count the same rows, a skipped key names what stays off, and
  `engenty setup` exits 1 on remaining gaps unless --allow-gaps.
- The first-space step creates the space when the tenant has no default
  instead of failing with nothing to skip to.
commits.raw_message:

commits.message:
docs(deploy): correct the upgrade runbook against the real 0.2.0 deploy

Running it on the live install broke it three times, and §1 had the central
fact backwards.

Exposed schemas: the list changes in BOTH directions, and the removal is what
hurts. §1 claimed naming a schema that does not exist is a no-op. It is not —
PostgREST answers `3F000 schema "module_memory" does not exist`, refuses to
build its cache at all, and every request becomes PGRST002. `engenty-edge`
then will not pass its server-lane preflight and the site serves 503. It is
configuration, not state, so it survives both a PostgREST restart and a
project restart. Say replace the field, never append, and give the
`Accept-Profile: __nope__` probe that enumerates the live list in one request.
Pre-creating the two new schemas empty (both migrations are `create schema if
not exists`) is what makes doing this before the deploy safe.

Proxy config files: `engenty-egress-proxy` and `engenty-browser-proxy` bind
four files beside the compose file and nothing delivers them. A panel-managed
compose has no git checkout, so Docker creates the mount points as
directories and the container cannot start — after the old containers are
already gone. Not mentioned anywhere before.

Migration ledger: the retired `memory` and `engenty-coordinator` modules leave
four rows with no matching files, and `supabase db push` refuses to run at
all. §0b could not have caught it: the rehearsal dump names data schemas only,
so the copy starts with an empty ledger and applies everything from scratch.
Dump `supabase_migrations` too.

Also §3: a pre-pull script pinning the old `engenty-<service>` names keeps
succeeding against the public images, so the real ones download inside the
outage window.

commits.message:
fix(ui): give the typecheck enough heap, and drop a static 100vh

apps/ui's tsc peaks at ~2.6GB since the spaces merge. Node's default
old-space on a GitHub runner is 2GB, so `@engenty/ui#typecheck` died with
"Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit" — it only ever passed locally
because a dev machine hands node a larger default. Reproduces exactly with
`NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=2048`.

The public mirror's CI is where this showed: pro's own run stops earlier,
at the viewport guard, which the merge tripped — SpaceAppearanceChooser's
popover caps its height with 100vh, and on iOS that is the large viewport,
so the picker overflows whenever the URL bar is up.

commits.message:
fix(publish): render the mirror's env templates from the tree being published

.env.example is generated from every engenty.plugin.json on disk, so pro's
copies document variables for modules the snapshot strips. The mirror
shipped them verbatim: `pnpm env:example:check` failed there on every
release, and an OSS reader was handed Remote-channels and Slack-bridge
settings for code the public tree does not contain.

The snapshot now materialises its filtered tree and runs the real
generator against it, via a new `env example --root`. Post-filtering pro's
file cannot stand in: a provider's setup steps are printed once, under
whichever variable needs them first, so dropping the wrong block would
strip the steps a surviving variable still points at.

publish-open.yml installs the workspace for it. `env` defers the plugin
boot, so the CLI warms only @engenty/environment and @engenty/telemetry.

commits.message:
feat(cli): ask which local Supabase stack a workspace owns

The Supabase CLI keys its containers by `project_id`, not by directory, so
every checkout that materialized config.toml from the template claimed the
same `engenty-local` stack. For a worktree of this project that is what you
want. For a second install it is not: a test install of the public mirror
ran its migrations into the dev database and would have shared it.

`engenty setup --local` now asks, defaulting to `engenty-local` — Enter
reproduces today's file byte for byte. A different id also gets its own
port band: the 543xx range shifts by a thousand (54321 -> 55321 -> 56321),
probing upward until a band is free, which is the offset the worktree
stacks were already shifted by hand. .env.local follows on its own, since
the env wizard harvests `supabase status`.

The prompt only runs when there is no config.toml or with --refresh, and
only on a TTY, so CI's `pnpm run setup` is unchanged. On --refresh the
default is the id this workspace already owns, not the template's, and its
band is reused — a blind Enter cannot silently re-point a custom install at
the shared stack.

Ports are probed by connecting, not by binding: on macOS a listen on
127.0.0.1 succeeds while a container holds the same port on 0.0.0.0, so a
bind probe called the running stack's ports free.

commits.message:
feat(scripts): materialize the open snapshot locally with OUT_DIR

The open tree only came into existence on a release tag, so testing the
install someone actually gets meant cutting a release and cloning the
mirror. That is why every mirror-only failure so far — the plugin slugs,
the env templates, the storage allowlist, the agent count — was found after
it shipped rather than before.

OUT_DIR writes the same filtered tree the next release would push into a
directory you can install and run the setup wizard in, with no GitHub round
trip and no tag. It builds from a commit like the publish path does, so
commit before you test. It refuses any directory it did not create, since
the target usually sits next to a real clone of the mirror, and keeps
node_modules so it can be re-run on every edit.

The public docs site advertised Time tracking, Apps, remote channels and the
Slack bridge to readers whose install has none of them — five pages whose

mechanical rule should touch — which is how the one sentence in team-chat
that sold Slack mirroring got found and rewritten here, where the pro reader
sees it too.

commits.message:
docs: state the real prerequisites, and lower the Node floor to what is tested

`engines.node` said >=24.11.0 and the README said "you need Node 24", but
nothing enforced either: pnpm only warns, and no source uses a 24-only API.
A full run on v22.21.0 — cold install, workspace build, Supabase with 226
migrations, `pnpm dev` with core, ai, ui and docs all listening, the app
served through the gateway, `engenty doctor` green — says 22 works. The
floor is now >=22.18.0, the highest 22.x any dependency declares. 24 stays
the recommendation, because CI and every deploy image run it; it is no
longer a gate.

The prerequisites now have their own section, and say what they are for:
Supabase is what provides sign-in, storage, realtime and row-level tenant
isolation over the one Postgres database, and running it locally is the only
reason a container daemon is needed. Docker Desktop is named as what this is
developed against, OrbStack as also working, and Dory as wired up but
untested rather than a peer recommendation.

Portless is no longer "recommended": plain `pnpm dev` is complete and
verified, and Portless is the optional upgrade for HTTPS origins and
parallel checkouts.

The 0.2.0 release banner becomes one line — early preview, feedback welcome.

commits.message:
fix(db): let a database be built from scratch again

`pnpm db:reset` could not rebuild this database. The expenses baseline
grants to `engenty_server`, a role created by
20260809200000_core_engenty_server_lane.sql — but the file carried the
backdated timestamp 20260616000800, so a from-zero replay ran the grant
two months before the role existed:

  ERROR: role "engenty_server" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42704)
  At statement 7 of 20260616000800_plugin_expenses.sql

It is the only migration of the 40 that name that role which sorted
before it. Existing installs never noticed: they applied it in June when
it was written, against a database where nothing else needed the role
yet. A fresh clone is the path every new self-hoster takes, and it died
there.

Renamed to 20260809290000 — after the server lane, before the
20260908 migrations that alter the same table. An install that already
applied it under the old name sees the new name as one it has not run,
so every statement is now guarded (`if not exists`, drop-policy-first,
`on conflict do nothing`); the four `expenses_*_own_scope` policies were
the only ones that would have failed a second time.

Verified both ways on a local stack: re-applied over an install holding
the old row with its data intact, and `pnpm db:reset` rebuilding from
zero — 253 migrations, 34 core tables, role created by its own
migration.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(setup): name the tenant the wizard actually signs you in to

Step 1 already created a tenant: `createInitialAdmin` calls
`ensureDefaultTenant`, which inserts "Default Tenant" (slug `default`)
and puts the administrator in it. Step 2 then POSTed a SECOND tenant
that nobody joined, so the name typed there applied to a tenant the
admin never saw. A local stack carrying both `default` and the named
tenant, with users split across them, is what this looked like.

Step 2 now renames the admin's own tenant, and the wizard asks what a
team is actually called rather than for an `engenty.app/<slug>` URL that
does not exist in this product — the slug is derived and never shown.

A third step names the tenant's default space, which the
`tenants_ensure_default_space` trigger has already created as "Company",
and re-keys it off that name: the trigger has only a tenant id to go on,
so it uses a placeholder, and `/s/<key>/…` routes on the key. This is the
one moment re-keying is free — nobody has a link to the space yet — so
`PUT /api/spaces/:id/setup` takes an optional `key`. The setup dialog
never sends it.

`ensureDefaultTenant` no longer looks the tenant up by `slug = "default"`.
Renaming the first tenant would otherwise make the next sign-up find no
`default` row and create a second "Default Tenant" beside the one
everybody is in; it now joins the oldest tenant, whatever it is called.

Steps 2 and 3 need a bearer while still on `/initial_setup`, so they sign
in on a detached Supabase client — signing the shared one in flips the
app to authenticated and the router sends `/initial_setup` to the
copilot chat, ending the wizard early. The shared client signs in once,
at the end.

Verified end to end against an empty local database: one tenant named
from step 2 with the admin in it, the default space renamed AND re-keyed,
all seven mounts intact, `/s/<key>` loading. Also the three paths around
it — a second sign-up joining the renamed tenant as a member, step 3's
Skip leaving `company` alone, and a name colliding with an existing
space key landing on `-2`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(cli): install / generate / dev / doctor / reset / deploy replace setup --local

Three spellings of "first run" (setup --local, init, db init), a setup that
only regenerated files, and 20 package.json aliases with a second name for
every verb. Now:

- engenty install: first run, repeatable, no dev preflight
- engenty generate: derived files from engenty.plugins (was setup / db sync)
- engenty dev: preflight -> build -> stack (pnpm dev is the alias)
- engenty doctor: read-only local checks; --remote for a deployment
- engenty db up|down|status|restart|migrate|reset|snapshot|restore
- engenty reset [--light] [--db]  (was purge)
- engenty deploy [--dry-run], deploy migrate

Version read from package.json; checkout-bound commands refuse outside a
workspace; a missing helper script is an error, never a skip.

Fixes on the way: the empty-database probe looked for an "Applied" column
the Supabase CLI no longer prints, so every install offered db reset with
default yes; the running-stack probe missed the JSON spelling API_URL;
config.toml managed markers are matched by prefix so existing files parse.

Docs, CI workflows, AGENTS.md, skills, deploy guides and the www quick
start follow the new names.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

yet. A fresh clone is the path every new self-hoster takes, and it died
there.

Renamed to 20260809290000 — after the server lane, before the
20260908 migrations that alter the same table. An install that already
applied it under the old name sees the new name as one it has not run,
so every statement is now guarded (`if not exists`, drop-policy-first,
`on conflict do nothing`); the four `expenses_*_own_scope` policies were
the only ones that would have failed a second time.

Verified both ways on a local stack: re-applied over an install holding
the old row with its data intact, and `pnpm db:reset` rebuilding from
zero — 253 migrations, 34 core tables, role created by its own
migration.

commits.message: state the real prerequisites, and lower the Node floor to what is tested
commits.body:
`engines.node` said >=24.11.0 and the README said "you need Node 24", but
nothing enforced either: pnpm only warns, and no source uses a 24-only API.
A full run on v22.21.0 — cold install, workspace build, Supabase with 226
migrations, `pnpm dev` with core, ai, ui and docs all listening, the app
served through the gateway, `engenty doctor` green — says 22 works. The
floor is now >=22.18.0, the highest 22.x any dependency declares. 24 stays
the recommendation, because CI and every deploy image run it; it is no
longer a gate.

The prerequisites now have their own section, and say what they are for:
Supabase is what provides sign-in, storage, realtime and row-level tenant
isolation over the one Postgres database, and running it locally is the only
reason a container daemon is needed. Docker Desktop is named as what this is
developed against, OrbStack as also working, and Dory as wired up but
untested rather than a peer recommendation.

Portless is no longer "recommended": plain `pnpm dev` is complete and
verified, and Portless is the optional upgrade for HTTPS origins and
parallel checkouts.

The 0.2.0 release banner becomes one line — early preview, feedback welcome.

commits.message: materialize the open snapshot locally with OUT_DIR
commits.body:
The open tree only came into existence on a release tag, so testing the
install someone actually gets meant cutting a release and cloning the
mirror. That is why every mirror-only failure so far — the plugin slugs,
the env templates, the storage allowlist, the agent count — was found after
it shipped rather than before.

OUT_DIR writes the same filtered tree the next release would push into a
directory you can install and run the setup wizard in, with no GitHub round
trip and no tag. It builds from a commit like the publish path does, so
commit before you test. It refuses any directory it did not create, since
the target usually sits next to a real clone of the mirror, and keeps
node_modules so it can be re-run on every edit.

commits.message: stop asserting pro's agent count in the starter catalogue
commits.body:
The guard read `manifests.length >= 13` — the number of
modules/*/ai/agents/*/agent.json files in this tree. The open snapshot
ships nine: engenty-apps, engenty-remote and time-tracking are filtered
out, taking four agents with them. So the mirror failed this test on every
release while pro stayed green, which is the fourth artifact found to
encode pro's module set and the reason nothing caught it — the failure is

commits.message: ask which local Supabase stack a workspace owns
commits.body:
The Supabase CLI keys its containers by `project_id`, not by directory, so
every checkout that materialized config.toml from the template claimed the
same `engenty-local` stack. For a worktree of this project that is what you
want. For a second install it is not: a test install of the public mirror
ran its migrations into the dev database and would have shared it.

`engenty setup --local` now asks, defaulting to `engenty-local` — Enter
reproduces today's file byte for byte. A different id also gets its own
port band: the 543xx range shifts by a thousand (54321 -> 55321 -> 56321),
probing upward until a band is free, which is the offset the worktree
stacks were already shifted by hand. .env.local follows on its own, since
the env wizard harvests `supabase status`.

The prompt only runs when there is no config.toml or with --refresh, and
only on a TTY, so CI's `pnpm run setup` is unchanged. On --refresh the
default is the id this workspace already owns, not the template's, and its
band is reused — a blind Enter cannot silently re-point a custom install at
the shared stack.

Ports are probed by connecting, not by binding: on macOS a listen on
127.0.0.1 succeeds while a container holds the same port on 0.0.0.0, so a
bind probe called the running stack's ports free.

commits.message: document the public image pipeline
commits.body:
The shipping doc described a `v*` tag as triggering build-images.yml and
nothing else. Since 0.2.0 the same tag also tags the mirror, which builds
and publishes the public `engenty-*` images from the open tree — the images
an OSS install actually pulls, and the half of the pipeline that was
undocumented.

Records the two things that cost a release to learn: the mirror's copy of
publish-images.yml is installed by hand and has already drifted, and a GHCR
package belongs to the repo that created it — pushing to one another repo
owns fails as `permission_denied: read_package`, which names neither the
package nor the owner.

commits.body:
The table was hand-written and said what was true when someone last looked.
It listed Time Tracking — which the open tree does not ship — and left out
nine modules that it does: a reader takes that table for the feature list,
and it undersold the product by half while promising one thing absent.

Rendered now from `engenty.plugins` plus each module's manifest, between
markers, with `pnpm readme:modules:check` in CI so adding a module without
touching the README fails there instead of on someone's first read. Nested

"Connections" on its own does not say which services are covered.

The snapshot re-renders it for the tree it publishes, like the env
templates: pro's table names the closed modules, and the mirror must not.

Also states WHY Node 24 rather than how to install it — nvm is one of five
version managers a reader might use, and the block spent four of its seven
lines telling a developer something they know.

commits.message: give the typecheck enough heap, and drop a static 100vh
commits.body:
apps/ui's tsc peaks at ~2.6GB since the spaces merge. Node's default
old-space on a GitHub runner is 2GB, so `@engenty/ui#typecheck` died with
"Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit" — it only ever passed locally
because a dev machine hands node a larger default. Reproduces exactly with
`NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=2048`.

The public mirror's CI is where this showed: pro's own run stops earlier,
at the viewport guard, which the merge tripped — SpaceAppearanceChooser's
popover caps its height with 100vh, and on iOS that is the large viewport,
so the picker overflows whenever the URL bar is up.

commits.message: correct the upgrade runbook against the real 0.2.0 deploy
commits.body:
Running it on the live install broke it three times, and §1 had the central
fact backwards.

Exposed schemas: the list changes in BOTH directions, and the removal is what
hurts. §1 claimed naming a schema that does not exist is a no-op. It is not —
PostgREST answers `3F000 schema "module_memory" does not exist`, refuses to
build its cache at all, and every request becomes PGRST002. `engenty-edge`
then will not pass its server-lane preflight and the site serves 503. It is
configuration, not state, so it survives both a PostgREST restart and a
project restart. Say replace the field, never append, and give the
`Accept-Profile: __nope__` probe that enumerates the live list in one request.
Pre-creating the two new schemas empty (both migrations are `create schema if
not exists`) is what makes doing this before the deploy safe.

Proxy config files: `engenty-egress-proxy` and `engenty-browser-proxy` bind
four files beside the compose file and nothing delivers them. A panel-managed
compose has no git checkout, so Docker creates the mount points as
directories and the container cannot start — after the old containers are
already gone. Not mentioned anywhere before.

Migration ledger: the retired `memory` and `engenty-coordinator` modules leave
four rows with no matching files, and `supabase db push` refuses to run at
all. §0b could not have caught it: the rehearsal dump names data schemas only,
so the copy starts with an empty ledger and applies everything from scratch.
Dump `supabase_migrations` too.

Also §3: a pre-pull script pinning the old `engenty-<service>` names keeps
succeeding against the public images, so the real ones download inside the
outage window.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): add the Space tier between Project and Global

A space is neutral core infrastructure — a client, a topic, a team, or just
"your space" on a one-person tenant. It sits in the containment ladder as

  Thread > Task > Goal | Routine | Phase > Project > SPACE > Global

and is a PATH SEGMENT, not merely a foreign key: object keys become
`tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/…`, so a space-scoped engenty cannot address another
space's bytes because no path leads there — containment by construction rather
than by a membership check someone has to remember to write.

- core.spaces with one-default-per-tenant, a key-format CHECK (it lands in
  routes, so a key with a slash would be a path-traversal shape) and an
  AFTER INSERT trigger + backfill, so "every tenant has a space" is a database
  invariant rather than something the UI hopes for
- core.space_mount: one table, four resource kinds. Mount = grant — a space's
  capability set is derived from its mounts by ONE function, so the count the
  UI shows and the grants an agent gets cannot disagree
- space-rooted storage keys (fileStorageSpaceObjectKey, workWorkspacePrefix)
  alongside the tenant-level ones, which skills and the Global commons keep
- the Drive as a PROJECTION over four existing stores, not a fourth store
- scripts/check-space-storage-scope.mjs: every tenant-rooted key builder must
  be classified, and the guard reads each owner's own migrations for space_id,
  so a module that later gains a space column becomes an error rather than a
  discovery

NO authorization is inferred from space membership, and there is no per-space
access control: every tenant user sees every space, rights come from roles.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(spaces): make the space the entry point in the UI

`/s/<key>` is a LAYOUT route owning three tabs (Apps · Drive · Tasks), with
every module route mirrored beneath it — so a module opened inside a space
keeps the space around it, and no module re-registers anything.

Three decisions worth keeping:

- There is no new SpaceContext. `WorkspaceContext.currentSpace` already
  existed; it is now driven by the URL. A second context would have given two
  answers to one question.
- EVERY module route is mirrored, not only `placement: "space"` ones.
  Placement is where a module appears by default, not whether a space may
  contain it — filtering by it would 404 contacts and commercial settings
  inside a space. Placement decides only which legacy `/mdl/*` links redirect.
- Reachability comes from the route table, labels from the setup catalog.
  Deriving both from adminMenuItems silently dropped the copilot from every
  space's Apps tab, because its rail entry is built separately.

A module's absolute `/mdl/…` link would otherwise relocate the user across
spaces: eleven modules build links from a `/mdl/<module>` base constant, so an
internal navigation from inside space B hit the legacy redirect and landed in
the tenant default. The redirect now prefers record space → last space in the
URL → default.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): bind work containers and knowledge bases to a space

`space_id` becomes `not null` on goals, tasks, projects and knowledge bases,
and the bytes follow the rows below the space boundary. NULL no longer means
"not yet" — it would mean "escaped the tier".

Constraints:
- the FKs become `on delete restrict`: `set null` cannot coexist with
  `not null`. Checked against a live Postgres rather than reasoned about — a
  TENANT delete still cascades fine (the cascade removes referencing rows in
  the same statement); what restrict blocks is deleting a space that still
  holds work, which is the intent
- `on delete set null` on a COMPOSITE FK nulls EVERY column, tenant_id
  included: deleting a space emitted `SET space_id = NULL, tenant_id = NULL`
  and died on knowledge_bases.tenant_id — an error naming the wrong table, one
  nullable column away from a tenant-less row. Fixed with
  `set null (space_id)`, then superseded by the not-null flip

Knowledge bases lose the tenant-wide tier they had: a library is part of a
space's file tree, so it lives in exactly one space. A library several spaces
shared now belongs to one of them.

Storage re-root (new uploads only — the key is computed once and stored on the
row, so existing files keep resolving from their stored key):
- KB media   → tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/knowledge-base/<slug>/…
- project files → tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/files/project/<id>/<entry>

The browser stopped composing KB keys. That was the actual cause of the drift:
the layout lived in a UI helper that read as string formatting, not storage
code, so when the row learned about spaces nobody looked there. Keys are minted
server-side now. `defaultBuildStorageKey` throws for a non-space owner with no
space rather than falling back — a fallback would silently restore the root
this change closes.

Also fixes: tasks created inside a project ignored the project's space, so
every task added to a project in a non-default space landed in Company.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(spaces): bind triggers to a space so fired tasks stay in it

`module_tasks.triggers` and `module_tasks.task_templates` gain `space_id`
`not null`, matching the goals/tasks shape: composite `(space_id, tenant_id)`
FK to `core.spaces` with `on delete restrict`, backfilled to the tenant
default.

The column is not the point. `fireTrigger` had no space to pass to
`createTask`, so `resolveCreateSpaceId` fell through to its last resort and
every trigger-materialized task landed in the tenant default regardless of
where the routine lived — the one creation path with no human in the loop was
quietly collapsing the tier. The fix is one line: `triggers` joins
`createTask`'s inheritance chain after parent/goal/project, so a fired task
follows its routine and `fireTrigger` itself is untouched.

Verified against local Postgres by driving the real DAL: a template created in
`marketing` produced a trigger in `marketing` and a fired task in `marketing`.
`trigger-fire.test.ts` mocks the DAL away and so passes identically before and
after — a mocked-DAL test cannot see an inheritance chain.

Space-scoped in the same pass, because a column nothing filters on is
decoration: `triggers_list` / `task_templates_list` take `space_id`,
`GET /ai/v1/triggers` forwards `?space_id=`, and `useRoutinesListQuery` scopes
to the current space by default with a `"tenant"` opt-out — scoping in the hook
rather than at six call sites, as the tasks queries already do. The space is
part of the react-query key; `list()` stays a valid prefix so existing
invalidations still clear every space. Create is symmetric.

`taskTemplateUpdateInputSchema` omits `space_id` deliberately:
`updateTaskTemplate` maps a fixed field list, so accepting one would parse
cleanly and then do nothing.

Channels remain open and are a different question — a `module_remote` binding
is one external workspace bound to one tenant, an entry point rather than a
work container.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): one sidebar column with the space on top and modules inside it

The space now HOSTS a module's nav instead of reproducing it. A module's
secondary nav is not data anywhere in this repo — Tasks and KB publish an
opaque ReactNode through usePageConfig — so the only way to show Work/Data/Plan
above a real module sidebar is to own the column and let the page keep filling
its slot.

Two levels in one column: level 1 is the space switcher + Work/Data/Plan tabs +
the mount list; level 2 is a Work-opened module's own nav behind a back arrow.
Data and Plan stay at level 1 because their TAB is the navigation.

app-shell gains route-level column props (secondaryNavHeaderOverride,
secondaryNavLeadingSlot, secondaryNavRouteTransition, secondaryNavRouteBreadcrumb).
Route-level, not page-level, because usePageConfig is last-writer-wins on one
global and these are route facts.

Fixes found on the way:

- SpaceLayout called usePageConfig for a breadcrumb, which silently wiped the
  child page's sidebar: layout effects run after children's and the hook writes
  `secondaryNavAfterItems ?? null` unconditionally. Layouts must never call it.
- The column header inherited the page's topbarChrome, so it was 52px on Work
  and 44px on Plan — the "jumping and refreshing" between tabs. routeOwnsChrome
  pins it.
- TasksRedirectPage hops through the absolute /mdl/tasks base; LegacyModuleRedirect
  now resolves from the remembered space without a round trip, and App.tsx holds
  the space chrome across the hop. The hop itself remains (11 modules hardcode
  /mdl/ bases) — it is just no longer visible.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): real personal spaces, built the home-directory way

A personal space is a NORMAL space plus a general permission mechanism plus a
thin convention — not a special type. A Unix home directory is an ordinary
directory; owner + mode bits + the useradd convention are what make it personal.
Here: `visibility` (open|private) and core.space_member are the mechanism,
`owner_user_id` + a trigger on core.user_tenant_roles are the convention.

This retires "there is NO per-space access control" deliberately. The §1c
non-goal survives REFINED, not reversed: space_member answers human
access/visibility, space_mount's existing agent rows answer agent
authorization, and the capability system stays authoritative for what an agent
may do.

RLS is only half the enforcement, and the smaller half. The server lane's JWT
subject is the nil UUID, so Postgres sees a tenant and never a user: the
policies here bind the browser lane, and listAccessibleSpaces /
requireSpaceAccess / accessibleSpaceIds are what actually hold on every
server-mediated path. A membership rule believed to be "enforced by RLS" on a
server path is enforced by nothing.

Inaccessible is 404, never 403, everywhere. Personal spaces are named after
people, so confirming one exists is itself the disclosure.

Three findings from the leak audit reshaped the work:

- The Drive was the symptom, not the leak. It fans out to /api/projects and
  /api/kb/… with a space_id — MODULE routes that trusted the id they were
  handed. The gate lives at the single plugin-http dispatch, so a module gains
  a space filter and is covered without knowing the gate exists.
- search.documents had no space at all while the KB source indexes every
  article, and knowledge bases are space-scoped. Search never passes a
  /s/<key> route, so no route guard was in its path. Adding the RPC parameter
  created an OVERLOAD rather than replacing the function — PostgREST calls by
  named args, so a call omitting it matched both; the old signature is dropped.
- PrincipalContext has no `userId` (a user IS principalId; agents carry
  actingForUserId). Reading the wrong field silently fell back to the nil UUID
  and the symptom was people unable to open their OWN space. Unit tests missed
  it because their fixtures were kinder than reality; the live two-user run
  caught it, and the fixtures now mirror PrincipalContext.

Also: space setup is owner-OR-admin, because admins deliberately cannot see
private spaces and admin-only setup would have left personal spaces
unconfigurable by anyone at all.

Verified at three levels, both directions: RLS via psql as each user, the
guards via unit tests, and live HTTP with two tokens — each user sees their own
personal space and not the other's, and every cross-user module-route read 404s
while the same request for the owner returns 200.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): personal spaces have no members; space roster lives in Settings

Two corrections from Matthias, and the second reshapes the concept.

A personal space is a SPECIAL type of space, not an ordinary one that happens
to start private. It belongs to one person and has no members, ever —
`owner_user_id` is the whole of its access grant, and `core.space_member`
becomes exclusively a shared-space table. That is smaller than what Phase P
built, not larger: the creation trigger no longer seeds an owner row, a new
trigger refuses any member row on an owned space, and existing rows are
removed.

The first cut of that migration deleted only rows where the member WAS the
owner. That left a member row sitting on a personal space — a state the new
trigger forbids anyone from creating — so the invariant would have read as
enforced with a violating row still in the table. Widened to every member row
on an owned space. Found immediately, by a row left over from live testing.

`core.protect_space_owner_member` is dropped rather than left inert: a trigger
that guards nothing is a claim that some rule is still enforced there.

The roster moved out of the space sidebar and into Settings, as the People tab
of `/settings/spaces/:spaceId` — beside Team in the settings menu. Managing
people is administration: you check a roster occasionally and change it rarely,
so it does not belong next to the things you open every day. The tab is absent
entirely on a personal space, because a tab that could only ever say "nobody
here" is worse than no tab.

Supporting work:

- `GET /api/users/directory` — names and ids only. `/api/users` was `select("*")`
  and would have handed a picker everyone's private phone number and home
  address. Registered BEFORE `/api/users/:id` or the literal is read as an id.
- `listSpaceMembers` embeds the person's name, with a narrow three-column
  projection for the same reason.
- Owner-first ordering, sorted in TypeScript: `order("role")` is ALPHABETICAL,
  so "member" sorted before "owner" and put the owner at the bottom of their own
  space's roster. Caught in the browser; now pinned by a test.

Verified live: Company (shared) shows Drive · People · Files and lists both
people; matthias (personal) shows Drive · Files with no People tab; the database
refuses an inserted member row on a personal space.

This commit also carries the `/api/users` field-narrowing from the background
task running concurrently in this worktree (CORE_USER_COLUMNS + toCoreUserWire,
with its tests). It could not be separated — that work and the directory
endpoint touch the same DAL and route files, and `crud-routes.ts` imports
`toCoreUserWire`, so committing one without the other would not build.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(spaces): read-only roster, Settings in the sidebar foot, spaces on Team profiles

Four changes, all from review feedback.

**People is read-only in the Work tab.** An × beside a colleague's name in the
sidebar you open all day is an invitation to a mistake — one click from a list
you are only glancing at. The roster stays visible there because "who else is
in here" is worth seeing; changing it is administration and moved behind
Settings. Shared spaces only: a personal space has no members by construction,
so the section is absent rather than empty.

**A Settings link pinned to the foot of the space sidebar**, where this
application already puts Settings. It needed a new `secondaryNavFooterSlot` on
the shell column, rendered OUTSIDE the level transition — the footer is the
column's own furniture, not part of what slides when a module opens — and it
shows at both levels for the same reason.

**A person's spaces on their Team profile**, via `GET /api/spaces/memberships`.
The signature takes two subjects on purpose (`subjectUserId`, `viewerUserId`)
and returns the intersection: a profile listing every room someone belongs to
would be a directory of private spaces and their occupants, which is the one
thing per-space access control exists to prevent. Personal spaces cannot appear
at all — they hold no member rows — and that property is what makes the
endpoint safe on a profile page.

The route is registered BEFORE `/api/spaces/:spaceId/…`, or `memberships` is
read as a space id and 404s. The section fetches through `requestApiJson`, not
a bare `fetch`: the first draft used raw fetch, which sends no bearer token and
would have 401'd on every profile.

**Team is back on the rail**, in the admin stack above Settings. Phase 5a moved
it off entirely on the grounds that it is a directory rather than a place you
work; that argument holds for zone ③ (tools you carry between spaces) and is
why this is not a revert. "Who works here" is administration, and
settings-menu-only put it two clicks from everywhere.

Verified live: Company lists all seven people with no controls; the personal
space shows no People and still shows Settings; Anna Berger's profile lists
Company and not her personal space; /mdl/team is on the rail.

Five dummy colleagues were seeded into the dev database (each got a personal
space and Company membership from the trigger, plus a linked team profile) —
data only, no code.

commits.message:
fix(dev): scope the predev Supabase check to the worktree's own stack

predev-check.sh probed a hardcoded 127.0.0.1:54321 and hardcoded
`supabase_*_engenty-local` container names, so from any worktree it reported
the MAIN checkout's stack as healthy while this one was down — a false green.
Worse, soft_heal_supabase_rest() ran `docker restart` on that literal name:
healing from here would have bounced another checkout's PostgREST out from
under a colleague's running dev server.

Both now derive from this worktree's own gitignored supabase/config.toml
(project_id + [api] port) — the same file `supabase start` reads, so probe and
stack cannot diverge. Verified against both: engenty-spaces/54821 and
engenty-local/54321.

The openapi.json half of the original commit is dropped: main fixed the same
z.custom bug independently (and better, without z.custom) after it caused the
v0.1.117/118 prod outage.

commits.message:
fix(spaces): reconcile the rebase with main

Four things the replay onto main could not settle on its own:

- app-sidebar kept the `SidebarSpacesZone` import after the shell rework
  removed its only use. The removal hunk did not apply against main's changed
  import block, so the import survived alone — invisible until `noUnusedLocals`.
- The `buildNavigationSections` fixture this branch added predates
  `backgroundComponents`/`chatCommands`/`tabs` on `UiContributions`; every
  fixture main already had carries them.
- KB and Project fixtures that main added or rewrote after the fork do not
  carry `space_id`, which Phase 6 made non-optional on those entities. The
  types are right; the newer fixtures simply had not met them yet.

Still red and NOT from this branch (no commit here touches these files or the
types they consume): tenant-settings + user-settings mock `registerHttpRoute`
as returning void where it returns `PluginRegistrationReceipt | undefined`,
and team-chat passes a dispatch union where the queue wants a
`Record<string, unknown>`.

fix(spaces): restore the check:space-storage-scope gate lost in the rebase

The package.json entry for this check rode along in `chore(dev): start the
local Supabase stack lean`, which was skipped during the rebase because main
had landed that change independently. Skipping it took the unrelated passenger
with it: `scripts/check-space-storage-scope.mjs` and its allowlist were still
in the tree, but nothing could run them, so acceptance criterion 7 — every
tenant-rooted storage key is a classified, argued choice — was silently
unenforceable.

Green on restore: 11 classified tenant-level entries, no debt.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): chat lives in a space (Phase C1 + C2)

The copilot becomes a per-space surface: in a space you see that space's
chats, and a chat opened outside any space binds to your personal one. This is
VISIBILITY, not authorization — what an agent may reach is still the capability
system and the space mount set. C3a is where the thread's space starts
selecting tools, and it must validate the space against the caller's accessible
set first; `spaceIdFromRouteContext` says so at the seam.

C1 — placement. The manifest says `space`, so the existing route mirror serves
`/s/<key>/engenty-copilot/…` and legacy `/mdl/*` links redirect. Two seams did
not see it: the rail reads placement off `adminMenuItems` and the copilot
contributes no menu row, so the tile stayed put no matter what the manifest
said, and `spacePlacedModuleIds` was blind for the same reason. Placement now
rides on `UiCopilotAppContribution` too, enriched exactly where menu items are.

C2 — the thread carries a space. `ai.thread.space_id` (nullable; null reads as
"pre-space" and shows only under All spaces), composite `(space_id, tenant_id)`
FK, backfilled to the creator's personal space. The UI puts the space in
`routeContext.scope` because the affinity key hashes it — the drawer in
Marketing stops resuming Company's thread with no second mechanism.

Three things that had to be built differently than planned:

- **`/s/me` cannot be emitted into a deep link.** React Router ranks by
  specificity, not declaration order, so a mirrored module route under
  `/s/:spaceKey` out-ranks the `/s/me/*` splat: the alias arrived as a literal
  space key, no space has it, and the shell fell back to the tenant default.
  Found live — the chat opened, its history came back empty, nothing errored.
  The redirect resolves the real key now. The same trap applies to every other
  mirrored module (`/s/me/tasks/briefing` has it today); that one is untouched
  here and belongs with the routing, not with each caller.
- **Invalidation needs a space-agnostic PREFIX.** A full list key ends in the
  space and the copilot provider builds its key without one, so invalidating
  with it yielded `…/"all-spaces"` — prefix-matching nothing but itself, which
  left the space-scoped history stale after every run.
- **The RPC coalesces the space rather than assigning it.** Every sibling
  column takes `excluded`; this one must not, because upsert is also the
  idempotent re-save path and a save that omits the space must not un-space a
  thread. The service reads the merged route context for the same reason.

The migration DROPS the old 10-argument signature in the same file: adding a
parameter creates an overload, PostgREST calls by named args, and a request
omitting the new one would match both. Grants are restated because recreating a
function drops its ACL — engenty_server included, or creating a chat fails
outright.

Verified live: `/mdl/engenty-copilot/chat` lands on `/s/matthias/…`; zone ③ is
contacts/inbox/time-tracking with no copilot tile; the route answers 2/0/2
threads for no-filter/Company/personal. In Postgres: one signature, grants
intact, and the FK's `confdelsetcols` is `{space_id}` alone — tenant_id is not
nulled by a space delete.

Known and deliberately left: the active thread is remembered per host key, not
per space, so Company can show a personal chat in the content pane while the
list beside it is correctly empty.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): the copilot knows its space, and space URLs read like places

The copilot inside a space could not tell you where it was. `/mdl/` was
hardcoded in the one regex that resolves which module the user is looking
at, so once a space mirrored every module route the agent resolved NO
module at all — no page prompt, no skill-catalog hint, and "where am I?"
answered by asking the user which page they were on.

Fixed there, plus the space itself: the runtime block now names the
current space (name, key, id, and whether it is the user's personal one),
resolved against the caller's own membership-filtered list so a prompt can
never name a space they are not in. The space id comes from the route
context the client sends — the same value C2 binds the thread to — so what
the agent is told and where the chat lives are one fact, not two that
drift. An unresolvable space degrades to a single line rather than taking
the whole runtime block down.

Space URLs lose the vendor prefix: `/s/company/copilot/chat/…`, not
`/s/company/engenty-copilot/chat/…`. Only the URL segment changes; the
module ID is untouched everywhere it means something. The alias table
lives in ai-core because the shell and the agent's page-context resolver
are two readers of the same scheme — two tables in packages that cannot
import each other's tests is how the agent ends up resolving `copilot`
against a registry that only knows `engenty-copilot`. Aliases are opt-in
per module, never derived by stripping `engenty-` (that would silently
claim `/s/x/core`). Pre-alias space links stay mounted rather than
redirected, so a bookmark or notification still opens the page.

Rail: the `+N` overflow chip becomes a stack of the hidden spaces' own
tiles, which says WHICH places are down there rather than only that there
are more — and a stack of cards visibly wants to be fanned out. Hovering
unfolds it into the named list; the count does not survive as a leftover
chip beside the tiles it stood in for. Fixed-height box so fanning out
cannot shove zone ③ around, and the rolled-up mention indicator still
rides on the stack.

`core.spaces.color` and `.icon` have existed since Phase 5a and the API
accepted both on create and edit, but nothing could set them, so every
space was grey. The setup dialog now has a palette, an emoji row and a
preview at rail size. A fixed palette rather than a colour input: the
rail's readability rests on white text over the tile, and a free picker
can produce one that cannot carry it.

Verified live on the spaces stack: a fresh chat in Marketing answers
"Marketing / marketing / engenty-copilot" — the module ID resolved
through the short URL, so the de-alias round trip holds end to end.
Marketing set to violet + megaphone from the dialog and the rail tile
followed.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): a run reaches only what its space mounts (Phase C3a)

C2 gave a thread a `space_id`. This is where that column stops being a
label and starts deciding what the run can do.

**The plan's seam was wrong, and the live behaviour is what showed it.**
C3a was specced as `allowedToolIds` on `assembleDynamicAgent` — correct
for an agent carrying module tools directly, and worth nothing for the
copilot: its `toolIds` are the six catalog meta-tools, and every module
operation it ever runs arrives through `engenty_tool_execute` by id.
Narrowing a list that holds no module tools would have looked like
enforcement and enforced nothing. The check therefore sits on the call.

Two strengths, deliberately different. The catalog HIDES what the space
does not mount, so the copilot stops proposing Company's offers inside
Marketing; `engenty_tool_execute` REFUSES it, because a model that
remembers an operation id from its own history never asks the catalog.
Either alone is a hole or a bad turn. Core stays authoritative behind
both — it re-checks every invoke — but "failed at the HTTP boundary" is a
broken product even when it is a safe one.

Validation is not a second membership list here: the surface endpoint is
already gated by `requireSpaceAccess`, so asking it for the mounts IS
asking whether the caller may have them, and an unbacked claim gets a 404
instead of a mount list. That closes the hole C2 left open on purpose.

Unresolvable degrades rather than denies — no space claimed, a deleted
space, core slow — all fall back to the pre-Phase-C tenant-wide
behaviour with a warn. The surface narrows; it never grants. Denying on
unknown would turn a core hiccup into a dead copilot.

The workspace roots at the run's own space, so a chat opened in Marketing
puts its files under Marketing. A task-bound run still wins with
`resolveWorkVisibility` — a task does not move because someone opened it
from another space — and the disagreement is logged, because a chat in
one space checking out work from another is either a legitimate hand-off
or a containment bug and neither is diagnosable from silence.

Filtering silently was its own bug, caught on the first live run: asked
for offers in a space without them, the copilot searched, got only the
mounted module back, and reported "the offers module has no read tool
registered" — confident, wrong, and unavoidable, because nothing said
anything had been removed. Catalog results now carry `space_scope`
naming what the space does mount.

Verified live in Marketing (mounts invoices, not offers):
- `engenty_tool_execute` with `offers_list` → `module_not_in_space`, the
  full refusal surfaced verbatim to the user
- the same request through search → only `invoices_list` came back
- `POST /api/tools/invoices_list/invoke` still runs — the space narrows
  the surface without breaking the chat

commits.message:
feat(spaces): connectors and delegation follow the space too (Phase C3b)

Two of the three C3b narrowings, each a reader of the same surface C3a
already fetches. The third is blocked, and says so rather than pretending.

**Connections.** A connector is mounted one provider-account at a time
(`google-gmail`) while its operations live in a shared module
(`connections-google`, ops named `gmail_*`). So the module check is the
wrong grain in both directions: mounting Gmail would hand the space all
of Google, and refusing on the module would block a connector the space
explicitly mounts. The connector check therefore runs before the module
check and instead of it, matching by tool prefix with longest-match
wins — a connector whose prefix prefixes another's (`g` vs `gmail`) must
not claim its operations. The connections module's OWN plumbing (the
catalog, the account list) stays reachable once any connector is
mounted: a space able to call Gmail and unable to ask which account to
call it with is not a coherent state.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): headless task runs follow their task's space; fix appearance saves

**Headless was the one lane with no narrowing at all.** A routine firing
in Marketing could reach every module in the tenant while a person
sitting in Marketing could not — the widest reach in the system belonged
to the runs nobody is watching.

The task's own space now narrows it, through the same gate the chat lanes
use. `resolveWorkVisibility` already ran there and already knew the
space; the step was discarding it and rooting on the tenant default.

The lane differs from chat in a way worth stating rather than papering
over. A chat's space is CLIENT-supplied, so fetching the surface doubles
as the access check. A task's space is a server-side lookup off the task
row — there is no claim to check, and the run's principal is the AI
service, which holds no membership in anything. Core still gates the
surface on space access and a service principal resolves to the nil user,
so an OPEN space answers and narrows the run while a PRIVATE one 404s and
the run keeps its old tenant-wide reach, with a warn carrying the task id.
Strictly better than no narrowing anywhere, and greppable instead of
silent. Closing that gap means teaching the space access rule about
`actingForUserId` — an auth-seam change with its own blast radius, not a
rider on this one.

The reflect step is deliberately untouched: it runs with
`allowedToolIds: ["memory_save", "memory_record_search"]`, both platform
tools, which the gate never touches.

**Appearance: colour saves now.** `SpaceAppearanceFields` built each next
value from the `value` PROP — a snapshot captured at render — so two
changes inside one React batch both computed from the same stale base and
the first was silently overwritten. Picking a colour and then an icon
saved the icon, dropped the colour, and left the form showing both, which
is why this looked verified when it was not. `onChange` is now an updater.

**And the space header tile shows the icon**, using the shared
`railSpaceInitials` instead of a second local copy of the rule: that tile
and the rail tile are the same object seen twice, so a space showing a
megaphone on the rail and "MA" in the header is the one thing that
component exists to prevent.

Verified: colour + icon persist to `core.spaces` and render on both the
rail and the space header. The headless wiring is typechecked and the
gate it feeds is unit-tested, but it is NOT exercised end-to-end — firing
a real dispatched task job needs the scheduler, which this run did not do.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): a real space settings page, under the space's own URL

`/settings/spaces/<uuid>` → `/s/<key>/settings`.

The old URL could not be read, typed or sent to a colleague, and it put a
space's settings in a different tree from the space — so configuring
Marketing meant leaving Marketing. Under `/s/<key>` the way out is one
segment back, and the sidebar keeps the space's own switcher and
Work/Data/Plan tabs instead of borrowing the Setup nav, which had nothing
to say about a space and left the column empty.

**One page, not tabs.** Drive / People / Files meant three clicks to
answer "what is this space and who is in it", and a tab bar that grew
every time a module contributed a surface. Tenant settings already solved
this shape — identity header, then stacked cards you scroll — and a space
is a smaller version of the same object, so it gets the same treatment
rather than a second idiom. Sections are ordered by why people come here:
appearance, people, what is mounted, the Drive, then module surfaces.

Colour and icon are editable HERE, saved on their own, so changing a
colour is no longer a trip through the mount dialog.

Three duplications the first render exposed, each the same mistake — a
component bringing its own chrome to a place that already had chrome.
`SpaceAppearanceFields` and `SpaceMembersSection` now take `showHeader`,
and module-contributed surfaces render BARE rather than inside a titled
card: they were built as tab panels and carry their own header, so a card
printed the module's name twice.

**`settings` is a reserved segment, and both URL readers now know it.**
Every reader inferred a module called "settings": the shell slid the space
sidebar away to show that module's (empty) nav, and the agent would have
reported `page_module: settings` and gone looking for tools under it. The
answer lives beside the alias table in ai-core, because the shell and the
agent's page-context resolver are the same two readers that already share
it — one fact, not two that drift.

The uuid URL redirects rather than 404s (it is in bookmarks and in the
sidebar link as shipped), resolving the key from the id through the
membership-filtered list, so an id the viewer cannot see falls through to
the spaces list instead of confirming the space exists.

Verified live: the old uuid link lands on `/s/marketing/settings`; Company
renders identity + People (7) + Apps counts + Drive + Files with the space
sidebar intact; the personal space shows no People section and is editable
by its owner.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): space settings become settings, not a second home screen

The page carried the Drive tree and the files module's contributed tab —
neither is a setting; both are things you go into the space to USE. Gone.
What remains is what the space IS (name, colour, who is in it) and what it
CONTAINS (its mounts).

Apps was a count badge: it said "2" and left the actual question — which
ones — to a dialog. Each mount kind is now a flush card listing what is
mounted in the row idiom /settings already uses, with a footer that opens
the picker. Module rows link into the module inside the space where it is
reachable. The access chip says "Engentys · No access" rather than a bare
"No access", which read as "you cannot open this".

Colour and icon move off the column and onto the tile — an edit pen on
hover, the same move tenant settings makes on its logo. The palette was
the least-used thing on the page and was sitting above the things people
came for. A draft with Cancel/Save, because a modal with a Cancel button
has to be cancellable.

People stops being the sidebar's component with its header suppressed —
that flag was the giveaway. SpaceMembersCard is the administration
surface (avatar rows, owner chip, remove, add); SpaceMembersSection keeps
the sidebar's glance. Visibility rides at the top of the card: same
question, who gets in.

Known gap: with the Drive card and the spaces.detail host removed,
SpaceDriveTree and the files module's space tab render nowhere. Both are
left intact — the Drive belongs under Data beside the KB and Files wants a
real Work-list route, and neither is this commit's call.

Verified live: colour+icon round-trips to core.spaces with mounts intact;
personal space shows no People card and stays owner-editable; fresh load
with no console errors. apps/ui 153 tests, typecheck and biome clean.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): one modal per mount kind, and a create dialog that only creates

The setup dialog asked everything at once. That is right when you are
CREATING a space — you answer "what is this place" once, in order — and
wrong when you are changing one list: you arrive from a card that already
showed you what is mounted, and the dialog re-asks the name and the other
three lists before letting you touch the one you came for.

So editing is now per kind. Each card's footer opens exactly the list that
card shows: Apps, Engentys, Skills, Connections — the last two split out of
the card they had shared, so no footer edits a list you cannot see. The
other kinds' mounts ride along untouched on save, because the setup
endpoint reconciles the COMPLETE desired set and sending one kind alone
would unmount the rest.

SpaceSetupDialog keeps create and loses edit. The two dialogs share the
selection model they always shared plus a new space-mount-catalog.ts —
category grouping, rows for mounts the catalog no longer lists, the
server's locked baseline keys. Shared as code, not as one component doing
two jobs. The spaces admin list's Edit button now links into the space's
own settings page: one place authors a space's mounts.

The count moved off the title row, where it rendered underneath the
dialog's own close button.

Verified live: each footer opens its own kind; ticking a skill adds only
that mount and leaves the other five intact; unticking removes it again.
(A first attempt failed on a 15s stalled request — core logged "Body is
unusable"; the retry round-tripped.) apps/ui 153 tests, typecheck and
biome clean.

Visibility moves out of People into its own General card. It had been at

reachable by keyboard while it is transparent.

Selected-counts are gone from both dialogs. The ticks are the count, and in
the per-kind modal the number sat in the same inch as the close button.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): a mount stops claiming a record scope nobody chose

`core.space_mount.record_scope` was required on every module mount, and
every writer filled it with 'space'. No query, policy or agent assembler
ever read it — and for the modules people actually mount it was false:
contacts, invoices, offers and time tracking are ONE tenant-wide book a
space borrows, and their tables have no `space_id` to scope by.

Two questions were sitting in one column. Whether a module's records CAN
be space-scoped is a fact about its schema, knowable from the module and
not worth storing once per space. Whether a space's VIEW of them should
be narrowed is a real per-space choice — and that feature (module objects
as virtual folders in the data tree) is not designed yet.

So the column stays and stops being written. NULL means undecided, which
is the truth, and the first reader to arrive will not find rows claiming
a decision nobody made. `agent_access` is untouched and still required on
a module mount: that one IS read, and carries authorization.

Also fixes the baseline SQL pin, which read a hard-coded migration path.
`core.space_baseline_mounts()` is a `create or replace`, so a later
migration supersedes it silently — the guard caught this redefinition
only because the two happened to disagree. It now follows the last
migration that defines the function.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): contacts, the inbox and time tracking leave the app rail

The last three modules declaring `placement: "global"` move into spaces.
They are reached inside a space now, and their legacy `/mdl/*` links
redirect there through the same path the copilot has used since C1 — no
new machinery, since rail zone ③ is already built by filtering on
placement rather than by a list of module ids.

Their records do not move: contacts is one address book per tenant and
the inbox one set of accounts. A mount decides REACH — whether the app
appears in a space's Work list and whether that space's engentys get its
tools — not which records exist.

That empties zone ③ on a default install, so a section with no items is
now dropped instead of rendered. The renderer gives every section a label
and a trailing separator, so an empty one drew an "Apps" heading over
nothing with a rule under it — the same stray separator that got the
`primary` section deleted in 5a. Two tests asserted the old shape,
written when nothing forced the question.

Neither the inbox nor time tracking is mounted anywhere yet, so both are
reachable only where someone mounts them.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): connections are mounted per account, agents get grants (Phase CN)

Mounting Gmail into a space granted every Gmail account in the tenant: the
mount key was the CONNECTOR, though the schema comment always said "connection
id". This closes that and builds the flows around it.

CN.3 — accounts, not connectors. `space_mount.resource_key` now holds a
connection id. The run's space reaches core as `x-engenty-space-id`, alongside
the agent/goal/task ids already forwarded there; the connections policy
intersects it with the candidates the principal may already use and denies
`connection_not_in_space` with a reason that names the space. Safe to take from
a header because it can only NARROW — sharing, capabilities and the action
policy still decide what is in that set. Hard cutover, no backfill: nothing is
in production, so pre-CN mounts simply stop matching and are remounted by hand.

CN.4 — one flow. The browser carries the space on every request, so a module
page inside a space sees that space's accounts (inbox account list narrows).
"Add account" from a space carries the space through the OAuth round trip on
the pending flow row — not the redirect URL, since a mount is a grant and the
redirect is attacker-visible — and auto-mounts on the callback, best-effort:
the account exists either way, and failing the callback would report a connect
failure that did not happen. Shared spaces are offered org accounts only.

CN.5 — agent grants. `connection_agent_grants` lets an owner lend an account to
an agent for unattended work, checked in the sharing clamp. Keyed on
`auth.agentId` rather than the principal type: headless runs already forward
x-engenty-agent-id, so this works on today's service-principal lane and on an
agent-principal lane later, with neither a precondition for the other. Managed
from the AGENT's settings — people ask "what can the Marketing Agent do", not
"which of my agents may touch this mailbox"; the connection card shows the
inverse read-only. A grant means the agent may REACH the account, nothing more:
autonomous_mode and the per-action policies still apply.

CN.2 — "Needs setup" was a disabled button for everyone: an admin who could fix
it in a minute was sent hunting, a member was told to do something they cannot.
Now a link for whoever can act, a sentence naming the ask for everyone else.

CN.6 — three pre-existing holes, found while verifying the above:
  * a new org share defaulted to UNCAPPED, handing every member the full
    surface; new shares now start at `read` (insert only, so a reconnect cannot
    undo a cap the owner widened)
  * org connections were self-servable — `module.connections.write` is in the
    member profile, so any colleague could rewrite the company mailbox's
    policies or flip its sharing; now owner-or-admin
  * any tenant user could decide any approval, while the reason string claimed
    it went to the connection owner; the policy now stamps `owner_user_id` into
    the approval context and core restricts on it, falling back to tenant scope
    when absent so other modules are unchanged

Also adds `PluginOperationError` to plugin-sdk: handler errors that are answers
("no such connection", "not yours") were reported as 500 internal_error, which
tells the client, the retry policy and the alerting that the server broke.
Checked structurally, not with `instanceof` — modules load through jiti and can
hold a different copy of the SDK than core imports.

Verified: typecheck clean across plugin-sdk, api-client, connections-sdk, core,
ai, ai-ui, connections, inbox, ui. Tests green — core 831, ai 1011, ui 154,
connections 26 (6 new), inbox 53, connections-sdk 63, plugin-sdk 69,
api-client 6. Both migrations applied locally and confirmed in
information_schema. Smoke-tested live: the space header on the wire, the flow
row carrying space_id + back path through a real connect start, both new grant
operations, and the setup link.

Not verified: the OAuth callback auto-mount, which needs this worktree's core
port registered as a redirect URI with the provider.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): the Data tab — files as protocol, one tree, module-rendered nodes

One tree per space with three node classes: real bytes (file spaces and
connected folders), stores (knowledge pages, projects, artifacts), and RECORD
nodes rendered on demand by per-module adapters. Postgres stays store of
record; nothing here syncs or stores. Every adapter call goes through
`invokeOperation` with the caller's principal, so an agent editing a file
raises the same approval card as calling the operation — because it is
calling it.

- plugin-sdk: `SpaceDataAdapter` contract, node types, frontmatter/CSV/index
  serialization, refs, archive. Path traversal is gated in
  `splitSpaceDataPath`, before dispatch.
- core: `/api/spaces/:id/data/{roots,list,read,write,import,export}`.
  `resolveVisibleSpaceDataRoots` is the pure seam where mount = grant lives.
  Writes carry the version they read; a mismatch is 409 `data_conflict`,
  never a silent overwrite.
- adapters: contacts (flat `.contact.md`), offers and invoices (bundles).
  Invoices carry the legal boundary — an issued invoice's members are
  read-only and a write is refused before the operation.
- agent: the `/data` mount in every workspace preset, plus a staging cache.
- ui: the tree lives in the space SIDEBAR, where navigation belongs; the page
  is the pane the selection opens. Modules contribute renderers through the
  ordinary `registerTab` seam — `spaces.data.page` by kind, and
  `spaces.data.node:<nodeTypeId>` for records, because every adapter emits
  `record`/`bundle` and only the namespaced type cannot collide.
- a module contributes ITS ACTUAL PAGE, not a lookalike, and the phase picks
  the view: a draft renders the module's real draft editor.

`Invoice` gained `updatedAt` — without a version token every conflict is a
silent overwrite.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): one grid for CSV and .xlsx, and a pane that tells the copilot what is open

The Data pane rendered a CSV as one long line and markdown as its own source —
the bytes, not the document. Both already had a renderer in this codebase, so
the pane now hands each file to the right one, and the grid grew the
interactions people already have in their fingers.

The grid (packages/csv-import)
- `CsvGrid` draws a matrix; `CsvTable` is the text wrapper over it. Splitting
  there is what let a worksheet reuse selection, clipboard and the row window
  without either side knowing about the other.
- Selection is anchor + focus → a normalized rectangle, header as row -1 so a
  column select spans it. Drag, shift-click, header takes the column, row
  number takes the row, arrows/Tab/shift-arrows, Cmd-C copies as TAB-separated
  text (what Excel and Sheets paste back as cells), Cmd-V pastes a block and
  GROWS the table, Delete clears, Enter/double-click/typing edits.
- Cells are NOT inputs until being edited: an always-on input eats the
  mousedown, and without the mousedown there is no drag-select.
- All of it pure functions in `csv-matrix.ts`, 25 tests.

Workbooks (.xlsx, read-only)
- `exceljs` (MIT), dynamically imported so a space with no spreadsheet never
  downloads the parser. Columns are the sheet's own letters, not row 1 — a
  worksheet does not promise a header row, and assuming one moves every value
  up a row.
- exceljs repeats a merged range's value in every covered cell; rendered as-is
  one banner becomes three, so covered cells are blanked.
- A formula with no cached result shows its formula: a blank claims the sheet
  is empty where it is merely uncomputed.
- `worksheet.rowCount`/`columnCount` are computed getters that walk every row.
  Read inside the scan they made 25,000 cells take 66 seconds; hoisted into
  locals the same pass is ~5ms. The comment saying so is the point.
- Hidden sheets are shown and marked, capped sheets say they were capped, and
  legacy .xls is refused on purpose (OLE2 — a different container).
- Read-only because writing back means styles, formulas and number formats this
  viewer does not model must survive the round trip.

The pane
- Actions and identity live in the topbar; the document gets the whole window
  with a bottom info bar for counts, delimiter, selection size and warnings.
- A collection CSV's save is the bulk IMPORT, not a file write — it reports
  created/updated/refused, the first caller of the /data/import endpoint.

Copilot context
- `useRegisterAgentUiSlice` had zero consumers anywhere in the repo, so every
  AG-UI snapshot was the base one and `selection` was `{}`. The pane is the
  first publisher: the node's own agent path, its members and version, and a
  bounded excerpt — cut by ROWS for a CSV, never by characters, because a byte
  cut hands the model a broken record.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): a folder is a thing you can open, and its module can render it

Clicking a folder in the Data tree did nothing. Four gaps sat behind that, and
the first one was also why a knowledge page with children could not be opened.

The tree
- `SpaceDriveTree` had `selectable = !expandable && …`, so a container was NEVER
  selectable and `onSelect` never fired for a folder. Containers are selectable
  now; `activate()` OPENS rather than toggles, because the pane is about to show
  what is inside and collapsing the row on the same click would fight it.
- The chevron became a real button (`aria-expanded`), so a folder you can open
  can still be closed.
- `href` stays leaf-only on purpose: a project row that navigated away from the
  Data page on the click that expands it would make the tree unusable.

Folders have a type
- `SpaceDataFolder.nodeType` and `SpaceDataAdapter.rootNodeType`, carried
  through the roots endpoint, the client and the drive projection. A folder here
  is a virtual object — `People` is the contacts whose type is `person`, `sent`
  is the offers in that state — and neither is a directory.
- `SpaceDataListing.self` is the folder's OWN row. A listing otherwise describes
  only what is inside, which leaves the type reachable only by listing the
  parent and unreachable at a root. The server fills it in for roots from the
  adapter's `label` and `rootNodeType`, so no adapter describes a row it never
  lists. This is what makes a folder URL openable by link, not only by walking.
- Typed: `contacts.folder`/`.root`, `offers.status`/`.root`,
  `invoices.status`/`.root`. Invoice statuses are deliberately NOT offer
  statuses: an offer's stages are a pipeline you push through, an invoice's are
  Festschreibung, and a view of one is not a view of the other.

The pane
- `spaces.data.folder:<nodeType>`, keyed like the node surface and for the same
  reason — one shared `spaces.data.folder` would let contacts render the offer
  pipeline. Untyped folders get a generic list, which is the honest view of a
  folder nobody claimed.
- `as=folder` rides in the URL because the pane must choose `read` vs `list`
  before it has fetched anything. Sniffing the name for an extension works only
  because every node type today happens to declare one; read-first-and-fall-back
  costs a round trip per folder and reports cleanly only at a root.
- For a module-rendered FOLDER the host keeps the chrome — the opposite of a
  module-rendered NODE. A folder's identity is its path and its only action is
  leave, both already known here; handing the topbar over would make every
  module re-derive the same breadcrumbs. It also keeps the chrome stable across
  the fetch, since `self` (and so the renderer) is unknown until the listing
  lands.
- File-space folders and connector mounts open too, at `?folder=<id>&fs=<key>`.

One real consumer, not just a seam
- Offers registers `spaces.data.folder:offers.status`: number, title, client,
  date and validity, with an expired `valid_until` in the destructive colour.
- The host passes the LISTING it already fetched through `params`. It is the
  only place the nodes' data paths exist, so a module refetching from its own
  API would get its records back without them and would have to rebuild each
  path from the adapter's naming convention to link a row back into the pane.

Also in this commit: file content can be SAVED (`PUT …/files/:id/content`,
`replaceContent` on the file sources), built in parallel in this worktree and
entangled with the above in `SpaceDataPage.tsx` — there was no clean way to
split the two.

Verified live on `forschung-kueste`: `Offers` lists its stages, `Offers/draft`
renders the offers table under `Offers / draft` breadcrumbs, `Research` lists
its files, and the chevron collapses without touching the URL. 140/140 test
tasks green.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): a real list in the folder pane, and modules that own their index

The folder overview shipped as rows carrying a name and a chip that repeated
what the icon already said, and every module root fell back to it — so `Offers`
was three words and `Contacts/Organisations` was a column of
`acme-gmbh__01a00056-c22e-….contact.md`. The id is in a node name so resolving
one costs no scan; it is not something a person should read past to find
"Acme GmbH".

The generic view
- Containers and leaves are separate sections, in the order the tree sorts
  them, so the pane reads as the folder the tree row points at rather than as a
  second, differently-ordered tree. The headings drop when there is only one
  group — a lone "Items" label over the only list on the page names nothing.
- One bordered block with dividers, a date column and a chevron: a LIST, not a
  grid of cards. These rows are a name and a date, the name is the only thing
  being scanned, and a card grid puts three per line so the eye has to track
  sideways through a column that is already alphabetical.
- The kind chip is gone. The icon carries it, and "Folder" written next to a
  folder icon is the label saying what the picture says.

Modules own their index
- `spaces.data.folder:offers.root` — the pipeline's stages with how much is IN
