commits.message:
feat(spaces): the app the copilot builds lands in the space's Data tree

An agent built an HTML app in a space chat and the space could not see it:
the artifact was visible only as a panel in the chat that happened to build
it. The trace found one hardcoded line and two never-wired seams.

Publish to the space (apps/ai)
- app_build's publish step scoped every artifact handle `thread` — even in a
  space chat whose ALS already carries the space, validated against the
  caller's access (Phase C3a). It now publishes space-scoped when the run has
  a space, thread-scoped otherwise; the row keeps `thread_id` either way.
- The trap this exposed: the chat's artifact tab strip is a scope LISTING,
  not a transcript projection — a space-scoped artifact would vanish from the
  chat that built it. The full-page chat's pane now merges the space scope
  (`extraScope`), so the tab stays, wearing a Space badge. Inline cards were
  never affected (they fetch by id).
- 3 tests pin the scope choice: space / thread / no-ALS resume.

Pin to space (packages/ai-ui)
- The pin menu's target type was `task | project | goal` while the server's
  /store route accepted `space` all along. The current space is now the
  one-click target at the top of the menu, read from the same workspace
  context every module page reads.

Artifacts open in the pane (apps/ui)
- A tree row for an artifact did nothing: `artifact` was left out of
  `opensInPane` and no client ever built its href. It now navigates to
  `?artifact=<id>` and the pane renders through the SAME renderer registry
  the chat panel uses — `app` mounts the running App in its sandboxed frame.
  The pane adds nothing of its own; versions and publishing stay the chat
  panel and the Apps section.
- The copilot is told what is open: a `space-data:artifact` slice names the
  artifact, and for an `app` says it is a running App with its `app_id` and
  that its source lives in the Apps module — excerpting the handle JSON
  would have told the agent three ids and nothing it can use.

One toolbar for the pane (apps/ui)
- PaneChrome now appends the common controls after whatever the branch
  contributes: expand, an overflow menu when a branch has entries, close.
  Six per-branch Close buttons deleted.
- Expand gives the document the whole window. It must PORTAL to body: the
  shell's content column is `relative z-0` — its own stacking context — so a
  fixed overlay inside it paints under the shell's fixed sidebar at any
  z-index. z-[120] clears the layout layers and stays under the guide
  overlays. The toggle remounts the children, which is safe because every
  branch keeps draft values above PaneChrome; Escape collapses via a
  document listener since the overlay covers the topbar.

Includes the file-text extraction (`preserveTrailingNewline` + useFileText's
fetch half) the page already imports.

Live-verified end to end: pin → tree → pane → expand → Escape, on the app
artifact and the contacts.csv collection grid. 186 apps/ui tests green,
ai-ui + apps/ai suites green, biome clean.

commits.message:
feat(invoices): the space Data folders are receivables, not a list of five words

`Invoices` rendered as five folder names and `Invoices/issued` as a column of
node filenames. Both now come from this module, through the
`spaces.data.folder:<type>` surface the host offers.

- `invoices.root` — one card per lifecycle state with its count AND what it is
  worth, plus a banner for how much of the outstanding money is already late.
  `invoices_list` takes no filter and no paging, so the whole list arrives once
  and every figure is grouped from that same array; nothing is counted twice
  and no two cards can disagree.
- `invoices.status` — number, recipient, date, due date and gross. No status
  badge: every row in one of these folders has the same status, so it would be
  one word repeated down the page. What differs, and what anyone opening `sent`
  is looking for, is which of them are overdue.

**An invoice due TODAY is not overdue.** `due_date` is a `date` column, so
`dueDate` is `"2026-08-15"`, `new Date(…)` of it is midnight, and midnight is
behind `Date.now()` for all but the first instant of the day — an instant
comparison paints every invoice due today red. Caught it on screen: the one
seeded invoice was due today and showed red. Compared as calendar days now, in
`lib/invoice-overdue.ts` so the folder's colouring and the root's money cannot
drift apart, with the today/yesterday/tomorrow cases pinned in tests.

commits.message:
fix(app-shell): keep the space rail's stack front tile still while it opens

The front of the collapsed overflow stack was a copy of `hidden[0]` painted
inside the stack. Opening the stack destroyed that copy and re-created the same
space as a fresh tile in the fanned list a few pixels lower, so the one tile
that should anchor the animation was the one that visibly jumped.

Promote it to a real `SpaceTile` in the rail's normal flow, rendered identically
in both states. The dealt cards behind it become pure decoration that only
fades, and the 8px hang they need trades its space with the unfolding list.

Both boxes now animate `grid-template-rows: 0fr ↔ 1fr` instead of `max-height`.
A max-height transition interpolates the cap, not the rendered height: the list
snapped fully open in the first fifth of the animation while the collapsing
stack still held its 48px, so everything below jumped down a tile and slid back
up.

Verified in the browser with the transition slowed to 3s — the front tile sits
at the same y in the collapsed, mid-flight and expanded frames, and the rail
below it moves monotonically.

commits.message:
fix(spaces): stop the space's Settings link bleeding into module sidebars

A module pins its own settings entry to the foot of its nav, and the space
footer rendered on top of that, so with a module open the column ended with two
rows both labelled "Settings", one under the other, pointing at different
things — and the module's is the one being looked for there.

Render the space footer only on the space's OWN pages. The condition is "a
module is open", not `spaceNavLevel`: the promoted Plan module keeps the tab
strip and so stays at the space level, but its column is still a module's
column with a module's footer in it, and it duplicated too.

The footer wrapper in the shell's nav panel gets `empty:hidden`, because the
slot is an element rather than its output — a footer that renders nothing would
otherwise still draw its divider and padding at the foot of the column.

Verified across /s/marketing, /data, /tasks, /projects and /settings: the space
link appears on the space's own pages only, and the wrapper measures 0px where
it is empty.

fix(spaces): raise sidebar contrast — opaque when pinned, weight for selection

Two separate causes of the same washed-out column.

The pinned nav was translucent. `ui-canvas-floating` paints `--popover`,
which is the card at 85% plus a 12px backdrop blur — right for a panel
drawn over the page, wrong for a column that IS part of the layout, and
the page's own text ghosted through it. The shell now takes an explicit
`surface` prop; the pinned column passes "docked" and gets `bg-card`.
The hover panel passes nothing and keeps its glass, which is the case
where reading what is behind is the point.

Keyed on a new prop rather than the existing `toggleMode` because that
answers a different question: the mobile sheet also passes "collapse"
while being an overlay.

The lists inside it were muted grey, with selection carried by colour on
top of a filled row — saying it twice for the selected row and leaving
every other one faint. These are the space's own things, so every row is
now full ink and WEIGHT marks the selection. Applied to the Data tree
and the Work list together, so the two tabs agree.

commits.message:
fix(spaces): close the migration hazards the v0.2.x audit found

Four findings from the pre-release migration audit:

- core.spaces owner FK used the bare composite `on delete set null`, which
  nulls tenant_id along with the owner — and tenant_id is not null, so
  deleting any user (every user owns a personal space) aborted. New
  migration re-adds it as `set null (owner_user_id)`, the same PG15 form
  20260810070200 used for module_kb.
- deploy/scripts/migrate.sh pushed without --include-all, so a v0.1.x
  install upgrading to v0.2.x would refuse the 15 branch migrations that
  timestamp-sort before main's newest applied version.
- module_connections.connection_agent_grants granted only engenty_server;
  the schema has no default privileges, so service_role got nothing and
  check:grants-coverage went red. Grant added plus default privileges so
  later tables stay covered.
- 20260811110000 replaced ai.upsert_thread_with_owner's signature without
  a pgrst reload — chat creation would PGRST202 on a live upgrade until
  the cache expired.

check-foreign-schema-scope gains TENANT_ONLY_TABLES for
module_connections.connections: the table has tenant_id but no scope_id
column, so the scope half of the rule is unsatisfiable there; tenant_id
stays required.

commits.message:
feat(files): folder rows in the files admin expand in place

The files admin could only browse one folder at a time: clicking a folder
replaced the listing with its contents, so comparing two folders — or seeing
where a file actually sits — meant walking the breadcrumb back and forth.

Folder rows now carry a chevron that expands them in place, recursively, at any
depth. Each branch owns its own children query rather than the page fetching the
whole tree up front: a bucket is arbitrarily deep and mostly unvisited, so the
tree costs one request per folder actually opened, and a folder closed and
reopened is served from the prefix-keyed cache.

The chevron toggles and the row still navigates. Both earn their place —
expanding compares folders side by side, drilling in gives one folder the whole
table and the breadcrumb path back out.

Notes on the details that are easy to get wrong:

- The indent rides on the thumbnail cell, the one cell that is always directly
  after selection. Indenting the filename column instead would lose the nesting
  the moment a user reorders columns.
- Collapsing drops the whole subtree from the expanded set. Leaving descendants
  behind would silently re-open them the next time the parent was expanded.
- Sorting moved to a shared `sortFilesBy`, because the tree renders more than
  one batch now and a child batch sorted by a different rule than its parent
  reads as a bug, not as a nested list.

commits.raw_message:
feat(files): folder rows in the files admin expand in place

The files admin could only browse one folder at a time: clicking a folder
replaced the listing with its contents, so comparing two folders — or seeing
where a file actually sits — meant walking the breadcrumb back and forth.

Folder rows now carry a chevron that expands them in place, recursively, at any
depth. Each branch owns its own children query rather than the page fetching the
whole tree up front: a bucket is arbitrarily deep and mostly unvisited, so the
tree costs one request per folder actually opened, and a folder closed and
reopened is served from the prefix-keyed cache.

The chevron toggles and the row still navigates. Both earn their place —
expanding compares folders side by side, drilling in gives one folder the whole
table and the breadcrumb path back out.

Notes on the details that are easy to get wrong:

- The indent rides on the thumbnail cell, the one cell that is always directly
  after selection. Indenting the filename column instead would lose the nesting
  the moment a user reorders columns.
- Collapsing drops the whole subtree from the expanded set. Leaving descendants
  behind would silently re-open them the next time the parent was expanded.
- Sorting moved to a shared `sortFilesBy`, because the tree renders more than
  one batch now and a child batch sorted by a different rule than its parent
  reads as a bug, not as a nested list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(search): reset space-blind index rows and scope artifact docs

search.query_chunks treats a NULL space_id as visible from every space —
correct for tenant-level sources, a leak for space-bound ones: KB documents
indexed before search.documents.space_id existed answered from every space,
private ones included, and space-pinned artifacts (D9) never wrote space_id
at all. The artifact source now stamps space_id for scope_type='space'

machinery — the superadmin Rebuild button or the next ingest event —
re-indexes them with the space attached. Reset over backfill per Matthias:
absent from search until rebuilt beats answering from the wrong space.

commits.message:
feat(kb): retire the filesystem-sync module — the space Data lane is the sync

Matthias, 2026-08-15: "if spaces already provide the sync - we can drop it."
They do: agents read and write articles live through the /data mount
(adapter ops, approval-gated), bulk export is the space archive
(GET /api/spaces/:id/data/export, same OKF frontmatter shape), and import
is /data/import. The one thing the module did that the space lane does not
— an event-driven OKF mirror in the kb-sync bucket — has zero consumers.

The released bucket migration moves to apps/core verbatim (its version is
applied on installs; deleting it would break db push), the bucket stays in
the tenant-bucket registry so pre-v0.2 mirror blobs remain covered by
tenant-data lifecycle, and the OKF format helpers live on in plugin-sdk's
space-data-format, which is where D5 folded them.

commits.message:
feat(files): select all means the files, and the tree opens in one go

Two things the tree made wrong, both reported from the screen.

"Select all" selected nothing. The header checkbox was wired to the top-level
listing only, so in a folder that holds nothing but folders — which is most of
this bucket — it had an empty set to work with and dutifully selected none of
it, while rows sat visible underneath it. Selection now covers every file row
actually rendered: the top level plus everything the expanded folders reveal.
Those come from the same query keys the expanded rows already use, so nothing is
fetched twice, and reading them through the hook (rather than out of the cache)
is what makes the count follow a folder that finishes loading.

⌘A selected the page's characters. Rows were plain selectable text, so a drag
highlighted glyphs and the browser's own "Select all" took the whole document —
the list looked like it was doing something bizarre because it was doing nothing
at all. The table is `select-none` now, and ⌘A is bound to selecting the files.
Typing in the search box still gets the native behaviour, since a shortcut that
eats ⌘A inside an input is its own bug.

Also adds expand/collapse all. It walks the tree a level at a time through the
query cache, so already-open folders cost nothing. It is bounded at 8 levels and
400 folders, because "expand all" on a storage root is otherwise an unbounded
number of requests, and it says so when it truncates — a partially expanded tree
is indistinguishable from a complete one.

One tradeoff worth naming: `select-none` means filenames can no longer be
drag-selected to copy. That is the standard file-manager bargain, and the key
is still copyable from the detail panel.

commits.message:
feat(db-checks): a single-signature rule guards query_chunks

Adding a parameter to a PostgREST-called function creates an overload, not
a replacement — a call omitting the new param matches both and the old body
quietly answers, which for search.query_chunks means searching without the
space filter. The branch hit this once; and because the space-aware
definition lives in apps/core while packages/retrieval owns the function,
a retrieval migration re-created from an old template would silently bring
the second signature back. Rule 6 fails the nightly the moment pg_proc
holds more than one signature; negative-tested by injecting an overload.

commits.message:
fix(ui-plugin-sdk): the types catch up with the plugin runtime

Type drift the apps/ui typecheck blind spot had been hiding: the facade
implemented chatCommands, expose/get and diagnostics fields the SDK types
never declared. EngentyPluginsApi splits into a named core + the indexed
shape (Omit<T, string> over an index signature is {} — an implementation
typed that way loses every method); UiPluginSummary gains the
manifestPath/packageName/rootDir/sourceType the loader actually sends,
with sourceType as the manifest enum; the hook engine accepts interface
event maps (interfaces never satisfy Record<string, unknown>); the
resolver's invalid-scope strip keeps routes typed as UiRouteContribution
instead of poisoning every downstream .scope read.

commits.message:
feat(ui): apps/ui joins the typecheck gate

The last blind spot: every other app typechecks, apps/ui never did, and
~130 errors had pooled under it. The catalog's 21 module imports are now
declared dependencies (Vite resolved them workspace-wide; tsc honestly
could not), @engenty/import points its types at SOURCE — the hand-written
d.ts re-exported from a dist with no declarations, so every consumer
type-checked against `any` — and the sweep of what that surfaced lands
here: the deleted `page` node kind's icon and the never-set readOnly
guard in SpaceDataPage, four grid labels nothing consumed, a required
description nine shipping import fields never had, QueryClient imported
through the seam instead of @tanstack directly, Badge's missing
destructive variant, undefined-leaf guards in the local-files FSA lib,
and a redirect Fallback that now accepts any component.

noUnusedLocals/noUnusedParameters stay off in apps/ui on purpose: this
project compiles dependency sources, and those flags would re-lint every
package under rules its own gate does not enforce — unused-code
enforcement is biome's lane.

commits.message:
feat(ai): graph action primitives, data model and save-path validation

Phase 1a-1c of PLAN-workflow-designer.md: an Action can be a multi-step
declarative Mastra stored graph instead of a single agent + prompt.

Four engenty-owned primitives are the ONLY tools a graph may reference:
run_specialist (tenant registry resolves the agent at run time, which is
why declarative `agent` entries are unusable), engenty_tool (module ops
through the existing gateway invoker, so the capability check is
unchanged), approval_gate (HITL as a node via workflow suspend — proven
durable across process restart by the Phase-0 spike), apply_field_updates
(today's fixed tail, generalized).

Run identity travels only on the request context: a graph carries no
tenant, no user, no credential, so a graph copied between tenants is
inert.

Versions are immutable and runs pin the version they started on, so a
long-lived run (sleepUntil) never wakes into an edited graph. Adds a
`sleeping` run state so a run parked until Thursday is not shown as
awaiting a human.

Save-path validation rejects what cannot be governed: non-primitive tool
references, declarative agent entries, a graph that asserts its own
tenant, a gate inside a foreach, and — the load-bearing rule — any
primitive whose governing argument is not a constant. A computed tool_id
could not be capability-checked at save time, so it fails closed.

commits.message:
feat(ai): dispatch, resume and HTTP surface for graph actions

Phase 1d of PLAN-workflow-designer.md. A stored graph is itself the durable
workflow — it has its own pg snapshot, suspend/resume and crash-resume — so
it is not wrapped in an outer job; the route starts it and run-lifecycle
records the outcome. Wrapping would mean an outer step mirroring every inner
suspension, and two places where a run's state can disagree.

Each dispatch rehydrates the pinned version onto a throwaway Mastra carrying
only the primitives. Registering tenant graphs globally would let another
tenant's nested-workflow reference resolve them.

Adds `sleeping` bookkeeping distinct from `requires_action`: a run parked by
a sleep node is not waiting on a human and must not sit in the inbox looking
stuck.

Routes cover create/list/read/update/delete, preflight validate, version
mint, publish (the human gate — a saved version is inert until approved),
run, and gate resume. Mastra's own /stored/workflows routes stay unmounted.

Integration test against real Postgres proves the exit gate: a graph gates
before writing, nothing is written while suspended, and a SEPARATE
rehydration of the same stored JSON — what a process restart looks like —
resumes and applies the approved patch. A rejected gate writes nothing.

Migration timestamp moved to 20260807190000: main's live session already
holds 20260807120000, and a collision makes `supabase migration up` skip the
newer file silently.

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): action canvas — one picture for authoring, monitoring and approving

Phase 3 of PLAN-workflow-designer.md. React Flow (@xyflow/react, the same
dependency modules/team already uses) renders a stored graph as the flow it
actually is.

One component with a mode rather than three screens, because the definition
IS the run view: a user approves a picture, then watches that same picture
fill in. Author shows problems on nodes; monitor overlays run state; approve
highlights the pending gate.

The node visual language answers two questions at a glance — what does this
do, and where does it stop for me. Work nodes are calm cards that recede.
Gates differ in kind, not degree: amber, shielded, tinted. Waits are dashed
and quiet because nothing is happening. A kind chip names the role, which
matters most for Agent — the only kind that costs a model turn and can vary
between runs.

Problems render on the node that has them, never in a side console: a
missing capability is a property of that step. Tool nodes read as sentences
("Send invoice") with the raw operation id underneath, so a flow scans like
prose instead of config.

Layout is derived, not persisted — graphs arrive from the LLM position-less,
so a chat-authored flow looks exactly as good as a hand-dragged one. Two
passes: an estimate, then a re-stack using React Flow's measured heights,
because a node's height depends on how its text wraps and guessing short
makes tall nodes overlap.

Gate and wait tints mix into the card colour instead of replacing it; a flat
bg-amber-500/6 would override bg-card and leave the node stranded light in
dark mode.

Verified in the browser across all three modes, light and dark.

commits.message:
feat: LLM authoring, run monitoring and gate approval for graph actions

Phase 2 of PLAN-workflow-designer.md, plus the run views that make the
canvas's monitor and approve modes reachable.

action_graph_propose is the primary authoring path, not a convenience: a
user describes a flow in chat, the model emits the graph, and a human
reviews it on the canvas. Same governance shape as agent_propose — the
version is saved unapproved and publishing is a separate, human-only route
deliberately not exposed as a tool. Validation failures come back as the
exact issue list so the model repairs and retries instead of the user
hitting a dead end.

Capabilities are checked at PUBLISH, not propose, and that is the right
place: what matters is whether the human turning this on could perform the
calls themselves. A model drafting a flow it couldn't personally execute is
harmless — it cannot publish it.

Run views: a runs list whose status column answers "which are waiting on
me, which are asleep, which failed", and a run view that draws the run
against the version it STARTED on — never the current one, or a run in
flight would be rendered as a graph it isn't executing. Polling stops when
the run settles, because a finished run never changes again.

Breaks two import cycles found by the failing validator suite: the
save-path validator is a pure function over JSON, but reaching into the
primitives and run-context modules for ids and key names dragged in the
whole agent runtime — which imports the propose tool, which imports the
validator, leaving the constants undefined at module init. Ids and
request-context keys now live in dependency-free modules.

apps/ai: 852 tests pass, both typechecks clean.

commits.message:
feat: invoke_action tool, and fix two bugs found by rendering the real UI

invoke_action lets an open-ended run call a governed deterministic flow as
one step instead of improvising it — the bridge in the taxonomy where tasks
meet actions. Only published actions are callable, so a draft is inert to
agents exactly as it is to buttons. When the flow pauses at a gate the tool
says so and stops rather than letting the agent redo the work by hand.

Two real bugs, both caught by putting the shipping components on screen
rather than trusting the typecheck:

  · Infinite render loop. `issues = []` and `runState = {}` default
    parameters allocate a fresh object every render, so the layout memo's
    deps never settled: memo → effect → setState → render → memo. It only
    triggered when a caller omitted the optional prop, which is exactly
    what the run views do. Defaults are now module constants.

  · The detail and run screens rendered at content width, leaving half the
    viewport empty — they sit in a flex row and were missing flex-1/w-full.

The harness now renders ActionGraphDetail, ActionRunsList and ActionRunView
against a pre-seeded react-query cache, so it exercises the shipping code
path with the network swapped out rather than a mockup of it. All six views
verified in light and dark.

commits.message:
fix(ai): refuse waits the engine cannot durably hold

Pinned the actual behaviour first: Mastra awaits a sleep IN-PROCESS —
run.start() does not return until the timer elapses. Short waits are fine.
A multi-day one is not: it would be held open by a live process, and the
next deploy would strand it. `wake_at` is recorded but nothing re-arms the
timer at boot.

So the validator rejects waits over 15 minutes until that boot sweep
exists. Finding out at author time is a small annoyance; finding out
because a "chase in 5 days" silently never fired would erode trust in
every other flow the tenant has published.

sleep-behaviour.integration.test.ts pins the engine contract so a Mastra
upgrade that changes it fails here rather than in production.

fix: two bugs only the signed-in app could show

Verified the feature end to end in the real app via /auth/agent-login (which
is documented in AGENTS.md and which I should have used from the start
instead of treating the sign-in screen as a blocker). Ran a published flow
from the UI, watched the gate suspend it, approved it on the run screen, and

Two things that neither the typecheck nor the harness could have caught:

  · The approval card rendered the suspend ENVELOPE — "kind: field_updates",
    a request UUID — instead of the decision itself. The gate suspends with
    {kind, title, payload, request_id, context_*} and only the inner payload
    is what a human is deciding about. Showing the actual effect is the whole

    which out-specifies utility classes — in dark mode the zoom controls were
    white buttons with near-white icons. Themed in action-canvas.css against
    a wrapper class so it wins on specificity rather than !important.

commits.message:
feat: durable long waits, and a create dialog that drafts the flow

Two things the plan called out as missing: "chase in 5 days" did not work,
and there was no way to make a flow except by asking the copilot in chat.

DURABLE WAITS. The plan framed this as "build the wake_at boot sweep", but a
sweep alone could not have worked. Mastra's default engine awaits a sleep
IN-PROCESS — executeSleep calls engine.executeSleepDuration, and the suspend
handed to a dynamic sleep fn is an explicit no-op — so a sleeping run is held
by a live process no matter who is scanning wake_at. The wait itself had to
become a suspension.

wait_until is that: a primitive that records wake_at, suspends via the same
mechanism the Phase-0 spike proved for approval gates, and leaves the run
parked in the pg snapshot where a deploy cannot touch it. The graph-wake
system job then rejoins the two durable halves — the snapshot holds WHERE the
run is, wake_at holds WHEN it continues. Boot is not a special case: a process
down for a week just finds a bigger backlog, because "due" is a fact in the
database rather than a timer that was lost. Claiming is a compare-and-swap, so
two instances cannot wake the same run.

Raw sleep stays capped at 15 minutes — the cap is not a limit on how long a
flow may wait, it is which of the two mechanisms is honest at which duration,
and the issue message now names the right one.

CREATE DIALOG. "New flow" in the Flows topbar takes a name and a description
and returns a drawn flow. Same governance as the chat path: the version lands
unapproved and a human still publishes it, which is what lets drafting be this
frictionless. One repair round is built in, and it is kept only if it actually
reduces the issue count.

Five bugs found by running it, four of which only the real thing could show:

- validateStoredWorkflow THROWS on some malformed graphs rather than reporting
  them (its schema-flow pass walks entry.steps unguarded). Every caller hands
  it untrusted JSON, so a 500 was the response to exactly the input it exists
  to reject. A graph Mastra cannot analyze is now an invalid graph.
- An LLM's most natural mistake is writing the toolId as the entry type —
  { type: "run_specialist", args: … }. That is meaningless to the engine but
  slipped past every type === "tool" check, saved, and rendered as a row of
  blank steps. Unknown entry types now fail closed, and the message names the
  fix. The guidance also SHOWS a tool entry now instead of only describing one.
- The constant-arguments rule was too strict across container boundaries: a
  mapping before a conditional really does feed the first node in each branch,
  and rejecting that rejected correct graphs. `previous` now comes from the
  walk, which knows that branches are alternatives, not a sequence.
- The canvas read predicate fields the DSL does not have (conditions/arg, bare
  right), so branches rendered with no label at all — worse than a wrong one,
  because the flow then looks unconditional.
- Drafting takes 60-90s against a 15s client timeout, so the UI reported "lost
  connection" while the server kept working and the flow appeared a minute
  later. Both a failure message and a duplicate.

The primitive id list had drifted into three hand-maintained copies; the one
in validate-graph fed Mastra's tools index, so a new primitive validated as a
missing reference while running perfectly. All three now derive from one.

apps/ai: 870 tests pass, both typechecks clean. Verified in the signed-in app:
a described flow comes back as agent -> approval -> branch -> Wait 5d -> agent
-> approval, with the wait stored as wait_until {duration_ms: 432000000} and
the graph-wake job ticking every minute.

commits.message:
feat: teach and draw every control-flow entry type

Answering "do we cover all of them?" — runtime and validation always did
(rehydrateWorkflow handles the ten stored entry types; the validator descends
into every container). The two layers that did NOT were the two that decide
whether anyone ever sees one, which is why every drafted graph came out as a
straight line.

AUTHORING. The guidance described conditional/parallel/foreach/loop in a single
clause and never gave their shapes, so the model could not write them. Most
starkly for loop: `loopType` is exactly "dowhile" or "dountil", and that was
never stated anywhere a model could read it. Each container now has its exact
JSON shape spelled out, including the traps — conditional and parallel take
plural `steps`, foreach and loop take a singular `step`, and none of them take
an `id`.

The validator now backs each of those instead of letting Mastra crash on them:
a foreach that used `steps`, a loop with no loopType or no predicate (it can
never stop), and a conditional whose branch and predicate counts disagree —
they pair by position, so a mismatch silently leaves a branch unguarded or
unreachable, which is invisible on the canvas because the branch simply never
runs. That last check immediately caught a wrong fixture in our own test suite.

DRAWING. A container was rendered as one flat box labelled "Branch", which hides
the exact thing a reviewer opens the canvas to check. Containers are now frames
that enclose their children: `steps` are alternatives laid out side by side,

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): draw a branch as a branch

"That doesn't look like a branch" — correct. Enclosing the alternatives in a
frame put the branches on screen but not the BRANCHING: no split, no merge,
just two cards in a box. The fork and the join are the meaning, so they have to
be drawn.

A container now forks. Its branches sit in a row beneath it with an edge out to
each one — labelled with that branch's predicate for a conditional — and an
edge from each one down into whatever follows. That join is what stops a
branch from reading as a dead end.

A loop additionally draws a dashed edge from its body back up to itself, which
is the only thing on the canvas that says "this repeats". It leaves sideways
through dedicated hidden handles: routed between the normal top/bottom handles
it travels straight back up through the nodes it just left, collapses into the
forward line, and is invisible — which is how it first shipped in the previous
commit.

The nesting machinery goes away with it: no parentId, no parent-relative
positions, no container sizing, no separate frame component. Layout regroups
from `data.segmentIndex` / `data.childIndex`, which also fixes the measured
second pass — it re-runs the SAME layout function with real heights instead of
re-stacking by hand, so it can no longer disagree with the first pass about
where a branch row belongs.

Verified in the signed-in app, both themes: a conditional forks to
"approval1.approved = true" / "= false" and merges back into Wait 5d; the loop
shows its dashed return edge and reads "Repeats while recheck.unpaid_count > 0
and cancel-approval.approved = false".

commits.message:
feat: draft flows on the planning tier, and give the designer a toolbar

MODEL. Flow drafting ran on the wrong model, and not by a near miss. It called
runDelegatedConversation without a modelConfig, which makes assembleDynamicAgent
short-circuit to the agent's compiled-in default — so the tenant's configured
bindings were bypassed entirely and it landed on the copilot's own
`purpose: "routing"` default. Routing is a supervisor tier for delegation
decisions; writing declarative graph JSON against a strict schema is planning
and coding work. The mistakes that forced the last three commits of validator
hardening — a toolId used as an entry type, a conditional written as an inline
if — are exactly what a router-tier model produces.

Drafting now resolves the tenant's planning_coding tier through the same
bindings + tenant-settings path the session runtime uses, and pins the run to
it. All three ids in the config are set to that model deliberately: the copilot
resolves by its OWN declared purpose, so `routingModelId` is the field it reads
and pinning only `planningCodingModelId` would change nothing. This says "run
this delegation at planning quality" without editing the shared agent's purpose,
which would affect every other copilot turn.

UI. The header was one row carrying identity, state and the primary action at
once, which left Publish sitting beside a description reading as decoration.
Now: identity on its own row, a compact toolbar row beneath it for the things
you read and switch (validity, version, Flow/Runs), and the primary action
lifted into the app topbar where every other page keeps its CTA. Both rows are
bg-card, matching the app's other headers.

The detail component still renders the action — which button it is depends on
the selected version and error count, state the page doesn't have — and hands
the node up. It depends on `mutate` and `isPending` rather than the mutation
objects, so the topbar doesn't re-register on every render.

apps/ai: 877 tests pass. ai-ui: 743 tests pass. Both typechecks clean.

commits.message:
fix(ui): blend the flow header into the topbar, and let skill cards breathe

FLOW HEADER. Matched the offers document header: the transparent topbar now
floats over the white header (`topbarOverlap`) so the two read as one surface
instead of two stacked bars, and the toolbar strip is bracketed by a divider
above and below rather than only beneath.

SKILL CARDS. The name and slug shared a row, so both truncated — "Contacts
content m… contacts-content-…" — hiding the one thing you scan a card for.
Stacked now: the name gets the full width and only the slug can clip. Paired
with a wider grid track, because a skill is chosen by READING what it does; a
catalog of short labels (tools, files) still reads better dense, so the wider
track is opt-in per list rather than a new default.

Cards are also the default view for skills now. The table leads with
identifiers, which is the right default only once you already know what you're
looking for. Only affects users with no stored preference.

One trap avoided while widening: the first cut interpolated the track width into
the arbitrary class (`minmax(min(100%,${x}),1fr)`). Tailwind scans source
statically, so a class assembled at runtime emits no CSS at all and the grid
silently collapses to one column. The track classes are literals, and a test
pins that they stay that way.

ui-core: 80 tests pass. ai-ui: 743 tests pass. Typecheck clean.

commits.message:
fix(ai): resolve the tenant's models for every graph delegation

A delegated run handed no `modelConfig` does not fall back to the tenant's
configuration — `assembleDynamicAgent` short-circuits to the agent's compiled-in
`config.model`, so bindings and tenant AI settings were bypassed entirely.
`run_specialist` passed none, which meant every agent node in every flow ran on
its static default no matter what the install had configured.

Resolves the same config the chat path does, via a shared helper: model
resolution now takes only the two deps it actually uses, so it can be called
without a thread service. Not pinned to a tier here — each node runs at the tier
ITS agent declares. The drafter keeps its planning-tier pin, but as an override
on top of the shared resolution rather than a second hand-rolled copy, so it
also picks up governance grants and the safeguard model it was missing.

commits.message:
fix(ui-core): open the filter row on the first click, not the second

The filter toggle is anchored to the right edge of the search field, and that
field widens on focus-within. Taking focus on mousedown therefore slid the
button out from under the cursor mid-press — measured on the Flows toolbar, the
wrapper goes 196px → 448px and the button moves ~250px right. mouseup landed
somewhere else, so the browser never synthesized a click: the first press only
expanded the field and the filter row stayed shut.

Suppressing the mouse-press focus keeps the button still so the click lands.
Keyboard is untouched — Tab still reaches it and Enter/Space still fire onClick,
which does not depend on position.

Affects every catalog using the shared toolbar; verified on Flows and Agents.

The create dialog showed one static spinner line for the 3-6 minutes a

of the partially streamed graph JSON, append-only across reparses.

controller under the client id spanning both model rounds, the cancel
route aborts it, the route answers 409 draftCancelled, and no graph rows
are left behind.

optional; fall back to the chat tier as documented).

fix(ai): teach the drafting model the mapConfig rules it kept breaking

The flow "Check for new incoming receipts" resisted two live repair
rounds: one reply had a surplus interior brace, the other wrote mapConfig
as an object literal - which fails twice over (Mastra can't parse the
config AND every constant it was supposed to supply counts as missing,
so dynamic-agent-key and missing-output-schema fire together). The
guidance never spelled any of this out.

wrong shape shown and named as the most common mistake); the four source
shapes verbatim from Mastra's analyzeMapConfig (value / initData:true+path
/ step+path / template with ${} placeholders), including that the FIRST
mapping has no earlier steps to reference; paths are plain dotted
segments only; a complete worked run_specialist mapping-pair with
output_schema as a {value} constant; and a bracket-balance warning at
the end of the guidance and in the draft output contract.

The worked example is validated in a scratchpad check: extracted verbatim
from GRAPH_GUIDANCE, it parses and passes validateGraphAction with zero
issues. Live proof: the previously unfixable flow repaired 6 -> 0 in ONE
round under the new guidance - v2 saved, auto-selected, badge flipped to
Valid.

commits.message:
feat(ai,tasks): let a scheduled task run a flow without an agent turn

A flow could not recur. `triggers.task_template_id` is NOT NULL, so a
schedule can only create a Task, and the only way from a Task to a flow
was an agent deciding to call `invoke_action` — a model turn spent
pressing a button on a graph that is deterministic by construction.

Variant D keeps the June invariant ("Routine = Trigger(schedule) -> Task,
always") and makes the Task the control plane instead: a task template
may target an action graph, the materialized task carries that target,
and the task job dispatches the published graph directly.

The lane branches inside the existing run-specialist step rather than
adding one. Mastra resumes an interrupted run by replaying its snapshot
against the current step list, so a new step would strand every
in-flight task job mid-pipeline on deploy; the shape stays identical.
Reflection is skipped for the flow lane — there is no judgement to learn
from, and no specialist to reflect as.

Outcome mapping is the part worth reviewing: a suspended gate becomes
`needs_approval` (a human really is required), a sleeping run becomes
`ran` so the task rests visibly instead of holding its checkout, and
publish state is re-checked at fire time because a flow can be
unpublished between configuring the routine and the tick.

`ai.action_request` gains `owner_task_id`, which is what lets settle
find its way back to the board: a gate answered tomorrow or a sleeper
woken next week both re-enter `settleGraphRun`, and without the link the
board would keep showing work the system already finished. The mirror is
fail-open by construction — the flow's effects are already real, so a
throw there could roll back a completed run.

commits.message:
fix(core,ai): unbreak db:migrate and the thread-run route test after the merge

Three things the merged tree surfaced, none of them from the flow work:

`db:migrate` failed outright. When kb-filesystem-sync was retired its
migration moved into apps/core to keep continuity for released installs,
but kept the module's `plugin_` prefix — and aggregate-module-migrations
rejects that prefix in core, so every migration run died before applying
anything. Only the slug is renamed: `supabase_migrations` tracks the
timestamp, so 20260616180000 stays applied and nothing re-runs.

The thread-run route test 500'd because the harness's bare `{}`
conversation store has no `listMessagesOrdered`. The attachment-history
load only catches a rejected promise, so a store missing the method
throws synchronously rather than degrading — the default now carries it.

The rest is biome: formatting and interface-member ordering across files
the merge brought together.

commits.message:
fix(core,ai): backdate server-lane JWT iat so PostgREST clock skew cannot reject scheduled fires

PostgREST validates iat against its own clock with a hard-coded ~30s leeway
(bisected on v14.16: +29s passes, +31s is 401 PGRST303 "JWT issued at future")
and no config knob. A minter clock ahead of the database container — the Docker
VM lagging after host sleep — failed every server-lane query, surfacing as
"Scheduled trigger fire failed: Failed to load trigger: JWT issued at future".
Mint with iat = now - 30s (~60s total tolerance); exp stays anchored to the
real clock so token lifetime and refresh margin are unchanged. Applied to both
tenant-db replicas, with regression tests pinning the leeway and exp anchoring.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): create a task in two steps, not one wall of pills

The dialog wrote its metadata as a sentence of muted pills — "[Projekt] Für
[Zuständig] in [Ziel]" — which only parses if you already know the model, and
it asked for a workflow status the creator has no opinion about yet.

Now it asks two questions in order. What: title, description, project, goal.
Who and when: agent or team, start now or just plan, priority, due date. The
assignee section defaults to the Coordinator so the common path is one click,
and it states the consequence — assigning to an agent IS the dispatch, which
the gateway has always done on create but nothing ever said out loud.

Status leaves the create path entirely. "Start now" and "Plan only" map onto
todo/backlog; the full enum belongs on the board.

Scheduled and triggered are rendered disabled rather than hidden, so the shape
of the model is visible before those paths are wired.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): put where-it-belongs back under the title, and phases in it

Step one had grown a boxed "Wo es hingehört" section at the bottom for two
fields that were fine as pills. They are back on the line under the title,
reading "[Projekt] in [Ziel]" again — but with the values in the foreground so
a chosen project no longer looks like an empty placeholder.

Picking a project swaps the goal slot for a phase slot, because that is what
belonging-somewhere means inside a project: a task sits in one of its phases,
and it cannot sensibly sit in a phase of a project it is not part of. The
phase rides in the project context's metadata, which is where the projects
module already reads it from — tasks have no phase column of their own.

Phases come from the project detail endpoint; there is no GET /phases route,
only create/update/delete.

commits.message:
feat(ui): show that a scrollport has more, without painting over it

A description longer than its box just stopped mid-line, which reads as a
rendering fault rather than "keep scrolling". It now fades out at the bottom
edge and carries a slim always-visible scrollbar.

The fade masks the content instead of overlaying a gradient. An overlay
cannot work on engenty chrome: the glass surfaces are translucent on purpose
(`--popover` is `color-mix(… 85%, transparent)`), so a gradient in the same
colour stacks a second layer over the first and shows up as a darker band
across the field. A mask has no colour of its own, so it holds on any
surface and in both themes.

Both utilities live next to `.ui-canvas-glass` since they exist to serve the
same chrome, and are reusable by any small scrollport.

commits.message:
fix(tasks): "plan only" now actually plans instead of starting

Creating an agent task in the backlog dispatched it immediately, so the
Start choice changed which column the task landed in and nothing else.

`isDispatchableTask` was doing two jobs. It answers "could an agent check
this out", and `backlog` belongs in that set because a routine's standing
task rests there between fires and is re-dispatched from fireTrigger. But
creating a task *into* backlog is someone saying "not yet", which is a
different question. The create paths now ask that one instead.

Both create paths were patched — the gateway op and the REST route each ran
their own dispatch, and fixing one silently left the other, which is how the
UI kept starting tasks after the first fix looked complete.

Also from the same pass: the selected segment is a tint of the brand colour
rather than a near-black fill, the chip nests concentrically in its track
(no ring — a ring paints outside the button box and lands on the track's own
border), and priority is a pill like project and goal, not a fourth
segmented control.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): let a run speak on the task it is working

A specialist reaches its tools through the space it runs in, and a
contacts space mounts contacts ops and nothing else. That is right for
which records an agent may touch and wrong for the task it was
dispatched onto: a run could read contacts but could not comment,
could not ask anything, and could only end and let finalize mirror a
status. Runs kept landing in review having said nothing.

The task is a run's output channel, the headless equivalent of the chat
thread, so `task_comment` and `task_ask_user` ride as extraTools next to
artifacts and workspace files — bound to this run's task id, never
mounted from a space, never able to reach another task.

Asking ends the run: the tool posts the question and signals the step,
which parks the task `blocked` with a `task_question` inbox row. The
answer arrives as a reply comment on a later dispatch, which the brief
already replays.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): answer an agent's question from the task

Three shapes of waiting now have three cards. TaskReviewCard judges a
finished run and TaskPendingApprovalCard grants a tool; this adds the
one in between — the run that stopped because only a person has the
fact it needs.

The question is a comment, not a row, so "is one open" is a property of
the end of the thread: an agent question nobody has replied to. Reading
it that way keeps the answer in the same place as the question, and the
brief already replays both to the next run.

Answering posts the reply and dispatches the task in one gesture. An
answer nobody resumes on is just another comment.

Also: a flow gate can be answered from the task now that the graph runs
under the checkout run id — the task's newest run IS the graph run, so
no lookup is needed. And a task waiting on an answer no longer claims
its run failed.

commits.raw_message:
feat(tasks): answer an agent's question from the task

Three shapes of waiting now have three cards. TaskReviewCard judges a
finished run and TaskPendingApprovalCard grants a tool; this adds the
one in between — the run that stopped because only a person has the
fact it needs.

The question is a comment, not a row, so "is one open" is a property of
the end of the thread: an agent question nobody has replied to. Reading
it that way keeps the answer in the same place as the question, and the
brief already replays both to the next run.

Answering posts the reply and dispatches the task in one gesture. An
answer nobody resumes on is just another comment.

Also: a flow gate can be answered from the task now that the graph runs
under the checkout run id — the task's newest run IS the graph run, so
no lookup is needed. And a task waiting on an answer no longer claims
its run failed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): a task run's transcript was never saved, and never readable

Opening a finished run's details showed an empty box. Three separate
causes, all of them the headless lane falling through rules written for
a human's chat.

The transcript was never written. `saveMessages` put the raw scope user
into `author_user_id`, an FK to `core.users` — and a service principal
is not a user row. The insert threw on the run's FIRST message and the
throw abandoned the whole save loop, so not even the assistant turn
survived. `saveThread` right above it already goes through
`scopeAttributionUserId` for exactly this reason.

It was not readable either. `listMessages` and `getThread` compare the
thread's owner to the caller, and a task-job thread has no owner, so
`null !== callerUserId` locked out everyone — including the person
looking at the task. A run's transcript is not a private chat, it is
the work record of a task, so whoever may read the TASK may read its
runs. We ask core with the caller's own credential rather than
re-deriving that permission; a caller who cannot see the task still
gets a 404.

And Mastra's own thread lookup rejected the unowned thread for the same
reason, this time to the run itself.

The run then opens on its brief — the whole rendered task, hundreds of
words the reader is already looking at — so that turn folds away and
the agent's actual work leads.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): a comment has a kind, instead of a leading emoji

Comments are a task's output channel: a person's note, an agent's
progress report, a run's result, a question that blocks the run, and
lifecycle notices nobody typed. The code told those apart by string
prefix — the result lookup ran `content like '🤖%'` and "is a question
open" matched a leading '❓'. That is typing user-visible text: reword
the copy, translate it, or let someone paste an emoji, and the meaning
moves.

`kind` is note | progress | question | result | system, checked in the
database and backfilled from the prefixes it replaces. Every emitter
now names one and no reader parses text: the result lookup selects
`kind = 'result'`, the answer box looks for a `question` at the tail of
the thread. Hard cutover — the prefixes are gone from the writers, so
nothing is left reading them.

The thread renders the kinds: a system notice is one quiet line rather
than a voice in the conversation, a question carries the same sky rail
as the box that answers it, and the agent's name is no longer prefixed
into its own text when the row already says who wrote it.

commits.message:
fix(tasks): read the activity feed in the same direction as comments

Comments run oldest-first with the newest at the bottom; activity ran
the other way, so switching tabs reversed the reading direction
mid-thought. The API answers newest-first because its index is
`(task_id, created_at desc)`, which is right for the API — so the order
is settled at the render point instead, where the two tabs cannot drift
apart again.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): a question carries how it can be answered

`task_ask_user` could only produce prose and a free-text box. Most of
what an agent needs to ask is a choice — which of these three, may I
proceed, which of these apply — and asking that as prose makes the
person retype an option the agent already enumerated, then makes the
agent re-parse it. ENG-47 asked "Choose one: #E63946 (red), #2A9D8F
(teal), or #F4A261 (orange)" into a textarea.

The tool now takes `answer_type` (text | confirm | single_choice |
multi_choice) with `options`, and the shape rides in a new
`task_comments.metadata` column — not in the text, for the same reason
`kind` does not. The card renders one control per type: two buttons for
a confirm, one-click rows for a single choice, checkboxes plus submit
for a multi. A choice that arrives with no options degrades to a text
box rather than rendering an empty list and stranding the run.

The card also stopped repeating the question. The comment carrying it
sits directly above, and printing it twice was the first thing anyone
noticed; what the card contributes is the control.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): hand a task to a flow, not just to an agent

A task could only target a flow if a TEMPLATE made it — direct create had no
flow fields at all, so the one thing Variant D exists for was unreachable from
the UI (T1b).

The create schema now takes `action_graph_id` + `flow_input`, refined one notch
weaker than the template rule: agent XOR flow, or NEITHER, because an unassigned
task is a perfectly good plan while an unassigned template could never
materialize anything. `.partial()` for updates is taken on the unrefined shape,
same reason as the templates above it.

Fixes a flow task that could not be created at all: `normalizeTaskAssignees`
rejected the very shape `fireTrigger` passes — kind `agent` with a NULL agent
key, which is how a headless flow task is stored — so a flow template threw
`primary_assignee_agent_required` on materialization and the trigger looked
configured while producing nothing. The rule now reads the flow target, and
normalizes an unassigned flow task onto the dispatchable kind so no caller has
to know the convention. Editing a flow task's collaborators threw for the same
reason; the update path now carries the row's flow target into the check.

Wizard: "Wer erledigt das" gains a third answer — Agent | Team | Flow — offered
only when the tenant has a published, active flow (the task job re-checks both
at dispatch, so a draft would only produce a run that fails). Picking one shows
the fields the published version declares in its `inputSchema`; flat scalars
only, anything else is skipped rather than guessed at, and required fields block
submit — a flow started without its subject fails on its first tick.

Verified live: ENG-49 created from the wizard dispatched, ran the graph, and
parked at its approval gate; ENG-50 with "Nur planen" persisted
`{"offer_id": "…"}` and correctly did not dispatch.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): say what a flow task is actually doing

Four things a flow task got wrong on the page it lives on, all found by running
one (ENG-49) end to end:

- The status badge said "Lauf fehlgeschlagen" about a task parked at an approval
  gate. A flow gate is a graph node, not a tool grant, so it leaves no pending
  operation id and the reason fell through to `failed`. `blockedReason` now
  takes hints rather than a lone boolean, and a parked gate reads as "wartet auf
  Freigabe" — the same reason, because it is the same question.
- The assignee read "9c53 25cb252a3e15": the pseudo checkout key
  `action-graph:<uuid>` split like a normal agent key into two uuid fragments.
  It resolves to "Flow" now, and WHICH flow gets its own property row beside the
  routine row.
- There was no account of the run at all. A specialist has a transcript to
  watch; a flow runs tools, so its steps ARE the account — TaskFlowStepsPanel
  lists them in GRAPH order (a snapshot only holds what has been reached) with
  each state. The run query already polls while a run moves, so it is live
  without a stream of its own (T3).
- Reassigning on the detail page dispatches immediately and nothing said so
  (T2). The picker now carries that sentence — on an existing task only, where
  the choice IS the dispatch; in create dialogs "Sofort starten | Nur planen"
  decides and the wizard already says it.

The gate lookup is lifted into `useTaskFlowRun` so the card, the badge and the
timeline read one answer instead of three.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): filter the list down to work that runs itself

T6's first half: a "Läufe" segment beside Person and Agent, showing only tasks
nobody has to pick up — materialized by a routine (`trigger_id`) or supervising
a flow (`action_graph_id`). Either origin counts; both are machine-run work,
and both are what D4 will want to look at.

"runs" is not an assignee kind and does not travel as one: the list page turns
it into `machine_run`, its own filter. That param takes the wire's "true"/"false"
as well as a real boolean, because the same schema parses `c.req.query()` and
gateway op input — `z.coerce.boolean()` would have read the string "false" as
TRUE and shown a filtered list to someone who asked for everything.

Verified live: the Aufgaben list drops from 5 tasks to the 2 flow tasks.

Not included: the auto-done display for short-lived runs, which needs D4's
definition of "short-lived" before it can be anything but a guess.

commits.message:
feat(routines): a routine can run a flow instead of an agent

Phase 7 #1 + #2. Variant D's whole point is recurring deterministic work, and
until now nothing could CONFIGURE it: the trigger route's task-template schema
required an `agent_type_key`, so the one target that skips the model turn was
unreachable from any UI.

"Neue Routine" gains a "Was läuft" switch — an agent, or a published flow. On
flow the agent picker and the instructions box disappear rather than sitting
there ignored: a flow's steps ARE its instructions. Only published, active
graphs are offered, because `runTaskFlow` re-checks both when the routine fires
and a draft would only produce a run that fails at 02:00.

Both target keys always travel in the payload, and the unset one travels as
null — a routine switched agent→flow must CLEAR the old key, or the template
carries two targets and its check constraint refuses the write.

#2, the event guard: an event trigger may not target a flow. The event's
payload reaches a task as PROSE in the description, and a graph cannot read
that (D5 owes the mapping). Refused on create and on patch, with the reason
stated in the form the moment the pair is selected, rather than saving a
routine that fires forever with an empty input.

Verified live end to end: a flow routine created from the dialog materialized
ENG-51 on "Jetzt ausführen", which dispatched, ran the graph, parked at its
approval gate (steps panel showed `gate` waiting, `apply` still idle), and
settled on reject. That path threw `primary_assignee_agent_required` before
today's normalizer fix — a flow template could not materialize a task at all.

commits.message:
feat(authz): grant a role to an agent by name, not by uuid

Phase 7 #8, first half. The assignments tab asked for an "agent uuid" in a
free-text box, so granting a role to an agent meant looking its principal up in
the database first — and the granted list then read "agent 019fc98c-…" back at
you, which is how fifteen hand-grants ended up unreadable.

Both halves of the picker now select by name, backed by
`GET /api/tenants/:tenantId/agents` — the agent-shaped sibling of the
`GET /api/users` the user half already used. `core.agents.name` IS the
agent_type_key, so the list needs no join.

The granted list falls back to the raw id when a principal is gone: an
assignment can outlive what it names, and "agent <uuid>" is still the truth.

Not included: per-module DEFAULT role assignments (the other half of #8).
`ensureCoreAgentId` is the single seam where a principal is minted, but it
lives in the AI plane while authz writes belong to core — that boundary is a
decision, not a detail.

commits.message:
feat(authz): a module's agent can read its own module from the start

Phase 7 #8, second half. "The contacts agent may read contacts" is not a
decision anyone makes differently — it is what installing that agent MEANS —
but it was a hand-grant per tenant, so every fresh tenant shipped with agents
that parked on their first read.

Minting moves to core as `core_agents_ensure`: an agent principal is an authz
subject and the grant that comes with it is an authz write, so core owns both.
The AI plane keeps what it knows — agent KEYS, and the registry's
`core_agent_id` link, which is an AI-plane column.

The default is deliberately narrow: the agent's OWN module, viewer (read) only,
and only when that role exists. Writing stays an explicit grant. `engenty.*` is
the platform prefix, not a module, so the coordinator and copilot get nothing
here — how far a cross-module orchestrator may read is its own decision.

The grant lands ONLY on the call that CREATED the principal, which is why
`ensureAgentPrincipal` reports `created` instead of upserting blindly: granting
on every call would re-add a role a human revoked and make the revoke
impossible to make stick. Existing principals therefore keep exactly what they
have — fixing an already-provisioned tenant stays a visible act (now two clicks,
since the roles picker learned names).

Verified live: dispatching a task to `offers.manager` for the first time minted
its principal AND granted `offers.viewer` in one step. (That run then failed on
`unknownTool` — the offers module is not mounted in that space, which is the
mount mismatch already logged under Phase 7's live issues, not an authz gap.)

commits.message:
feat(triggers): run a trigger now and watch the run it started

A manual fire used to hand the task to the dispatch queue and return
nothing to watch: the button spun until the POST came back — the moment
the work STARTS — and then went idle over a run nobody was following.

commits.message:
feat(flows): compile an Action into the one-node flow it always was

An ACTION.md is one agent, one prompt, an input schema and a tool allow
list — a one-node flow written in a second format. `compileActionToGraph`
derives the stored graph from that declaration, so the parallel runtime can
go without touching authoring: the markdown stays the source of truth.

Two things had to give first, both of them honest fixes rather than
concessions to the compiler:

The save validator demanded a constant `output_schema` on EVERY
run_specialist, though its own reason was "so downstream nodes can be
type-checked". An action is terminal and answers in PROSE — the button
renders it as markdown — and `output_schema` puts the agent under a
"respond with ONLY a JSON object" contract, so the rule made "end by
having an agent answer" unexpressible. It now applies where its reason
does: the graph's last top-level step may go without one; anything nested
stays fail-closed, because inside a container "what follows" is the
container's business.

`run_specialist` never told the specialist WHAT the run was about, so a
graph node had to be handed the subject as prose. It now renders the run
context's subject as the `## Subject` section `buildActionBrief` has always
written for the action lane.

Input travels as `{initData: true, path: ""}` — Mastra resolves an empty
path to the source object — so a press's values arrive intact and the
compiler never tracks the input schema. The compiled graph passes the same
save-path validator as hand- and LLM-authored graphs, with no exemption.

Phase 7 #4 (part).

commits.message:
feat(flows): seed an Action's flow on first use, not by migration

Actions have no per-tenant rows at all — `listAllActions` resolves them per
request from module capabilities — so giving each one a flow means new
persistence. Seeding the fleet would write rows for buttons nobody has
pressed and need a reconcile to stay honest as declarations change.
`ensureActionFlow` does it on USE instead: find-or-create, compare the
stored graph with a fresh compile, and mint + publish a new version only
when the declaration has actually moved. Same shape as
`core_agents_ensure`, and for the same reason.

Identity is a new `source_action_id` column, not the name: a tenant may
already have a flow called "Enhance contact", and (tenant_id, name) is
unique, so keying on the name would either hijack their flow or refuse to
seed ours. Null on every authored flow — which is the distinction that
matters: a row with a source may be rewritten by a recompile, a row
without one belongs to whoever wrote it.

Auto-publishing is deliberate and limited to this path: what governs a
module action is installing the module, and its markdown shipped as code.
A compiled graph is still put through the same save-path validator first —
a flow that could not be saved must not be published either.

Phase 7 #4 (part). Migration 20260816020000, applied locally.

commits.message:
fix(flows): a flow with an agent node could not run headlessly at all

`created_by_user_id` on the child run is a core.users FK, and a headless
lane runs as the AI SERVICE principal — whose id is a service_credential
id. Writing it raw failed the insert, which failed the specialist node,
which failed the whole graph: "agent_run insert: violates foreign key
constraint". Same trap `triggers_fire` and `registerTaskJobRun` already
handle; `runDelegatedConversation`'s observe path was the one place left
writing the raw scope id.

Invisible until now because no flow that ran from a task had an agent node
— the seeded gate/apply flows have none — and the button lane passes a
real user's scope, where the raw id was correct all along.

Found by running a compiled Action end to end: ENG-58 ran
`contacts.enhance-contact` as a flow, the specialist researched the
contact, proposed two field updates, and the task settled to in_review.

Also drops a false drift signal in the Action seeder: `jsonb` does not
preserve key order, so comparing raw JSON text made every press look like
a change and mint an identical version. Caught on the second real run.

Phase 7 #4 (part).

commits.message:
feat(tasks): review the field updates a flow's agent proposed

A specialist inside a flow proposes updates and finishes — it does not
suspend the way the action job does — so the suggestions ended up on its
CHILD run with the task holding the decision and no way to reach them. The
task showed "the flow completed", the agent's two researched corrections
sat in a run nobody could open, and that was the end of it.

Three pieces close it:

The flow run snapshot now reports `agentRuns` — the runs its agent nodes
started. A specialist runs under its own id, so from outside, a flow that
had an agent do all the work looks like it did nothing; the child ids are
the only path from a task to what its agent actually said.

`TaskFieldSuggestionsCard` reads those runs and shows what was proposed,
with the evidence and sources the agent cited. Sibling of
TaskFlowGateCard: that one answers a gate the GRAPH declared, this one
answers what the AGENT proposed inside a node.

`POST /ai/v1/tasks/:taskId/field-updates` applies the approved fields
through the module's own update operation, as the CALLER — approving a
suggestion is a human act and is gated by that human's capabilities, like
editing the record by hand. The subject comes from the task's own binding,
never from the request, so an approval cannot be pointed at another record.

Live: a compiled Action researched a contact, proposed a corrected phone
number and registration number with Impressum sources, and the card
rendered both with checkboxes; the route applied a patch through
contacts_update and left the audit comment on the task.

Phase 7 #4 — this was the standing precondition for retiring the action
lane ("field-update approval verified on the task path").

commits.message:
feat(actions): a button press is a trigger fire, and the action lane is gone

Pressing an Action button started an `action-job` workflow directly — the
one invocation lane with no work record, which is why its approvals had
nowhere to live and `ask_user` asked into the void. A press now takes the
same path as every other invocation: trigger → task → flow.

Everything the press needs is derived from the ACTION.md on demand: the
flow it compiles to, a manual trigger pointing at it (keyed by module_key
`action:<id>`), and a task carrying the press's input and subject. Nothing
is seeded ahead of time; the second press reuses what the first created.

Identity is split on purpose: provisioning runs as the SERVICE principal,
the fire records the person who pressed. Someone allowed to press a button
on a contact is not thereby a routine administrator, and demanding
`module.tasks.write` of them would leave the button to admins only. What
the flow may DO is still gated inside the run. `triggers_fire` therefore
accepts an explicit creator, honoured only when the caller has no user
identity of its own — a user always attributes to itself, so it cannot be
used to blame someone else.

The button reads the task instead of one run: the flow run says whether it
is still going, and the agent's CHILD run carries the steps, the answer
and any proposed updates. Approving them goes to the task's field-updates
route, so the same approval works from the button and from the task page.

Deleted with the lane, not left as a fallback: the action-job start path
and `POST /ai/v1/actions/:actionId/approve` (nothing suspends any more).

Live: pressed "Kontakt anreichern" on a real contact → trigger and flow
provisioned on the spot → task ENG-61 → the agent researched the company →
button went to "Needs approval" → the modal showed both suggestions with
their Impressum sources. Not applied: the contact is real data.

Phase 7 #4.

commits.message:
feat(admin): one catalog for everything this workspace can run

Two catalogs described one runtime. An ACTION.md compiles to a one-node
flow the first time it is pressed, so /actions and /flows were the same
list twice — and after the press cutover the Actions catalog described a
lane that no longer exists.

Flows is now the only catalog: stored graphs and declared ACTION.md files
merged into one list, deduped on `source_action_id` so a compiled action
appears once, as the flow that actually runs. Where a runnable was
written (file / canvas) and what shape it has are filter chips. A
declared action that nobody has pressed is a fourth status, not a hidden
row.

The admin sidebar drops to the five building blocks (Overview, Agents,
Flows, Skills, Tools); Artifacts, Connections and Activity move to a
second group until their fold-ins land.

Also closes the loose end from the press cutover: the run panel on an
ACTION.md read its history from `ai.action_request` rows keyed on the
ACTION.md id, which a press stopped writing — the audit row is written
against the compiled graph now, so the panel reads the flow's history and
names the task the press created.

commits.message:
feat(triggers): an event can start a flow, because its payload becomes the input

An event payload reached a task as PROSE appended to the description —
readable by an agent, unreadable by a flow, which is why event triggers
were rejected at save time whenever they pointed at one.

A trigger may now carry an input mapping in the SAME grammar the graph
canvas uses for its mapping nodes ({value} / {initData,path} /
{template}), with the event payload as initData, so there is one mapping
language platform-wide. With no mapping the payload IS the input, which
is what a flow authored against that event would map internally anyway.
Only a flow target gets this layer: an agent still reads the event as
prose in its brief.

Also fixes what the first live fire exposed: a run that stopped to ASK
(gate, capability, ask_user) rested as `blocked`, and the briefing lists
todo/in_review/backlog — so every question the convergence model routes
to that surface was invisible on it. Waiting on a person is `in_review`;
only a failure is blocked. Nothing re-dispatches either (neither is a
checkout entry status).

Verified live: a webhook fire with {record:{id}} mapped to the flow's
{offer_id}, ran the published flow, hit its approval gate, and the task
came to rest in review with the mapped input on it.

commits.message:
feat(flows): a gate decision is written where the question was asked

The question a flow's approval gate raises lands on the task as a
comment; the answer did not — the thread held half a conversation, and
the only record of a decision was the run resuming.

That asymmetry is harmless while every pause parks on the row, and
load-bearing the moment a run can be suspended instead (Phase 8 tier 1):
degrading a suspended run back to the park path must lose nothing, and
it only can if both halves are always in the comments. So the decision
is now recorded there, with the reason a person typed and, as metadata,
who answered — the caller is the service principal, so claiming
authorship would be a lie.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): run a dispatched task on Mastra's background-task substrate

The queue, the boot resume and two-thirds of the task-job workflow were
infrastructure Mastra did not have when we built them: persistence,
per-agent concurrency, backpressure, stale-task recovery and a lifecycle
stream all ship now. So the six steps become an ordinary function and a
BackgroundTaskManager carries it — which also dissolves the frozen step
list, since a run no longer resumes into the code it was suspended under.

Both substrates run that same function, and a test asserts the workflow's
chain still equals it, so a task cannot behave differently depending on
which carrier picked it up. The switch is `ENGENTY_TASK_DISPATCH_SUBSTRATE`
and the workflow stays the default: the plan requires crash-recovery
parity to be proven before anything is deleted.

Proven, and it found a real trap. `recoverStaleTasks` returns a task the
crash caught to `pending` only when `maxRetries > 0`; with the default 0
it marks it failed and the task row stays `in_progress` forever. Killed a
process mid-run twice: without retries the task was stranded, with them
the next boot re-dispatched it, re-entered on its original run id (the
checkout is idempotent for the same id) and settled it correctly. The
executor is registered by NAME for the same reason — recovery has no
per-task closure to call.

commits.raw_message:
feat(tasks): run a dispatched task on Mastra's background-task substrate

The queue, the boot resume and two-thirds of the task-job workflow were
infrastructure Mastra did not have when we built them: persistence,
per-agent concurrency, backpressure, stale-task recovery and a lifecycle
stream all ship now. So the six steps become an ordinary function and a
BackgroundTaskManager carries it — which also dissolves the frozen step
list, since a run no longer resumes into the code it was suspended under.

Both substrates run that same function, and a test asserts the workflow's
chain still equals it, so a task cannot behave differently depending on
which carrier picked it up. The switch is `ENGENTY_TASK_DISPATCH_SUBSTRATE`
and the workflow stays the default: the plan requires crash-recovery
parity to be proven before anything is deleted.

Proven, and it found a real trap. `recoverStaleTasks` returns a task the
crash caught to `pending` only when `maxRetries > 0`; with the default 0
it marks it failed and the task row stays `in_progress` forever. Killed a
process mid-run twice: without retries the task was stranded, with them
the next boot re-dispatched it, re-entered on its original run id (the
checkout is idempotent for the same id) and settled it correctly. The
executor is registered by NAME for the same reason — recovery has no
per-task closure to call.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
refactor(tasks): the background substrate IS the dispatch path now

Cutover, after the parity the plan required was proven live: a dispatched
task runs on Mastra's background-task manager, and the six-step workflow,
its registration and the two-substrate switch are deleted rather than
left as a fallback. Verified through the real service on both lanes — a
flow task (gate → in_review) and an agent task (the coordinator answered,
its comment landed, task in_review) — each carried by the manager with
its retry budget intact.

The queue survives, and the comment now says why: `dispatchTaskIfReady`
runs in CORE, which has no Mastra instance, so something must carry "run
this task" across the process boundary. What it stopped carrying is
durability — the consumer hands the message over and acks, because
awaiting the run would only race a redelivery timer against a substrate
that already guarantees it.

Swept with it: the action-job workflow, its steps, schema and brief. That
lane's runtime went in the press cutover; this is the file it left behind.
One pre-cutover action run sits parked at `requires_action` from before
that change — it was already unanswerable (its approve route is gone) and
is left alone rather than silently rewritten.
