commits.message:
feat(agent): Manage tab; fix admin showing no routines for an agent

The admin personnel file said "No routines target this agent" for an
agent that plainly had one. The card queries routines at the CURRENT
Space's scope, and `/admin/engenty/...` sits outside the Space the
routine lives in — so it listed another Space's routines and found no
match. The hook already has `scope: "tenant"` for exactly this case,
described as "surfaces that are about the PERSON or the whole tenant
rather than one space", which is what a personnel file is. It now lists
the agent's routines wherever they live.

Adds a Manage / Verwalten tab in the Space: the mandate, the skills it
loads, the connections it can reach, and its identity — the questions
someone working in the Space asks about an agent before trusting it,
without leaving for an admin screen built for a different job.

It reads from the desk feed the other tabs already use rather than
rendering the admin file twice: admin keeps editing (tools, instruction
files, model, workspace) and this links there. Duplicating those panels
would have meant pulling the whole admin data layer into the Space and
maintaining two ways to draw the same thing.

Tab labels are translated now (en + de) instead of hardcoded English.

commits.message:
chore(deps): @mastra/editor 0.14.0 drops a stale transitive tree

`@mastra/editor@0.13.8` pulled `@mastra/schema-compat@1.3.4` (through
`@composio/mastra`) and `@mastra/memory@1.23.1`, each installed alongside the
copy the rest of the workspace uses. 0.14.0 drops both: schema-compat resolves
to a single 1.3.7, and editor's memory copy moves 1.23.1 → 1.27.0.

Four duplicate @mastra packages become three. What is left is `@mastra/rag`
(declared twice — knowledge-base 2.3.0 vs retrieval 2.4.2) and
`@mastra/server` (1.52.1 via the dev-only `mastra` CLI).

`@mastra/memory` stays declared at 1.26.2 on purpose. Declaring 1.27.0 to close
its duplicate fails at run time: memory 1.27.0 imports
`assertKnowledgeScopeWithinCeiling` from `@mastra/core/storage`, which core
1.59.0 does not export and 1.61.0 does. Its peer range (`>=1.4.1-0 <2.0.0-0`)
does not catch that, and neither does tsc — 52 apps/ai test files failed to
import before the revert. That duplicate is coupled to the core bump, not
independent.

apps/ai: typecheck clean, 215 files / 1529 tests passing — the pre-bump baseline.

commits.message:
feat(agent): routine detail in the Plan tab, and leaving/deleting an agent

Three things the agent page needed.

**Routines open IN the Plan tab**, behind a back link, instead of
navigating to the task page — which leads with comments and activity when
what you came for was the setup. The routine UI is the one that already
existed: the drawer's body moved into RoutineDetailBody, so the drawer,
the admin card and this tab show one routine rather than three readings
of it. The work half (runs, comments, files) stays on the task, one
"Open work" link away.

**Remove from Space / Delete agent** in the overflow menu, each behind a
dialog that says what is attached before it acts. Neither is one call:
core's unmount removes the mount and nothing else, and the registry's
delete removes only the agent row — so routines would keep waking and
tasks would sit assigned to someone who is no longer there. The dialog
counts both, offers to hand the open tasks to another mounted agent (or
to nobody), then cascades. Unmount PAUSES routines, following core's own
"unmounting hides, never deletes"; delete deletes them, because a routine
without its agent can never run again. Every non-/ai URL this needs is
collected in agent-space-removal.ts so the coupling is one file.

**The header eyebrow** said "engenty. · Spezialist". The brand word told
you nothing — every agent here is an engenty one — and the role read as
prose next to it. Both are the admin badges now.

commits.message:
feat(tasks): routines declare an outcome and a report floor

A routine now carries a promise (outcome, prose) and a declared report
mode on its standing task. The mode is a FLOOR, not an override: a run
may escalate above it (quiet < report < review), never end below it.
Null stays undeclared and reads as quiet — pre-existing routines change
behaviour in no way.

- module_tasks.tasks: nullable outcome + report_mode (checked enum)
- floor applied in write-result and finalize via applyReportFloor;
  read once in build-brief and carried on the job envelope so both
  consumers judge against the same value — including the flow lane,
  which skips the rest of the briefing
- task brief renders "## Outcome" and a per-mode run protocol
- spawn-per-event children inherit outcome + report_mode: a child IS
  one cycle of the routine that got its own row

commits.message:
feat(ai): unpressed Actions in the routine flow picker; copilot declares invoke_action

The flow picker used to show only compiled graphs — and Actions compile
on first PRESS, so a tenant where nobody had pressed anything saw an
empty list and concluded flows were broken. The picker now builds from
the same catalog the Flows page uses: declared Actions appear beside
published graphs, and choosing one compiles it on the spot.

- POST /ai/v1/actions/:id/flow — the press's ensureActionFlow without
  the run; returns the compiled graph id
- buildRoutineFlowOptions keeps compiled graphs only when active with a
  current version (a draft here would only produce a 02:00 failure) and
  marks declared Actions with an `action:` prefixed value
- selecting a declared row compiles, then swaps in the real graph id;
  failure clears the field instead of storing a namespaced value
- action-routes.ts header rewritten — it still described the retired
  action-job lane

invoke_action joins ENGENTY_COPILOT_TOOL_IDS: the tool existed and was
registered but declared by nobody, so the copilot simply could not
reach a flow. action_graph_propose stays deliberately undeclared, with
the reasoning recorded in copilot-agent.ts — running a governed flow
spends an approval a human already gave; authoring one mid-chat is the
other side of that gate.

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): inline routine editor, the routine drawn as a diagram, corpses swept

Editing a routine on the agent's Plan tab now happens INLINE — the same
panel swaps to the form with a back link — instead of a modal over the
detail. RoutineEditor is the one implementation of "save a routine";
RoutineCreateDialog is reduced to Dialog chrome around it.

Every routine also draws itself: wake sources on the left, what runs in
the middle, the declared outcome on the right —

  [trigger] --+
              +--> [ what runs ] --> [ outcome ]
  [trigger] --+

routine-shape.ts derives that picture from the data model (the middle is
ALWAYS a list of steps: length one for an instruction routine, the graph
spine for a flow — the picture never changes kind, it only gets longer),
and routine-diagram.tsx renders it: expandable per row in the Plan list,
and after the instructions on both routine detail screens, where it
absorbs the separate trigger card and outcome card. Step icons/chips are
imported from the canvas vocabulary (KIND_ICON / KIND_CHIP now exported)
so two pictures of one flow cannot disagree.

The editor grows the Outcome fields (promise + report floor) and the
detail views show them; naming pass — Flow is the noun, Action is kept
only where it names the file/shape.

Swept after whole-tree verification (only hits were their own
definitions): RoutinesList + its embed export, and the tasks module's
unused CreateTaskDialog.

commits.message:
fix(actions)!: a press is a subject-bound run, never a task

Two correct decisions composed into a defect: on 17 Aug the press
converged onto trigger -> task to give its approvals a home, when every
fire still minted a fresh task — per-press isolation held. On 23 Aug
routines became standing tasks and fires started WAKING one task instead
of creating one; the press rode the same rail and silently inherited
standing-task semantics. Every press of one action shared ONE work
record, the subject was dropped (manual fires never read `contexts`, so
apply-field-updates 400'd on noSubject), and a second press was skipped
while the first ran — with B's button watching A's run. No test covered
a manual fire with two subjects, so nothing went red.

The fix is not a better task shape but no task at all. A Task is a work
item assigned to a person or an agent; a press is an INVOCATION. The
schema always said so: `action_request.owner_task_id` is "Null for
button/agent-started runs."

- dispatch-published-run.ts: the ONE way to run a published graph
  outside a Task — per-subject dedup (an in-flight run for this
  (action, subject) wins), subject bound into the run context (where
  run_specialist reads `## Subject` from), an audit row pinning caller,
  subject and version, stable ids for idempotent retries. Shared by the
  canvas Run button, the ActionButton/slash press and invoke_action's
  out-of-task path, so the press cannot drift from the canvas again.
- pressAction: ensure flow -> dispatch. Returns run identity; the
  route answers {run_id, request_id, thread_id, deduped} — no task_id.
- invoke_action out-of-task -> startPublishedActionRun on the same
  dispatcher; tool's task_id output is optional (nested-only).
- manual-flow-task.ts DELETED — zero consumers, no fallback kept.
- POST /ai/v1/action-runs/:runId/field-updates: run-scoped apply twin;
  subject from the run's own audit row, never from the request.
- ActionButton/run panel follow the run; the run query polls while
  snapshot is still null (it froze on the first fetch before, leaving
  the button "running" forever).

Contract pinned red-first in action-press.test.ts. Live-verified:
press on a contact -> audit row subject-bound with owner_task_id NULL,
0 new triggers/tasks, run settles, the agent names its subject in the
answer, button reaches "View result". The old broken shape never left
feat/spaces, and this dev DB holds zero press-provisioned triggers —
no cleanup migration is needed.

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: rename action_graph -> flow_graph, ring 1 — the database

The definition table was named after one of its callers. `ai.action_graph`
holds every governed flow — pressed as a button, targeted by a routine,
called via invoke_action, run from the canvas — and "Action" is the first
of those callers promoted to the name of the thing they all call, which is
why a scheduled flow and a pressed button felt like different species.

Ring 1 renames the database objects and nothing above them:

- ai.action_graph -> ai.flow_graph, ai.action_graph_version ->
  ai.flow_graph_version (+ column flow_graph_id), and
  action_request.action_graph_version_id -> flow_graph_version_id —
  constraints, indexes and policies renamed with them; grants and
  policies bind by OID and survive; data untouched.
- module_tasks.tasks.action_graph_id -> flow_graph_id (guarded module
  migration; the soft cross-schema reference stays soft by design).
- The two ai-schema stores and the tasks DAL are the only code that
  touches the columns; they now write the new names and MAP the rows
  back to the unchanged API field names at their boundary, so the
  identifier ring can land later as a pure mechanical sweep. The
  duplicate-name detector follows its index to flow_graph_tenant_name_idx.

Rings still to land, in order: TypeScript identifiers (~97 files),
HTTP paths (/ai/v1/action-graphs, with a redirect window), and the tool
ids last — invoke_action/action_graph_propose live in core.agents.tool_ids
jsonb, so that ring needs a data migration a compiler cannot verify.

Applied to the dev stack and live-verified: zero old-named objects
remain; rows, version pins and the engenty_server grants survived; the
flows catalog lists v1 with no version churn (the compile-on-use
comparison held through the mapping); a routine's flow target reads
through the renamed column; a fresh press dispatched, pinned its version
under the new column and settled completed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: rename action_graph -> flow_graph, ring 2 — identifiers

The mechanical sweep the ring-1 boundary mappers existed to enable:
every TypeScript identifier, type, wire field and file name moves from
action_graph/actionGraph/ActionGraph/action-graph to the flow_graph
family — 96 files — and the three DAL mappers, now identities, are
deleted. The API surface speaks flow_graph_id end to end (task rows,
routine DTOs, trigger routes, graph version rows, the copilot
work-routing SKILL.md that documents the trigger contract).

Files renamed with their exports: dal/action-graphs -> dal/flow-graphs
(flow-graph-store.ts), flow-graph-routes.ts, flow-graph-propose-tool.ts,
and ai-ui's flow-graph-{api,queries,detail} in action-canvas.

Deliberately NOT renamed (each is data or a later ring):
- `action-graph:` id prefix — stored in ai.agent_run agent ids, flow
  tasks' pseudo assignee keys and Mastra workflow names; renaming it
  would orphan existing rows for zero benefit.
- `/ai/v1/action-graphs` HTTP paths — ring 3, with a redirect window.
- tool ids `invoke_action` / `action_graph_propose` and invoke_action's
  `action_graph_id` input field — ring 4; the ids live in
  core.agents.tool_ids jsonb and need a data migration.

Envelope safety checked before renaming the task-job field: zero
suspended action_requests and zero Mastra snapshots carrying
action_graph_id on this stack, and feat/spaces is unreleased — no
in-flight state can strand on the schema change.

Verified: apps/ai + ai-ui + tasks typecheck clean; full suites green
(2891 tests); dev stack reloaded and live-checked — routine detail and
the Flows catalog render through the renamed wire fields.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
chore(deps): Mastra core 1.59 → 1.61, with the spine that must move with it

@mastra/core 1.61.0, and everything whose peer range is a lie about what it can
actually run on: hono 1.7.1, pg 1.21.1, docker 0.6.0, memory 1.27.0. All nine
core declarations move together — apps/ai and the eight modules — so the
duplicate closed in 035683d14 does not come back.

memory 1.27.0 is the point of the group. It imports
`assertKnowledgeScopeWithinCeiling` from `@mastra/core/storage`, which 1.59 does
not export; declaring it against 1.59 installed clean, typechecked clean, and
failed at module evaluation across 52 test files. On 1.61 it resolves, and the
@mastra/memory duplicate is gone. Two duplicates left: @mastra/rag (declared
twice) and @mastra/server (dev-only, via the mastra CLI).

The patch is re-authored for 1.61 (`agent-DSxJoGjY.js`, `agent-NkjbehmN.cjs`).
The unowned channel-render `driverPromise` rejection is still unfixed upstream —
verified against the published 1.61.0 tarball — and the dist chunk names are
content-hashed, so the patch cannot survive a bump untouched.

Core 1.61 narrowed Agent's `tools` to DynamicArgument<ToolsInput>, which
`Record<string, object>` no longer satisfies. Widened at the two call sites that
already import Agent, not in packages/ai-core: `MastraToolDefinition = object`
is deliberate there, keeping ai-core free of any @mastra/core dependency, and
importing Mastra types to satisfy a typecheck would trade that boundary for two
casts. `ChannelHandlerContext.signalMetadata` also became required; the gate
test's fixture needed it, no production code reads it.

apps/ai: typecheck clean, 215 files / 1529 tests — the pre-bump baseline.
All modules typecheck clean. (@engenty/tasks fails on an unrelated pre-existing
error, identical at 1.59.)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

chore(deps): one @mastra/rag, at 2.6.0

knowledge-base declared 2.3.0 and retrieval 2.4.2, so both installed. Retrieval
carries rag as an optional peer (`>=2.3.0`) plus a devDep for its own tests, and
knowledge-base is the only real consumer — nothing pinned either side to an old

manifest, so it was carrying a version pin for a dependency it never imported.
It rode along in 035683d14 and again in 0931244e4 because those commits only
moved versions.

@mastra/server is now the last duplicate — 1.52.1, dev-only, via the mastra CLI.

knowledge-base 77 files / 402 tests, retrieval 5 / 24, 33 turbo tasks green.

commits.message:
chore(scripts): re-apply the @mastra/core patch by content, not by line

The patch targets built dist chunks whose filenames are content hashes
(`agent-DSxJoGjY.js`), so they change on every release and a stored diff can
never re-apply — it has been hand-authored on each bump since 1.57.

This matches the ChatChannelOutputProcessor block on its log string instead, so
the next bump is `pnpm patch` → script → `pnpm patch-commit`. It refuses loudly
rather than patching the wrong thing if upstream reshapes the block, and is
idempotent on a tree that already carries the patch.

Ported to .mjs to match the other 37 scripts here; the Python original was
written mid-sweep and had no precedent in this repo.

Delete this and the patch once a release carries mastra-ai/mastra#22164.

commits.message:
fix(tasks): updateTask persists flow_graph_id and flow_input

updateTask's explicit allow-list never copied the two Variant D fields
its callers patch: trigger-gateway-methods re-targets a routine's
standing task between agent and flow, and trigger-fire re-stamps a
manual/flow fire's input — both were accepted and silently dropped, so
the standing task kept its previous target/values.

The assignee normalization now sees the merged patch-over-row view
(a re-target re-derives "agent with no key" from the NEW flow target),
and an explicit null in the patch actually clears the field instead of
falling back to the row's value via ??.

The existing coverage mocked the repo (which spreads the whole patch),
so it asserted the patch was passed, not applied. New DAL-level test
runs the real createTasksRepoSupabase against a fake PostgREST client
and asserts on the actual update payload.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(tests): ring-2 sweep fallout + the long-standing TS2571

Two repairs routed by peer sessions after the mastra-sweep merge:

- invoke-action-tool.test.ts: the ring-2 sweep renamed the test fixture's
  input field to flow_graph_id, but `action_graph_id` is the TOOL-SURFACE
  name, deliberately protected until ring 4 — the sweep protected the tool
  file and missed its fixture. Mastra 1.61 now validates tool input and
  returns an error object rather than throwing, so the mocks recorded zero
  calls with no exception — the failure mode is documented at the fixture
  so the next rename doesn't repeat it.

- trigger-gateway-attribution.test.ts: the operation registry's `handler`
  returns `unknown`, so `.catch` on its result was TS2571 — an error that
  predated the rename rings, the press fix and the Mastra bumps, and
  reproduced on pristine source. createDaily now returns a typed Promise
  and the one catch site narrows explicitly. @engenty/tasks typechecks
  clean for the first time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
refactor(ai): rename action_graph -> flow_graph, ring 3 — the HTTP surface

The route base moves from /ai/v1/action-graphs to /ai/v1/flow-graphs;
the ai-ui client follows. /ai/v1/actions/:id/* stays untouched — those
paths name the ACTION.md, and Action survives as the concept for a
module-shipped declared single-node flow.

The retired base answers 308 onto the canonical one for one release
window: with no external consumer on feat/spaces, the only caller that
can still hold the old path is a browser tab running pre-rename JS
across the deploy. 308 (not 301/307) so every verb survives with its
body, and fetch follows silently. The redirect fires before scope
resolution — it is a path alias, not an endpoint.

flow-graph-legacy-redirect.test.ts pins the window's contract and says
in its header how to close it: delete the legacy block and flip the
expectations to 404 — removal should show up in a diff, not as a
silent disappearance.

Live-verified on the dev stack: canonical base auth-gates (401 anon),
legacy POST answers 308 with the rewritten Location, and the Flows
catalog loads through GET /ai/v1/flow-graphs -> 200.

Remaining: ring 4 — tool ids invoke_action/action_graph_propose and
invoke_action's action_graph_id input field, with the
core.agents.tool_ids jsonb data migration a compiler cannot verify.

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: rename action_graph -> flow_graph, ring 4 — the tool ids

The last ring, and the one a compiler cannot verify: the ids models call
by name. `invoke_action` -> `invoke_flow`, `action_graph_propose` ->
`flow_graph_propose`, and invoke_flow's input field `action_graph_id` ->
`flow_graph_id`. Files follow (invoke-flow-tool.ts,
invoke-flow-execution.ts + their tests); the tool's model-facing prose
now says Flow, matching what the catalog and the routine picker taught.

The data half: any custom agent that declared one of the old ids carries
the string in ai.engenty_ai_agents.tool_ids (jsonb) — renaming the
constant alone silently strands it, the tool just vanishes from its
surface. The migration rewrites both ids in place, preserving array
order and bystanders. Zero rows carry them on this stack; the rewrite
was proven against a synthetic row in a rolled-back transaction.

Registry proof after reload: all 29 declared copilot tool ids resolve
against the builtin registry, both new ids present, no stale
invoke_action anywhere. Full apps/ai suite green.

The rename is COMPLETE across all four rings: tables (e325c52a7),
identifiers (fdfddd1ac), HTTP paths with a 308 window (df27090cd), and
tool ids + data (this commit). What deliberately keeps the old word:
`ai.action_request` (the audit row was always about invocations),
the stored `action-graph:` id prefix (data), /ai/v1/actions/:id/*
(names the ACTION.md), and "Action" itself as the shape a
module-shipped single-node declared flow takes.

commits.message:
feat(routines): promote an instruction routine to a flow — nothing is deleted

Decision 2 of the flow_graph round, implemented. Two halves:

1. The target switch stops destroying. routineFormToPayload used to null
   the instructions and the outcome when a routine moved to a flow
   target — a one-way door that got easy to walk through once the
   picker filled up. Both now survive every switch: the flow lane
   ignores the description and judges no prose promise, but what a
   person wrote stays theirs until they change it.

2. POST /ai/v1/triggers/:id/promote — the growth path. The routine's
   own instructions compile into a ONE-node published flow
   (compileInstructionToGraph: same two-entry shape an ACTION.md
   compiles to, thread_mode "reuse" so the promoted flow keeps the
   routine's thread continuity, open input schema — tightening the
   contract is canvas work AFTER promotion). The standing task is
   retargeted through the same gateway path the editor uses; the patch
   carries ONLY the target keys, so description and outcome stay.
   Auto-publish is deliberate and argued in the route comment: the
   graph's only content is text the same human already runs unattended
   — promotion changes its shape, not its authority. Name collisions
   disambiguate with the task identifier.

UI: "Promote to flow" on the routine detail (custom, agent-target,
instructions present), which compiles on click and swaps the diagram to
the flow. One consequence worth knowing: a promoted routine leaves the
AGENT's Plan tab — a flow routine has no executing agent — and lives on
in the space-level Routinen list, where its standing task still shows
the preserved instructions with the flow-target chip.

Verified: 4 route tests (red-first contract: instruction becomes node
one's brief, publish stamped by the caller, retarget patch carries only
target keys, name collision path) + form tests; live end-to-end on the
dev stack — created a probe routine, promoted it, confirmed in the DB
that instructions and outcome survived, the flow published as v1 with
the brief in node one, then removed the probe.

commits.message:
feat(routines): Agent Space routine UI — canvas, in-place designer, prompt edit rounds

The routine experience lives in the Space now, end to end.

Ownership: an agent's Plan tab (and the admin routines card) claim flow
routines whose published graph RUNS the agent — the task-level agent
column is null on a flow target (one-of rule), but the agent moved into
node one, it did not leave. GET /ai/v1/triggers enriches flow targets
with standing_task.flow_agent_keys (collectFlowAgentKeys walks
run_specialist mapConfigs, container children included);
routineBelongsToAgent() is the one filter. Fixes the promoted-routine
vanish found in live verify.

Canvas: RoutineCanvas (ReactFlow) replaces the CSS routine-diagram at
all three call sites — TriggerNode and OutcomeNode join the ActionNode
vocabulary, three left-to-right bands, flow-spine ids pass through
untouched so run overlays can key on entry ids later. ActionNode grew an
invisible left side-in handle; the outcome edge reuses loop-out.
routine-diagram.tsx deleted, no fallback.

Designer in place: clicking a routine's flow opens FlowGraphDetail
EMBEDDED in the Plan tab (?flow= param, back link) — a Space user is
never ejected to /admin/engenty. Editing is prompting, per ruling — no
manual node editor: a permanent "Describe a change" button opens the
repair dialog, and the repair lane accepts zero issues + an instruction
as an EDIT round (brief carries the previous graph, acceptance = changed
and still valid, result is the next draft; a human still publishes).

Detail + edit sections: instructions render truncated with a fade and a
hover/focus expand pill; a Triggers section lists the wake sources under
the canvas from the same routineTriggers() derivation; the edit form is
re-sectioned to mirror the view (Anweisungen / Ablauf / Auslöser /
Ergebnis) and instructions are edited in the tiptap markdown editor.

commits.message:
feat(ai): copilot and coordinator can see, run, and author flows

Closes the three gaps found auditing what the two orchestrating agents
can actually do with agents, routines, connections and flows.

flows_list (new): the catalog read that was missing. invoke_flow runs a
flow BY ID and flow_graph_propose writes one, but nothing turned a name
into an id — so "use the invoicing flow" had no path, and a writer blind
to the catalog re-proposes what exists. Read-only: ids, names, status,
and `runnable` meaning exactly what invoke_flow enforces at dispatch
(published version AND active definition). The graph body is
deliberately not returned; describing a change is how a flow is edited.

flow_graph_propose is DECLARED now, reversing the earlier hold-back. The
objection was that authoring mid-conversation puts the model on the
authoring side of the publish gate. It does not: the tool saves an
unapproved version and publishing stays a human-only route — the same
shape as agent_propose, which both agents already declare on exactly
that reasoning. The review lives on the canvas, which now opens inside
the Space and takes changes as prose.

The coordinator gains all three flow verbs (it had none — it is the
surface where "every morning, the same way" gets said), and its skill
gains Step 5b: repeating work becomes a ROUTINE with an owner that is
never a live chat agent, and fixed-step work targets a FLOW. The
copilot's work-routing skill gains the matching Flows section.

Live-verified: both agents called flows_list and returned the real
catalog with correct runnable flags.

commits.message:
fix(routines): promote 500, edit mode as the view, flows authored in place

Three things reported as broken, all real.

"In Flow umwandeln" was DEAD — a 500 the UI swallowed. Promote resolves a
tenant-unique flow name by falling back from "<name>" to
"<name> (ENG-49)", and that fallback was a SINGLE attempt: promoting the
same routine twice left both names taken, the second insert violated the
unique index, and the route answered 500 while the button rendered
nothing at all. The fallback now counts ("(ENG-49 2)", "(ENG-49 3)", …),
retries ONLY a name collision (a storage outage must not disappear
behind nine renames), and answers a plain 409 when every candidate is
taken. The UI surfaces both outcomes: failures print, and a success
opens the flow it just created.

Edit mode now IS the view with the fields unlocked. The state row stays,
the title and description are the heading and subtitle rather than two
labelled inputs above them, and Anweisungen / Ablauf / Auslöser /
Ergebnis are the same four sections in the same order and the same card
chrome. Switching between reading and editing no longer reshuffles the
page.

Instructions are edited as BLOCKS — the RichEditor the instruction files
already use (headings, lists, slash menu, drag handles) instead of a
plain surface that gave no sign it was anything but a text box.

Authoring a flow for a routine no longer dead-ends: the Ablauf section
offers "Create a flow" (the same describe-it dialog) and "Edit this
flow", both opening in place through the host's onOpenFlow — never a
bounce to the admin area.

release-timed and closes with the next release, per

commits.message:
refactor(ai-ui)!: one list, one name — Actions

Matthias's model, stated plainly: an Action holds the input parameters and
is what a button, a slash command, a routine or an agent calls. Its steps
are one agent turn or a whole graph. "Flow" describes the SHAPE of those
steps — it is not a second species, so it must not be a second list, a
second name or a second URL space. An Action can have a complex flow.

The schema already said so: flow_graph.context_type is the binding,
flow_graph_version.input_schema the parameters, allowed_tools the
narrowing — every runnable carries all three. The only columns that
differ are module_id / source_action_id, i.e. WHO SHIPS IT.

So:
- The catalog is Actions, at /admin/engenty/actions. One list, unchanged
  contents — no split by provenance, which was an earlier wrong turn.
- /admin/engenty/actions/:id is the one detail address. It takes either id
  the catalog can produce — a declared ACTION.md id or a stored graph uuid
  — and ActionDetailRouter picks the declaration view or the steps view.
  buildActionFlowDetailPath now points into that space, so every caller
  (routine canvas included) converges on one path.
- Nav, sub-tab, overview cards and search copy all say Actions.
- The row chip stops saying "Action" (everything is one) and says
  provenance instead: Modul / Eigene.

Also fixes a number that never matched its list: the German overview card
interpolated only {{live}} and {{draft}}, silently dropping the 9 declared
actions, so it read "2 live · 1 im Entwurf" beside a list of 12. Both
locales now show total · live · draft · declared.

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): unify the action detail screen; count readiness, not plumbing

ONE screen for one thing. An Action's declaration and the workflow it runs
are two views of the same Action, so the steps are now a tab on the action's
own page (Ansicht · Schritte · Code) instead of a separate destination. A
module action nobody has pressed has no compiled graph yet — compile-on-use
plumbing — so the tab offers "Schritte anzeigen" and compiles on demand
rather than reporting an internal state.

That same plumbing was leaking into the overview card, which read
"12 Actions · 2 live · 1 Entwurf · 9 deklariert" — three numbers nobody can
act on. "Declared" only ever meant "no graph row yet" and those actions run
perfectly; "live" only meant "happens to have been compiled already". The
question a person actually has is whether it can run, so counts gain
`ready = live + declared` and the card reads "12 Actions · 11 bereit ·
1 Entwurf". The row chip says Bereit for both states, and the version chip
(v1) still shows where the difference is real.

commits.message:
feat(ai): a graph node may ask for approval mid-run

Matthias's governance ruling, 2026-08-24. Until now a specialist node ran
with the delegate default `approvalPolicy: "deny"` — it could not perform a
gated operation at all, because run-specialist.ts held that "what needs a
human is visible on the canvas, not buried in an agent's judgment". That
rule is what kept an instruction routine (whose agent has always been
allowed to ask, and whose task parks for a human) from being expressible as
a one-node graph.

The node can now ask — but only when the RUN says so, never by graph
authorship: the policy rides the run context (`approvalPolicy`), absent
means `deny`, and an unknown value fails closed to `deny`, so every
already-published graph keeps the original behaviour untouched.

With "request" the node collects what its agent was refused
(`onApprovalRequired`) and SUSPENDS the graph run carrying those calls —
the same suspend/resume seam `approval_gate` uses, so the inbox card and a
cold restart both work. On resume the approved calls ride `resumeData` into
the delegated run, which replays them once before the model gets a turn;
Mastra clears the suspend payload atomically when a resume claims the run,
which is what makes the replay single-use.

Two things the tests caught, both fixed here rather than asserted around:
- the node suspended without DECLARING suspendSchema/resumeSchema, and
  Mastra validates both — the same trap that has bitten this codebase twice;
- a second, bare ask for the same operation OVERWROTE the first, throwing
  away the concrete arguments that let an approval replay the exact call.
  Requests now merge, richest wins.

Next: route instruction routines through this as a one-node graph, so
every runnable is a Mastra workflow.

commits.message:
fix(ai): a graph node inside a task gets the task's tools

Found while unifying the lanes, and it is a live bug rather than a
refactor: a FLOW routine's agent node was MUTE. `run_specialist` passed no
extraTools, so a specialist inside a graph could not comment on the task or
ask the human anything — while an instruction routine's agent always could.
Same run, same task, same standing work; the only difference was which lane
built the run. `report_mode` and mid-run questions therefore silently did
nothing for every flow-target routine.

The Task now travels in the graph run context (`taskId`, written by the
flow lane from `env.task_id`), and a specialist node mounts
`createTaskSelfTools` from it — with TASK_SELF_TOOLS_GUIDANCE appended to
the brief, because a tool the agent is not told about is a tool it does not
use. No task in the context (a button press, an agent call) mounts nothing:
there is no task to speak on.

A question parks the run, the same way an approval does — both mean "a
human is needed" — carrying `{kind: "question", payload: {question}}` on
the suspend the node already declares.

Verified: 1574 apps/ai tests green, and the primitives barrel still
initialises with real imports (this neighbourhood has a documented
module-init cycle hazard, and the node now reaches into the task tools).

With this the two lanes differ only in who assembles the run, not in what
the agent may do — the prerequisite for routing instruction routines
through a one-node graph.

Updated `ModuleSecondaryNavColumnShell` and `ModuleSecondaryNavPanel` to improve footer behavior. Added support for a sticky footer that prevents content from being obscured during scrolling. Introduced a new prop `footerSurfaceClassName` to ensure the footer paints the column's surface correctly. commits.message:
fix(ai): a run that cannot start says so instead of reporting "queued"

`invoke_flow` answered `status: "queued"` for a run that had already
failed: dispatch is fire-and-forget by design, so the graph's own input
schema only rejected the call inside the background run. Live on
2026-08-24 the copilot passed that on to the user as "waiting" while
two runs had failed seconds in on a missing `connection_id`.

Input the graph requires and the caller does not carry is now checked
before anything is registered, in `dispatchPublishedActionRun` — the one
way into a published graph outside a Task, so the press, the slash
command, the canvas Run button and the tool all get it. HTTP answers 400
naming the fields; `invoke_flow` answers `failed` with the same names, so
the next call can carry them. No failed audit row for a call that could
never have worked.

Two more places the same mistake was invisible:

- a routine could target a flow with no published version, or one needing
  input a schedule never supplies (a schedule passes only the static
  `flow_input`). Both are refused at write time now — a routine that
  cannot fire is not a routine, and the person creating it is right there.
- `flows_list` reported `runnable: true` for a flow that needed an
  undeclared `connection_id`. It now reports `required_input`.

commits.message:
fix(copilot): a recurring job gets an agent and a routine, not a lone flow

Asked to "create an agent" for a pasted use-case, the copilot proposed a
FLOW and stopped: no `agent_propose`, no `triggers_create`. Verified in
the DB — no trigger row, no task row, and no such call in the thread. In
a Space that leaves nothing anyone can open, own or manage, and nothing
that ever runs.

The rule lived only in the `work-routing` skill, which that run never
loaded (no `skill` call at all). A skill's `allowed-tools` is
documentation, not a runtime grant, so the tool cannot be gated behind
the playbook. It goes where it cannot be skipped instead:

- AGENTS.md, always loaded, names the shape that misfired — a pasted
  use-case describing an agent's work — and answers it: hire, then one
  routine. A Flow is a body a routine can use, never the deliverable.
- `flow_graph_propose` now REQUIRES `run_by`. Naming the caller is the
  point: `run_by: "routine"` answers that the hire and the routine are
  still missing, and the note names any input every call must carry.
- work-routing no longer offers "fixed steps → a Flow" as a peer lane.
  Judgement inside a cycle argues FOR the instruction routine.

Also fixed: AGENTS.md still described a "Task template plus Trigger"
(task_templates was dropped), and gained two rules the same run broke —
never report a schedule or run state no tool returned, and never click
Publish or Approve on the user's behalf.

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): open a run from the Runs tab, and date the ones that predate the hire

A run row said "succeeded" or "failed" and that was the end of it. Rows
are buttons now: the detail opens IN the tab — back button on top, state
in `?run=<id>` so browser back and reload land where you were — with the
run's header (trigger, finished, duration, tokens, error) and the event
timeline. The timeline keeps the events that carry a fact and drops the
AG-UI envelope: Started / Called <tool> / Result / Error, not
TEXT_MESSAGE_START and a hundred TOOL_CALL_ARGS deltas.

The second half answers "why are old runs attached to a fresh agent?".
They are keyed by the agent KEY, which outlives any one registry row, so
re-hiring a key inherits the work done under it. That is real history and
hiding it would lose it on every rehire — `/ai/v1/runs` now returns
`agent_registered_at` and the list marks the boundary instead.

commits.message:
fix(ai): a hired specialist keeps the catalog floor whatever it declares

An "Inbox Contact Importer" hired with six module OPERATION ids ran with
no `engenty_tool_execute` and reported it had no interface: no threads
read, no contacts created. Naming narrower tools REPLACED the catalog
floor, and the catalog is the only path to module work.

Approvals are the boundary, not `tool_ids` (Matthias's call) — the
catalog reaches only what the Space allows and each gated operation still
asks. So the floor is unioned in and never lost. Applied at assembly, not
only at hire: flooring the payload alone would leave every existing row
broken. Unioned BEFORE the allow-list filter, so an action's guardrail
can still narrow a node deliberately.

The go-live gate is unchanged and pinned by a test: eligibility still
reads the REQUESTED ids, so naming extras still routes through a human,
and the decision card still shows what the model asked for rather than
three tools nobody chose. (The gate never leaked here — six operation ids
made this hire ineligible, and it went live because a human approved it.)

`POST /ai/registry/agents` now rejects ids the registry cannot resolve,
naming them: module operations are reached THROUGH the catalog and
pre-approved via approval grants; they are not tools.

commits.message:
fix(connections): grant an account to the agent id an agent actually has

`connections_agent_grant_set` demanded `agent_id` as a uuid — the
core.agents principal — but nothing hands an agent that uuid:
`registry_agents_list` returns the key. So the copilot passed
`contacts.inbox-importer`, the only id it has, and the operation was
uncallable from chat.

Both grant operations take either form now and resolve the key through
`core.agents.name` on the service handle (platform data, no `scope_id`,
so foreignSelect does not apply). The stored row still keys on the
principal uuid — the same identity `x-engenty-agent-id` carries at run
time, which is what makes the grant match. An unknown agent is a 404
pointing at registry_agents_list, not a 500.

Live: granting by key wrote the grant on the right uuid, the list filter
accepts the key, and a bogus key 404s.

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): a run's timeline shows the call, its arguments and its answer

Three identical "Called skill" rows with a loose result below them. The
run had loaded three DIFFERENT skills — contacts-email-extraction,
inbox-triage, contacts-search — but the name lives in TOOL_CALL_ARGS and
the answer in TOOL_CALL_RESULT, tied to the call only by `toolCallId`.
Rendered event-by-event, the arguments were dropped and the results were
orphaned.

`buildRunTimeline` folds the stream back into what happened: one row per
call, arguments joined from their chunks, result attached and expandable.
`_background` is stripped — it rides on every call and is transport
config, never what was asked. The row is one line with the full value on
hover; a `contacts_list` call carries 200 characters of arguments and was
running off the right edge.

commits.message:
feat(ai): record how a run actually started, instead of calling everything a message

`ai.agent_run` never recorded its trigger, so the run API filled the field
with the constant "message". Every run in an agent's Runs tab claimed a
person had typed something — including the ones a schedule fired at 07:00
with nobody watching. That is the one question the tab exists to answer.

The column is nullable on purpose: rows written before it cannot be
attributed after the fact, and inventing "message" for them is the bug
being fixed. The reader shows an unrecorded trigger as unknown.

Each lane now states what it knows, because each one does know:
  · chat (session + conversation run) — message
  · a delegated child run (graph node, message_agent) — direct
  · the flow designer drafting a graph — direct
  · a press / slash command / API dispatch — already carried by
    dispatchPublishedActionRun, now passed on to the run record
  · a routine fire — the trigger's own kind IS the answer, mapped in the
    tasks module (schedule → cron, event → hook, manual → button) and
    carried on the dispatch envelope through checkout

Callers that genuinely cannot say (core's own dispatchTaskIfReady sites)
pass nothing and the run records no trigger.

Live: a chat turn wrote `trigger = message`; older rows stayed null and
the header reads "unbekannt".

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): show what was asked above the run

A run's header said when it ran and how long it took, but not what it was
for — the reader had to infer the job from the tool calls underneath.

The prompt is already in the run's own event stream, just not in one
piece: a `role: "user"` TEXT_MESSAGE_START, then content deltas that
carry no role of their own, then an END. `readRunPrompt` remembers the
role across that span and joins the deltas.

Null for a run nobody typed into — a routine's brief reaches the model
another way — and the block is then absent rather than empty.

commits.message:
fix(ai): a hire for recurring work is told the routine is still owed

Asked again for the Import-contacts agent, the copilot got the hire right
this time — and then stopped. It announced the agent, navigated to its
page, and said the trigger action "was not available here". It never
searched for one: `triggers_create` is in the catalog, among 378
operations the caller could reach.

The guidance said hire-then-routine, but the last thing the model read
said otherwise. `agent_propose` answered:

  "The agent is active and mounted — message it with message_agent now."
  "The user approved this hire — you can assign tasks to it now."

Both point away from the routine, and the second one is the note that
came back after the approval card — exactly where this run stopped.

`for_work` is now required on the call (routine | tasks | chat), same
shape as `run_by` on flow_graph_propose: naming the purpose is what makes
the answer specific. A routine hire is told, by id, that it has NO
standing work yet and which call is still owed — and the purpose rides
the tool's own input, so it survives the approval suspend and the resumed
turn gets the same instruction.

Also: the resumed run recorded no trigger (my own gap from the previous
commit — a resume continues the person's turn, so it is `message`).

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: the Action is the word — no agent surface says "flow" anymore

Matthias's ruling: flows are a technical internality and must NOT be
exposed to any agent. The 2026-08-24 tool-id rename (ac5cb6294) went the
OPPOSITE way and put flow vocabulary directly into the models' mouths —
which is why the copilot talked to users about "Flows". Reversed and
settled:

- Tool ids: invoke_flow -> invoke_action, flow_graph_propose ->
  action_propose, flows_list -> actions_list. Schema fields follow
  (action_id; list returns `actions` rows). All model-facing prose,
  results and error messages say Action. Migration 20260824190000
  rewrites stored ai.engenty_ai_agents.tool_ids and also folds the
  pre-detour ids forward, so any installation lands right.
- Triggers wire surface: task.action_id / task.action_input on
  create/update, action_input on fire, standing_task.action_id /
  action_input / action_agent_keys on reads — mapped once in
  rowToStandingTask and the trigger services. The module_tasks COLUMNS
  keep their storage names; the wire never says flow. Error keys:
  triggers.actionNotPublished / actionNotFound / actionInputMissing /
  alreadyActionTarget.
- Agent guidance rewritten in Action vocabulary: work-routing SKILL.md
  ("Actions — a body, never the deliverable"), coordinator Step 5b,
  copilot AGENTS.md and tool-list comments.
- Deliberately still flow-named (internal only): ai.flow_graph storage,
  /ai/v1/flow-graphs, the action-graph: id prefix, internal identifiers.

apps/ai 1589 green, modules/tasks 449 green, migration applied and
verified against the dev stack (zero stale tool_ids rows).

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): one Action screen — sectioned detail, inline steps, honest list

An Action with a stored graph had a whole second UI: its own header,
version picker and Flow/Runs toggle on a separate designer page, while
the declared ACTION.md page had an unreachable Steps tab (the URL
builder could only encode view=code, so clicking Schritte bounced back
to Ansicht). Merged into ONE screen shape, styled like the agent
personnel file:

- Detail: sections instead of tabs — Identity (colored source/module
  pills + fact rows), Instructions (the rendered ACTION.md; the file
  chooser is gone — an Action carries exactly one instruction document,
  the files API returns [] by design), Inputs (schema table, only when
  fields exist), Steps (the canvas inline with versions, validity,
  describe-a-change and the runs view), and the run panel. No card in
  card; the spec card is decomposed into the sections.
- Steps auto-compile: opening the page prepares a missing graph
  silently (compile-on-use is plumbing, not a button). Concurrent
  ensure calls now share one request — React's dev double-mount raced
  two compiles and gave a fresh graph two identical versions.
- Routing: a list row is the ACTION — declared ids always open their
  own page; only canvas-authored Actions are addressed by graph uuid,
  and legacy uuid links to compiled ACTION.md graphs redirect to the
  declared address. The uuid page uses the same sectioned layout.
- List: columns are Action | Source | Status; the always-empty Subject
  column is gone (it stays a filter), and status is one colored-pill
  vocabulary — Ready (emerald) / Draft (amber) / Disabled — instead of
  "v1" pretending to be a state.
- Chrome: topbar and header blend into one surface, the topbar CTA
  (Publish / Run now) is primary, intro copy one step smaller.
- i18n: every remaining user-facing "Flow" string in en/de says Action.

Verified live end to end: list -> declared detail -> auto-compiled
steps, uuid redirect, error/retry state; ai-ui 1031 green.

commits.message:
fix(inbox): make agent-granted mailboxes visible to headless reads (CN.5)

A personal mailbox its owner granted to the acting agent vanished from
every inbox read in a headless run: inbox_accounts_list filtered on
sharing/owner (a service principal is neither), and the owner-visibility
arm hid all of the mailbox's threads the same way — so a routine hired to
scan the very account it was granted reported "no mailbox connected".
The connections EXECUTE path already applied the grant set; the inbox
READ path never adopted the rule.

- connections-sdk client gains listAgentGrantedConnectionIds (the
  core.agents principal uuid the grant rows store, from auth.agentId)
- inbox accounts/threads/thread-get/digest/chat reads ride an
  agent-aware repo whose visibility adds the granted connections' rows
- list_threads is recreated with p_granted_connection_ids uuid[]
  (null keeps the pre-grant behaviour; execute granted to service_role
  and engenty_server)

Only ever ADDS the granted accounts' rows; every other personal row
stays owner-only.

commits.message:
feat(ai)!: a routine is a job that produces runs, not a standing task

A daily standup is not one forever-task with a cron on it. Until now a
routine was a `module_tasks.triggers` row plus a "standing task" it woke on
every fire: the job's instructions lived in a work item, the run mutex was
that item's checkout column, and a board full of cards nobody could ever
finish was the price.

Three things the product had collapsed into one are now separate:

  - a Specialist is who you talk to,
  - a Routine is a job that runs (a row in `ai.routines`: an Action to run,
    or its own operating text, plus a wake source),
  - a Task is a work item.

Every execution is a Run. A routine fire, a button press, a chat turn and
"work this task" are different triggers of a run, not different systems —
they share one dispatcher, one run index and one version-pinning rule.
Overlap is decided on the run, so a fire is skipped while the previous run
is still active instead of parking a work item in `in_review`. A task can be
the SUBJECT of a run; completing the run does not silently complete it.

Routines leave `@engenty/tasks` — they are agent runtime, not a CRM object.
`module_tasks.triggers` and the task runtime columns are dropped;
`task_runs` stays, because it is the record of runs against a work item.

Event routines need one edge the in-process bus cannot cross on its own:
apps/core subscribes and forwards to `POST /ai/v1/routines/events`, and an
inbound webhook lands on `/ai/v1/routines/hooks/:id/:secret`.

The knowledge half ships in the same commit, because text is the part that
bites twice — an agent greps the repo, finds a confident sentence describing
the old model, and rebuilds it. Docs, skills, prompts, tool descriptions,
ROUTINE.md declarations and i18n are rewritten, and
`scripts/check-work-vocabulary.mjs` fails CI if the retired vocabulary comes
back. `docs/content/dev/work-model.md` is the one canonical glossary.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): make a routine fire actually reach its Space and its desk

Five bugs found by running the loop for real — hire a specialist, give it a
routine, fire it — none of which the unit tests could see, because each one
lives in a seam the old model got for free from the standing task.

A routine run is unattended: nobody typed it. That has consequences the task
lane used to absorb.

  - Its thread has no owner. Stamping the human who configured the routine
    made it a private chat that the service principal executing the run was
    then refused from ("a thread can only be used by the resource that owns
    it"), and every fire died in 200ms.
  - Its memory belongs to the Space, not to whoever ran it. `isSharedMastraRoom`
    knew that for task-bound threads only; routines used to qualify through
    their standing task, so the rule now has its own branch.
  - It resolves its Space as the human who configured it while EXECUTING as
    the service. Core's private-Space exemption was task-bound for the same
    historical reason — a routine names itself instead, and core looks the
    Space up from the routine row, so a forged id unlocks nothing.
  - Without that, `engenty_tools_discover` withheld every module result and the
    run "succeeded" having read nothing — the worst failure shape there is,
    because it looks like success.
  - Its thread is filed under the compiled action (`action-graph:<id>`), which
    is what pins the version, so the desk feed listed it under nobody. The run
    now carries the owning specialist and the routine's name for the desk, and
    the feed includes an agent's unattended run threads alongside the caller's
    own conversations.

Live-verified end to end: Copilot hires `contacts.daily-summary`, creates
"Daily New Contacts Summary" (0 7 * * *, Europe/Vienna), scheduler-sync links
the Mastra schedule, and a fire discovers Contacts, calls `contacts_list` and
renders 24 new contacts. Zero tasks created, `owner_task_id` null throughout.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): say what the specialist is doing while a routine runs

A routine fire runs in its own unattended thread, so the chat a person
has open showed nothing at all while the agent worked — the fire only
became visible once it was over and its thread turned up in the feed.
The only reason to trust an agent that works on a schedule is seeing it
work, so the lane now reports the fire while it happens: the routine's
name, its tool calls as they land, and the result or the error at the
end. It reads the RUN's outcome, not the thread's status, so a fire that
failed says so.

- `useAgentRoutineActivity` finds the newest in-flight run nobody typed
  (`trigger !== "message"`), names the routine from the run thread, and
  HOLDS it through its terminal state — a run leaves the in-flight list
  at exactly the moment the person needs to be told how it went.
  Discovery is a poll on purpose: nothing pushes "a routine started" to
  the browser, and once a run is found its SSE stream carries the rest.
- `AgentDeskRunActivity` rides that stream through the existing
  `ActionRunStatus`, so steps, cancel, error and the final markdown come
  from the same component the Actions surface uses. It stands down while
  the lane is already bound to that fire's thread rather than narrating
  the transcript twice.
- `CopilotPanelContent` gained a `transcriptFooter` slot for it.

Fixes a bug this uncovered: leaving a desk tab drops the open
conversation from the URL so you return to "the newest thread", and
before routines had threads that always meant "the newest chat". After
the cutover it could mean the machine's last run — a blank screen when
that fire had written nothing yet. Desk conversations now carry
`metadata.routine_id` and the Chat default skips them. Fires stay
reachable from the feed and from the card.

Live-verified on a scheduled tick: starting → six web_search steps →
"Routine finished" with the quotes table, in a chat nobody had touched.

commits.message:
fix(ai): type the author-less thread honestly, and answer what it means

`ThreadRow.created_by_user_id` was typed `string` while the routines
cutover writes NULL there on purpose: an unattended thread — a routine
fire, a task run — has no human author, and stamping one would make its
transcript a private chat the service principal executing the run is
then refused from. The lie sat in exactly the area this cutover has
broken three times, and it is why nothing warned about the author-less
case in the listing path, the access path, or the default-selection one.

Widening it forced real answers rather than `??` fallbacks:

- `sessionToThread` is the row-only FALLBACK for memory calls that pass
  no resourceId; the run path always passes one and `getThreadById`
  overrides with it, so `createEngentyMastraResourceId` stays the
  authority. The fallback now takes the same two steps for the case a
  row can decide — no author means a shared room, so Space then thread —
  instead of emitting the author verbatim, which for those threads is a
  `null` Mastra's own `resourceId: string` forbids. An authored thread
  still answers with its author: telling a shared specialist room from a
  personal one needs the agent's scope, which a row does not carry.
- Chat search: null is CORRECT and means the transcript reaches nobody.
  This source declares `visibility: "user"`, whose rule in
  `search.query_chunks` is `owner_user_id = p_user_id` — never true of
  NULL — so a fire's transcript is indexed and returned to no one. Typed
  honestly and documented; making fires findable needs `space_id` on the
  document and a visibility decision, which is not this change.
- Guest auth: the `chatbot.*` fallback resolver minted a scope straight
  from the thread's author with no null check. The grant means "this
  guest may act as the person whose thread this is"; with no such person
  there is nobody to act as, so it falls through to the original denial
  instead of handing a null `userId` to every DAL filter.

fix(ai): type the author-less thread honestly, and answer what it means

`ThreadRow.created_by_user_id` was typed `string` while the routines
cutover writes NULL there on purpose: an unattended thread — a routine
fire, a task run — has no human author, and stamping one would make its
transcript a private chat the service principal executing the run is
then refused from. The lie sat in exactly the area this cutover has
broken three times, and it is why nothing warned about the author-less
case in the listing path, the access path, or the default-selection one.

Widening it forced real answers rather than `??` fallbacks:

- `sessionToThread` is the row-only FALLBACK for memory calls that pass
  no resourceId; the run path always passes one and `getThreadById`
  overrides with it, so `createEngentyMastraResourceId` stays the
  authority. The fallback now takes the same two steps for the case a
  row can decide — no author means a shared room, so Space then thread —
  instead of emitting the author verbatim, which for those threads is a
  `null` Mastra's own `resourceId: string` forbids. An authored thread
  still answers with its author: telling a shared specialist room from a
  personal one needs the agent's scope, which a row does not carry.
- Chat search: null is CORRECT and means the transcript reaches nobody.
  This source declares `visibility: "user"`, whose rule in
  `search.query_chunks` is `owner_user_id = p_user_id` — never true of
  NULL — so a fire's transcript is indexed and returned to no one. Typed
  honestly and documented; making fires findable needs `space_id` on the
  document and a visibility decision, which is not this change.
- Guest auth: the `chatbot.*` fallback resolver minted a scope straight
  from the thread's author with no null check. The grant means "this
  guest may act as the person whose thread this is"; with no such person
  there is nobody to act as, so it falls through to the original denial
  instead of handing a null `userId` to every DAL filter.

rows and the desk reads them. That surfaced the Activity page rendering
`shortActivityId(null)` in its User column (now "Unattended") and owner
search throwing on an author-less row.

commits.message:
test(ui): give apps/ui its own vitest project so `@/` resolves

SpaceHomeComposer.test.tsx never ran. It failed to LOAD — the component
imports `@/components/spaces/SpaceComposerControls` and the root vitest
config has no `@` alias — and vitest reports that as "1 failed | 0 tests",
which reads as noise rather than as an untested component.

`@` is a per-app convention, not a workspace one: it means `apps/ui/src`
here and the app root in apps/docs, and both sit under the root runner's
`apps/**` globs. A single `@` in the root config would therefore make the
first docs test that imports one resolve silently into apps/ui. apps/manage
already has its own project for exactly this reason.

The new config EXTENDS the root one rather than restating it, so the forks
pool, the --localstorage-file execArgv, the shared env setup, the repo-root
chdir and the ai-core/plugin-sdk source aliases cannot drift. `include` and
`exclude` are replaced rather than merged: mergeConfig concatenates arrays,
and that was already load-bearing — apps/ui/scripts/ exists, and its test
was being collected only because the root's `scripts/**` glob re-anchored
onto it (33 files silently became 32 until it was listed on purpose).

Also marks IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT in the revived test: without it React
does not treat act() as act and gives no guarantee effects have flushed, so
the assertions could read state the render had not committed.

apps/ui: 33 files / 255 tests green. Root run: 1115 passed, 0 failed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): resolve every kind of Mastra resource id to its threads

Resource-scoped observation lists the resource's threads on every turn, and
the storage forwarded that resourceId straight into the participant query.
Only a personal room's resource is a `thread_participant.principal_id`:

- the shared observational-memory key is a synthetic `tenant:…:agent:…:user:…`
  composite, which the uuid column rejected outright — `22P02` took down the
  whole output-processor workflow, so shared observations never recorded
  anything for a personal-scope agent;
- a shared room's resource is the Space id (or, with no Space, the thread id),
  which passed the cast and then quietly matched nobody.

The composite is now parsed back to its audience and read through the owner or
the room, filtered to the agent it names so observations cannot reach across
agents or tenants; a Space or thread resource resolves the same way it is
minted. The personal path still costs one query.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): give headless runs a real computer, and bound the host

An agent that can write and run a script when a person is watching, and
cannot when a schedule fires it, is not the same agent. Task jobs and
routine fires built no workspace at all — they got two flat storage tools
where a chat of the same agent got its mounts, its skills and its sandbox.
Both lanes now build the workspace from the same declaration, through one
shared resolver.

That only holds if the host survives it, so the sandbox stops being
unbounded: every container gets memory, CPU, PID and capability ceilings, a
tmpfs for its scratch, and no network unless its agent asked for one.
Admission is capped per host, per tenant and per space, so one busy tenant
cannot take every slot. Staging dirs and package caches are reaped on TTL
and on a byte budget, with a bind-aware in-use check.

Per-fire approval was the wrong mechanism for scheduled work — at 03:00
there is nobody to answer, so a fire that asks is a fire that does nothing.
A routine's standing grants now reach its runs, and the sandbox gate reads
them, so an approval can actually be spent instead of re-asking forever.

- Space-rooted sandbox scratch and caches; task scope keys carry tenant and
  space (a task identifier is unique per tenant, not globally)
- `/routine` mount so successive fires share a folder; `/space` added
  alongside `/shared` rather than renaming it
- Sandbox image ships node + npm next to bun, jq, and a non-root user;
  NODE_PATH so a global `require("zod")` resolves on both runtimes
- Egress proxy with a default-deny allowlist for the runs that fetch
- Compute leases metered as `compute_ms` on `ai.usage_event`
- Prefix workspace file tools deleted — the task lane was their only caller

Verified against a live daemon: limits and network land on the container,
the allowlist admits pypi and refuses the rest, a warm cache halves an
install, and Code Mode round-trips with no network.

commits.message:
fix(ai): give each agent in a thread its own sandbox container

A session sandbox was keyed by thread alone, so the copilot and the
`engenty.cli` sub-agent it delegates to resolved to one container. A
container keeps the HostConfig of whoever created it first, so the CLI
agent's `network: "egress"` silently became the copilot's `none` — its
sandbox had no network at all, and a package install there would have
failed for a reason nothing reported.

The session identity is now (thread, agent). Keying by the PARENT thread
still does what it was for — one container across repeated delegations in a
conversation — it just stops that container being handed to a different
agent. The storage prefix carries the agent too: separate containers sharing
one staging dir would be worse than the original bug.

`destroySessionLifecycleSandbox` derived a single id from the thread, so
with two containers per thread a closed conversation would have left the
sub-agent's running. It looks them up by label now and destroys every
session container for the thread.

Containers created before this parse fine but no longer resolve to a thread,
so a close cannot target them; the age sweep clears whatever a deploy finds
on the host.

Verified in a live chat: two containers, `-engenty.cli` on bridge and
`-engenty.copilot` on none, and curl to pypi.org from the CLI sandbox
returns 200 where it previously had no network.

commits.message:
feat(ai): give registered specialists a computer, not just files

A specialist created through `agent_propose` could never run a line of
code. `ai.engenty_ai_agents` has no workspace column, so every registered
agent's declaration comes from one default in `mapAgentRow` — and that
default had files and no sandbox. In chat and in a routine alike, the
tool simply was not there.

That is the gap the compute plan's specialist-parity rule names: a
specialist is expected to pull data, transform it and write a script, and
doing that through tool calls alone is the thing it exists not to have to
do. The default now carries a sandbox.

Cheap to hand out, because the container is lazy: it is created when a
command is actually run, so a specialist that never runs one never costs
one. `run` lifecycle keeps it to the run that asked for it. Approval is
required and the network is off — a specialist that needs either gets it
from its routine's standing grants, not from this default.

Verified live: `contacts.daily-summary` called execute_command (a tool it
did not previously have), the call suspended on the approval gate with no
grant, and its container came up as `engenty-run-<id>` with Net=none,
Mem=512M, User=sandbox.

commits.message:
feat(ai): let a registered specialist declare its network tier

A specialist that installs a package or calls an API needs the wire, and
had no way to ask for it: `ai.engenty_ai_agents` carries no workspace
declaration, so every registered agent got one hardcoded default and the
network tier was always `none`. The sandbox arrived last commit; this is
the half that lets an agent say what it needs from it.

A `sandbox` jsonb column holds the sandbox slice of the declaration and is
merged over the default at read time, so a row that says nothing keeps the
safe default and a row that says `network: "egress"` gets the wire.

Only the sandbox slice. The preset — which mounts an agent gets — stays
derived from `agent_scope`, because that is platform policy about what an
agent may see rather than a request an agent makes about itself.

`requireApproval` is deliberately NOT read from the row. An agent describes
itself through `agent_propose`, and a description that could clear its own
approval gate would make unattended command execution a matter of writing
it down. That comes from a grant against a routine, decided per job by a
person, and the clamp is asserted in a test.

Verified live on the dev tenant: two specialists, one declaring `egress`
and one not, produced containers on `bridge` and `none` respectively.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): space computer, one worker default, and the space switch

The space computer (PLAN-space-computer.md): a fourth sandbox lifecycle
`space` — one long-lived container per space, idle-stopped (docker stop
keeps installed programs; the next command wakes it), Reset removes the
container while the bind-mounted drive survives. Commands serialize per
machine; a run holds an admission slot only while it uses the machine. The
machine's $HOME is a drive bind, so dotfiles and venvs survive stop AND
Reset. Ships with the engenty-browser service (own image, socat CDP face,
profile bind for logged-in sessions) and Stop/Reset/queue rows in Computers.

Personal spaces act with their owner's connections (PLAN-space-computer §2):
resolveVerifiedSpaceOwnerForRun opens the personal-sharing clamp only for a
non-user principal whose routine is stored as bound to exactly that space;
autonomy ceilings, mount levels and approval asks all keep applying. Also
closes the executor parity hole (mount narrowing + level on execute).

Compute per agent class (PLAN-agent-computers.md P0-P3): the per-agent
placement column/UI is removed; WORKER_SANDBOX_DEFAULT applies at the
composite-registry read seam so module and hired agents share ONE default
(gated shell + Code Mode), with explicit opt-outs on Coordinator and Remote.
En route this fixed the seed pipeline silently dropping every module agent's
workspace declaration. Placement is one space-level switch
(spaces.computer_enabled) riding the surface; run-lifecycle sandboxes route
to the machine, session/task declarations keep their own containers. Queue
depth is visible per machine and waits are logged; DEPLOY.md documents the
operator knobs. Measured: the workspace tool set costs 17.2KB per model
call (~32% of an inbox.assist request) — mitigation lanes recorded.

commits.message:
feat(ai): space computer always on + shared-room thread ownership fix

The space computer switch is gone: run-lifecycle sandboxes always target
the space machine when a space resolves (drop migration for
core.spaces.computer_enabled; resolveRunSandboxLifecycle keeps only
declared + spaceResolved; computerEnabled off surface/DAL/routes/clients;
the Computer card is informational).

Shared-room runs no longer die on Mastra's thread-ownership assert: the
session memory storage now answers the Space key for the run's own
shared-room thread when Mastra fetches it without a resourceId, mirroring
createEngentyMastraResourceId — a shared child thread carries both
created_by_user_id and space_id, and the row alone cannot tell it from a
personal space-bound thread. This unblocks message_agent to hired
(shared-scope) agents in a space.

commits.message:
feat(ai): space engenty roster in the prompt + harmony leak scrub

The runtime space block now renders the mounted Engentys with registry
name and description (address-by-id roster) instead of bare ids — users
say display names, and an id-only list made the model ask what a name it
was never shown refers to. Identities come from the same endpoint the
registry_agents_list tool calls; any failure degrades to the id line.

Thread messages are scrubbed of leaked Harmony channel markup at the DAL
seam, on write and on read: a small Harmony model can emit its tool
traffic into the text channel and the serving side passes it through raw;
persisted, it rides the next prompt as history and every turn degrades
further. The scrub keeps only the final channel's content (token form and
the fully degraded glued `assistantfinal` form) and leaves user rows
verbatim.

commits.message:
feat(ai): mounted engentys — actions are workflows, triggers are bindings

An Action is now a verbatim Mastra DynamicWorkflowGraph stored in
ai.flow_graph with immutable versions, rehydrated at dispatch. Modules
ship ai/workflows/<id>.workflow.json; the boot reconcile materializes
them per tenant. There is no compile step and no prose lane.

A trigger is a binding on the specialist: ai.routines names a
workflow_id, never instructions. Schedule bindings fan out per space
that mounts the declaring module, and unmounting disables them.

Agents declare what they are — kind, interfaceRole, moduleId — instead
of being guessed from their id string, and mounting a module mounts its
agents. run_specialist refuses a specialist that is not mounted in the
run's Space; validation happens at install and save, never at fire.

Owner-scoped graphs: flow_graph.owner_agent_id null means library, and
publish-to-library copies with provenance. Discovery is the library plus
the caller's own.

Retired with no fallback: ACTION.md/ROUTINE.md loaders, compile-action,
ensure-action-flow, ensure-routine-action, ModuleActionCapability, the
routine prompt lane, routines.target_kind, agent-space-removal, and the
bundled-agents UI list. Three migrations truncate and reshape the
affected tables.

Also carries adjacent work that had not landed yet: the LLM call trace,
skill-gated tool visibility, the schema-compat and gateway strict-schema
patches, run outcome records, the space-setup skill, inbox space scope,
and space mount connection access.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): per-space internet access for the space computer

The space computer's network reach was an env var and nothing else:
`ENGENTY_SPACE_COMPUTER_NETWORK_TIER`, defaulting to `none`. Every space
on a host got the same answer, and the agents that most need to install a
package or call an API — the ones a schedule wakes — got the sealed one.

Default is now `egress`, overridable per space on
`core.spaces.computer_network_tier` (null inherits the host). Resolution is
space -> host env -> egress, in one function, so the container a run gets
and the "## Your computer" sentence in its prompt cannot disagree. The tier
rides the space surface, which is the call a headless run already makes to
learn its own space.

Still never per-agent: the machine is one per space and its HostConfig is
fixed by whichever run creates it, so an agent-level declaration would make
reach depend on run ordering.

Space settings grows a Security section — the former General card held only
visibility and approvals, so it already was one. Both inherit options now
name what they resolve to ("Tenant default - Manual"), from two new entries
on GET /ai/v1/settings/effective. The People description follows the
visibility switch: on an open space that roster gates nothing, and saying
"who can open this space" over it was flatly untrue.

commits.message:
feat(ai): the workspace timezone rides into every sandbox as TZ

A container boots on UTC, so an agent reading its own clock answered in
UTC and everything derived from it — "good evening", "due today", "this
morning's mail" — was off by the offset. The tenant setting is the only
place that knows better.

`ai.config.timezone` (IANA, null inherits UTC) is set on the Limits &
budgets tab of AI settings and read fresh on every container create. No
cache: the only caller is starting a container, which costs seconds, so
a settings round trip is free next to it — and a cache would need an
invalidation hook in apps/core, where the write actually happens.

A zone Intl rejects is stored as null. Docker ignores a bad TZ, so a
setting that looked saved and did nothing would be worse than an empty
one. A failed lookup never blocks a sandbox: a container on UTC is a
working container with a wrong clock, and no container is no work.

Adding the field also needed the two ai.config round trips in
ai-settings-api.ts, which rebuild the object field-by-field, and
configSignature in use-ai-settings.ts — hasChanges compares signature
strings, so a field missing there leaves the Save button disabled and
the control moves without saving anything.

Verified by falsification: same agent, same prompt, zone flipped to
Pacific/Kiritimati behind its back returned GMT+1400 (Line Islands
Time) — a different day of the week. Env is fixed at container create,
so a space computer keeps its old zone until Reset.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(notifications): core notification package, bell, streams

Notifications become a core package instead of a tasks-module inbox:
`packages/notifications` (kind: "package", mandatory) owns
`core.notifications` + delivery ledger + push subscriptions + streams/routes,
the service (audience ladder, class gate, dedupe), `/api/notifications/*`
on core and the host every module reaches as `server.notifications`.
apps/ai keeps `emitInboxNotification` as a thin adapter, so no producer
call site changed.

- Four classes (decision / alert / todo / update) derived from a
  registered kind table replace the two drifting kind sets; the badge and
  the lanes read `record.class`.
- One emit seam / one resolve seam bound to the run: graph gates and
  failures announce from `settleGraphRun`, delegate suspends from
  `delegate-run`, task dispatch/finalize resolve by subject. The per-
  component dismiss wiring in the tasks UI is gone.
- `packages/notifications-ui`: the bell (new `topbarEndSlot`),
  `/notifications` and `/s/:key/notifications`, the space card, realtime
  via postgres_changes, client channels (browser, desktop), a per-kind
  renderer registry (tasks contributes the tool_approval body). The tasks
  module drops its inbox page, sidebar row and app-bar badge.
- Channels are registrations: in_app/web_push/email built in, `remote`
  registered by engenty-remote; apps/ai and core each run the delivery
  loop for their own channels over a compare-and-swap ledger.
- Streams + routes (API, settings page, `notifications.manage`), the
  `notify` tool in every Engenty's catalog, saved views, team-chat cut
  over to the host (its queue + apps/ai consumer deleted).
- Per-user channel prefs (on/off/digest) and quiet hours applied at emit;
  profile settings section.
- plugin-sdk: `approval.requested`/`approval.decided` were missing from the
  events runtime's reserved core set, so the platform-wide approval event
  could neither be subscribed nor (silently) emitted.

Schema only — nothing is copied from the earlier Mastra-backed inbox.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>
