commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): desk header on the canvas, agent names instead of ids

Five things the desk got wrong, all visible on one screen.

The identity header was a white card band centred in the page while every
message sat in a narrower column, so the name never lined up with what it
named. It now draws on the page canvas, in the chat's own column — including
the lane the floating thread-context card reserves. That reserve was a number
the pane published as a CSS variable on its own root, which the header, a
sibling above that pane, could never see; it is a shared token now and the
header reads the mode from the store the pane already writes.

The header also flickered near the top of a transcript. It animates its
height over 200ms, and every frame of that animation resizes the chat's
viewport and fires a scroll event — which a single 16px threshold read as a
reason to toggle back. Two thresholds, a settle window longer than the
animation, and scroll anchoring off leave it unable to re-trigger itself.

A run hands the UI an agent ID, never a name, and the only answer was a
hardcoded map of two platform agents plus a title-cased id — which is how a
delegation to `inbox.overview` read as "Inbox.Overview", and why the id often
stood until something unrelated re-rendered. Names the app has actually
loaded now live in a registry that the space roster publishes into and that
the context box and both tool-call cards subscribe to. `message_agent` stores
the bare id when its own lookup misses at run time; a loaded name beats that.

The context box drew its group headings as full-width triggers that lit up
under the pointer. They are the space sidebar's headings now: a label, then a
chevron button right after it.

Who an agent reports to was in the mount rows and on no screen. It reads as
"Reports to <name>" under the mandate, on the roster row and the Desk header.

Also: `subscribePostgresChanges` gave every subscription its own channel
topic. `client.channel(topic)` returns an EXISTING channel when one is still
registered, and `.on("postgres_changes", …)` throws on a channel that has
joined — so a remount racing its own async removeChannel threw out of the
effect and took the component tree with it.

line came from a second grey system (`--sidebar-border`, neutral, L .85) next

  dark one step below the canvas. The Ember preset's `dark.sidebar` is empty so

  column header and the rail's first tile share one centre line; the rail's
  user-menu row and the column's Settings row are one lineless row and sit
  level.

  later `border-border/NN` sweep.

commits.message:
feat(connections-external): integrations.sh v3, guarded fetch, official MCP client

Update the external connector importer to the current integrations.sh schema,
route every outbound request through the SSRF guard, and replace the
hand-written MCP transport with the official v2 client. Scope stays OpenAPI +
MCP; GraphQL, CLI and a second registry are out.

Registry (v3). The registry publishes a service's surfaces in two views that
do not agree: /api/{domain}/surface carries the rich facts (slug, spec,
specAlternates, requiredHeaders, variables, transports, per-credential auth
mechanics) while /api/search carries a catalog summary that today is the only
place specOverrides appear — and for some domains the same spec is listed
under two different URLs. registry-source.ts re-derives one surface from both
views by exact URL match; nothing is matched fuzzily, so a correction
published against one spec URL is never applied to another. Import and preview
re-resolve this server-side from domain + source URL instead of trusting
client metadata.

Identity. The registry surface slug is the connector's identity: it seeds the
suggested id and tool prefix, is persisted, and a domain may import each
surface only once. Manual URLs stay possible and carry no slug.

Import decisions are now explicit rather than best effort. HTTP surfaces need
an OpenAPI spec; MCP surfaces need a supported remote transport (a declared
stdio-only server is blocked, an undeclared transport defaults to streamable
HTTP). Registry specOverrides are applied as RFC 6902 patches before
normalization and a patch that does not apply fails the import. Static
required headers are stored and forced onto every HTTP and MCP request;
env-sourced headers, URL variables and auth we cannot express block the import
with a reason. An MCP server with unknown auth is no longer imported as
anonymous.

SSRF. createGuardedFetch validates the host on every hop for any method —
web-ingest's safeFetchFollowingRedirects is GET/HEAD only and the MCP
transport POSTs and DELETEs. It is injected into the MCP SDK's fetch option
and wraps spec fetches and connector HTTP calls. Spec size is checked from
content-length and again while the body streams.

MCP. A small adapter over @modelcontextprotocol/client: streamable HTTP with
an SSE fallback for legacy endpoints, Connections-managed credentials as
request headers, and terminateSession() + close() in finally — the SDK's
close() alone leaves the server-side session behind.

Schema. Additive migration for registry_surface_slug, required_headers and
mcp_transport plus a unique (domain, surface) index. Existing connectors keep
their stored actions and auth config; there is no re-import and no backfill,
and records without the new fields still boot and execute.

Deps: add @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.0.0, @engenty/web-ingest and rfc6902;
bump @executor-js/plugin-openapi 1.5.29 → 1.6.7. Drop spec_snapshot_text from
the import intermediate — it was neither persisted nor read.

Tests run against recorded v3 fixtures; CI never calls integrations.sh.

specAlternates, requiredHeaders, variables, transports, per-credential auth
mechanics) while /api/search carries a catalog summary that today is the only
place specOverrides appear — and for some domains the same spec is listed
under two different URLs. registry-source.ts re-derives one surface from both
views by exact URL match; nothing is matched fuzzily, so a correction
published against one spec URL is never applied to another. Import and preview
re-resolve this server-side from domain + source URL instead of trusting
client metadata.

Identity. The registry surface slug is the connector's identity: it seeds the
suggested id and tool prefix, is persisted, and a domain may import each
surface only once. Manual URLs stay possible and carry no slug.

Import decisions are now explicit rather than best effort. HTTP surfaces need
an OpenAPI spec; MCP surfaces need a supported remote transport (a declared
stdio-only server is blocked, an undeclared transport defaults to streamable
HTTP). Registry specOverrides are applied as RFC 6902 patches before
normalization and a patch that does not apply fails the import. Static
required headers are stored and forced onto every HTTP and MCP request;
env-sourced headers, URL variables and auth we cannot express block the import
with a reason. An MCP server with unknown auth is no longer imported as
anonymous.

SSRF. createGuardedFetch validates the host on every hop for any method —
web-ingest's safeFetchFollowingRedirects is GET/HEAD only and the MCP
transport POSTs and DELETEs. It is injected into the MCP SDK's fetch option
and wraps spec fetches and connector HTTP calls. Spec size is checked from
content-length and again while the body streams.

MCP. A small adapter over @modelcontextprotocol/client: streamable HTTP with
an SSE fallback for legacy endpoints, Connections-managed credentials as
request headers, and terminateSession() + close() in finally — the SDK's
close() alone leaves the server-side session behind.

Schema. Additive migration for registry_surface_slug, required_headers and
mcp_transport plus a unique (domain, surface) index. Existing connectors keep
their stored actions and auth config; there is no re-import and no backfill,
and records without the new fields still boot and execute.

Deps: add @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.0.0, @engenty/web-ingest and rfc6902;
bump @executor-js/plugin-openapi 1.5.29 → 1.6.7. Drop spec_snapshot_text from
the import intermediate — it was neither persisted nor read.

Tests run against recorded v3 fixtures; CI never calls integrations.sh.

commits.message:
feat(kb): one knowledge base per space, /s/<key>/kb URLs, settings by scope

A space has exactly one knowledge base. Every URL segment, chooser, switcher,
scope picker and per-KB select that assumed several is gone; routes carry no
:kbSlug and resolve to the space's KB. The rule is enforced in the DB (partial
unique index on (tenant_id, space_id) where deleted_at is null) and in the DAL
(space_has_knowledge_base → 409 / tool error) for create and space move.

The space URL segment is `kb` (`/s/<key>/kb/…`) via SPACE_MODULE_URL_ALIASES;
the `knowledge-base` segment stays mounted for links already in flight, and
tool results link with the short form.

Settings by scope (PLAN-kb-settings.md): the module page keeps only tenant-wide
index infrastructure (embedding model + index status/rebuild, retrieval knobs,
test search); chunking is persisted per KB (`kb.chunking`) and applied by the
splitter per document; the KB's own page carries space, chunking and delete.
auto_generate_* and default_kb_id/is_default are removed with their KV rows.

Search is scoped: search.documents rows carry space_id + metadata.kb_id, the
host injects space_ids for space-owned sources, backfill/listDocuments accept a
metadata filter, and a KB moved to another space is re-indexed
(knowledge-base.kb.space_changed). Deleting a KB soft-deletes its articles so
the index follows.

commits.message:
feat(spaces): module mountOperation — a module's first-use setup runs on mount

A manifest may name a `mountOperation`, sibling of `connections[].bindOperation`.
Core runs it with `{ space_id }` from every path that mounts the module — the
create wizard (POST /api/spaces), the setup dialog (PUT /setup) and the
`space_setup` tool (POST /setup/add) — for the mounts the call added or changed;
re-adding a module is the retry. The answer carries `mounted[]`
({ module_id, ready, needs, error? }); a failing setup never fails the mount.
Re-adding a module WITHOUT agent_access keeps the level the space gave it.

Knowledge base: the space's one library is created by `kb_space_mount` and
nowhere else — named `<space name>-kb`, slug `<space key>-kb`, `needs:
["ai_gateway"]` when AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY is unset. Removed: `kb_create`,
POST /api/kb/knowledge-bases, the create dialog, the editor's hidden "Default"
library create, and the Data tree's on-write library create (now
`kb_not_found` pointing at the space's setup). The hub's empty state re-posts
the mount.

Fix: `callOperation` in server.ts handed the route's ResolvedRouteAuth straight
to invokeOperation; evaluatePolicy reads `auth.moduleIds` and crashed for every
user principal (bind and ceiling ops had the same latent bug). Now
toPrincipalContext(auth).

commits.message:
feat(spaces): mountOperation for Inbox and Files

`inbox_space_mount` binds every mailbox the space has placed (the same
binding as `inbox_account_bind`, so the create wizard and the setup dialog
end at "the mail is here" too) and reports `needs: ["mailbox"]` while the
space has none. `files_space_mount` mounts every placed drive's root; a
space's Files needs no row and works with native folders, so it is always
ready. Both bind handlers are shared with the per-account bind operations.

Core skips the pair binding for a module that is being added and has a
mountOperation — the mount operation binds all of the space's accounts, and
the pair binding on top would pull every mailbox twice. An account placed
later into a space that already has the app still goes through the pair
binding.

commits.message:
feat(ai-ui): workflow detail header, sync button, canvas expand, persisted catalog filters

Workflow detail pages used a hand-rolled non-sticky header under the
floating transparent topbar, so a scrolled page drew its title over the
breadcrumb row. Both now use DetailPageHeader (blended + sticky), which
collapses and frosts once stuck; ActionDetailHeader is deleted with them —
both call sites passed isEditing={false} and no-op handlers, so its whole
EditableText half was dead.

A "Sync" action on the module detail page runs the boot reconcile, so an
edit to a module's workflow file reaches the app without restarting the AI
service. Core still has to have re-read the file — it is the process that
loads it.

The canvas card takes an expand toggle: the page header and the other
sections step aside and the Steps card fills the content area. Every
element keeps its place in the tree, so the editor is restyled rather than
remounted — expanding to look closer must not drop the version you picked.

Sidebar catalog group/filter/sort now ride in the existing
admin_agents_sidebar_nav_state user setting, per tab. The search box stays
local: a query restored on the next visit hides most of the catalog with
nothing on screen saying why.

That setting had in fact never saved. Its PATCH added
`Content-Type: application/json` on top of the client's own lowercase
`content-type`, which fetch sends as `application/json, application/json`;
the route does not read that as JSON, the body never parses, and the
schema then fails on `type` — a field the caller did send. So pins, aside
width, folders and sections were being discarded too.

feat(ai): TASKS.md — a private task pad per engenty, next to MEMORY.md

copilot) keeps a TASKS.md: standing goals on top, dated checkbox tasks
below. It lives as `metadata.tasks_md` on the same ai.mastra_resources row

delegated or visible to anyone else, and the instructions say so.

TS-declared scopes were dropped on the way into apps/ai.

compact markdown (checkboxes, done lines struck through) with an edit
toggle; pads are editable by whoever may manage agents in the Space,
independent of the identity's `canManage`.

bucket, and that bucket was badged from `!card.routine` — an absent routine

workflow's own status. A published workflow nobody wrapped says it runs on
request.

commits.message:
feat(ai): agent-run tracing through Mastra observability sinks

Langfuse was wired for the Vercel-AI-SDK era and never moved: its OTel
bootstrap ran only in core, while every agent run lives in apps/ai. Replace
that path with Mastra's own observability, fed by whichever sinks the
installation configures:

- apps/ai/ai/observability.ts builds a Mastra `Observability` with
  LangfuseExporter (LANGFUSE_*), OtelExporter (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*) and
  MastraStorageExporter (ENGENTY_TRACE_STORE → ai.mastra_ai_spans); none
  configured = Mastra's no-op.
- Run identity (tenant, user, session=thread, space, agent, run, lane) is set
  on the RequestContext at the three seams that create it and copied onto
  every root span via requestContextKeys.
- apps/ai hydrates platform settings before importing app.js, because the
  Mastra instance reads the sink keys at module evaluation; observability is
  flushed on shutdown.
- The seven observability keys move to the copilot module's env
  contribution as platform-configurable, so /setup/platform shows them and
  the deploy template carries them.
- packages/telemetry loses its OTel/Langfuse bootstrap and dead span
  helpers; the AI-SDK `telemetry: { isEnabled }` flags in core-process
  callers are removed with it.

Also fixes platform-settings hydration dropping boolean and numeric values,
which left every Setup-UI toggle unset in the process that read it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(notifications): first to answer wins — space audience, seen per viewer, desk interrupts

A notification is a pointer to something a person can decide; the right to
decide lives on that thing, never on the row. Shared work is now addressed to
its place: audience_kind "space" (readable by everyone who may enter the
space, mirroring listAccessibleSpaces), tenant when there is no space. A
person is the audience only when the subject is theirs — assigned work, a
private room's participants, a task outside any space. The run's initiator
and the routine's owner become subscribers (pushed, mailed), never the
audience; whoever answers first closes the row for everyone.

Seen is per person (core.notification_seen); the row's status is pending,
dismissed or resolved, a decision is never dismissed, a merged re-ask is new
for everyone, and delivery skips a target who already looked.

Desk interrupts (requestDecision, requestFeedback, gated tool calls, frontend
tools) file agent_question / tool_approval rows — except a gate core already
filed a request for, which has its approval_requested row. The answered
interrupt resolves at the top of the resume route, on the orphan heal, on a
fresh turn past the card, and in the sweep when no thread holds it. Core's
decide route answers 409 approvals.alreadyDecided for a request someone
else got to first; the card says so.

commits.message:
Sidebar lists conversations, not agents

The Work tab is a list of conversations, the way Slack's is: Favoriten,
then this person's own sections, then the built-ins Agenten (the desks),
Räume and Direktnachrichten. A row lives in exactly one place; pinning
moves it to Favoriten, hiding drops it until the next message, and a desk
can never be hidden.

Four kinds, one server-side answer (`threadKind`): a desk is the agent's
single shared line, a room carries `route_context.room`, a DM carries
`route_context.dm` — one per person × agent × Space, stable id, private —
and a pair thread stays what it was. Rooms are listed by participation
only; everything else in the Space is in `/s/<key>/chats` with a join
button.

The nav state is per person and lives in the user-settings document
`shell.spaces.conversation_nav.v1` — sections, order, placement, pins,
hidden_at — so nothing about one person's arrangement touches another's.
The old `agent_nav.v1` folds into it once on read.

Rooms also say who is speaking: every assistant row is stamped with the
agent that wrote it, the message list resolves the name through the
registry, and the transcript prints it above the bubble on desks and in
rooms — never in a DM, where there is only one voice to attribute. A
room's breadcrumb names the room and its members instead of offering the
host's agent switcher.

commits.message:
A new Space starts with its creator on the roster

`core.space_member` was written in exactly two places — an explicit invite
and claiming an orphaned personal space — so a freshly created Space had
no rows at all, not even for the person who made it. An open Space is
enterable without them, so nothing noticed: its People section, the room
bar's add-someone picker and the composer's `@` list were empty in a Space
somebody was working in every day. Creating one now writes the creator's
row as `owner`, which is also the row that keeps them in when the Space
later goes private. A failed write is logged, not fatal — the Space
exists and is usable.

`useSpacePeople` is the one place those rows are read, so the three
surfaces cannot disagree about who is here. The composer's `@` list also
offers every agent on the roster, the desk's own included: in a room the
host is one participant among the others, and Game Master was the one
name you could not mention.

commits.message:
Mention a room or an artifact, not just a colleague

The `@` picker offered agents and people only, so the two things a Space chat
talks about most — the rooms its agents work in and the artifacts they built —
could only be named in prose. Rooms and artifacts join the list, and every row
now leads with a glyph: each agent as its own Engenty, an artifact by its type,
a room by the chat mark. Without one a mixed list is a single column of text
where a room reads like an agent.

Each ref kind carries its own instruction instead of one undifferentiated
"here are some references": an artifact says read it with `artifact_read`
first, a room says speak in it with `message_agent`'s new `room_id`.

`room_id` is what makes a mentioned room addressable. `agent_ids` names a room
by its member set, which from a desk always opens a NEW one — so the agent
would have answered in a second room beside the one the person named. With
`room_id` the room is the id: everyone in it takes a turn, `agent_ids` narrows
that to the members named. Membership, the turn budget and the pause stay
`deliverToRoom`'s; this refuses only a thread that is not a room of this Space.

Reading a room from a desk is still not possible, and the room entry says so
rather than letting the agent claim it read one.

commits.message:
Upgrade agentOS to 0.2.19 and carry the build patch forward

deployApp() is still broken as published: the build VM has the guest tar
write the packed release through a host directory mount, and the guest
cannot write to it — "tar: Permission denied (os error 2)" — so every
deploy fails, including the package's own README example. createBuildVm
is byte-identical to the 0.2.14 original, so the patch is regenerated
unchanged against the new version.

Verified on 0.2.19: an App backend deploys, serves requests, and has a
real filesystem — node:fs works and /home/agentos survives sleep and a
cold start. It does not survive a release: the actor key is
<appId>/<releaseHash>/default, so publishing a new version creates a
different actor with an empty disk. App data therefore cannot live in
the isolate.

commits.message:
feat(apps): give each App a /data volume

Every App backend now has /data: a real host directory keyed by App,
mounted read-write into its agentOS isolate via host_dir, so an App's
node:sqlite database and files outlive every release. One replica per
App (maxReplicas default 32 -> 1): node:sqlite in the guest is a
checkout that writes the whole file back on close, and one process must
own that file.

- patches/@rivet-dev__agentos-apps@0.2.19.patch: second hunk,
  setupApps({ replicaOptions }) spread into the replica actor's
  resolveOptions return; extra mounts appended after the read-only /app.
- app-host: dataDir from ENGENTY_APPS_DATA_DIR (default
  ~/.engenty/app-data), <dataDir>/<appId> created at deploy and mounted
  at /data on every replica boot; the guest runs as 0:0. The sidecar's
  node:sqlite write-back is DAC-checked against the HOST file's uid, so
  the default 1000:1000 identity failed EACCES on the first close of
  every process and later closes were silent no-ops until exit.
- compose: /opt/engenty/spaces bound 1:1 into app-host (same convention
  as the sandbox dir), ENGENTY_APPS_DATA_DIR=/opt/engenty/spaces/apps;
  Dockerfile guard checks both patch markers; DEPLOY/BLUE-GREEN notes.
- skills: app-authoring "The backend" documents /data and the
  open-per-request / close-in-finally rule; engenty-bridge points
  backend records at /data.

Live-verified through the dev app-host: three releases of a spike App,
row count carried 2 -> 4 -> 7, each close() visible on the host at once.
app_data is deliberately left in place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(apps): put an App's source in git on the spaces tree

An App is now a folder with a history. Its source lives in a git work
tree at tenants/<tenant>/spaces/<space>/apps/<slug>/src on the shared
spaces tree, beside the data/ directory the isolate already mounts at
/data, and the space computer binds the space's apps/ at /sandbox/apps —
so an agent edits the checkout and the running App reads the same files.
app-host owns the tree: it commits into it, reads a commit out of it,
and builds that commit. A version row in Postgres is one release attempt
of one commit (sha, manifest, built document, status) — files jsonb is
gone, and so is app_consent, which nothing ever read.

- app-host: AppStore (place, commit, read a tree at a ref) behind
  PUT/GET /internal/apps/:id/source; ENGENTY_SPACES_DIR replaces the
  data-dir-only setting; the container runs as uid 1000, the space
  computer's user, because both write these directories.
- module: app_file_write commits files and writes the manifest as
  engenty.json; app_release_propose commits the work tree, builds that
  commit and records it; rollback redeploys a commit. A commit that does
  not build is a `failed` version carrying its log.
- Two gates close at release: a manifest naming an operation that does
  not exist is refused with the unknown ids in the build log, and the
  approval banner names the module or connector each operation belongs
  to instead of listing bare ids.
- sqld is gone from the App path entirely: service, routes, client,
  compose network and image.
- backup-spaces.sh, because the tree is tenant data with no other copy.
- Cleanup: no PLAN-/SPIKE- references left in the touched files, stale
  migration comments corrected, skills and app-coder instructions
  describe the git model.

Live-verified against the dev app-host: two commits, a no-op commit on a
clean tree, a delete, and a read at an earlier sha.

commits.message:
The Space's home is its sidebar, unfolded

A card per conversation, in the sidebar's own order: Favoriten first, then
the rest. A pinned row always has a card; an unpinned one only while it is
live — waiting on you, paused at the room's turn budget, running, or
finished since your last visit. Everything else is one line of names.

`GET /ai/spaces/:id/home` answers the states in one round trip: open
interrupts, `room_paused`, `ai.agent_run` rows since a cursor, and each
thread's newest message. `active-thread-runs.ts` is deliberately not a
source — it is an in-process map a second instance cannot see.

A thread shows at most one LIVE job per state (one room takes one run at a
time), while finished runs are counted rather than listed. Verdicts stay
where they can be given: the room's pause lifts on the card, an interrupt
opens the conversation, where its decision card already waits.

Beside the cards, what the Space keeps: its promoted artifacts and its
mounts. The same artifacts get a Work-tab section with the Data tree's own
row menu, and the Work list's Inbox row becomes the Dashboard, whose count
moved to a bell on the home.

Spaces gain a description — a name, an icon and a colour could not say what
a space is FOR — shown in the home's heading and edited in settings.

commits.message:
Say what an App asks for, and let the person answer where they are

An App built by a colleague came to rest with nobody knowing they were the
blocker. The home said "Wartet auf deine Antwort" and offered to open a chat;
the chat offered a row of chips reading `expenses · expenses_list` and
`table · 01a0862f-…`. Identifiers, not consequences — and the card could not
even name which App, because a release is a marker message and a decision
notification, neither of which the home ever read.

It reads them now. The Space home unions the release markers, asks core once
per App whether those versions are still proposed, and the card carries the
verdict itself: `apps.approve` is a plain POST with no run to resume, so a
button there IS the decision rather than a weaker copy of the one in the chat.

And the consent surface reads like consent. The manifest is grouped by what
it lets the App DO — work in a module, read and write these tables, reach
these addresses, keep its own files, ask you again every time — each group
one collapsed line with a count, opening to the sentences that were already
being fetched and thrown away: the operation contract's summary, the table's
title. The high-risk group opens itself, because that is the part a person
most needs to have read. Card and banner derive their groups from the same
hook, so what the card promises is what the banner shows.

Around it, the smaller things that made the feature hard to use: the message
excerpt drops its markdown before it is cut, the App can move to the artifact
panel beside the conversation it belongs to, and closing the Data pane goes
back where you opened it from instead of stranding you in a file list.

commits.message:
Stop waiting on a question the conversation already moved past

A desk row said "Wartet auf dich" about an ask from the day before. Nothing
was open: `requires_action` is how a suspended run ENDS, it is never cleared,
and both the sidebar and the home read every run in the feed and let the
oldest parked one speak for the agent for good — even though a later run in
the same thread had since completed.

Each conversation now answers for itself, judged by its own newest run, and
the agent takes the most urgent of them. An ask in ANOTHER thread still
outranks work in progress, so a desk running jobs in parallel keeps saying
the thing a person can act on.

And an App now reloads when it is activated. The frame in the chat was built
while the version was still proposed, so every engenty call it made came back
`apps.operationNotDeclared` — and it had no way to learn that the answer had
changed. The decision refetches the frontend and the release's state rides in
the frame key, so approving reloads the App where it stands.

commits.message:
Never let the browser handle signal a host process; reach the browser by IP or loopback port.

Mastra's AgentBrowser reads the connected Chromium's PID over CDP and, on
disconnect or close, runs process.kill(-pid). Our Chromium is the container's
PID 1, so that was kill(-1) on the host — every process the apps/ai user owns.
It took the desktop down twice. The registry now makes the PID fields on our
handle write-ignoring, so the kill helper always returns before signalling;
a test pins it.

The container is created with the docker CLI carrying Mastra's labels. On a
dev host without a view network it publishes DevTools on an ephemeral
loopback port; on a deployment apps/ai dials the container's IP on the view
network — DevTools refuses a container-name Host header. Attaching a viewer
now launches the CDP session, waking a sleeping container, so the live view
shows a page without a tool call first.

commits.message:
Forget a burnt refresh token wherever the bearer is fetched, not only on first load.

The access token usually outlives the crash, so the first getSession() still
succeeds and the failure arrives minutes later, on the refresh inside the
next bearer lookup — thrown into ensure-current-user and shown verbatim on
the setup card. The bearer getter now treats that as a dead session (local
sign-out, no token) and the bootstrap's stale-session matcher knows the
message, so the shell reaches the login screen from either direction.

commits.message:
feat(deploy): check the two Supabase settings migrations cannot make

Exposed schemas and the Customize Access Token hook live in project config,
so nothing in this repo can guarantee them — and both fail silently. A
missing schema crash-loops engenty-ai on the schema cache; a missing hook
turns a correct password into Unauthorized and leaves realtime off.

`engenty doctor` checks both over HTTP, from a checkout, against any
deployment. Schemas come from one PostgREST request: an impossible
Accept-Profile answers PGRST106 and names every exposed schema. The hook
side calls the new core.deployment_self_check(), which reports the function
and each grant GoTrue needs, so "all false" reads as unmigrated rather than
as a hook fault. At runtime, edge now says the same thing once when a valid
Supabase token arrives with no tenant_id claim.

The list of required schemas is read from the committed migration sources
instead of the generated supabase/config.toml, so it is correct on a bare
clone — which is what the deploy wizard had wrong: config.toml is
gitignored, and its committed template carries only the five base schemas.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(global): one list decides what stays out of the public mirror

The open/closed boundary was three hand-kept lists: CLOSED_PREFIXES in
publish-open.sh, EXCLUDES in publish-open-snapshot.sh, and
CLOSED_PLUGIN_SLUGS. They drifted. modules/expenses and
modules/finance-reports were stripped from the published tree while
their slugs stayed in the published engenty.plugins, so a 0.2.0 snapshot
would have given the mirror a manifest naming two modules it does not
contain — `pnpm plugins:check`, which the public ci.yml runs, exits 1 on
exactly that.

scripts/lib/closed-paths.mjs is now the only list. Each entry carries the
path and, when the path is a plugin, the slug the manifest uses for it, so
the tree filter and the manifest strip cannot disagree. Both bash scripts
read it; the slug consumers import it.

The drift guard only ever checked that one list was a superset of the
other, which this bug satisfied. It is replaced by three tests: neither
script keeps its own array, every closed modules/ entry declares a slug
that matches its engenty.plugin.json, and no plugin enabled in the pro
manifest resolves to a directory behind a closed prefix without being
stripped. Removing a slug from one entry fails the last two.

Two paths the per-commit script was missing are now covered for it as
well: apps/ui/src/plugins/pro and .github/workflows/build-images.yml.

A filtered tree built from this branch now passes plugins:check with 25
plugins, where it exited 1 before.

commits.message:
fix(deploy): put engenty Apps behind the apps compose profile

engenty-app-host was a default service in docker-compose.yaml and
docker-compose.prebuilt.yaml, but the module that drives it —
modules/engenty-apps — is PRO-only. A public build therefore starts a
service nothing can call, and because app-host refuses to serve
unauthenticated internal calls in production it exits on the missing
ENGENTY_APP_HOST_TOKEN and crash-loops on restart: unless-stopped. The
first thing an open-source installer would see is a container they never
asked for, failing.

Gate it the way docs and studio are gated. Nothing depends_on app-host,
so skipping it costs the rest of the stack nothing.

PRO deployments on either of those two files now need --profile apps (or
COMPOSE_PROFILES=apps on Coolify) on BOTH build and up — profile-gated
services are skipped by `docker compose build`, so the image is otherwise
never built. Called out in DEPLOY.md next to the /docs 502 warning, which
is the same trap. The blue-green production layout is untouched:
docker-compose.backend.prebuilt.yaml runs app-host always.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(deploy): publish public images, and let one image serve any install

Installing on a VPS meant building two app images on the box, because the
open repo has no image pipeline: build-images.yml is pro-only and does not
sync. publish-images.yml builds the open tree on engenty/engenty and pushes
public ghcr.io/engenty/engenty-* packages; publish-open.yml now tags the
mirror so there is something to trigger it, and something for a user to pin.

A generic image was impossible while the Supabase URL and anon key were
baked into the bundle at build time — CI cannot know the install. The
gateway now writes them into each HTML document it serves, from the
deployment's own environment, through the same __ENGENTY_RUNTIME_ENV__ seam
the desktop shell already uses to point a bundled SPA at a chosen server.
Assets are untouched, unresolved keys fall back to what was baked, and the
values move on restart instead of on rebuild.

Both repos publish into the same org, so pro's images become engenty-pro-*
and the compose files take ENGENTY_IMAGE_PREFIX (plus ENGENTY_IMAGE_TAG to
pin a release). The default is the public prefix: a PRO deployment must set
it, or it comes up with none of the closed modules and no error to say so.
DEPLOY.md and BLUE-GREEN.md say that where the variables are configured.

publish-images.yml runs only on engenty/engenty — in pro the tree still
holds the closed modules — and has to be installed on the mirror by hand,
since the open-source sync keeps the mirror's own workflows rather than
overwriting them with pro's.

commits.message:
fix(deploy): name deploy images in full, and drop the -pro on publish

`${ENGENTY_IMAGE_PREFIX:-…}` in an `image:` field was the shape that took the
site down on 2026-07-07: Coolify's compose parser ignores the `:-default`
fallback, so an unset variable collapses the reference to a bare name that
cannot be pulled — and it fails after the old containers are already removed.
The comment saying so was directly above one of the lines this replaced.

Both repos' compose files now name their own packages in full, and
publish-open-snapshot.sh drops the `-pro` in the index on its way to the
mirror, the way it already rewrites package.json. No variable to set on the
host, nothing for a PRO deployment to remember, and no way for an OSS install
to end up pointed at packages it cannot read.

commits.message:
feat(deploy): ask for what only the operator knows, derive the rest

A deployment demanded eight variables. Four of them restated something the
install already had: VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY repeated
SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, and ENGENTY_CORS_ORIGINS repeated
PUBLIC_APP_URL. Restating a value is not configuration — it is a second
place to get it wrong, and a second place to forget when the first changes.

The UI pair became derivable when the gateway started writing those values
into the served page; the manifest just had not caught up. The /ai
allow-list now falls back to PUBLIC_APP_URL's origin, which for a
single-origin install is the entire list.

Requirement turns out not to be a property of a key but of a key in a file:
the UI pair is load-bearing for `pnpm dev`, where Vite serves the SPA with
no gateway in front of it, and an override in a deployment. So `required`
takes an optional per-scope form, resolved once per report by
requirementForScope. The templates show the split: .env.example still has
VITE_SUPABASE_URL uncommented, deploy/.env.example no longer does.

The wizard writes the three only when they differ from what would be
derived — today, never, so the file it produces is four lines shorter.

commits.message:
fix(banking,finance-reports): scope cross-schema expense reads to the scope too

module_expenses.expenses and module_banking.bank_transactions are both
`(tenant_id, scope_id)` with RLS on has_scope, and module DAL runs
service-role — so filtering tenant_id alone reads and writes every scope in
the tenant. Banking's matcher could clear or claim an expense belonging to
another scope; the finance summary counted their amounts.

scopeId was already a parameter of createBankingRepo and already on
ctx.auth, so loadSummary takes the TenantScope rather than the tenant id.

Expense receipts are classified tenant-level instead: module_expenses has no
space_id column and every expenses operation is tenant_shared, so the bytes
sit above every space the way company-profile's and pdf-templates' do. The
guard escalates the entry to an error if the module ever gains that column.

commits.message:
feat(deploy): a wizard for the database you already run, wherever it runs

The stepper only knew one installation: a Supabase Cloud project reached
through the Management API, deployed by Coolify. Everyone else met the same
two sentences telling them to go set something by hand, and then nothing
checked whether they had.

It now opens by asking where Supabase runs and how engenty runs, and the
rest follows. Self-hosted Supabase gets the exact PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS and
GOTRUE_HOOK_CUSTOM_ACCESS_TOKEN_* lines, because there is no Management API
to set them through and the schema list is far too long to retype. Docker
Compose gets deploy/.env, the pull/up commands, and the Caddy snippet for
TLS in front of engenty-edge:8787 — the step Coolify would otherwise have
hidden.

Both Supabase paths now end by asking the database what it actually did,
through the same probes as `engenty doctor`, instead of trusting the click.
Steps carry a `when`, so the stepper shows the path you chose rather than
one with dead stops in it.

Self-hosted also asks for the URL the containers use when it differs from
the browser's: that split is what the gateway's runtime env resolution was
for, and this is where it gets filled in.

commits.message:
docs(deploy): a runbook for the 0.1.x install, and a banner that tells the truth

0.2.0 is not a release you can ship by pulling images. It adds 107
migrations, three internal networks, two proxies and a host directory that
must exist and be owned by uid 1000 before anything starts — and it enables
two modules whose schemas have to be exposed in Supabase first, which no
migration can do and whose absence only shows up as engenty-ai
crash-looping on the schema cache.

It also deletes data on purpose: every tenant-authored flow and routine is
truncated by the 2026-08-29 cutover, goals and the tasks module's own
triggers/templates/settings tables are dropped. All deliberate, all
permanent, none of it converted. The runbook lists them with their
migrations so the backup decision is made with the facts.

Two more things a pull would get wrong: engenty-app-host moved behind the
`apps` profile, so it stops unless COMPOSE_PROFILES says otherwise, and the
per-user browser image is built by no pipeline — it exists only as a
build-only service, so on a prebuilt host starting a browser fails until
someone builds it.

The README banner claimed data is not rewritten. It is. Fixed, and pointed
at the runbook.

commits.message:
docs(deploy): rehearse the 0.1→0.2 upgrade, and correct what it disproved

Ran the chain against a copy of engenty.engrd.xyz's database: 106 migrations,
no errors, under five seconds. Four things in the runbook were wrong, and
one number was worth having.

The number: this install loses 18 rows, not a category of work. The tables
behind the loudest warning — ai.routines, ai.flow_graph — do not exist on
0.1.x at all; 0.2.0 creates them and truncates them empty. kb_settings is
not emptied either, only three named keys go, 7 rows to 4. flow_graph is
renamed to ai.workflow by the end of the chain, so a reader who goes looking
for it afterwards will not find it.

"Expect this deploy to take noticeably longer" was a guess, and wrong by two
orders of magnitude. The schema change is not the slow part; pulling images
is.

And the failure the rehearsal reproduced: exposed schemas reach PostgREST as
process configuration, so a new one needs it restarted, not its cache
reloaded. Migrations applied cleanly and doctor still could not read the
schema cache until the container came back. That is exactly why §1 runs
before the deploy, which the section now says instead of implying.

§0b writes the rehearsal down — including the two things that bite on the
way: pg_dump 17.6 emits \restrict, which breaks COPY through psql, and
Supabase's postgres role cannot disable FK triggers, where
session_replication_role can.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(global): stop engenty setup deleting the UI's module dependencies

`pnpm engenty setup` removed all 18 `@engenty/*` module dependencies from
apps/ui/package.json, a committed file. It survived unnoticed because
node_modules was already linked from that manifest, so Vite still resolved
and only the git tree went dirty — until an install ran after a setup, as a
branch switch does, and the app stopped loading with
`Failed to resolve import "@engenty/files-ui/ui/components/connect-folder-dialog"`.

Three bugs, each hiding the next.

`moduleHasUi` read a top-level `manifest.ui` field. No module declares one;
almost all of them ship `ui/plugin.ts` and say nothing, which is the
convention the UI artifact generator already resolves. So `hasUi` was false
for all 33 modules, the enabled-UI set was empty, and every module dep
qualified for removal. It now takes the module directory and checks the
convention file and `capabilities.ui` as well — and agrees exactly with the
generated catalog, which is the authority on what actually ships.

With the add path reachable for the first time, `packageName` turned out to
be derived from the slug: modules/files would have been written as
`@engenty/files`, which does not exist. It reads the module's own
package.json now, keeping `@engenty/files-ui` and
`@engenty/pdf-templates-module`.

And `tryReadClosedPrefixes` still parsed a `CLOSED_PREFIXES=(` bash array
out of publish-open.sh. That array became a loop over closed-paths.mjs, so
the parser scraped `$_prefix` and an error string, and `moduleTier` answered
"open" for every closed module — which would have put banking, expenses and
five other pro packages into the manifest the public mirror is served from.
It reads closed-paths.mjs, the one list, directly.

The sync now refuses to remove more than three dependencies at once and logs
what it removes. A wholesale removal means detection broke, not that the
product changed, and it should not be something you discover from a build
error two steps later.

apps/ui/package.json carries a one-time sort normalisation so the sync is a
true no-op; the test asserts that property, and fails without the fix.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

test(ai): assert what the memory tests are about, not list lengths

Three assertions counted `memoryProcessors` when the list held only the
shared observational processor. MEMORY.md and TASKS.md now ride the same
list and are deliberately independent of the OM switch, so the count says
nothing about the observer — check for the processor by name instead.

MEMORY.md pair) and in the copilot channel name, where live-cache appends a
per-subscription "#<n>" so a second subscriber cannot adopt a joined
channel; match the prefix rather than a sequence number that depends on how
many subscriptions ran first.

migrations, three internal networks, two proxies and a host directory that
must exist and be owned by uid 1000 before anything starts — and it enables
two modules whose schemas have to be exposed in Supabase first, which no
migration can do and whose absence only shows up as engenty-ai
crash-looping on the schema cache.

It also deletes data on purpose: every tenant-authored flow and routine is
truncated by the 2026-08-29 cutover, goals and the tasks module's own
triggers/templates/settings tables are dropped. All deliberate, all
permanent, none of it converted. The runbook lists them with their
migrations so the backup decision is made with the facts.

Two more things a pull would get wrong: engenty-app-host moved behind the
`apps` profile, so it stops unless COMPOSE_PROFILES says otherwise, and the
per-user browser image is built by no pipeline — it exists only as a
build-only service, so on a prebuilt host starting a browser fails until
someone builds it.

The README banner claimed data is not rewritten. It is. Fixed, and pointed
at the runbook.

commits.message: say what 0.2.0 actually promises about upgrades
commits.body:
"we do not guarantee data migrations" read as "we might eat your data",
which is not what happens: migrations run forward on every deploy and
nothing rewrites existing rows. What an upgrade can cost is a manual step —
0.1.x to 0.2.0 needs several on the host, and consolidating the migration
history afterwards will need one more — plus no way back down.

Say that instead, and tell people to take a backup, which is the advice the
old line was reaching for.

commits.message: a wizard for the database you already run, wherever it runs
commits.body:
The stepper only knew one installation: a Supabase Cloud project reached
through the Management API, deployed by Coolify. Everyone else met the same
two sentences telling them to go set something by hand, and then nothing
checked whether they had.

It now opens by asking where Supabase runs and how engenty runs, and the
rest follows. Self-hosted Supabase gets the exact PGRST_DB_SCHEMAS and
GOTRUE_HOOK_CUSTOM_ACCESS_TOKEN_* lines, because there is no Management API
to set them through and the schema list is far too long to retype. Docker
Compose gets deploy/.env, the pull/up commands, and the Caddy snippet for
TLS in front of engenty-edge:8787 — the step Coolify would otherwise have
hidden.

Both Supabase paths now end by asking the database what it actually did,
through the same probes as `engenty doctor`, instead of trusting the click.
Steps carry a `when`, so the stepper shows the path you chose rather than
one with dead stops in it.

Self-hosted also asks for the URL the containers use when it differs from
the browser's: that split is what the gateway's runtime env resolution was
for, and this is where it gets filled in.

commits.message: scope cross-schema expense reads to the scope too
commits.body:
module_expenses.expenses and module_banking.bank_transactions are both
`(tenant_id, scope_id)` with RLS on has_scope, and module DAL runs
service-role — so filtering tenant_id alone reads and writes every scope in
the tenant. Banking's matcher could clear or claim an expense belonging to
another scope; the finance summary counted their amounts.

scopeId was already a parameter of createBankingRepo and already on
ctx.auth, so loadSummary takes the TenantScope rather than the tenant id.

Expense receipts are classified tenant-level instead: module_expenses has no
space_id column and every expenses operation is tenant_shared, so the bytes
sit above every space the way company-profile's and pdf-templates' do. The
guard escalates the entry to an error if the module ever gains that column.

commits.message: ask for what only the operator knows, derive the rest
commits.body:
A deployment demanded eight variables. Four of them restated something the
install already had: VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY repeated
SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, and ENGENTY_CORS_ORIGINS repeated
PUBLIC_APP_URL. Restating a value is not configuration — it is a second
place to get it wrong, and a second place to forget when the first changes.

The UI pair became derivable when the gateway started writing those values
into the served page; the manifest just had not caught up. The /ai
allow-list now falls back to PUBLIC_APP_URL's origin, which for a
single-origin install is the entire list.

Requirement turns out not to be a property of a key but of a key in a file:
the UI pair is load-bearing for `pnpm dev`, where Vite serves the SPA with
no gateway in front of it, and an override in a deployment. So `required`
takes an optional per-scope form, resolved once per report by
requirementForScope. The templates show the split: .env.example still has
VITE_SUPABASE_URL uncommented, deploy/.env.example no longer does.

The wizard writes the three only when they differ from what would be
derived — today, never, so the file it produces is four lines shorter.

commits.message: publish public images, and let one image serve any install
commits.body:
Installing on a VPS meant building two app images on the box, because the
open repo has no image pipeline: build-images.yml is pro-only and does not
sync. publish-images.yml builds the open tree on engenty/engenty and pushes
public ghcr.io/engenty/engenty-* packages; publish-open.yml now tags the
mirror so there is something to trigger it, and something for a user to pin.

A generic image was impossible while the Supabase URL and anon key were
baked into the bundle at build time — CI cannot know the install. The
gateway now writes them into each HTML document it serves, from the
deployment's own environment, through the same __ENGENTY_RUNTIME_ENV__ seam
the desktop shell already uses to point a bundled SPA at a chosen server.
Assets are untouched, unresolved keys fall back to what was baked, and the
values move on restart instead of on rebuild.

Both repos publish into the same org, so pro's images become engenty-pro-*
and the compose files take ENGENTY_IMAGE_PREFIX (plus ENGENTY_IMAGE_TAG to
pin a release). The default is the public prefix: a PRO deployment must set
it, or it comes up with none of the closed modules and no error to say so.
DEPLOY.md and BLUE-GREEN.md say that where the variables are configured.

publish-images.yml runs only on engenty/engenty — in pro the tree still
holds the closed modules — and has to be installed on the mirror by hand,
since the open-source sync keeps the mirror's own workflows rather than
overwriting them with pro's.

commits.message: put engenty Apps behind the apps compose profile
commits.body:
engenty-app-host was a default service in docker-compose.yaml and
docker-compose.prebuilt.yaml, but the module that drives it —
modules/engenty-apps — is PRO-only. A public build therefore starts a
service nothing can call, and because app-host refuses to serve
unauthenticated internal calls in production it exits on the missing
ENGENTY_APP_HOST_TOKEN and crash-loops on restart: unless-stopped. The
first thing an open-source installer would see is a container they never
asked for, failing.

Gate it the way docs and studio are gated. Nothing depends_on app-host,
so skipping it costs the rest of the stack nothing.

PRO deployments on either of those two files now need --profile apps (or
COMPOSE_PROFILES=apps on Coolify) on BOTH build and up — profile-gated
services are skipped by `docker compose build`, so the image is otherwise
never built. Called out in DEPLOY.md next to the /docs 502 warning, which
is the same trap. The blue-green production layout is untouched:
docker-compose.backend.prebuilt.yaml runs app-host always.

commits.message: one list decides what stays out of the public mirror
commits.body:
The open/closed boundary was three hand-kept lists: CLOSED_PREFIXES in
publish-open.sh, EXCLUDES in publish-open-snapshot.sh, and
CLOSED_PLUGIN_SLUGS. They drifted. modules/expenses and
modules/finance-reports were stripped from the published tree while
their slugs stayed in the published engenty.plugins, so a 0.2.0 snapshot
would have given the mirror a manifest naming two modules it does not
contain — `pnpm plugins:check`, which the public ci.yml runs, exits 1 on
exactly that.

scripts/lib/closed-paths.mjs is now the only list. Each entry carries the
path and, when the path is a plugin, the slug the manifest uses for it, so
the tree filter and the manifest strip cannot disagree. Both bash scripts
read it; the slug consumers import it.

The drift guard only ever checked that one list was a superset of the
other, which this bug satisfied. It is replaced by three tests: neither
script keeps its own array, every closed modules/ entry declares a slug
that matches its engenty.plugin.json, and no plugin enabled in the pro
manifest resolves to a directory behind a closed prefix without being
stripped. Removing a slug from one entry fails the last two.

Two paths the per-commit script was missing are now covered for it as
well: apps/ui/src/plugins/pro and .github/workflows/build-images.yml.

A filtered tree built from this branch now passes plugins:check with 25
plugins, where it exited 1 before.

commits.message: check the two Supabase settings migrations cannot make
commits.body:
Exposed schemas and the Customize Access Token hook live in project config,
so nothing in this repo can guarantee them — and both fail silently. A
missing schema crash-loops engenty-ai on the schema cache; a missing hook
turns a correct password into Unauthorized and leaves realtime off.

`engenty doctor` checks both over HTTP, from a checkout, against any
deployment. Schemas come from one PostgREST request: an impossible
Accept-Profile answers PGRST106 and names every exposed schema. The hook
side calls the new core.deployment_self_check(), which reports the function
and each grant GoTrue needs, so "all false" reads as unmigrated rather than
as a hook fault. At runtime, edge now says the same thing once when a valid
Supabase token arrives with no tenant_id claim.

The list of required schemas is read from the committed migration sources
instead of the generated supabase/config.toml, so it is correct on a bare
clone — which is what the deploy wizard had wrong: config.toml is
gitignored, and its committed template carries only the five base schemas.

commits.message: call it Fair Source, not open source
commits.body:
FSL-1.1-MIT is source-available with a delayed MIT grant, not an OSI
open-source licence. Say so on the landing page, the docs front page,
the README and CONTRIBUTING, so the public launch does not claim a
licence the project does not carry.

Third-party dependency credits keep "open-source" — those really are.
The internal open/closed vocabulary (publish-open, "the open tree") is
about which code is published, not about the licence, and stays.

commits.message:
Forget a burnt refresh token wherever the bearer is fetched, not only on first load.

The access token usually outlives the crash, so the first getSession() still
succeeds and the failure arrives minutes later, on the refresh inside the
next bearer lookup — thrown into ensure-current-user and shown verbatim on
the setup card. The bearer getter now treats that as a dead session (local
sign-out, no token) and the bootstrap's stale-session matcher knows the
message, so the shell reaches the login screen from either direction.

A burnt refresh token means "sign in again", not "check your env vars".

has already used, and getSession() reports it as an error. The shell showed
that message on the setup card with no way out. Now the dead token is
forgotten locally and the shell falls through to the login screen; any
other auth failure still shows its message.

commits.message:
Never let the browser handle signal a host process; reach the browser by IP or loopback port.

Mastra's AgentBrowser reads the connected Chromium's PID over CDP and, on
disconnect or close, runs process.kill(-pid). Our Chromium is the container's
PID 1, so that was kill(-1) on the host — every process the apps/ai user owns.
It took the desktop down twice. The registry now makes the PID fields on our
handle write-ignoring, so the kill helper always returns before signalling;
a test pins it.

The container is created with the docker CLI carrying Mastra's labels. On a
dev host without a view network it publishes DevTools on an ephemeral
loopback port; on a deployment apps/ai dials the container's IP on the view
network — DevTools refuses a container-name Host header. Attaching a viewer
now launches the CDP session, waking a sleeping container, so the live view
shows a page without a tool call first.

commits.message:
Stop waiting on a question the conversation already moved past

A desk row said "Wartet auf dich" about an ask from the day before. Nothing
was open: `requires_action` is how a suspended run ENDS, it is never cleared,
and both the sidebar and the home read every run in the feed and let the
oldest parked one speak for the agent for good — even though a later run in
the same thread had since completed.

Each conversation now answers for itself, judged by its own newest run, and
the agent takes the most urgent of them. An ask in ANOTHER thread still
outranks work in progress, so a desk running jobs in parallel keeps saying
the thing a person can act on.

And an App now reloads when it is activated. The frame in the chat was built
while the version was still proposed, so every engenty call it made came back
`apps.operationNotDeclared` — and it had no way to learn that the answer had
changed. The decision refetches the frontend and the release's state rides in
the frame key, so approving reloads the App where it stands.

commits.message:
Say what an App asks for, and let the person answer where they are

An App built by a colleague came to rest with nobody knowing they were the
blocker. The home said "Wartet auf deine Antwort" and offered to open a chat;
the chat offered a row of chips reading `expenses · expenses_list` and
`table · 01a0862f-…`. Identifiers, not consequences — and the card could not
even name which App, because a release is a marker message and a decision
notification, neither of which the home ever read.

It reads them now. The Space home unions the release markers, asks core once
per App whether those versions are still proposed, and the card carries the
verdict itself: `apps.approve` is a plain POST with no run to resume, so a
button there IS the decision rather than a weaker copy of the one in the chat.

And the consent surface reads like consent. The manifest is grouped by what
it lets the App DO — work in a module, read and write these tables, reach
these addresses, keep its own files, ask you again every time — each group
one collapsed line with a count, opening to the sentences that were already
being fetched and thrown away: the operation contract's summary, the table's
title. The high-risk group opens itself, because that is the part a person
most needs to have read. Card and banner derive their groups from the same
hook, so what the card promises is what the banner shows.

Around it, the smaller things that made the feature hard to use: the message
excerpt drops its markdown before it is cut, the App can move to the artifact
panel beside the conversation it belongs to, and closing the Data pane goes
back where you opened it from instead of stranding you in a file list.

commits.message:
The Space's home is its sidebar, unfolded

A card per conversation, in the sidebar's own order: Favoriten first, then
the rest. A pinned row always has a card; an unpinned one only while it is
live — waiting on you, paused at the room's turn budget, running, or
finished since your last visit. Everything else is one line of names.

`GET /ai/spaces/:id/home` answers the states in one round trip: open
interrupts, `room_paused`, `ai.agent_run` rows since a cursor, and each
thread's newest message. `active-thread-runs.ts` is deliberately not a
source — it is an in-process map a second instance cannot see.

A thread shows at most one LIVE job per state (one room takes one run at a
time), while finished runs are counted rather than listed. Verdicts stay
where they can be given: the room's pause lifts on the card, an interrupt
opens the conversation, where its decision card already waits.

Beside the cards, what the Space keeps: its promoted artifacts and its
mounts. The same artifacts get a Work-tab section with the Data tree's own
row menu, and the Work list's Inbox row becomes the Dashboard, whose count
moved to a bell on the home.

Spaces gain a description — a name, an icon and a colour could not say what
a space is FOR — shown in the home's heading and edited in settings.

commits.body:
The desk row cut the message at 280 characters. That row is not only a
card: a person reads the desk, answers there, and that answer's run
reads the row as its brief — so a cut brief was answered as a cut brief.
Seen live: a manager handed over an App spec, the coder's desk showed
"Zweck: Mitarbeitende erfassen eine Reiseabrechnung…", and the coder

commits.message: put an App's source in git on the spaces tree
commits.body:
An App is now a folder with a history. Its source lives in a git work
tree at tenants/<tenant>/spaces/<space>/apps/<slug>/src on the shared
spaces tree, beside the data/ directory the isolate already mounts at
/data, and the space computer binds the space's apps/ at /sandbox/apps —
so an agent edits the checkout and the running App reads the same files.
app-host owns the tree: it commits into it, reads a commit out of it,
and builds that commit. A version row in Postgres is one release attempt
of one commit (sha, manifest, built document, status) — files jsonb is
gone, and so is app_consent, which nothing ever read.

- app-host: AppStore (place, commit, read a tree at a ref) behind
  PUT/GET /internal/apps/:id/source; ENGENTY_SPACES_DIR replaces the
  data-dir-only setting; the container runs as uid 1000, the space
  computer's user, because both write these directories.
- module: app_file_write commits files and writes the manifest as
  engenty.json; app_release_propose commits the work tree, builds that
  commit and records it; rollback redeploys a commit. A commit that does
  not build is a `failed` version carrying its log.
- Two gates close at release: a manifest naming an operation that does
  not exist is refused with the unknown ids in the build log, and the
  approval banner names the module or connector each operation belongs
  to instead of listing bare ids.
- sqld is gone from the App path entirely: service, routes, client,
  compose network and image.
- backup-spaces.sh, because the tree is tenant data with no other copy.
- Cleanup: no PLAN-/SPIKE- references left in the touched files, stale
  migration comments corrected, skills and app-coder instructions
  describe the git model.

Live-verified against the dev app-host: two commits, a no-op commit on a
clean tree, a delete, and a read at an earlier sha.

commits.message: give each App a /data volume
commits.body:
Every App backend now has /data: a real host directory keyed by App,
mounted read-write into its agentOS isolate via host_dir, so an App's
node:sqlite database and files outlive every release. One replica per
App (maxReplicas default 32 -> 1): node:sqlite in the guest is a
checkout that writes the whole file back on close, and one process must
own that file.

- patches/@rivet-dev__agentos-apps@0.2.19.patch: second hunk,
  setupApps({ replicaOptions }) spread into the replica actor's
  resolveOptions return; extra mounts appended after the read-only /app.
- app-host: dataDir from ENGENTY_APPS_DATA_DIR (default
  ~/.engenty/app-data), <dataDir>/<appId> created at deploy and mounted
  at /data on every replica boot; the guest runs as 0:0. The sidecar's
  node:sqlite write-back is DAC-checked against the HOST file's uid, so
  the default 1000:1000 identity failed EACCES on the first close of
  every process and later closes were silent no-ops until exit.
- compose: /opt/engenty/spaces bound 1:1 into app-host (same convention
  as the sandbox dir), ENGENTY_APPS_DATA_DIR=/opt/engenty/spaces/apps;
  Dockerfile guard checks both patch markers; DEPLOY/BLUE-GREEN notes.
- skills: app-authoring "The backend" documents /data and the
  open-per-request / close-in-finally rule; engenty-bridge points
  backend records at /data.

Live-verified through the dev app-host: three releases of a spike App,
row count carried 2 -> 4 -> 7, each close() visible on the host at once.
app_data is deliberately left in place.

Upgrade agentOS to 0.2.19 and carry the build patch forward

deployApp() is still broken as published: the build VM has the guest tar
write the packed release through a host directory mount, and the guest
cannot write to it — "tar: Permission denied (os error 2)" — so every
deploy fails, including the package's own README example. createBuildVm
is byte-identical to the 0.2.14 original, so the patch is regenerated
unchanged against the new version.

Verified on 0.2.19: an App backend deploys, serves requests, and has a
real filesystem — node:fs works and /home/agentos survives sleep and a
cold start. It does not survive a release: the actor key is
<appId>/<releaseHash>/default, so publishing a new version creates a
different actor with an empty disk. App data therefore cannot live in
the isolate.

commits.message:
A colleague's turn is somebody else's words

A room is one thread several agents answer in, and recall handed every
member the other members' answers as bare assistant messages — its own
words, as far as the model could tell. Live on 2026-09-08 a woken player
reasoned "I am the one agent in this conversation", concluded it had
already moved, answered nothing, and the room fell silent with every run
reported completed: no error, no pause, just a game that stopped at move
three.

Another agent's row now arrives as a user turn under the same
**Message from <name>** header the room's relays already carry — the
shape the shared-room instructions promised all along. Only what it
posted survives; its reasoning and its tool calls were its own work, and
read as the reader's they are the confusion itself. Rows carry the
author's name alongside the id so the header reads as a name.

commits.message:
Mention a room or an artifact, not just a colleague

The `@` picker offered agents and people only, so the two things a Space chat
talks about most — the rooms its agents work in and the artifacts they built —
could only be named in prose. Rooms and artifacts join the list, and every row
now leads with a glyph: each agent as its own Engenty, an artifact by its type,
a room by the chat mark. Without one a mixed list is a single column of text
where a room reads like an agent.

Each ref kind carries its own instruction instead of one undifferentiated
"here are some references": an artifact says read it with `artifact_read`
first, a room says speak in it with `message_agent`'s new `room_id`.

`room_id` is what makes a mentioned room addressable. `agent_ids` names a room
by its member set, which from a desk always opens a NEW one — so the agent
would have answered in a second room beside the one the person named. With
`room_id` the room is the id: everyone in it takes a turn, `agent_ids` narrows
that to the members named. Membership, the turn budget and the pause stay
`deliverToRoom`'s; this refuses only a thread that is not a room of this Space.

Reading a room from a desk is still not possible, and the room entry says so
rather than letting the agent claim it read one.

commits.message:
A new Space starts with its creator on the roster

`core.space_member` was written in exactly two places — an explicit invite
and claiming an orphaned personal space — so a freshly created Space had
no rows at all, not even for the person who made it. An open Space is
enterable without them, so nothing noticed: its People section, the room
bar's add-someone picker and the composer's `@` list were empty in a Space
somebody was working in every day. Creating one now writes the creator's
row as `owner`, which is also the row that keeps them in when the Space
later goes private. A failed write is logged, not fatal — the Space
exists and is usable.

`useSpacePeople` is the one place those rows are read, so the three
surfaces cannot disagree about who is here. The composer's `@` list also
offers every agent on the roster, the desk's own included: in a room the
host is one participant among the others, and Game Master was the one
name you could not mention.

whenever the Space holds anything, not only when the current chat does.

commits.message: agent-run tracing through Mastra observability sinks
commits.body:
Langfuse was wired for the Vercel-AI-SDK era and never moved: its OTel
bootstrap ran only in core, while every agent run lives in apps/ai. Replace
that path with Mastra's own observability, fed by whichever sinks the
installation configures:

- apps/ai/ai/observability.ts builds a Mastra `Observability` with
  LangfuseExporter (LANGFUSE_*), OtelExporter (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_*) and
  MastraStorageExporter (ENGENTY_TRACE_STORE → ai.mastra_ai_spans); none
  configured = Mastra's no-op.
- Run identity (tenant, user, session=thread, space, agent, run, lane) is set
  on the RequestContext at the three seams that create it and copied onto
  every root span via requestContextKeys.
- apps/ai hydrates platform settings before importing app.js, because the
  Mastra instance reads the sink keys at module evaluation; observability is
  flushed on shutdown.
- The seven observability keys move to the copilot module's env
  contribution as platform-configurable, so /setup/platform shows them and
  the deploy template carries them.
- packages/telemetry loses its OTel/Langfuse bootstrap and dead span
  helpers; the AI-SDK `telemetry: { isEnabled }` flags in core-process
  callers are removed with it.

Also fixes platform-settings hydration dropping boolean and numeric values,
which left every Setup-UI toggle unset in the process that read it.

commits.message: workflow detail header, sync button, canvas expand, persisted catalog filters
commits.body:
Workflow detail pages used a hand-rolled non-sticky header under the
floating transparent topbar, so a scrolled page drew its title over the
breadcrumb row. Both now use DetailPageHeader (blended + sticky), which
collapses and frosts once stuck; ActionDetailHeader is deleted with them —
both call sites passed isEditing={false} and no-op handlers, so its whole
EditableText half was dead.

A "Sync" action on the module detail page runs the boot reconcile, so an
edit to a module's workflow file reaches the app without restarting the AI
service. Core still has to have re-read the file — it is the process that
loads it.

The canvas card takes an expand toggle: the page header and the other
sections step aside and the Steps card fills the content area. Every
element keeps its place in the tree, so the editor is restyled rather than
remounted — expanding to look closer must not drop the version you picked.

Sidebar catalog group/filter/sort now ride in the existing
admin_agents_sidebar_nav_state user setting, per tab. The search box stays
local: a query restored on the next visit hides most of the catalog with
nothing on screen saying why.

That setting had in fact never saved. Its PATCH added
`Content-Type: application/json` on top of the client's own lowercase
`content-type`, which fetch sends as `application/json, application/json`;
the route does not read that as JSON, the body never parses, and the
schema then fails on `type` — a field the caller did send. So pins, aside
width, folders and sections were being discarded too.

commits.message: mountOperation for Inbox and Files
commits.body:
`inbox_space_mount` binds every mailbox the space has placed (the same
binding as `inbox_account_bind`, so the create wizard and the setup dialog
end at "the mail is here" too) and reports `needs: ["mailbox"]` while the
space has none. `files_space_mount` mounts every placed drive's root; a
space's Files needs no row and works with native folders, so it is always
ready. Both bind handlers are shared with the per-account bind operations.

Core skips the pair binding for a module that is being added and has a
mountOperation — the mount operation binds all of the space's accounts, and
the pair binding on top would pull every mailbox twice. An account placed
later into a space that already has the app still goes through the pair
binding.

commits.message: module mountOperation — a module's first-use setup runs on mount
commits.body:
A manifest may name a `mountOperation`, sibling of `connections[].bindOperation`.
Core runs it with `{ space_id }` from every path that mounts the module — the
create wizard (POST /api/spaces), the setup dialog (PUT /setup) and the
`space_setup` tool (POST /setup/add) — for the mounts the call added or changed;
re-adding a module is the retry. The answer carries `mounted[]`
({ module_id, ready, needs, error? }); a failing setup never fails the mount.
Re-adding a module WITHOUT agent_access keeps the level the space gave it.

Knowledge base: the space's one library is created by `kb_space_mount` and
nowhere else — named `<space name>-kb`, slug `<space key>-kb`, `needs:
["ai_gateway"]` when AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY is unset. Removed: `kb_create`,
POST /api/kb/knowledge-bases, the create dialog, the editor's hidden "Default"
library create, and the Data tree's on-write library create (now
`kb_not_found` pointing at the space's setup). The hub's empty state re-posts
the mount.

`callOperation` in server.ts handed the route's ResolvedRouteAuth straight
to invokeOperation; evaluatePolicy reads `auth.moduleIds` and crashed for every
user principal (bind and ceiling ops had the same latent bug). Now
toPrincipalContext(auth).

commits.message: one knowledge base per space, /s/<key>/kb URLs, settings by scope
commits.body:
A space has exactly one knowledge base. Every URL segment, chooser, switcher,
scope picker and per-KB select that assumed several is gone; routes carry no
:kbSlug and resolve to the space's KB. The rule is enforced in the DB (partial
unique index on (tenant_id, space_id) where deleted_at is null) and in the DAL
(space_has_knowledge_base → 409 / tool error) for create and space move.

The space URL segment is `kb` (`/s/<key>/kb/…`) via SPACE_MODULE_URL_ALIASES;
the `knowledge-base` segment stays mounted for links already in flight, and
tool results link with the short form.

Settings by scope (PLAN-kb-settings.md): the module page keeps only tenant-wide
index infrastructure (embedding model + index status/rebuild, retrieval knobs,
test search); chunking is persisted per KB (`kb.chunking`) and applied by the
splitter per document; the KB's own page carries space, chunking and delete.
auto_generate_* and default_kb_id/is_default are removed with their KV rows.

Search is scoped: search.documents rows carry space_id + metadata.kb_id, the
host injects space_ids for space-owned sources, backfill/listDocuments accept a
metadata filter, and a KB moved to another space is re-indexed
(knowledge-base.kb.space_changed). Deleting a KB soft-deletes its articles so
the index follows.
