commits.message: render timezone-carrying routine schedules verbatim
commits.body:
An agent-created trigger stores its cron in the named IANA zone's local
time, but the routine UI assumed every cron is UTC: the chip converted
07:00 Europe/Vienna to 09:00 local, and editing round-tripped the hours
through the preset picker's UTC conversion, silently shifting the
schedule. Timezone-carrying routines now render their hours verbatim
suffixed with the zone, and the edit form falls back to the custom-cron
preset so a PATCH never mangles what the agent wrote.

commits.message: make agent-created routines actually fire, attribute, and honor pre-approvals
commits.body:
Three gaps between the gateway write path (an agent's triggers_create) and
a working routine:

- Gateway trigger writes never reached the Mastra scheduler, so an
  agent-created routine had heartbeat_id null and stayed inert until the
  next restart, and a gateway delete left a live orphan schedule. The boot
  reconcile's schedule pass is extracted as syncTenantSchedules and runs
  every 2 minutes as the scheduler-sync system job; deleted-trigger fires
  are skipped quietly instead of spamming trigger_failed cards.
- A bad cron or timezone persisted as a configured-looking routine that
  could never fire (the HTTP route rolls back via Mastra, the gateway
  never asked). Both gateway write paths now validate with croner — the
  parser the scheduler itself runs on — plus an Intl timezone check.
- Unattended fires carried no acting user, so a routine in a private space
  resolved no Space surface and ran with every module tool refused. Fires
  now fall back to the trigger's own creator; triggers_create stamps
  created_by_user_id for user-token callers.

Also closes the approval split-brain for pre-configured approved tools:
approval_grants written via triggers_create/update (the picker and the
agent path) only satisfied the AI pre-gate while core still 202'd the run.
The gateway now dual-writes trigger-scope grants into core.approval_grants
(revoking delisted ops, reaping on trigger delete) and a backfill brings
along existing config entries. The copilot work-routing skill teaches the
timezone contract and pre-approval etiquette.

commits.message: add OpenRouter as a second model gateway
commits.body:
The catalog already carried a `gateway` column and a registry built for a
second adapter. The runtime did not: every model was constructed from an id
alone, so the gateway a role was bound to was read from the binding row,
carried through resolution, and then dropped.

A model is named by ONE string in six places — tenant `ai.config`, an agent's
`modelOverride`, a session pick, an `AI_*_MODEL` seed, a select value, a role
seed. Rather than add a parallel gateway field to each, a model **ref** names
both: `<gateway>:<model id>`, with a bare id meaning the default gateway. So
`openai/gpt-4o` and `vercel:openai/gpt-4o` are the same model, nothing stored
needed migrating, and a Vercel-only install sees byte-identical strings.

The ref head is matched against the registered gateway set rather than split
on the first colon, because OpenRouter's own ids carry colons
(`meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct:free`). It is deliberately not the
`openrouter/openai/…` slash spelling — that ambiguity with `provider/model`
is what the gateway column was added to fix.

No new dependency: OpenRouter speaks the OpenAI wire protocol, and
`@ai-sdk/openai` already resolves to the `@ai-sdk/provider` version `ai@7`
expects, so `createOpenAI` with a base URL is the whole integration.

- `resolveLanguageModel` replaces three private copies of a predicate that
  asked "does this look like a gateway id?" instead of "which gateway serves
  it?". The safeguard and observational-memory models consequently gain the
  gateway file-data middleware the agent path always had — a no-op on the
  text-only prompts they see.
- Model calls are not confined to apps/ai, and `modules/inbox` reads the
  binding table itself, so the gateway-aware `AI_SDK_DEFAULT_PROVIDER` lives
  in ai-core and is installed by both hosts. Embeddings and images stay on
  Vercel: OpenRouter serves chat only, and routing them would break search
  for an install that merely moved its chat roles.
- The adapter's real work is vocabulary translation. `isCapableAgentModel`
  asks for a `tool-use` tag; OpenRouter reports `supported_parameters`.
  Untranslated, every OpenRouter model would look tool-incapable and vanish
  from every agent picker.
- Pickers key options by ref. Keyed by id, two gateways' rows for one model
  collapsed into a single unselectable entry — in the binding console, the
  model matrix, and the picker dialog's React keys.
- A grant names a model, not a route, so the allow-list compares with the ref
  head stripped: which gateway serves a role is a platform binding the tenant
  cannot see or set.
- Catalog sync is fail-soft per gateway. With one adapter, "a gateway threw"
  and "the run failed" were the same event; with two, an OpenRouter outage
  would have skipped Vercel's pricing pass and reported a total failure over
  a catalog that refreshed fine.

Known gap: `ai.model_pricing` is keyed by model id alone, so a model served by
both gateways gets one price row. Registration order makes that deterministic
(Vercel first, so existing billing is never repriced), but gateway-keyed
pricing needs a migration on the pricing table and a gateway on the usage
event, which records the model id only.

  from every agent picker.
- Pickers key options by ref. Keyed by id, two gateways' rows for one model
  collapsed into a single unselectable entry — in the binding console, the
  model matrix, and the picker dialog's React keys.
- A grant names a model, not a route, so the allow-list compares with the ref
  head stripped: which gateway serves a role is a platform binding the tenant
  cannot see or set.
- Catalog sync is fail-soft per gateway. With one adapter, "a gateway threw"
  and "the run failed" were the same event; with two, an OpenRouter outage
  would have skipped Vercel's pricing pass and reported a total failure over
  a catalog that refreshed fine.

Known gap: `ai.model_pricing` is keyed by model id alone, so a model served by
both gateways gets one price row. Registration order makes that deterministic
(Vercel first, so existing billing is never repriced), but gateway-keyed
pricing needs a migration on the pricing table and a gateway on the usage
event, which records the model id only.

commits.message: pick and propose article templates during ingest
commits.body:
The wizard's Output step had no template control at all, and hard-coded
`templateHasStructure={false}` — so the content checkboxes could not know
that a structured template already carries the body. It now resolves what
`inherit` actually points at by walking the category chain, names it in the
picker, and persists the binding. Only the explicit binding carries an id:
`inherit` and `none` are modes, and leaving a stale id beside them is how a
source ends up bound to a template the user thought they had switched off.

Choosing a template before reading the crawl is the same problem the concept
analyzer solves for the agentic brief, one level down — the useful template
is the shape the entries already share, and only the entries know it. So
`POST /api/kb/sources/:id/suggest-template` reads a sample and proposes one:
an H2 skeleton plus the typed fields those entries repeat. It creates
nothing; the user creates it from the proposal, in the wizard or on the
source's Ingest tab.

The model proposes labels and types only. Keys and ids are minted here,
because a property key must be a unique lowercase slug and a model inventing
them is how you get `property_definitions` the API rejects — after the user
has already waited for the suggestion. Umlauts transliterate before NFD
strips combining marks, so "Zuständigkeit" becomes `zustaendigkeit` rather
than `zustandigkeit`.

Neither response schema uses `.optional()`: strict structured output requires
every property to appear in `required`, and one optional field makes the
provider reject the whole schema with no hint about which.

commits.message: open the add-source wizard as a large modal
commits.body:
A full page was the wrong shell for it: adding a source is something you do
from wherever you are, and routing away meant losing the page you were on to
a flow you might abandon two steps in. The wizard is now a dialog on the
sources list, sized to the widest thing it shows — the index browser and the
analyzer's concept list — with only the step body scrolling, so the progress
rail and the Back/Next footer stay put.

`/sources/new` survives as a deep link that redirects to the list and asks it
to open the wizard. That request travels as a search param, not router state:
a Space rewrites `/mdl/...` to `/s/<key>/...` with its own navigation, and
state does not survive the hop — which is why the first attempt silently
landed on the list with no dialog.

The wizard remounts per opening. Reopening on step four of an abandoned run,
pointing at a source someone has since deleted, is worse than starting over.

commits.message: add sources through a guided wizard
commits.body:
Adding a source was a dropdown of adapter ids feeding a dialog: you had to
know which adapter you wanted, what its settings meant, and how the result
should be filed — all before seeing a line of the material. The wizard asks
those questions in the order they can actually be answered.

Art → Einrichten → (Auswählen) → Testabruf → Ergebnis. The selection step is
derived, not hard-coded: an adapter that indexes a list earns it, one that
resolves to a single document does not.

The test fetch is the step that earns the design. It creates the source and
fetches up to five entries, then shows what came back, so the plan step —
and the analyzer inside it — works from real text instead of a guess. That
also means the source exists from step four on; abandoning the wizard after
that leaves a valid, un-armed source rather than a half-written draft in
some parallel table.

The plan step persists as the source's standing ingest configuration, and
always writes both activation flags: the wizard is where the mode is
decided, and leaving the other flag undefined would let a stale `true`
survive as a second armed mode nobody asked for.

Step sequencing, the sample cap, the adapter grouping and the plan → config
mapping are pure and unit-tested; the id reader accepts both the enveloped
and unwrapped create responses rather than trusting either.

commits.message: let one large item fill the analysis budget
commits.body:
The excerpt loop sliced each item's text to the per-item allowance and then
rejected any block that pushed past the total. With a sample of one, those
two numbers are the same — so the block overflowed by exactly the length of
its own header and was dropped, every time. The analyzer then reported that
no source material had been provided, which was true and useless: a single
long document is the case it exists for.

The budget is now charged for the whole block, header included, and the
assembly moves into `buildAnalysisExcerpts` so the boundary is testable
without a model call.

commits.message: read uploaded documents, not just store them
commits.body:
A `file_upload` source put the bytes in the vault and left `raw_markdown`
null, so its one item had a file and no content. Every consumer downstream
reads text — ingest, analysis, search — and none of them can read a PDF, so
the source produced empty articles and the analyzer reported, accurately,
that it had been given nothing.

Uploads now go through `/api/kb/convert-document`, which stores the original
under the KB root and extracts markdown in one pass, and the extracted text
rides `settings.body_markdown` into the inbox item the source bootstraps.
A caller that skips conversion still gets a valid source; it just has
nothing to say until the text arrives.

commits.message: analyze concepts first, then derive the pages
commits.body:
The analyzer proposed the source's own table of contents back. On the Wiener
Bauordnung it returned eight pages like "Überblick und geltende Fassung" and
"Übergangsbestimmungen und Änderungshistorie" — document sections, not things
anyone would look up. A wiki organised by document section is just the document
again.

It now works in two steps, and the ordering is the fix. Step one extracts the
concepts and claims: the terms the material establishes, in its own vocabulary,
with what it actually says about each. Step two derives pages from those, one
per major concept, merging only concepts too thin to stand alone — and each
page names the concepts it carries, so nothing is silently dropped. The prompt
says outright that a list reading like a table of contents means the wrong
thing was done.

Same source, after: 25 concepts — Bauplatz, Flächenwidmung, Bauklasse,
Baulinien, Abstandsbestimmungen, Baubewilligung, Nachbarrechte, Bauführer,
Baugebrechen — becoming 24 pages. The drafted brief now tells the agent to name
pages after the law's terms rather than paragraph headings, unprompted.

Two things had to be fixed for concept extraction to be possible at all:

- The per-item excerpt was a flat 3k, so one enormous item (a whole law) got
  the same slice as one of fifty and the analyzer only ever saw the page
  header — it could not have proposed anything but the contents page. The
  prompt budget is now split across the sample, so a single item gets all 40k.
- Manual entries and uploaded files keep their text on the inbox item, not in
  sections, so every such source read as empty. The analyzer now falls back the
  way ingestion does, ignoring promotion status — analysis consumes nothing,
  and an item already made into an article is still evidence of the subject.

The agentic skill follows the same shift: the unit of output is a concept, not
a document; a page named after a section is almost always wrong. Two additions
from the compiled-second-brain loop this is modelled on — new pages must link
into pages that ALREADY existed, not only each other, and where the source
contradicts an existing page the run flags both claims for a human instead of
silently overwriting or quietly keeping both. The summary closes with what
changed.

commits.message: make agentic ingestion plannable and repeatable
commits.body:
Agentic ingestion had three problems: nobody could write the brief, the output
was not really a wiki, and it ran exactly once.

**Analyze** (`kb_source_analyze`, `POST /api/kb/sources/:id/analyze`) answers
the blank instructions box. Writing an authoring brief asks the user to
describe a structure before they have read what the crawl returned, so the
analyzer reads a sample and drafts it for them — returning an overview, the
pages the material actually supports, and a ready `agentic_instructions` value
they edit rather than invent. It writes nothing, so re-running is free. The
sample is spread evenly across the items rather than taken as a prefix: a
crawl is ordered, and the first N pages of one are all front matter.

**Wiki output.** The skill now asks for a hub page plus topic pages nested
under it, where the unit is a topic rather than a crawled document, and the hub
is written twice because its index cannot link to children that do not exist
yet. It also says plainly what agentic ingestion is FOR now that plain
ingestion can split a long document into sub-pages on its own: structure,
synthesis and connections — not the same pages with tidier headings. The step
budget scales with item count; the flat 40 truncated larger sources mid-build
and left an unlinked hub behind.

**Arming.** `ingest_config.authored_active` / `agentic_active` make a mode run
after every successful sync, and both can be armed at once — they write
different things and were never alternatives. The hook is
`RunKbSourceOptions.onSyncComplete`, supplied by the callers that hold auth and
the gateway, so the sync engine stays free of ingestion concerns. An armed run
sends `strategy` only and lets the source's own config supply the rest, and a
failing ingest never turns a sync that fetched its items into a failed one.

Because runs now repeat, the agent is told to survey existing articles first
and update them, and to always pass `original_document_url` — it is the dedup
key, so the URL stays the source URL even for uploaded documents. Agentic runs
also write `source_references` and honour `attach_original`, which the authored
path gained in the previous commit.

Verified live: the analyzer produced a German brief for the Wiener Bauordnung
with structure, naming, nesting depth and grounding constraints, and applying
it filled the instructions field; arming a source made a plain sync create its
article with no ingest call. The agent's own wiki-authoring loop is covered by
tests and types but was not run end to end here.

commits.message: let long ingest calls outlive the client timeout
commits.body:
The api-client aborts after 15s, but an ingest pass runs the whole pipeline
inside the request — the 802 KB law took minutes. The server finished and the
articles landed; the browser had given up long before, so the toast never
fired, the "view article" navigation never happened, and the run looked like it
had failed.

Both long calls now carry their own signal. The real fix is to move ingestion
to a background job and poll it, the way agentic runs already do via a task —
this stops the UI lying about work that succeeded.

commits.message: one ingest flow, independent content options
commits.body:
"Artikel erstellen" and "Zusammenfassung" were never rival strategies — they
differed only in how many articles came out, and were identical in every other
respect. They are now one flow: pick the grouping (`per_entry` / `per_source`),
then tick what each article should contain.

The content axes become independent switches, replacing the `content_mode`
enum that conflated "apply the template structure" with "full text vs summary"
and so made a page carrying both inexpressible. A bound template's structure is
now simply applied whenever it has one, and the switches decide the rest:

- `include_full_content` / `include_summary` — combinable, and at least one
  must survive unless a template structure can carry the body on its own.
- `split_long_articles` — an oversized body becomes an index page plus
  sub-pages: with `per_entry` cut at the document's own shallowest repeating
  heading level, with `per_source` one sub-page per entry. The index is written
  twice, because the contents list can only link to children that already have
  ids, and a table of contents you cannot navigate is not one.
- `include_questions` — answers with citation links land in the body, where a
  link can actually render, while `questions_answered` keeps the plain question
  list retrieval already consumes. Widening that column into a structured type
  would have touched every reader, snapshot and version-restore path.
- `attach_original` — sets the document NAME as well as the url, without which
  the Files block never rendered and the original was invisible.

Two gaps found along the way: ingest wrote no `source_references` at all, so
the provenance block on an ingested article was always empty; and requested
flags now beat the source's stored defaults field by field, so an explicit
`false` is not swallowed by a stored `true`.

Renaming the strategy values needs no migration — `strategy` is a request
field, never persisted.

Verified live on the 802 KB Wiener Bauordnung: one index page plus 194
sub-pages, one per Artikel and per §, each linked from the contents list, with
12 answered questions carrying citations back to RIS and 137 provenance rows.

commits.message: open an attached web original instead of signing it
commits.body:
`original_document_url` holds a vault object key for uploaded documents but
a plain page URL for anything captured from the web, and the download button
fed both to `getFileStorageSignedUrl` — which can only sign a storage key, so
a web original failed instead of opening.

commits.message: ingest large documents whole
commits.body:
A consolidated law, a long reference page, anything book-sized arrived at
the knowledge base as a stub. The RIS page carrying the entire Wiener
Bauordnung is ~1.3MB of HTML; retrieval capped the body at 2MB with a 15s
timeout, then stored the extracted markdown as one section that
downstream consumers truncated — what survived covered §§ 0 to 5b out of
roughly 140 paragraphs. An agent asked to build a wiki from it could
either invent the rest or report the gap; both are failures we caused.

Raise the per-item retrieval cap to 10MB with a 30s timeout, since source
items are stored whole, and split oversized markdown into ordered
`markdown:N` sections instead of cutting it off, each carrying its part
number so a reader can tell a chunk from a document. Reassembly now takes
the readable kinds only (the provenance HTML sections sit next to the
markdown), falling back to everything for items stored before this.

commits.message: govern approvals and model per goal
commits.body:
Until now the trust dial ran tenant → space → agent, and the model came
from the tenant alone. But a goal is where the work actually differs: one
goal in a space may be routine enough to run unattended while its
neighbour touches customer data, and a planning-heavy goal may be worth a
stronger model than everything else in the tenant.

Two nullable columns on goals, surfaced as pills beside the target-date
and progress pills on the goal page: approval mode (inherit, manual,
auto, pass-all) and model (inherit, or one of the tenant's bound tiers).
The build-brief step stamps both into the run envelope, where the
consumers already wait for them — `goal_approval_mode` folds in as one
more most-restrictive-wins layer for tool gating and for done-vs-review
completion, and `model_id` rides the resolver's override slot.

A goal can only tighten what the tenant and space allow, never loosen it,
so the pill is a brake and not a bypass. Unset means inherit, and an
explicit null clears the override.

commits.message: only a human may resolve a tool approval
commits.body:
`tasks_resolve_tool_approval` is a tasks-module operation, and the
coordinator's execute policy allows every operation in that module. So
on 2026-08-22 a coordination run answered its own gate: a parked
`kb_source_delete` on a task it was unblocking came back as
"Approved kb_source_delete (this task). Re-running." An agent that can
lift its own human-approval gate is not gated at all.

Guard both endpoints (the gateway operation and the HTTP route) with
`assertHumanApprovalActor`: a non-user principal, or any call carrying an
agent id — an agent riding a user's token included — is refused. The
guard sits at the endpoints rather than inside the service on purpose,
so server-side callers acting on a decision the human already made
elsewhere (the connections-resume subscriber) keep working.

commits.message: headless runs survive token expiry and never repeat a write
commits.body:
Two failures from the same 2026-08-22 knowledge-base runs, both in the
seam between a long-lived run and the core it calls.

A service token lives 15 minutes and a task run can outlive it: the
28-minute ENG-34 run hit 401 on every module tool once its dispatch-time
bearer expired and finished reporting it could not write anything, while
a probe run started minutes later worked instantly. A service credential
can re-mint, so give the run's core clients a refresh seam: on 401 the
client re-mints once, retries only with a token different from the one
that just failed (so a 401 that is not about expiry cannot loop), and
keeps the fresh token for the rest of its life. Interactive user tokens
have no mint path — for them a 401 still surfaces unchanged.

Approval grants also make a repeated write free to execute: an approved
`kb_source_create` inserted two identical sources 35 seconds apart,
because the park had gone through the bulk pre-approval path, which
records no per-call arguments, so nothing was replayed on resume and the
re-briefed model created the source twice. The gate cannot catch that —
it passes both times. So the execute layer now registers every successful
non-read-only invoke under a canonical invocation key and refuses an
identical repeat with the first call's result attached, which also hands
the model back the record id whose loss caused the duplicate. `_repeat:
true` authorizes a deliberate second execution and is stripped before the
input reaches the gate or core.

commits.message: give the work coordinator its own model tier
commits.body:
The coordinator declared `purpose: "routing"`, and routing maps to the
`router` role binding — a small routing model (gpt-oss-20b here). Planning
a goal is not a route pick: on 2026-08-22 a coordination run died with
"reached its maximum output length before finishing" halfway through
writing its plan, leaving the goal with no tasks.

Add a distinct `coordinator` purpose that keeps the stored
`coordinator_model_id` knob (legacy field name, shared with routing) but
binds to the chat-grade `model.high` role, and resolve a
`coordinatorModelId` alongside the other tiers so `modelForPurpose` can
hand it to the agent. The coordinator declares the new purpose; the
compiled-in id stays the structural fallback for runs that resolve no
config.

`@engenty/ai-core` is consumed from dist — rebuild it after touching the
purpose tables, or apps/ai keeps resolving against the old union.

commits.message: replay an approved parked tool call exactly once on resume
commits.body:
A headless run that parks needs_approval now records the exact gated call
(operation + args) in the background task's suspend payload. The tier-1
resume hands it back as resumeData — Mastra clears the payload when a
resume claims the task, which makes the replay single-use — and the
resumed run executes it once inside its own ALS (attributed, space-gated,
pre-gated) before the model turn, briefing the model with the result.

Previously the resumed model turn restarted from the bare brief and had
to re-derive the call: on 2026-08-22 an approved tasks_create ran twice
(ENG-22 unattributed + ENG-23) on goal 01a02926. Fresh dispatches cannot
carry replay calls (resumeData-only), bulk pre-approvals and pre-change
parks record no args and keep the old behavior.

commits.message: reviews become to-dos and the trust dial governs completion
commits.body:
A finished agent run used to park every task at in_review while announcing
itself as task_completed — reviews blocked dependents with no to-do anywhere,
and the agent-approval mode (tenant → space → agent) had no say. Now a
review-parked run emits task_review_requested (high), which the briefing's
approvals lane and the inbox already treat as a to-do, and a new completion
policy resolves the same trust dial: manual parks for review, auto/pass-all
completes straight to done so dependents dispatch. Ordinary task/goal writes
are re-graded from blanket high risk to medium — the coordinator creates
tasks without a blind approval under auto — while deletes stay high.

commits.message: safe-area + dynamic viewport foundation, phone smoke lane
commits.body:
Phase 0 of PLAN-mobile.md: make the web app hold up at phone width, which is
also the UI layer the planned Tauri mobile shell will bundle.

footers.value:
- viewport-fit=cover, and a --ui-safe-* token set (design-tokens/ui-viewport.css)
  fed into --ui-scroll-safe-bottom and the copilot dock clearance, so pinned
  content clears the home indicator. Every inset is 0px off-device, so desktop
  layout is unchanged.

  full-height layouts sit under the URL bar and the composer is pushed

  onto an empty navigation: Settings and the avatar were the only reachable

  login. The readiness signal now matches either half of the shell.

descriptor emulates viewport and user agent, not notch insets.

next field added to agentConfigSchema fails loudly here instead of
arriving empty.

now render their own German chips.

commits.message: one chat-input base for every chat lane
commits.body:
The specialist desk drew its own composer: full width with a hard-coded
right pad to dodge the copilot FAB, no queue-while-running, no effort
chooser — a second chat that happened to look like the first. Both panels
also carried their own copy of the same ~150 lines of composer wiring, and
they had already drifted.

Extract that base as `components/copilot/chat-lane`:

- `chat-lane-layout` — the one column measure. Every lane surface now
  imports it instead of repeating `max-w-[42rem]`, which is how the desk
  drifted to full width in the first place.
- `use-chat-lane-composer` — draft recovery, the queue, interrupt
  resolution, sandbox approve/reject, stop-and-clear.
- `ChatLaneDock` — queued messages + the parked decision chooser (was
  `AgentDeskChatDock`, plus an inline twin in the copilot panel).
- `chatLanePanelBaseProps` — the shared panel configuration.

The copilot chat, the specialist desk and the space home landing now line
up on the same measure and offer the same composer, effort chooser
included (host-keyed, injected by the app since ai-ui cannot import the
copilot module).

A specialist stays in its lane: no position menu, so no drawer, sidebar or
floating window — and no realtime voice, which drives the app through the
copilot's frontend tools a specialist does not carry.

commits.message: rebuild the Data landing on the design system
commits.body:
The previous version was written without reading docs/agent/DESIGN.md,
which is canonical for look-and-feel. It broke six rules at once.

- **Title and CTA belong to the chrome.** The page had an `h1` plus a
  lead paragraph restating its own tab name, and no breadcrumb. Now the
  name is a breadcrumb and the content starts with content.
- **No intros.** The lead is gone. The mount note stays (P1.4 still
  requires the tab to say it) but moves to `CardSection.Caption`, below
  the card it describes — a footnote, which is what it always was.
- **Topbar actions are compact.** Pairing `topbarChrome: "contentBlend"`
  with the existing `contentStackBackground: "paper"` puts the CTA in the
  `app-topbar-actions` cascade (`h-7 px-2 text-xs`, `size-3.5` icons)
  instead of rendering a full-size outline button in the bar. The
  hand-rolled `mr-2` on its icon is gone too; the container sets `gap-1`.
- **Section headings are `CardSection`, not hand-rolled Tailwind.** This
  is a hub, so they take the `display` variant rather than the invented
  uppercase micro-label.
- **Card surfaces are `CardSection.Body`** (`.ui-canvas-panel`,
  `border-0`). The old cards carried their own `border bg-card`, which

commits.message: make the Data tab landing a real dashboard
commits.body:
It was three equally-weighted lists — Starred, Recent, "In this space" —
under two paragraphs of prose. Two of those lists are empty for anyone
who has not used the tab, so the page a new person met was mostly
apology text, and the one thing they needed (the way in) was a row of
small tiles at the bottom.

Now it answers two questions and stops. **Entry points**: the tree's own
top level — mounted modules, Projects, connected folders — as cards big
enough to aim at, derived by splitting the drive's nodes on kind
(container = a way in, everything else = an asset). **Latest**: the
space's own assets, newest first, with when they changed, using the
`updatedAt` the drive already loads. No new fetch, and deliberately no
item counts on the entry points: a root's size is a query over that
module's records, and a dashboard that ran five of them to draw its
first screen would be the store this projection promises not to be.

The personal shelf (starred, recently opened) drops below and renders
only once it holds something. The CTA moves into the page's real top bar
via `usePageConfig({actions})`, which is where the layout rule for this
pane puts it. The mount note (P1.4) stays but becomes a footnote to the
list it explains rather than a preamble to the page.

Also fixed, and the reason to check a German UI rather than a
screenshot: every string Phase 3 added was missing from the German
locale, so the tab read half-English ("LATEST", "Edited vor 11
Stunden"). Added, along with the delete/rename dialogs and the action
labels. The outcome classifier now returns a KIND and no message for the
two sentences that are ours — it is pure and has no `t`, so the caller
translates; the server's own message still passes through verbatim
because it names the module's action, which is the useful half.

commits.message: the Data tab becomes a place you can do things
commits.body:
The tree was a reader and the file manager was the editor — two screens
over one store, which is the split this design exists to remove. Phase 3
gives the tree the actions, and they go through `/data/*`: a person
renaming a folder and an agent renaming it are now one call with one gate
behind it.

**Gating happens before the click.** The roots and every listing carry
`capabilities` derived from the adapter's optional methods, so Contacts —
which deliberately has no `createNode` — shows no "New folder" rather
than one that 405s. Live: Contacts renders no row menu at all, Files
does. An app that offers actions which do not work teaches people it is
flaky, and they stop trusting the ones that do.

Caught while verifying: the Files ROOT was offering Rename and Delete,
which the server correctly refuses ("removed by unmounting the module").
A root is a module's presence in the space, not a folder in it — fixed,
and the root now offers only "New folder".

- Row menu on hover (a `⋯` button, not right-click alone: right-click is
  undiscoverable and unreachable on touch), staying open via
  `group-focus-within` so it does not vanish under the pointer.
- CTA in the TOP BAR, not a toolbar in the content — that layout was
  rejected once already for this pane. It asks which root only when more
  than one can hold a folder.
- P3.3: the four outcomes are told apart. An approval is not an error and
  must not wear an error's colour; a 409 offers a reload. The trap, now
  covered by tests: an adapter's refusal arrives FLAT through
  `invokeOperation`'s passthrough while core's own is wrapped, so the api
  client decodes it as `request_failed` and the real code survives only
  in `details`.
- P3.5: the copilot slice carries what may be DONE here, as a sentence —
  the negative half ("you cannot create or delete here from the tree")
  is what stops an agent discovering limits by attempting them.
- P1.4 / decision 2, said where a person can read it: module folders
  appear when the module is mounted; projects and pinned artifacts belong
  to the space itself and are always shown.
- P3.2: the files module's space Files tab is DELETED. It was the second
  editor over the space's own files; the file manager stays for the
  PROJECT file space, which has no Data tab.

commits.message: connected folders become write targets
commits.body:
P2.1's inventory corrected the plan's premise: the connector modules ARE
in this repo (modules/connections/providers/*), and only **S3** declares
`storage`. Drive and OneDrive have bespoke `create_file`/`upload_file`
actions that are NOT wired to the capability, and local-files cannot
write at all (its bridge protocol has no write verb). So the tree can be
taught to write today, and exactly one provider answers.

- connections-sdk: `filesWrite`/`filesDelete`/`filesMove` calling the
  SYNTHESIZED action ids, so the connection's policy, the ask-by-default
  gate on group `write`/`destructive`, approvals and audit all apply with
  no new gate code. Plus `isStorageCapable`, which answers the PRIOR
  question — can this provider be written at all — without attempting a
  write.
- connector-file-source implements deleteFile / moveFile / renameFile /
  replaceContent. Folder verbs refuse BY NAME: the capability is file-only,
  so creating a folder in a mount is not a permission we lack but a gesture
  the provider contract does not have.
- Capability is negotiated, not attempted: the listing reports `readOnly`
  from `isStorageCapable`, so a read-only mount renders read-only instead
  of offering an action that fails. A client that cannot be asked answers
  "not writable" — the safe direction.

Virtual node ids now carry the PARENT ref. A provider entry has no parent,
but the capability addresses a write by folder + name, so an id that knew
only the file could rename nothing. Appended, so ids minted before this
still decode and report `parentRef: null` — which reads as "position
unknown" and makes the write paths refuse rather than guess a destination
and relocate somebody's document.

Two honest limits, stated in code rather than discovered later: overwrite
semantics on `replaceContent` are the PROVIDER's (S3 replaces; another
connector might duplicate), and `expectedUpdatedAt` cannot be enforced
against a provider with no compare-and-set, so the native source's
conflict guarantee does not hold across a mount.

Also fixed: the read-only refusals threw SYNCHRONOUSLY from methods
declared to return a Promise, so a caller using `.catch()` — which the
declaration entitles them to — got an exception past their handler.

Decision 5 resolves itself: `sourceFolderId` is not editable after mount
creation (no PATCH route, no store update), so re-pointing cannot be a
silent privilege change.

commits.message: guard workspace delete, add move/copy, resume headless approvals
commits.body:
**P1.6 — the delete gate.** Mastra ships `mastra_workspace_delete`
UNGATED and it takes `recursive`, so one call could empty a prefix of
`/shared` and nothing asked. `EXECUTE_COMMAND` already had the answer:
the per-tool `WorkspaceToolsConfig`. The gate is DYNAMIC, so it sees the
call's args — an agent tidying one file in its own `/home` is not asked,
while anything recursive, anything on a shared/containment mount, and
anything in `/data` is. It fails closed: a target it cannot read gates.
There is deliberately no setting meaning "never ask".

**Move and copy, which Mastra has neither of.** The filesystem layer has
`moveFile`/`copyFile`; the gap was one layer thick. Ours work ACROSS
MOUNTS, which is the reason to have them: `Workspace.filesystem` is a
composite, so a single provider's `moveFile` cannot express
`/task/draft.md` → `/shared/reports/final.md`, and carrying an artefact
out of a run's scratch into the commons is the whole "store my work"
gesture. A folder move is a bounded batch that REPORTS truncation, and
it removes the source only when the copy was complete — deleting the
origin of a truncated move would destroy the files that did not make it.

**P1.6b — headless approval, resolved by reading the lane.** The earlier
"bridge it or disable it" framing was wrong. `requireApproval` is
evaluated at tool-EXECUTION time, and the leaf lane runs its whole
lifecycle inside `engentyToolsRunAls.run(...)`, so the gate closure reads
the same `approvalGrants` a gated module op consults. The one missing
piece was the `tool_suspended` case in delegate-run's existing subscribe,
forwarding to the same `onApprovalRequired` callback — so the task now
records it in `pendingByOp`, parks `needs_action` instead of reporting a
failure, and the grant a human writes is what the gate reads on
re-dispatch. Grant ids are PATH-scoped: approving one recursive delete
must not license every future one.

commits.message: /data becomes a real filesystem, and delete lands gated
commits.body:
**P1.5 — mkdir stops lying.** `//data` was a `FilesSDKFilesystem` over an
object-store adapter, whose `mkdir` is a documented no-op. An agent that
made a folder got success, listed it, found nothing, and made it again —
not a failure but a LOOP, indistinguishable from a slow write.

The `WorkspaceFilesystem` contract already declares mkdir/rmdir/moveFile/
copyFile/deleteFile. It was never Mastra that could not express a folder,
it was the wrapper we picked. `SpaceDataFilesystem` implements the
contract directly against the data endpoints, one method per endpoint,
and an adapter with no `createNode` surfaces a typed "not supported here"
instead of a silent success. `copyFile` composes read + create rather
than asking modules for a `copy` — a module-implemented copy would be a
second way to mint a record, sidestepping its own create's schema.

The files-sdk adapter STAYS for sandbox staging (D6), where an
object-shaped read-through cache is the right shape. Both faces now share
one HTTP client and, importantly, ONE `SpaceDataRequestError`: two
classes of that name would fail every `instanceof` across the seam and
silently break the force-delete and exists paths.

**Delete, with the cascade priced in.** `deleteNode` on the protocol,
`DELETE /data/delete` carrying `recursive` (default FALSE — a cascade
happens because someone asked, never because a default made it
convenient), and the files adapter implementing it. The folder operation
is `riskLevel: high`, which is not documentation: `evaluatePolicy`
escalates agent principals on high/critical, so that level IS the gate. A
non-empty folder without `recursive` is refused 409 naming its child
count, because the underlying delete cascades unconditionally.

commits.message: let the Files adapter save an edit
commits.body:
Live verification found the root reporting `writable: false` — an agent
could read a file in Files/ but not save it, which is half a face.

`files_space_write` maps onto the file source's existing `replaceContent`,
so `baseVersion` travels straight through to its REQUIRED
`expectedUpdatedAt` and the tree inherits the file manager's conflict
answer instead of growing a second one. Verified live: a stale write
answers 409 `data_conflict` carrying the current version.

Base64 is verified by re-encoding rather than trusted, the same check the
HTTP save route makes — `Buffer.from(…, "base64")` accepts a good deal of
near-base64 and quietly produces garbage.

commits.message: the space's own files become a Data adapter root
commits.body:
The file space was the last lane of the Daten tab no agent could reach:
everything else is a module adapter root or a store agents already have
tools for, while the space's own folders were visible to a person,
invisible to an agent, and editable only through a second screen.

- plugin-sdk: SpaceDataAdapter gains OPTIONAL createNode/moveNode.
  Absent means unsupported, exactly as an absent `write` already means
  read-only, so no existing adapter changes and no record module is
  forced to pretend it has folders. No deleteNode yet — a cascade that
  takes children AND blobs waits for the approval plumbing.
- core: POST /data/create and /data/move, dispatching like the existing
  four (same resolveTarget, same traversal gate, same rooting on the way
  out). A move stays inside one root: crossing roots is a different
  operation, not a slow move, so it is refused by name.
- files: registers its space file space as module OPERATIONS — an HTTP
  route lives in a different registry from a module operation, so the
  file manager's routes were reachable by a browser and by nothing else.
  Space-scoped deliberately: a free-form owner would make these the
  first agent-callable way into a PROJECT's file space, whose visibility
  is work containment's to decide.
- files: the Files/ adapter root. A file's name carries its record id
  because filenames are NOT unique per folder — resolving a duplicate by
  picking the first match would open the wrong file, silently — and
  `title` carries what a reader should see.

Files/ is mount-gated from day one and the old ungated drive lane is
DELETED rather than kept as a fallback: reading it as well would show
every folder twice and keep an ungated path alive beside the gated one.
Nothing is backfilled — spaces are unreleased, so mount `files` by hand
where a space should show its files.

commits.message: a module mounted in a space knows which of its pages is open
commits.body:
The copilot fix generalises: every module was written with matchers against
`/mdl/<module>/…`, and inside a space that is not the URL — the shell mirrors
each module at `/s/<key>/<segment>/…` and redirects canonical links there. So
each matcher quietly answered "no" for the whole time a user stood in a space,
and there is no error to notice.

The tasks sidebar was the loudest: `isTasksListPath` never matched, so opening
Aufgaben inside a space left the panel on its Routinen default, listing
routines where the tasks belong. Contacts, invoices, offers, projects and
time-tracking lost every active row. The inbox never knew it was on settings.
The knowledge base lost its nav state, and three list routes never fired the
redirect that supplies the KB slug. Link prefetching died wholesale: the root
gates on `startsWith("/mdl/")`, so no module prefetched anything in a space.

One `canonicalModulePathname` in ai-core, beside the alias table that already
exists because two readers needed it. Applied where each component takes
`useLocation().pathname` — one call, and every pure matcher below keeps
working unchanged. The space prefix says where a module is MOUNTED, never
which of its pages is open, so it is noise to all of them.

`canonicalCopilotChatPathname` now delegates rather than carrying a second
copy of the regex; it keeps only the part that is really copilot-specific,
returning another module's route untouched so `startsWith` cannot claim
`/mdl/offers/chat/…`.

Verified live in a space: the tasks sidebar lists tasks and selects Aufgaben;
contacts marks `data-active` on Alle and nothing else.

commits.message: do not offer a composer on a thread nobody may write to
commits.body:
U3 put a task's agent threads on the task page, and opening one lands in
the copilot with a full composer. `appendMessage` is owner-only, and a
headless agent thread has no owner at all — so every send from there was
going to be rejected, with the box still sitting there inviting the next
one.

`isThreadWritableByViewer` mirrors the server's rule (owner, never the
task escape hatch `listMessages` has: reading an executor's record is a
right the task can grant, writing into it is not), and the panel swaps
the composer for a read-only note through the same `composerOverride`
seam realtime voice already uses. A courtesy, never the gate — the gate
stays server-side.

Nothing loaded yet and a brand-new chat both stay writable; the composer
is the entire point of that surface.

commits.message: a chat link opens the chat it names, inside a space too
commits.body:
Every matcher that reads a chat URL was written against
`/mdl/engenty-copilot/chat/…`. Since chat became a per-space surface, that
is not the URL the app is on: `LegacyModuleRedirect` sends the canonical
form to `/s/<key>/copilot/chat/…`, so the matchers were answering "not a
chat route" about a chat route, and two things fell out of it silently.

The thread id in the link was never read, so `/chat/<id>` opened whatever
chat was last active — the link named one thread and the page showed
another, which is exactly what the task page's "linked sessions" row does
for a living. And with the full page mistaken for the drawer, nothing
synced the URL afterwards: selecting a chat in the sidebar swapped the
transcript while the address bar stayed frozen on the id it had ignored,
so reloading or sending that link landed somewhere else again.

One normaliser, `canonicalCopilotChatPathname`, applied by all four
readers. The space prefix says where the module is mounted, never which
chat is open, so it is noise below that line — and normalising the read
side beats teaching four matchers a second shape.

The write side needs the opposite: `resolveSessionPath` now builds a
space-prefixed path while standing in a space. Emitting `/mdl/…` there
worked only by bouncing through the redirect, which resolves the
REMEMBERED space rather than the one in the URL, and spent a history
entry per selection.

commits.message: a comment posted mid-run reaches the running agent (U4)
commits.body:
Typing "actually, use the other address" while an agent worked did
nothing. The comment was written to the task — correctly, it is the
collaboration record — and the observer's live-run branch then returned
without doing anything with it, so the loop finished on stale
instructions and the only recourse was to reject the result and dispatch
again.

A live task run now publishes a way to be reached, the same shape
`run-abort-registry` already uses for cancel: the delegated conversation
hands out a `deliver` bound to a second `sendMessage`, which the agentic
loop drains as inbound input, and the registry is keyed by TASK because
the caller is looking at a task and checkout makes that unambiguous.

The comment is written to `task_comments` FIRST and stays there whatever
happens next — this is delivery, never storage. `{delivered: false}` is
an ordinary answer (nothing live, another replica, the loop refused) and
the caller falls back to exactly what it did before: the comment waits on
the task and the next dispatch's brief replays it.

Verified live, both directions. A 20-step run given "the SECRET WORD is
PELIKAN" three steps in ended with `SECRET=PELIKAN` in the same run, no
park and no re-dispatch; a run that finished three seconds before the
same call answered `delivered: false` and ended `SECRET=NONE`.

Not built: the `sendNotificationSignal` + `ifIdle` wake the plan paired
with this. An idle task already dispatches a continuation run, and a
second mechanism for a case that is covered is exactly the fallback the
no-fallbacks rule forbids.

commits.message: surface a task's agent threads, and close an append hole (U3)
commits.body:
"Verknüpfte Sitzungen" was structurally empty for agent work, not
occasionally empty: the thread list joins on `thread_participant`, and a
headless task thread has no participants — nobody owns an executor's
working memory. Now that U1 makes those threads stable per (task, agent),
they are worth showing, so they get their own task-gated route:
`GET /ai/v1/tasks/:taskId/threads`, answering with the caller's right to
read the TASK, which is the same rule that already lets a task's watchers
open a run transcript.

Owned threads stay out of it. A person's chat that happens to name a task
is their private chat and belongs to the participant list; the panel
merges the two sources and labels which is which.

Two things found on the way:

- `appendMessage` had NO ownership check. `getRequiredSession` filters on
  tenant + thread, so any member holding a thread uuid could put a
  message into a colleague's conversation; RLS would have refused, but
  the AI service holds the service-role key and bypasses it, so the
  service method was the whole boundary. Owner only — deliberately
  without the task escape hatch that `listMessages` has: reading an
  executor's record is a right the task grants, speaking into it is not.
- Two `tasks_add_comment` callers passed no `kind` and so defaulted to
  `note`, rendering as a person's comment with no author to show. The
  applied-field-updates notice is `system` (nobody typed it); the KB
  ingest outcome is `result` (it IS the task's outcome, and that is what
  a dependent task inherits).

commits.message: an answer in the comment thread carries its question
commits.body:
The copilot's resolved chooser shows the question with the answer beneath
it; the task comment thread showed neither. A reply reads "Hans" with
nothing attached, and by the time anyone scrolls back the agent has
posted two more comments in between — so the record of what was decided
is only reconstructable, never readable.

Nothing is stored to fix this. The pairing is derived the way a person
reads a thread: a question is answered by the next comment from a
DIFFERENT author. An agent asking again before anyone replies has
superseded its own question, not answered it — otherwise a double
`task_ask_user` pairs question #1 with question #2 and hangs the real
answer off the wrong one.

Also renders the options a question OFFERED, marking the one taken. They
live in the comment's metadata and were drawn only by the live answer
card, so answering erased all trace of what the choice had been between.

commits.message: give an agent one durable thread per task (U1)
commits.body:
A task job derived its `ai.thread` from the RUN id, so every dispatch
minted a new thread. An agent that parked on a question, waited for an
approval, or crashed and recovered came back to an empty context: the
brief was the only carrier, and anything it had worked out in the
previous run was gone.

The thread is now derived from (task id, actor id) with the same sha1
recipe, so the same agent picking the same task back up continues on its
own working memory — what a person doing the task would have. The brief
still renders every run; it stops being the ONLY context and stays the
cold-start path for a new agent, a human takeover, or a post-deploy run.

The actor is in the key on purpose: reassignment must not hand the
successor the predecessor's notes. A new agent gets a fresh thread and
inherits the task_comments record, exactly as a human successor does.

Two consequences handled here:

- The thread now outlives the run, so `finishTaskJobRun` puts it back to
  `idle`. Registration flips it to `running` on every dispatch and
  nothing else would ever flip it back, leaving worked tasks permanently
  "running" in thread lists. The run's own outcome stays on
  `ai.agent_run`, which is what run history reads.
- A run card must still show ITS run, not the whole working history.
  `resolveRunTranscriptWindow` bounds each run by the next run on the
  same thread — checkout is exclusive, so runs never overlap, and
  partitioning by run START (not `finished_at`) cannot clip what a run
  wrote between its last save and its release.

Verified live: a probe agent invented a codeword, wrote it only into its
reply text, parked on a question; after the answer a LATER dispatch
recalled it, with no comment ever carrying it. Reassigning the task
produced a second thread whose id matches the derivation for the new
actor.

commits.message: upgrade Mastra 1.57.0 → 1.59.0 (U0)
commits.body:
@mastra/core 1.59.0, memory 1.26.2, pg 1.20.0, hono 1.6.1.

Carried forward: the channel-driver unhandled-rejection patch — 1.59 still
re-throws from the driverPromise catch with the same unowned window, so the
patch is recreated against the new dist (both ESM and CJS bundles).

Renames absorbed: validateStoredWorkflow → validateDynamicWorkflow (the
stored→dynamic workflows rename; rehydrateWorkflow is unchanged).

Fixed a real 1.59 regression the crash probe caught: Mastra now initializes
the BackgroundTaskManager in its CONSTRUCTOR (fire-and-forget init, which
runs recoverStaleTasks), so a task a crash left running was re-executed
before boot code could register the executor — "No executor registered for
tool engenty.task-job", record failed, task stranded. The one registration
the constructor performs synchronously before init is the config `tools`
map, so the task job now ships as a config-level tool
(taskJobRecoveryTool): recovery is guaranteed an executor on every manager
instance Mastra ever builds. Mastra's tool→executor adapter forwards no
`suspend`, so a RECOVERED run that stops for a person parks tier-2 — the
crash-degraded lane by design. Steady state still gets the suspend-capable
executor: registerTaskJobExecutor now runs AFTER startWorkers (which
discards a producer-mode manager, taking pre-startWorkers registrations
with it) and overwrites the adapter entry.

Verified live: dispatch → park (suspended, maxRetries carried) → answer →
same run resumed → completed; kill -9 three seconds into a run → next boot
recovered it through the config tool and completed on the original run id
with ONE task_runs row. Suites: 138/138 typecheck, apps/ai 1194.

Known 1.59 storage quirk: background-task `args` is persisted double-encoded
(jsonb string, was object). All our readers go through manager.listTasks(),
which parses — no raw-SQL consumer exists.

commits.message: one run-history row per run
commits.body:
A run that stops for a person parks the task and resumes under the SAME
run id. `tasks_checkout` inserted a run row unconditionally, so the second
checkout minted a second row: run history showed one run twice, split at
the point where it stopped to ask, each fragment carrying its own duration.

Checkout is now reopen-or-insert — an existing row for the run is cleared
of its ending (release only stamps a row whose finished_at is null) rather
than duplicated. A unique index makes the invariant structural, and the
migration collapses the rows already written onto the earliest row of each
group, which inherits the last segment's ending so it spans the whole run.

Verified live: same run id checked out twice across a park-and-answer
cycle, one row, reopened and re-closed as completed.

commits.message: hire an agent from a role instead of from an empty form
commits.body:
Creating a custom agent worked; starting one did not. The form opened
blank and asked a person to invent an id, a job description and a tool
list before knowing what any of them do — so the result was either
nothing or an agent with a one-line prompt that behaves badly.

Four roles now fill the form: art director, marketing writer, research
analyst, operations assistant. Each is a job description written the way
a good AGENTS.md is written — how the role works, and what it explicitly
does not do — because that text IS the agent. Tools stay minimal (the
gateway search/execute pair, plus what a role obviously cannot work
without): a preset that quietly grants more than its role needs is how
agents end up over-permissioned, and the tool picker is right there.

Picking a role is not a mode. It fills the draft and stops mattering;
every field is edited normally afterwards, and blank is one click.

every field is edited normally afterwards, and blank is one click.

commits.message: answering a question resumes the run, instead of starting another
commits.body:
Tier-1 HITL. A run that stops to ask has always parked — question
comment, task in review, inbox card — and that path stays exactly as it
was. What is new is that the run also SUSPENDS on top of it, so the next
dispatch resumes that run rather than enqueueing a second one. A task's
history stays one run across an answer instead of one run per round-trip.

Suspend is an optimization over park, never the only path: if the lookup
fails, the resume fails, or the snapshot is simply gone after a deploy, a
fresh run is dispatched and nothing is lost — both halves of the exchange
are in the comments, which is what P8-1 was for.

The pipeline now reports WHY a run ended rather than only that it ended:
finalize releases the task and reports `released` whatever the reason
was, so "it stopped for a person" has to be read between the steps. That
was a real bug in the first cut — the suspend never fired.

Verified live: the coordinator asked which supplier to use, the run
suspended with the task in review, an answer comment plus the same
"run now" the UI sends resumed that same background task, and the agent
replied "Supplier B" on the original run id.

commits.message: the background substrate IS the dispatch path now
commits.body:
Cutover, after the parity the plan required was proven live: a dispatched
task runs on Mastra's background-task manager, and the six-step workflow,
its registration and the two-substrate switch are deleted rather than
left as a fallback. Verified through the real service on both lanes — a
flow task (gate → in_review) and an agent task (the coordinator answered,
its comment landed, task in_review) — each carried by the manager with
its retry budget intact.

The queue survives, and the comment now says why: `dispatchTaskIfReady`
runs in CORE, which has no Mastra instance, so something must carry "run
this task" across the process boundary. What it stopped carrying is
durability — the consumer hands the message over and acks, because
awaiting the run would only race a redelivery timer against a substrate
that already guarantees it.

that change — it was already unanswerable (its approve route is gone) and
is left alone rather than silently rewritten.

commits.message: run a dispatched task on Mastra's background-task substrate
commits.body:
The queue, the boot resume and two-thirds of the task-job workflow were
infrastructure Mastra did not have when we built them: persistence,
per-agent concurrency, backpressure, stale-task recovery and a lifecycle
stream all ship now. So the six steps become an ordinary function and a
BackgroundTaskManager carries it — which also dissolves the frozen step
list, since a run no longer resumes into the code it was suspended under.

Both substrates run that same function, and a test asserts the workflow's
chain still equals it, so a task cannot behave differently depending on
which carrier picked it up. The switch is `ENGENTY_TASK_DISPATCH_SUBSTRATE`
and the workflow stays the default: the plan requires crash-recovery
parity to be proven before anything is deleted.

Proven, and it found a real trap. `recoverStaleTasks` returns a task the
crash caught to `pending` only when `maxRetries > 0`; with the default 0
it marks it failed and the task row stays `in_progress` forever. Killed a
process mid-run twice: without retries the task was stranded, with them
the next boot re-dispatched it, re-entered on its original run id (the
checkout is idempotent for the same id) and settled it correctly. The
executor is registered by NAME for the same reason — recovery has no
per-task closure to call.

commits.message: a gate decision is written where the question was asked
commits.body:
The question a flow's approval gate raises lands on the task as a
comment; the answer did not — the thread held half a conversation, and
the only record of a decision was the run resuming.

That asymmetry is harmless while every pause parks on the row, and
load-bearing the moment a run can be suspended instead (Phase 8 tier 1):
degrading a suspended run back to the park path must lose nothing, and
it only can if both halves are always in the comments. So the decision
is now recorded there, with the reason a person typed and, as metadata,
who answered — the caller is the service principal, so claiming
authorship would be a lie.

commits.message: an event can start a flow, because its payload becomes the input
commits.body:
An event payload reached a task as PROSE appended to the description —
readable by an agent, unreadable by a flow, which is why event triggers
were rejected at save time whenever they pointed at one.

A trigger may now carry an input mapping in the SAME grammar the graph
canvas uses for its mapping nodes ({value} / {initData,path} /
{template}), with the event payload as initData, so there is one mapping
language platform-wide. With no mapping the payload IS the input, which
is what a flow authored against that event would map internally anyway.
Only a flow target gets this layer: an agent still reads the event as
prose in its brief.

Also fixes what the first live fire exposed: a run that stopped to ASK
(gate, capability, ask_user) rested as `blocked`, and the briefing lists
todo/in_review/backlog — so every question the convergence model routes
to that surface was invisible on it. Waiting on a person is `in_review`;
only a failure is blocked. Nothing re-dispatches either (neither is a
checkout entry status).

Verified live: a webhook fire with {record:{id}} mapped to the flow's
{offer_id}, ran the published flow, hit its approval gate, and the task
came to rest in review with the mapped input on it.

commits.message: one catalog for everything this workspace can run
commits.body:
Two catalogs described one runtime. An ACTION.md compiles to a one-node
flow the first time it is pressed, so /actions and /flows were the same
list twice — and after the press cutover the Actions catalog described a
lane that no longer exists.

Flows is now the only catalog: stored graphs and declared ACTION.md files
merged into one list, deduped on `source_action_id` so a compiled action
appears once, as the flow that actually runs. Where a runnable was
written (file / canvas) and what shape it has are filter chips. A
declared action that nobody has pressed is a fourth status, not a hidden
row.

The admin sidebar drops to the five building blocks (Overview, Agents,
Flows, Skills, Tools); Artifacts, Connections and Activity move to a
second group until their fold-ins land.

Also closes the loose end from the press cutover: the run panel on an
ACTION.md read its history from `ai.action_request` rows keyed on the
ACTION.md id, which a press stopped writing — the audit row is written
against the compiled graph now, so the panel reads the flow's history and
names the task the press created.

commits.message: a button press is a trigger fire, and the action lane is gone
commits.body:
Pressing an Action button started an `action-job` workflow directly — the
one invocation lane with no work record, which is why its approvals had
nowhere to live and `ask_user` asked into the void. A press now takes the
same path as every other invocation: trigger → task → flow.

Everything the press needs is derived from the ACTION.md on demand: the
flow it compiles to, a manual trigger pointing at it (keyed by module_key
`action:<id>`), and a task carrying the press's input and subject. Nothing
is seeded ahead of time; the second press reuses what the first created.

Identity is split on purpose: provisioning runs as the SERVICE principal,
the fire records the person who pressed. Someone allowed to press a button
on a contact is not thereby a routine administrator, and demanding
`module.tasks.write` of them would leave the button to admins only. What
the flow may DO is still gated inside the run. `triggers_fire` therefore
accepts an explicit creator, honoured only when the caller has no user
identity of its own — a user always attributes to itself, so it cannot be
used to blame someone else.

The button reads the task instead of one run: the flow run says whether it
is still going, and the agent's CHILD run carries the steps, the answer
and any proposed updates. Approving them goes to the task's field-updates
route, so the same approval works from the button and from the task page.

Deleted with the lane, not left as a fallback: the action-job start path
and `POST /ai/v1/actions/:actionId/approve` (nothing suspends any more).

footers.value:
pressed "Kontakt anreichern" on a real contact → trigger and flow
provisioned on the spot → task ENG-61 → the agent researched the company →
button went to "Needs approval" → the modal showed both suggestions with
their Impressum sources. Not applied: the contact is real data.

Phase 7 #4.

commits.message: review the field updates a flow's agent proposed
commits.body:
A specialist inside a flow proposes updates and finishes — it does not
suspend the way the action job does — so the suggestions ended up on its
CHILD run with the task holding the decision and no way to reach them. The
task showed "the flow completed", the agent's two researched corrections
sat in a run nobody could open, and that was the end of it.

Three pieces close it:

The flow run snapshot now reports `agentRuns` — the runs its agent nodes
started. A specialist runs under its own id, so from outside, a flow that
had an agent do all the work looks like it did nothing; the child ids are
the only path from a task to what its agent actually said.

`TaskFieldSuggestionsCard` reads those runs and shows what was proposed,
with the evidence and sources the agent cited. Sibling of
TaskFlowGateCard: that one answers a gate the GRAPH declared, this one
answers what the AGENT proposed inside a node.

`POST /ai/v1/tasks/:taskId/field-updates` applies the approved fields
through the module's own update operation, as the CALLER — approving a
suggestion is a human act and is gated by that human's capabilities, like
editing the record by hand. The subject comes from the task's own binding,
never from the request, so an approval cannot be pointed at another record.

footers.value:
a compiled Action researched a contact, proposed a corrected phone
number and registration number with Impressum sources, and the card
rendered both with checkboxes; the route applied a patch through
contacts_update and left the audit comment on the task.

Phase 7 #4 — this was the standing precondition for retiring the action
lane ("field-update approval verified on the task path").

commits.message: a flow with an agent node could not run headlessly at all
commits.body:
`created_by_user_id` on the child run is a core.users FK, and a headless
lane runs as the AI SERVICE principal — whose id is a service_credential
id. Writing it raw failed the insert, which failed the specialist node,
which failed the whole graph: "agent_run insert: violates foreign key
constraint". Same trap `triggers_fire` and `registerTaskJobRun` already
handle; `runDelegatedConversation`'s observe path was the one place left
writing the raw scope id.

Invisible until now because no flow that ran from a task had an agent node
— the seeded gate/apply flows have none — and the button lane passes a
real user's scope, where the raw id was correct all along.

Found by running a compiled Action end to end: ENG-58 ran
`contacts.enhance-contact` as a flow, the specialist researched the
contact, proposed two field updates, and the task settled to in_review.

Also drops a false drift signal in the Action seeder: `jsonb` does not
preserve key order, so comparing raw JSON text made every press look like
a change and mint an identical version. Caught on the second real run.

Phase 7 #4 (part).

commits.message: seed an Action's flow on first use, not by migration
commits.body:
Actions have no per-tenant rows at all — `listAllActions` resolves them per
request from module capabilities — so giving each one a flow means new
persistence. Seeding the fleet would write rows for buttons nobody has
pressed and need a reconcile to stay honest as declarations change.
`ensureActionFlow` does it on USE instead: find-or-create, compare the
stored graph with a fresh compile, and mint + publish a new version only
when the declaration has actually moved. Same shape as
`core_agents_ensure`, and for the same reason.

Identity is a new `source_action_id` column, not the name: a tenant may
already have a flow called "Enhance contact", and (tenant_id, name) is
unique, so keying on the name would either hijack their flow or refuse to
seed ours. Null on every authored flow — which is the distinction that
matters: a row with a source may be rewritten by a recompile, a row
without one belongs to whoever wrote it.

Auto-publishing is deliberate and limited to this path: what governs a
module action is installing the module, and its markdown shipped as code.
A compiled graph is still put through the same save-path validator first —
a flow that could not be saved must not be published either.

Phase 7 #4 (part). Migration 20260816020000, applied locally.

commits.message: compile an Action into the one-node flow it always was
commits.body:
An ACTION.md is one agent, one prompt, an input schema and a tool allow
list — a one-node flow written in a second format. `compileActionToGraph`
derives the stored graph from that declaration, so the parallel runtime can
go without touching authoring: the markdown stays the source of truth.

Two things had to give first, both of them honest fixes rather than
concessions to the compiler:

The save validator demanded a constant `output_schema` on EVERY
run_specialist, though its own reason was "so downstream nodes can be
type-checked". An action is terminal and answers in PROSE — the button
renders it as markdown — and `output_schema` puts the agent under a
"respond with ONLY a JSON object" contract, so the rule made "end by
having an agent answer" unexpressible. It now applies where its reason
does: the graph's last top-level step may go without one; anything nested
stays fail-closed, because inside a container "what follows" is the
container's business.

`run_specialist` never told the specialist WHAT the run was about, so a
graph node had to be handed the subject as prose. It now renders the run
context's subject as the `## Subject` section `buildActionBrief` has always
written for the action lane.

Input travels as `{initData: true, path: ""}` — Mastra resolves an empty
path to the source object — so a press's values arrive intact and the
compiler never tracks the input schema. The compiled graph passes the same
save-path validator as hand- and LLM-authored graphs, with no exemption.

Phase 7 #4 (part).

commits.message: a fire carries the values and the subject it was fired with
commits.body:
A schedule repeats the same input forever, so `flow_input` living only on the
template was enough. A button is pressed ON something, WITH values a person
just typed — neither had anywhere to travel.

`triggers_fire` now takes `flow_input` (layered over the template's, fire
wins key by key) and `contexts` (stamped on the materialized task, where
`resolveTaskFlowSubject` already reads them back). `POST /triggers/:id/run`
accepts them as `{input, context}` — both optional, so a routine's "run now"
is unchanged.

A fire that carries input also re-stamps a standing task's, or the re-run
would silently use the previous press's values.

Phase 7 #4 (part) — the seam every button needs before it can fire a trigger.

commits.message: run a trigger now and watch the run it started
commits.body:
A manual fire used to hand the task to the dispatch queue and return
nothing to watch: the button spun until the POST came back — the moment
the work STARTS — and then went idle over a run nobody was following.

The fire now dispatches in the caller's own process and answers with the
run id (`defer_dispatch` leaves the materialized task un-queued for
exactly this). The blocker gate still decides: it is split out of
`dispatchTaskIfReady` so deferring the dispatch cannot smuggle a blocked
task past it, and the fire reports what it did — a standing task mid-run,
in review or blocked answers `skipped`, `run_id` is null, and the button
stops rather than lying about a run that never started.

footers.value:
"manual"` becomes creatable (no cron, no provider — a trigger a
person presses). It is a button, not a routine, so the routines list
stops before mapping one.

`taskSchema` gained `action_graph_id` / `flow_input`: a caller that
dispatches a task itself has no other way to learn which lane it is, and
an output schema that drops them hands back an unrunnable task.

Phase 7 #3 (D4, part). Live: manual trigger → fire → run id in 142ms →
flow ran → parked at its gate; a second press answered `skipped`.

commits.message: a module's agent can read its own module from the start
commits.body:
Phase 7 #8, second half. "The contacts agent may read contacts" is not a
decision anyone makes differently — it is what installing that agent MEANS —
but it was a hand-grant per tenant, so every fresh tenant shipped with agents
that parked on their first read.

Minting moves to core as `core_agents_ensure`: an agent principal is an authz
subject and the grant that comes with it is an authz write, so core owns both.
The AI plane keeps what it knows — agent KEYS, and the registry's
`core_agent_id` link, which is an AI-plane column.

The default is deliberately narrow: the agent's OWN module, viewer (read) only,
and only when that role exists. Writing stays an explicit grant. `engenty.*` is
the platform prefix, not a module, so the coordinator and copilot get nothing
here — how far a cross-module orchestrator may read is its own decision.

The grant lands ONLY on the call that CREATED the principal, which is why
`ensureAgentPrincipal` reports `created` instead of upserting blindly: granting
on every call would re-add a role a human revoked and make the revoke
impossible to make stick. Existing principals therefore keep exactly what they
have — fixing an already-provisioned tenant stays a visible act (now two clicks,
since the roles picker learned names).

Verified live: dispatching a task to `offers.manager` for the first time minted
its principal AND granted `offers.viewer` in one step. (That run then failed on
`unknownTool` — the offers module is not mounted in that space, which is the
mount mismatch already logged under Phase 7's live issues, not an authz gap.)

commits.message: grant a role to an agent by name, not by uuid
commits.body:
Phase 7 #8, first half. The assignments tab asked for an "agent uuid" in a
free-text box, so granting a role to an agent meant looking its principal up in
the database first — and the granted list then read "agent 019fc98c-…" back at
you, which is how fifteen hand-grants ended up unreadable.

Both halves of the picker now select by name, backed by
`GET /api/tenants/:tenantId/agents` — the agent-shaped sibling of the
`GET /api/users` the user half already used. `core.agents.name` IS the
agent_type_key, so the list needs no join.

The granted list falls back to the raw id when a principal is gone: an
assignment can outlive what it names, and "agent <uuid>" is still the truth.

Not included: per-module DEFAULT role assignments (the other half of #8).
`ensureCoreAgentId` is the single seam where a principal is minted, but it
lives in the AI plane while authz writes belong to core — that boundary is a
decision, not a detail.

commits.message: a routine can run a flow instead of an agent
commits.body:
Phase 7 #1 + #2. Variant D's whole point is recurring deterministic work, and
until now nothing could CONFIGURE it: the trigger route's task-template schema
required an `agent_type_key`, so the one target that skips the model turn was
unreachable from any UI.

"Neue Routine" gains a "Was läuft" switch — an agent, or a published flow. On
flow the agent picker and the instructions box disappear rather than sitting
there ignored: a flow's steps ARE its instructions. Only published, active
graphs are offered, because `runTaskFlow` re-checks both when the routine fires
and a draft would only produce a run that fails at 02:00.

Both target keys always travel in the payload, and the unset one travels as
null — a routine switched agent→flow must CLEAR the old key, or the template
carries two targets and its check constraint refuses the write.

#2, the event guard: an event trigger may not target a flow. The event's
payload reaches a task as PROSE in the description, and a graph cannot read
that (D5 owes the mapping). Refused on create and on patch, with the reason
stated in the form the moment the pair is selected, rather than saving a
routine that fires forever with an empty input.

Verified live end to end: a flow routine created from the dialog materialized
ENG-51 on "Jetzt ausführen", which dispatched, ran the graph, parked at its
approval gate (steps panel showed `gate` waiting, `apply` still idle), and
settled on reject. That path threw `primary_assignee_agent_required` before
today's normalizer fix — a flow template could not materialize a task at all.

commits.message: filter the list down to work that runs itself
commits.body:
T6's first half: a "Läufe" segment beside Person and Agent, showing only tasks
nobody has to pick up — materialized by a routine (`trigger_id`) or supervising
a flow (`action_graph_id`). Either origin counts; both are machine-run work,
and both are what D4 will want to look at.

"runs" is not an assignee kind and does not travel as one: the list page turns
it into `machine_run`, its own filter. That param takes the wire's "true"/"false"
