commits.message: headless task runs follow their task's space; fix appearance saves
commits.body:
**Headless was the one lane with no narrowing at all.** A routine firing
in Marketing could reach every module in the tenant while a person
sitting in Marketing could not — the widest reach in the system belonged
to the runs nobody is watching.

The task's own space now narrows it, through the same gate the chat lanes
use. `resolveWorkVisibility` already ran there and already knew the
space; the step was discarding it and rooting on the tenant default.

The lane differs from chat in a way worth stating rather than papering
over. A chat's space is CLIENT-supplied, so fetching the surface doubles
as the access check. A task's space is a server-side lookup off the task
row — there is no claim to check, and the run's principal is the AI
service, which holds no membership in anything. Core still gates the
surface on space access and a service principal resolves to the nil user,
so an OPEN space answers and narrows the run while a PRIVATE one 404s and
the run keeps its old tenant-wide reach, with a warn carrying the task id.
Strictly better than no narrowing anywhere, and greppable instead of
silent. Closing that gap means teaching the space access rule about
`actingForUserId` — an auth-seam change with its own blast radius, not a
rider on this one.

The reflect step is deliberately untouched: it runs with
`allowedToolIds: ["memory_save", "memory_record_search"]`, both platform
tools, which the gate never touches.

footers.value:
colour saves now.** `SpaceAppearanceFields` built each next
value from the `value` PROP — a snapshot captured at render — so two
changes inside one React batch both computed from the same stale base and
the first was silently overwritten. Picking a colour and then an icon
saved the icon, dropped the colour, and left the form showing both, which
is why this looked verified when it was not. `onChange` is now an updater.

**And the space header tile shows the icon**, using the shared
`railSpaceInitials` instead of a second local copy of the rule: that tile
and the rail tile are the same object seen twice, so a space showing a
megaphone on the rail and "MA" in the header is the one thing that
component exists to prevent.

colour + icon persist to `core.spaces` and render on both the
rail and the space header. The headless wiring is typechecked and the
gate it feeds is unit-tested, but it is NOT exercised end-to-end — firing
a real dispatched task job needs the scheduler, which this run did not do.

commits.message: connectors and delegation follow the space too (Phase C3b)
commits.body:
Two of the three C3b narrowings, each a reader of the same surface C3a
already fetches. The third is blocked, and says so rather than pretending.

**Connections.** A connector is mounted one provider-account at a time
(`google-gmail`) while its operations live in a shared module
(`connections-google`, ops named `gmail_*`). So the module check is the
wrong grain in both directions: mounting Gmail would hand the space all
of Google, and refusing on the module would block a connector the space
explicitly mounts. The connector check therefore runs before the module
check and instead of it, matching by tool prefix with longest-match
wins — a connector whose prefix prefixes another's (`g` vs `gmail`) must
not claim its operations. The connections module's OWN plumbing (the
catalog, the account list) stays reachable once any connector is
mounted: a space able to call Gmail and unable to ask which account to
call it with is not a coherent state.

**Delegation.** Restricted to the engentys the space mounts. Filtering
the tool list IS the enforcement here, unlike the module gate — a child
run is a principal with its own tools and its own workspace, so the only
safe answer for an unmounted engenty is that its tool never exists.

Verifying that found the narrowing defeating itself. `skipSubAgents` was
set from "we ended up with at least one delegation tool", so a space
mounting none of the copilot's specialists filtered the list to empty,
which flipped that false, which dropped the flag, which handed the run
Mastra's IN-PROCESS sub-agents — every specialist back through a second
door, in exactly the case the narrowing existed for. It now reads off
"the harness can build child workspaces and the agent declares
sub-agents", which is what it always meant.

footers.value:
catalog visibility now delegates to the gate rather than
re-deriving the rule, so what discovery shows and what execution allows
cannot drift; and the runtime context names the space's engentys, so a
filtered-out specialist reads as "this space does not have the CLI
agent" instead of "not available in this session" — the same lesson as
the C3a scope note, which the first live run taught the hard way.

**Skills are NOT narrowed, deliberately.** A run reaches skills two

the module hint, and Mastra's `skill`/`skill_search` workspace
tools — which discover by PATH (`/tenant-skills`, tenant-wide). A path
list cannot express "these four skill names", so the second way needs a
per-space skills prefix (Phase 6b, a storage change with a migration).
Filtering only the hint would leave `skill_search` returning everything
one call later: the same "looks like enforcement, enforces nothing" trap
that moved C3a's check off the agent tool list.

Verified live in Marketing (mounts slack + invoices; agents are the
baseline copilot + coordinator only):
- `gmail_list_labels` → `connector_not_in_space`, and core logs the
  contract fetch with NO following invoke
- `agent-engenty_cli` → the copilot reports the tool does not exist

commits.message: a run reaches only what its space mounts (Phase C3a)
commits.body:
C2 gave a thread a `space_id`. This is where that column stops being a
label and starts deciding what the run can do.

**The plan's seam was wrong, and the live behaviour is what showed it.**
C3a was specced as `allowedToolIds` on `assembleDynamicAgent` — correct
for an agent carrying module tools directly, and worth nothing for the
copilot: its `toolIds` are the six catalog meta-tools, and every module
operation it ever runs arrives through `engenty_tool_execute` by id.
Narrowing a list that holds no module tools would have looked like
enforcement and enforced nothing. The check therefore sits on the call.

Two strengths, deliberately different. The catalog HIDES what the space
does not mount, so the copilot stops proposing Company's offers inside
Marketing; `engenty_tool_execute` REFUSES it, because a model that
remembers an operation id from its own history never asks the catalog.
Either alone is a hole or a bad turn. Core stays authoritative behind
both — it re-checks every invoke — but "failed at the HTTP boundary" is a
broken product even when it is a safe one.

Validation is not a second membership list here: the surface endpoint is
already gated by `requireSpaceAccess`, so asking it for the mounts IS
asking whether the caller may have them, and an unbacked claim gets a 404
instead of a mount list. That closes the hole C2 left open on purpose.

Unresolvable degrades rather than denies — no space claimed, a deleted
space, core slow — all fall back to the pre-Phase-C tenant-wide
behaviour with a warn. The surface narrows; it never grants. Denying on
unknown would turn a core hiccup into a dead copilot.

The workspace roots at the run's own space, so a chat opened in Marketing
puts its files under Marketing. A task-bound run still wins with
`resolveWorkVisibility` — a task does not move because someone opened it
from another space — and the disagreement is logged, because a chat in
one space checking out work from another is either a legitimate hand-off
or a containment bug and neither is diagnosable from silence.

label and starts deciding what the run can do.

commits.message: the copilot knows its space, and space URLs read like places
commits.body:
The copilot inside a space could not tell you where it was. `/mdl/` was
hardcoded in the one regex that resolves which module the user is looking
at, so once a space mirrored every module route the agent resolved NO
module at all — no page prompt, no skill-catalog hint, and "where am I?"
answered by asking the user which page they were on.

Fixed there, plus the space itself: the runtime block now names the
current space (name, key, id, and whether it is the user's personal one),
resolved against the caller's own membership-filtered list so a prompt can
never name a space they are not in. The space id comes from the route
context the client sends — the same value C2 binds the thread to — so what
the agent is told and where the chat lives are one fact, not two that
drift. An unresolvable space degrades to a single line rather than taking
the whole runtime block down.

Space URLs lose the vendor prefix: `/s/company/copilot/chat/…`, not
`/s/company/engenty-copilot/chat/…`. Only the URL segment changes; the
module ID is untouched everywhere it means something. The alias table
lives in ai-core because the shell and the agent's page-context resolver
are two readers of the same scheme — two tables in packages that cannot
import each other's tests is how the agent ends up resolving `copilot`
against a registry that only knows `engenty-copilot`. Aliases are opt-in
per module, never derived by stripping `engenty-` (that would silently
claim `/s/x/core`). Pre-alias space links stay mounted rather than
redirected, so a bookmark or notification still opens the page.

footers.value:
the `+N` overflow chip becomes a stack of the hidden spaces' own
tiles, which says WHICH places are down there rather than only that there
are more — and a stack of cards visibly wants to be fanned out. Hovering
unfolds it into the named list; the count does not survive as a leftover
chip beside the tiles it stood in for. Fixed-height box so fanning out
cannot shove zone ③ around, and the rolled-up mention indicator still
rides on the stack.

`core.spaces.color` and `.icon` have existed since Phase 5a and the API
accepted both on create and edit, but nothing could set them, so every
space was grey. The setup dialog now has a palette, an emoji row and a
preview at rail size. A fixed palette rather than a colour input: the
rail's readability rests on white text over the tile, and a free picker
can produce one that cannot carry it.

Verified live on the spaces stack: a fresh chat in Marketing answers
"Marketing / marketing / engenty-copilot" — the module ID resolved
through the short URL, so the de-alias round trip holds end to end.
Marketing set to violet + megaphone from the dialog and the rail tile
followed.

commits.message: chat lives in a space (Phase C1 + C2)
commits.body:
The copilot becomes a per-space surface: in a space you see that space's
chats, and a chat opened outside any space binds to your personal one. This is
VISIBILITY, not authorization — what an agent may reach is still the capability
system and the space mount set. C3a is where the thread's space starts
selecting tools, and it must validate the space against the caller's accessible
set first; `spaceIdFromRouteContext` says so at the seam.

C1 — placement. The manifest says `space`, so the existing route mirror serves
`/s/<key>/engenty-copilot/…` and legacy `/mdl/*` links redirect. Two seams did
not see it: the rail reads placement off `adminMenuItems` and the copilot
contributes no menu row, so the tile stayed put no matter what the manifest
said, and `spacePlacedModuleIds` was blind for the same reason. Placement now
rides on `UiCopilotAppContribution` too, enriched exactly where menu items are.

C2 — the thread carries a space. `ai.thread.space_id` (nullable; null reads as
"pre-space" and shows only under All spaces), composite `(space_id, tenant_id)`
FK, backfilled to the creator's personal space. The UI puts the space in
`routeContext.scope` because the affinity key hashes it — the drawer in
Marketing stops resuming Company's thread with no second mechanism.

Three things that had to be built differently than planned:

- **`/s/me` cannot be emitted into a deep link.** React Router ranks by
  specificity, not declaration order, so a mirrored module route under
  `/s/:spaceKey` out-ranks the `/s/me/*` splat: the alias arrived as a literal
  space key, no space has it, and the shell fell back to the tenant default.
  Found live — the chat opened, its history came back empty, nothing errored.
  The redirect resolves the real key now. The same trap applies to every other
  mirrored module (`/s/me/tasks/briefing` has it today); that one is untouched
  here and belongs with the routing, not with each caller.
- **Invalidation needs a space-agnostic PREFIX.** A full list key ends in the
  space and the copilot provider builds its key without one, so invalidating
  with it yielded `…/"all-spaces"` — prefix-matching nothing but itself, which
  left the space-scoped history stale after every run.
- **The RPC coalesces the space rather than assigning it.** Every sibling
  column takes `excluded`; this one must not, because upsert is also the
  idempotent re-save path and a save that omits the space must not un-space a
  thread. The service reads the merged route context for the same reason.

The migration DROPS the old 10-argument signature in the same file: adding a
parameter creates an overload, PostgREST calls by named args, and a request
omitting the new one would match both. Grants are restated because recreating a
function drops its ACL — engenty_server included, or creating a chat fails
outright.

Verified live: `/mdl/engenty-copilot/chat` lands on `/s/matthias/…`; zone ③ is
contacts/inbox/time-tracking with no copilot tile; the route answers 2/0/2
threads for no-filter/Company/personal. In Postgres: one signature, grants
intact, and the FK's `confdelsetcols` is `{space_id}` alone — tenant_id is not
nulled by a space delete.

Known and deliberately left: the active thread is remembered per host key, not
per space, so Company can show a personal chat in the content pane while the
list beside it is correctly empty.

types they consume): tenant-settings + user-settings mock `registerHttpRoute`
as returning void where it returns `PluginRegistrationReceipt | undefined`,
and team-chat passes a dispatch union where the queue wants a
`Record<string, unknown>`.

commits.message: scope the predev Supabase check to the worktree's own stack
commits.body:
predev-check.sh probed a hardcoded 127.0.0.1:54321 and hardcoded
`supabase_*_engenty-local` container names, so from any worktree it reported
the MAIN checkout's stack as healthy while this one was down — a false green.
Worse, soft_heal_supabase_rest() ran `docker restart` on that literal name:
healing from here would have bounced another checkout's PostgREST out from
under a colleague's running dev server.

Both now derive from this worktree's own gitignored supabase/config.toml
(project_id + [api] port) — the same file `supabase start` reads, so probe and
stack cannot diverge. Verified against both: engenty-spaces/54821 and
engenty-local/54321.

The openapi.json half of the original commit is dropped: main fixed the same
z.custom bug independently (and better, without z.custom) after it caused the
v0.1.117/118 prod outage.

commits.message: read-only roster, Settings in the sidebar foot, spaces on Team profiles
commits.body:
Four changes, all from review feedback.

**People is read-only in the Work tab.** An × beside a colleague's name in the
sidebar you open all day is an invitation to a mistake — one click from a list
you are only glancing at. The roster stays visible there because "who else is
in here" is worth seeing; changing it is administration and moved behind
Settings. Shared spaces only: a personal space has no members by construction,
so the section is absent rather than empty.

**A Settings link pinned to the foot of the space sidebar**, where this
application already puts Settings. It needed a new `secondaryNavFooterSlot` on
the shell column, rendered OUTSIDE the level transition — the footer is the
column's own furniture, not part of what slides when a module opens — and it
shows at both levels for the same reason.

**A person's spaces on their Team profile**, via `GET /api/spaces/memberships`.
The signature takes two subjects on purpose (`subjectUserId`, `viewerUserId`)
and returns the intersection: a profile listing every room someone belongs to
would be a directory of private spaces and their occupants, which is the one
thing per-space access control exists to prevent. Personal spaces cannot appear
at all — they hold no member rows — and that property is what makes the
endpoint safe on a profile page.

The route is registered BEFORE `/api/spaces/:spaceId/…`, or `memberships` is
read as a space id and 404s. The section fetches through `requestApiJson`, not
a bare `fetch`: the first draft used raw fetch, which sends no bearer token and
would have 401'd on every profile.

**Team is back on the rail**, in the admin stack above Settings. Phase 5a moved
it off entirely on the grounds that it is a directory rather than a place you
work; that argument holds for zone ③ (tools you carry between spaces) and is
why this is not a revert. "Who works here" is administration, and
settings-menu-only put it two clicks from everywhere.

Verified live: Company lists all seven people with no controls; the personal
space shows no People and still shows Settings; Anna Berger's profile lists
Company and not her personal space; /mdl/team is on the rail.

Five dummy colleagues were seeded into the dev database (each got a personal
space and Company membership from the trigger, plus a linked team profile) —
data only, no code.

commits.message: personal spaces have no members; space roster lives in Settings
commits.body:
Two corrections from Matthias, and the second reshapes the concept.

A personal space is a SPECIAL type of space, not an ordinary one that happens
to start private. It belongs to one person and has no members, ever —
`owner_user_id` is the whole of its access grant, and `core.space_member`
becomes exclusively a shared-space table. That is smaller than what Phase P
built, not larger: the creation trigger no longer seeds an owner row, a new
trigger refuses any member row on an owned space, and existing rows are
removed.

The first cut of that migration deleted only rows where the member WAS the
owner. That left a member row sitting on a personal space — a state the new
trigger forbids anyone from creating — so the invariant would have read as
enforced with a violating row still in the table. Widened to every member row
on an owned space. Found immediately, by a row left over from live testing.

`core.protect_space_owner_member` is dropped rather than left inert: a trigger
that guards nothing is a claim that some rule is still enforced there.

The roster moved out of the space sidebar and into Settings, as the People tab
of `/settings/spaces/:spaceId` — beside Team in the settings menu. Managing
people is administration: you check a roster occasionally and change it rarely,
so it does not belong next to the things you open every day. The tab is absent
entirely on a personal space, because a tab that could only ever say "nobody
here" is worse than no tab.

Supporting work:

- `GET /api/users/directory` — names and ids only. `/api/users` was `select("*")`
  and would have handed a picker everyone's private phone number and home
  address. Registered BEFORE `/api/users/:id` or the literal is read as an id.
- `listSpaceMembers` embeds the person's name, with a narrow three-column
  projection for the same reason.
- Owner-first ordering, sorted in TypeScript: `order("role")` is ALPHABETICAL,
  so "member" sorted before "owner" and put the owner at the bottom of their own
  space's roster. Caught in the browser; now pinned by a test.

Verified live: Company (shared) shows Drive · People · Files and lists both
people; matthias (personal) shows Drive · Files with no People tab; the database
refuses an inserted member row on a personal space.

This commit also carries the `/api/users` field-narrowing from the background
task running concurrently in this worktree (CORE_USER_COLUMNS + toCoreUserWire,
with its tests). It could not be separated — that work and the directory
endpoint touch the same DAL and route files, and `crud-routes.ts` imports
`toCoreUserWire`, so committing one without the other would not build.

trigger forbids anyone from creating — so the invariant would have read as
enforced with a violating row still in the table. Widened to every member row
on an owned space. Found immediately, by a row left over from live testing.

`core.protect_space_owner_member` is dropped rather than left inert: a trigger
that guards nothing is a claim that some rule is still enforced there.

The roster moved out of the space sidebar and into Settings, as the People tab
of `/settings/spaces/:spaceId` — beside Team in the settings menu. Managing
people is administration: you check a roster occasionally and change it rarely,
so it does not belong next to the things you open every day. The tab is absent
entirely on a personal space, because a tab that could only ever say "nobody
here" is worse than no tab.

Supporting work:

- `GET /api/users/directory` — names and ids only. `/api/users` was `select("*")`
  and would have handed a picker everyone's private phone number and home
  address. Registered BEFORE `/api/users/:id` or the literal is read as an id.
- `listSpaceMembers` embeds the person's name, with a narrow three-column
  projection for the same reason.
- Owner-first ordering, sorted in TypeScript: `order("role")` is ALPHABETICAL,
  so "member" sorted before "owner" and put the owner at the bottom of their own
  space's roster. Caught in the browser; now pinned by a test.

Verified live: Company (shared) shows Drive · People · Files and lists both
people; matthias (personal) shows Drive · Files with no People tab; the database
refuses an inserted member row on a personal space.

This commit also carries the `/api/users` field-narrowing from the background
task running concurrently in this worktree (CORE_USER_COLUMNS + toCoreUserWire,
with its tests). It could not be separated — that work and the directory
endpoint touch the same DAL and route files, and `crud-routes.ts` imports
`toCoreUserWire`, so committing one without the other would not build.

commits.message: real personal spaces, built the home-directory way
commits.body:
A personal space is a NORMAL space plus a general permission mechanism plus a
thin convention — not a special type. A Unix home directory is an ordinary
directory; owner + mode bits + the useradd convention are what make it personal.
Here: `visibility` (open|private) and core.space_member are the mechanism,
`owner_user_id` + a trigger on core.user_tenant_roles are the convention.

This retires "there is NO per-space access control" deliberately. The §1c
non-goal survives REFINED, not reversed: space_member answers human
access/visibility, space_mount's existing agent rows answer agent
authorization, and the capability system stays authoritative for what an agent
may do.

RLS is only half the enforcement, and the smaller half. The server lane's JWT
subject is the nil UUID, so Postgres sees a tenant and never a user: the
policies here bind the browser lane, and listAccessibleSpaces /
requireSpaceAccess / accessibleSpaceIds are what actually hold on every
server-mediated path. A membership rule believed to be "enforced by RLS" on a
server path is enforced by nothing.

Inaccessible is 404, never 403, everywhere. Personal spaces are named after
people, so confirming one exists is itself the disclosure.

Three findings from the leak audit reshaped the work:

- The Drive was the symptom, not the leak. It fans out to /api/projects and
  /api/kb/… with a space_id — MODULE routes that trusted the id they were
  handed. The gate lives at the single plugin-http dispatch, so a module gains
  a space filter and is covered without knowing the gate exists.
- search.documents had no space at all while the KB source indexes every
  article, and knowledge bases are space-scoped. Search never passes a
  /s/<key> route, so no route guard was in its path. Adding the RPC parameter
  created an OVERLOAD rather than replacing the function — PostgREST calls by
  named args, so a call omitting it matched both; the old signature is dropped.
- PrincipalContext has no `userId` (a user IS principalId; agents carry
  actingForUserId). Reading the wrong field silently fell back to the nil UUID
  and the symptom was people unable to open their OWN space. Unit tests missed
  it because their fixtures were kinder than reality; the live two-user run
  caught it, and the fixtures now mirror PrincipalContext.

footers.value:
space setup is owner-OR-admin, because admins deliberately cannot see
private spaces and admin-only setup would have left personal spaces
unconfigurable by anyone at all.

Verified at three levels, both directions: RLS via psql as each user, the
guards via unit tests, and live HTTP with two tokens — each user sees their own
personal space and not the other's, and every cross-user module-route read 404s
while the same request for the owner returns 200.

commits.message: one sidebar column with the space on top and modules inside it
commits.body:
The space now HOSTS a module's nav instead of reproducing it. A module's
secondary nav is not data anywhere in this repo — Tasks and KB publish an
opaque ReactNode through usePageConfig — so the only way to show Work/Data/Plan
above a real module sidebar is to own the column and let the page keep filling
its slot.

Two levels in one column: level 1 is the space switcher + Work/Data/Plan tabs +
the mount list; level 2 is a Work-opened module's own nav behind a back arrow.
Data and Plan stay at level 1 because their TAB is the navigation.

app-shell gains route-level column props (secondaryNavHeaderOverride,
secondaryNavLeadingSlot, secondaryNavRouteTransition, secondaryNavRouteBreadcrumb).
Route-level, not page-level, because usePageConfig is last-writer-wins on one
global and these are route facts.

Fixes found on the way:

- SpaceLayout called usePageConfig for a breadcrumb, which silently wiped the
  child page's sidebar: layout effects run after children's and the hook writes
  `secondaryNavAfterItems ?? null` unconditionally. Layouts must never call it.
- The column header inherited the page's topbarChrome, so it was 52px on Work
  and 44px on Plan — the "jumping and refreshing" between tabs. routeOwnsChrome
  pins it.
- TasksRedirectPage hops through the absolute /mdl/tasks base; LegacyModuleRedirect
  now resolves from the remembered space without a round trip, and App.tsx holds
  the space chrome across the hop. The hop itself remains (11 modules hardcode
  /mdl/ bases) — it is just no longer visible.

commits.message: bind triggers to a space so fired tasks stay in it
commits.body:
`module_tasks.triggers` and `module_tasks.task_templates` gain `space_id`
`not null`, matching the goals/tasks shape: composite `(space_id, tenant_id)`
FK to `core.spaces` with `on delete restrict`, backfilled to the tenant
default.

The column is not the point. `fireTrigger` had no space to pass to
`createTask`, so `resolveCreateSpaceId` fell through to its last resort and
every trigger-materialized task landed in the tenant default regardless of
where the routine lived — the one creation path with no human in the loop was
quietly collapsing the tier. The fix is one line: `triggers` joins
`createTask`'s inheritance chain after parent/goal/project, so a fired task
follows its routine and `fireTrigger` itself is untouched.

Verified against local Postgres by driving the real DAL: a template created in
`marketing` produced a trigger in `marketing` and a fired task in `marketing`.
`trigger-fire.test.ts` mocks the DAL away and so passes identically before and
after — a mocked-DAL test cannot see an inheritance chain.

Space-scoped in the same pass, because a column nothing filters on is
decoration: `triggers_list` / `task_templates_list` take `space_id`,
`GET /ai/v1/triggers` forwards `?space_id=`, and `useRoutinesListQuery` scopes
to the current space by default with a `"tenant"` opt-out — scoping in the hook
rather than at six call sites, as the tasks queries already do. The space is
part of the react-query key; `list()` stays a valid prefix so existing
invalidations still clear every space. Create is symmetric.

`taskTemplateUpdateInputSchema` omits `space_id` deliberately:
`updateTaskTemplate` maps a fixed field list, so accepting one would parse
cleanly and then do nothing.

Channels remain open and are a different question — a `module_remote` binding
is one external workspace bound to one tenant, an entry point rather than a
work container.

commits.message: bind work containers and knowledge bases to a space
commits.body:
`space_id` becomes `not null` on goals, tasks, projects and knowledge bases,
and the bytes follow the rows below the space boundary. NULL no longer means
"not yet" — it would mean "escaped the tier".

footers.value:
- the FKs become `on delete restrict`: `set null` cannot coexist with
  `not null`. Checked against a live Postgres rather than reasoned about — a
  TENANT delete still cascades fine (the cascade removes referencing rows in
  the same statement); what restrict blocks is deleting a space that still
  holds work, which is the intent
- `on delete set null` on a COMPOSITE FK nulls EVERY column, tenant_id
  included: deleting a space emitted `SET space_id = NULL, tenant_id = NULL`
  and died on knowledge_bases.tenant_id — an error naming the wrong table, one
  nullable column away from a tenant-less row. Fixed with
  `set null (space_id)`, then superseded by the not-null flip

Knowledge bases lose the tenant-wide tier they had: a library is part of a
space's file tree, so it lives in exactly one space. A library several spaces
shared now belongs to one of them.

Storage re-root (new uploads only — the key is computed once and stored on the
row, so existing files keep resolving from their stored key):
- KB media   → tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/knowledge-base/<slug>/…
- project files → tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/files/project/<id>/<entry>

The browser stopped composing KB keys. That was the actual cause of the drift:
the layout lived in a UI helper that read as string formatting, not storage
code, so when the row learned about spaces nobody looked there. Keys are minted
server-side now. `defaultBuildStorageKey` throws for a non-space owner with no
space rather than falling back — a fallback would silently restore the root
this change closes.

Also fixes: tasks created inside a project ignored the project's space, so
every task added to a project in a non-default space landed in Company.

commits.message: make the space the entry point in the UI
commits.body:
`/s/<key>` is a LAYOUT route owning three tabs (Apps · Drive · Tasks), with
every module route mirrored beneath it — so a module opened inside a space
keeps the space around it, and no module re-registers anything.

Three decisions worth keeping:

- There is no new SpaceContext. `WorkspaceContext.currentSpace` already
  existed; it is now driven by the URL. A second context would have given two
  answers to one question.
- EVERY module route is mirrored, not only `placement: "space"` ones.
  Placement is where a module appears by default, not whether a space may
  contain it — filtering by it would 404 contacts and commercial settings
  inside a space. Placement decides only which legacy `/mdl/*` links redirect.
- Reachability comes from the route table, labels from the setup catalog.
  Deriving both from adminMenuItems silently dropped the copilot from every
  space's Apps tab, because its rail entry is built separately.

A module's absolute `/mdl/…` link would otherwise relocate the user across
spaces: eleven modules build links from a `/mdl/<module>` base constant, so an
internal navigation from inside space B hit the legacy redirect and landed in
the tenant default. The redirect now prefers record space → last space in the
URL → default.

commits.message: add the Space tier between Project and Global
commits.body:
A space is neutral core infrastructure — a client, a topic, a team, or just
"your space" on a one-person tenant. It sits in the containment ladder as

  Thread > Task > Goal | Routine | Phase > Project > SPACE > Global

and is a PATH SEGMENT, not merely a foreign key: object keys become
`tenants/<t>/spaces/<s>/…`, so a space-scoped engenty cannot address another
space's bytes because no path leads there — containment by construction rather
than by a membership check someone has to remember to write.

- core.spaces with one-default-per-tenant, a key-format CHECK (it lands in
  routes, so a key with a slash would be a path-traversal shape) and an
  AFTER INSERT trigger + backfill, so "every tenant has a space" is a database
  invariant rather than something the UI hopes for
- core.space_mount: one table, four resource kinds. Mount = grant — a space's
  capability set is derived from its mounts by ONE function, so the count the
  UI shows and the grants an agent gets cannot disagree
- space-rooted storage keys (fileStorageSpaceObjectKey, workWorkspacePrefix)
  alongside the tenant-level ones, which skills and the Global commons keep
- the Drive as a PROJECTION over four existing stores, not a fourth store
- scripts/check-space-storage-scope.mjs: every tenant-rooted key builder must
  be classified, and the guard reads each owner's own migrations for space_id,
  so a module that later gains a space column becomes an error rather than a
  discovery

NO authorization is inferred from space membership, and there is no per-space
access control: every tenant user sees every space, rights come from roles.

commits.message: call it Fair Source, not open source
commits.body:
FSL-1.1-MIT is source-available with a delayed MIT grant, not an OSI
open-source licence. Say so on the docs front page, the README and
CONTRIBUTING, so the public launch does not claim a licence the project
does not carry.

Third-party dependency credits keep "open-source" — those really are.
The internal open/closed vocabulary (publish-open, "the open tree") is
about which code is published, not about the licence, and stays.

The landing page (apps/www) carries the same wording on feat/spaces;
that app does not exist on main and ships with 0.2.0.

commits.message:
fix(ai): Mastra's native REST API is not ours to serve

`createApp` mounted `MastraServer` unconditionally, which put ~390 Mastra
routes on our Hono app. `prefix` REPLACES Mastra's `/api` rather than
prepending it, so they landed at `/ai/agents`, `/ai/workflows`,
`/ai/memory/*` — not `/ai/api/*`. Grepping for the latter finds nothing and
suggests the surface is absent; it wasn't.

`checkRouteAuth()` opens with `if (!effectiveAuth) return null`, so with no
`server.experimental_auth` on the Mastra instance every one of those routes
runs. Our `/ai/*` middleware only seeds `engentyToolsRunAls`, our registrars
authenticate per route and none covered Mastra's, and apps/core proxies the
whole `/ai` prefix with no allowlist — so the lot was live on the public edge.

Verified unauthenticated against a running stack:

  GET  /ai/agents                        66 KB, incl. the copilot's full prompt
  GET  /ai/agents/:id/suspended-runs     live runId + threadId + resourceId
  POST /ai/agents/:id/approve-tool-call  accepts exactly those ids

That pair is an anonymous approval-bypass around the core grant store. Also
open: /ai/tools/:id/execute, /ai/workflows/*/start-async, /ai/memory/threads,
/ai/stored/*, /ai/workspaces/*/fs/*, /ai/schedules, /ai/system/api-schema.

So don't guard the surface — don't mount it. Nothing here calls that API: no
@mastra/client-js in the repo, and the remote-channel webhooks mount
themselves onto our app independent of MastraServer. Its only consumer is
Mastra Studio, opt-in dev tooling, so the mount now follows the Studio flag
and production ignores that flag outright. `experimental_auth` would have been
weaker: it leaves eight routes public by design, `/auth/credentials/sign-up`
among them.

Not fixed in gateway-paths.ts: Studio reaches the API through the gateway
origin in dev, so an allowlist there breaks Studio while the single mount seam
does not.

The regression test asserts 404, not 401 — the routes must not exist. A 400 is
how this presented in the first place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(styleguide): engenty mascot system, fluffy renderer and manage styleguide

Move the engenties out of auth-ui into ui-core, give them a procedural fur
renderer for hero surfaces, and catalogue the whole visual system on a new
/styleguide page in manage.

Engenties now live in packages/ui-core/src/components/engenty and are exported
from @engenty/ui-core; the two auth-ui import sites were rewritten and no shim
left behind. The cast grows from five kinds to ten — bean, pebble, sprout,
tower and wedge join the founding round/drop/dome/flame/oval. The new fills are
derived from existing brand tokens by rotating hue rather than hardcoded, so
they keep tracking the tenant theme; the brand mark still cycles only the
founding five.

FluffyEngenty renders large-format engenties as procedural shell fur in a
WebGL2 shader, with no mesh, texture or library. forms.ts describes each kind
as metaballs and is the bridge between the two renderers: the flat SVG draws
outlines, the shader needs a field. The field is a metaball *sum* — smooth-min
of distances creases where a small blob meets a large one and the coat parts
along the valley, and smooth-min of normalised fields lumps instead. Strand
coverage is antialiased against the pixel rather than the cell, and shell
sampling gaps are closed at the tips, so the coat stays smooth rather than
speckled. One shared GL context serves every instance, since browsers cap live
contexts per document and evict silently.

Also lifts the dock icons off a near-grey wash by boosting only chroma on their
brand tokens, and fixes --rose, which was spelled out rather than aliasing
--danger and so never picked up the dark-mode override its siblings did.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(time-tracking): full AI face — 13 tools, 3 skills, tracker + reporter agents

The module registered 26 gateway operations but exposed only four of them as
agent tools (load/log/update/delete entry) behind a single skill, so anything
report-, row-, or calendar-shaped was reachable only through generic
`engenty_tools_search` discovery with no guidance attached.

Tools (9 new): summarize_time_entries (grouped hours — the report-shaped op,
with the full filter set including the `*_contains` pattern filters that
load_time_entries omits), move_time_entry, load_timesheet_week (the only tool
returning row ids), create_timesheet_row, delete_timesheet_row, and the four
calendar ones: load_calendar_sources, load_calendar_events,
get/set_calendar_sync_settings.

Skills (2 new): time-tracking-reporting covers summarizing plus the saved
reports and snapshots that exist only as operations; time-tracking-calendar-sync
keeps overlay (read, Google + Outlook) apart from push sync (write, Google
only) and encodes the traps — isolated per-calendar errors, per-calendar event
caps, background backfill, no dedupe between meetings and logged hours.

Agents: time-tracking.tracker (write surface, timekeeping) and
time-tracking.reporter (read-only on entries, saved reports). Role names rather
than `.manager` because the split is write-heavy vs read-only.

time_tracking_calendar_sync_run deliberately gets no tool: it runs as the
service principal over every enabled connection in the tenant, so it stays
behind engenty_tool_execute with a confirm-first rule in the skill.

Also fixes engenty.plugin.json declaring `capabilities.ai: false` while the
module has registered an AI face all along (metadata only, nothing gates on it).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(copilot): an approval is not a decision, and an answered one must say what it approved

Every tool approval rides the decision-artifact pipeline — the gate returns
a decision-shaped artifact tagged `tool-approval|<op>` — so the transcript
part is named `requestDecision` and every reader that looks at the tool name
alone called it a decision. Answering then replaced the artifact in `output`
with `{approved, operation_id}`, which no decision reader recognises: the row
kept "Decision needed", was still counted as UNANSWERED, and hid a raw
`approved: true` behind a chevron. Four of those stacked up in one chat with
nothing to say which operation the user had let through.

- `ag-ui/tool-approval.ts` reads both shapes (the gate's artifact and the
  resolution it is overwritten with), tolerating raw-JSON output because the
  reloaded thread hands it over unparsed.
- The transcript row now reads `Approved "tasks_list"` / `Denied "…"`, with
  `+N more` for a bulk pre-approval, and an OPEN card leads with the gate's
  own question instead of "Decision needed".
- An answered approval renders its own compact card (verdict + operations)
  rather than falling through to the generic tool row.
- `pendingInterruptFromTranscript` stops at an answered approval. It only
  ever recognised a decision's `choice_label`, so it walked past the answer
  to an OLDER row and could re-dock a card the user had already answered.

Ports 64a74354d ("an answered question must still show the question") from
feat/spaces, which never reached main: a natively-suspended chooser resumes
with a model-facing sentence, so its question survives only in the tool's
`args`. Same symptom, same rows — the transcript now leads with the question
and trails the answer, and the resolved card renders the body it dropped.
The upstream test that pinned an answered approval to "Decision needed" is
replaced by the approval rows above.

Verified live on main (engenty.localhost, German UI): the reported thread's
four "Decision needed" rows now read "Freigegeben · time_tracking_context_get
/ projects_list / tasks_list / projects_list_tasks", and an answered chooser
shows title, body and "ANTWORT Ja, prüfen".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(copilot): an approval is not a decision, and an answered one must say what it approved

Every tool approval rides the decision-artifact pipeline — the gate returns
a decision-shaped artifact tagged `tool-approval|<op>` — so the transcript
part is named `requestDecision` and every reader that looks at the tool name
alone called it a decision. Answering then replaced the artifact in `output`
with `{approved, operation_id}`, which no decision reader recognises: the row
kept "Decision needed", was still counted as UNANSWERED, and hid a raw
`approved: true` behind a chevron. Four of those stacked up in one chat with
nothing to say which operation the user had let through.

- `ag-ui/tool-approval.ts` reads both shapes (the gate's artifact and the
  resolution it is overwritten with), tolerating raw-JSON output because the
  reloaded thread hands it over unparsed.
- The transcript row now reads `Approved "tasks_list"` / `Denied "…"`, with
  `+N more` for a bulk pre-approval, and an OPEN card leads with the gate's
  own question instead of "Decision needed".
- An answered approval renders its own compact card (verdict + operations)
  rather than falling through to the generic tool row.
- `pendingInterruptFromTranscript` stops at an answered approval. It only
  ever recognised a decision's `choice_label`, so it walked past the answer
  to an OLDER row and could re-dock a card the user had already answered.

Ports 64a74354d ("an answered question must still show the question") from
feat/spaces, which never reached main: a natively-suspended chooser resumes
with a model-facing sentence, so its question survives only in the tool's
`args`. Same symptom, same rows — the transcript now leads with the question
and trails the answer, and the resolved card renders the body it dropped.
The upstream test that pinned an answered approval to "Decision needed" is
replaced by the approval rows above.

Verified live on main (engenty.localhost, German UI): the reported thread's
four "Decision needed" rows now read "Freigegeben · time_tracking_context_get
/ projects_list / tasks_list / projects_list_tasks", and an answered chooser
shows title, body and "ANTWORT Ja, prüfen".

commits.message:
fix(time-tracking): wire agents and skills to operation contracts

Live testing on the agent desk surfaced that manifest agents (agent.json)
resolve toolIds against the AI registry, which for module functionality
carries ONLY operation contracts from core's /api/tools/contracts — the
defineModuleAi Mastra tool wrappers never cross the process boundary (the
capability seed ships agent_configs/skills/actions, never tools). Every
module tool id in the agent manifests failed with
agent_threads.unknownTool, and invoke_frontend_tool (copied from the
invoices/offers manifests) is a dead legacy id — frontend tools register
per-run natively now.

Both agent manifests now declare operation ids (time_tracking_entries_*,
rows_*, week_get, context_get, saved-report reads for the reporter) plus
tasks_list/projects_list for resolution, and the three skills teach the
operations with their snake_case wire shape instead of the unreachable
camelCase wrappers. This also retro-fixes the pre-existing time-tracking
skill, whose phantom log_time_entry reference is what pushed models to
improvise raw entries_create calls with manual "#21" titles.

Verified end to end against a live space: task + project resolution, date
math (gestern), linked project rows, manual-title fallback disclosed for
identifiers that resolve to nothing (now: ask first), week summary. The
wrappers in ai/tools stay: they serve the dynamicCapability channel and
its tests; whether that channel should survive is a separate decision.

commits.message:
fix(invoices,offers): drop the dead invoke_frontend_tool id from the manager manifests

Same landmine as time-tracking (0da6fcf8a): apps/ai's dynamic assembly
resolves every agent.json toolId against the registry and 400s the whole
run with agent_threads.unknownTool on the first miss. invoke_frontend_tool
is a legacy meta-tool id — frontend tools register per-run natively now
(modules/engenty-copilot/ai/agents/engenty.copilot/tools.ts) — so any
desk/dynamic run of invoices.manager or offers.manager failed before the
model saw the first token. The remaining ids in both manifests are all
builtin (engenty_tools_search, engenty_tool_execute, memory_*) and
resolve.

Sweep of the other module manifests: tasks.assist, inbox.assist,
knowledge-base.manager/.answers, engenty-remote, engenty-coordinator, and
engenty.app-coder all carry resolvable ids. contacts.manager and
company-profile.manager do NOT — their manifests declare camelCase module
wrappers (createContact, loadCompanyProfile, …) that exist neither as
builtin tools nor as operation contracts, so both are broken on the
dynamic lane the same way; they need a time-tracking-style rewiring to
operation ids, which is a bigger change left out of this fix.

commits.message:
feat(ai): show_artifact becomes a backend presentation tool

A frontend tool suspends the run until a browser resumes it. That makes
presentation impossible anywhere without a browser: headless task jobs, and
messaging channels, where a suspend nobody can resume parks the run forever
(the lesson Slack taught us in remote-channels.ts:738).

But presentation touches no client-local state. `offer_file_downloads`' handler
validates its input and returns an envelope; its buttons render from the tool
RESULT. `show_objects` is already an ordinary backend tool. `show_artifact` was
the odd one out, so it moves: the server returns a presentation handle
{artifact_id, title, type, mime_type} and each surface renders it as it can — a
pane tab here, a link on a channel, nothing at all headless.

Two things fall out of that:

- The pane opens on the host the transcript actually belongs to. The browser
  handler addressed ENGENTY_COPILOT_HOST_KEY, so a specialist's Agent Desk
  popped the global copilot drawer instead of its own pane. The card now reads
  the host from context, and auto-opens only for show_artifact on a live run —
  a fresh artifact_write already surfaces via useArtifactListSync.
- The active-artifact multi-window sync is written server-side, by the one
  writer that always runs, instead of by a browser round trip.

The tool's description says RE-OPEN, and says calling it is never required for
the work to count as done — otherwise models call it after every write, and
headless runs treat a no-op surface as a failure.

commits.message:
feat(ai): a file in storage can be an artifact

Artifacts held four types of text. A spreadsheet, a PDF or a generated image
had no representation at all, which is the only reason `offer_file_downloads`
existed: a chat-only download card, no preview, nothing to reopen, nothing
scoped to the task that produced it.

`file` follows the precedent `app` already set — the content is a handle
({key, name?, mime_type?}), the bytes stay where they were written. That is
what lets a 40 MB xlsx ride the ordinary artifact machinery: pane list, unseen
badges, realtime, store_to promotion to task/goal/project, the catalog.

The pane already knew how to do this and nothing could reach it: WorkFilePreview
(text/json/markdown/csv/images/pdf, office via preview-pdf) and downloadWorkFile
were wired only to the Files tab. A `file` artifact now renders through the same
preview, and the header's Download resolves the stored object instead of handing
the user the handle JSON.

`artifact_write` takes a typed `file` rather than making the model hand-write
JSON into a string field, and infers the type from it. ARTIFACT_HANDLE_TYPES
stops the storage mirror from writing a handle out to a bound folder and calling
it the document — a bug `app` already had.

commits.message:
feat(ai): delete offer_file_downloads

It existed only because a stored file could not be an artifact. Now that it
can, keeping it means two ways to hand over a file, and the worse one wins by
being easier to reach: a download-only chat card with no preview, nothing to
reopen, and no link to the task that produced it.

It was also never really a frontend tool. Its handler validated its input and
returned an envelope — the buttons render from the tool RESULT — so it paid a
suspend/resume round trip through the browser to compute nothing.

The parser and its tool-call card STAY. Threads written before this still
contain `offer_file_downloads` calls, and deleting the renderer would blank out
download buttons in transcripts the user can still scroll back to. Both are
marked legacy; nothing emits the shape any more.

Prompts follow the same rule now — one mechanism, two shapes of input:
artifact_write with `content` for what you write, with `file` for what you
generated.

commits.message:
feat(ai): only the copilot gets frontend tools

Nothing declared these. `assemble-dynamic-agent` merges the run's extraTools
over every root agent's manifest tools, and the executor filled extraTools from
the base catalog — so a specialist on its own desk silently carried ~18 tools it
never asked for: navigate, theme, locale, the copilot's own open/close/dock
controls, and seven browser_* tools for driving the page.

Restricting the server catalog was not enough to fix it. The shell registers the
same tools client-side and App.tsx ships the whole registry to every agent host,
so `includeServerTools: false` would have dropped nothing for a desk specialist.
The gate has to be an allow-list over the merged set.

Tiers: copilot lane gets everything, chatbot.* keeps its own tools, everything
else gets none. And a caller that sent neither tools nor state gets none either
— that is a run with no browser (a script, a bot, a channel bridge), and it was
previously handed a catalog whose first call would suspend the run for a client
that will never resume it.

Same seam for the prompt block, so the model can no longer be told about tools
it does not hold — and the navigate guidance is gated on navigate being present,
because an agent told to navigate without the tool will invent one.

commits.message:
feat(ai): an unattended run can say what it needs

Three gaps, one theme: a headless run had no honest way to deal with needing a
human.

requestDecision already degraded when the run could not park for an answer, but
returned the bare artifact — which reads as "the chooser was shown", so the model
waits for a pick that cannot come or invents one. It now says plainly that
nobody saw it, and carries the question so the run can report it.

requestFeedback had no such split at all: it always told the model "Feedback
artifact shown to the user. Wait for the user's typed response." On a background
task job that is simply false. Same runtime-capability check now decides.

Nothing told the agent it was unattended, while the skills it loads are written
for chat and say "ask the user…". The task brief now states the contract once,
up front, instead of leaving the ask tools to correct it after the turn has
already been spent planning around a question nobody will answer.

And the only way to stop and wait was the TOOL-APPROVAL gate — an ungranted
operation. A missing decision, an ambiguous record, something only the requester
knows: none of it had anywhere to go, so the run guessed, or wrote its question
into a result that reads like a report and parks in in_review beside finished
work. `TASK_BLOCKED: <what I need>` now lands the same way an approval does —
comment, `blocked`, an inbox row whose subject IS the question — for every task,
not just routines.

commits.message:
fix(copilot): the approval row's colour belongs to the verdict, not the shield

An ember-coloured ShieldCheck read as an alert about the operation — the eye
lands on a warning glyph before the word that says the user approved it. The
shield now only marks the row as an approval and stays neutral; the verdict
carries the colour, as a green check or a red cross beside the label. Matches
how run status is coloured elsewhere in ai-ui (emerald-600/400, destructive).

commits.message:
fix(copilot): an answered approval reaches its final row immediately

Answering wrote the optimistic label and nothing else, so until the run
resumed and the transcript refetched the server's `{approved, operation_id}`,
the row kept rendering the full question card with the picked option under it
— the "in between" version of something that ends as one compact line.

The artifact is still in `output` at that point and it carries the answer:
match the resolved label against the gate's own choices and read the verdict
off the choice id. `resolveToolApprovalChoiceVerdict` returns null for
anything that is not one of the three — a custom typed answer falls back to
the decision card rather than being reported as an approval nobody gave.

commits.message: delete offer_file_downloads
commits.body:
It existed only because a stored file could not be an artifact. Now that it
can, keeping it means two ways to hand over a file, and the worse one wins by
being easier to reach: a download-only chat card with no preview, nothing to
reopen, and no link to the task that produced it.

It was also never really a frontend tool. Its handler validated its input and
returned an envelope — the buttons render from the tool RESULT — so it paid a
suspend/resume round trip through the browser to compute nothing.

The parser and its tool-call card STAY. Threads written before this still
contain `offer_file_downloads` calls, and deleting the renderer would blank out
download buttons in transcripts the user can still scroll back to. Both are
marked legacy; nothing emits the shape any more.

Prompts follow the same rule now — one mechanism, two shapes of input:
artifact_write with `content` for what you write, with `file` for what you
generated.

commits.message: a file in storage can be an artifact
commits.body:
Artifacts held four types of text. A spreadsheet, a PDF or a generated image
had no representation at all, which is the only reason `offer_file_downloads`
existed: a chat-only download card, no preview, nothing to reopen, nothing
scoped to the task that produced it.

`file` follows the precedent `app` already set — the content is a handle
({key, name?, mime_type?}), the bytes stay where they were written. That is
what lets a 40 MB xlsx ride the ordinary artifact machinery: pane list, unseen
badges, realtime, store_to promotion to task/goal/project, the catalog.

The pane already knew how to do this and nothing could reach it: WorkFilePreview
(text/json/markdown/csv/images/pdf, office via preview-pdf) and downloadWorkFile
were wired only to the Files tab. A `file` artifact now renders through the same
preview, and the header's Download resolves the stored object instead of handing
the user the handle JSON.

`artifact_write` takes a typed `file` rather than making the model hand-write
JSON into a string field, and infers the type from it. ARTIFACT_HANDLE_TYPES
stops the storage mirror from writing a handle out to a bound folder and calling
it the document — a bug `app` already had.

commits.message: show_artifact becomes a backend presentation tool
commits.body:
A frontend tool suspends the run until a browser resumes it. That makes
presentation impossible anywhere without a browser: headless task jobs, and
messaging channels, where a suspend nobody can resume parks the run forever
(the lesson Slack taught us in remote-channels.ts:738).

But presentation touches no client-local state. `offer_file_downloads`' handler
validates its input and returns an envelope; its buttons render from the tool
RESULT. `show_objects` is already an ordinary backend tool. `show_artifact` was
the odd one out, so it moves: the server returns a presentation handle
{artifact_id, title, type, mime_type} and each surface renders it as it can — a
pane tab here, a link on a channel, nothing at all headless.

Two things fall out of that:

- The pane opens on the host the transcript actually belongs to. The browser
  handler addressed ENGENTY_COPILOT_HOST_KEY, so a specialist's Agent Desk
  popped the global copilot drawer instead of its own pane. The card now reads
  the host from context, and auto-opens only for show_artifact on a live run —
  a fresh artifact_write already surfaces via useArtifactListSync.
- The active-artifact multi-window sync is written server-side, by the one
  writer that always runs, instead of by a browser round trip.

The tool's description says RE-OPEN, and says calling it is never required for
the work to count as done — otherwise models call it after every write, and
headless runs treat a no-op surface as a failure.

commits.message: drop the dead invoke_frontend_tool id from the manager manifests
commits.body:
Same landmine as time-tracking (0da6fcf8a): apps/ai's dynamic assembly
resolves every agent.json toolId against the registry and 400s the whole
run with agent_threads.unknownTool on the first miss. invoke_frontend_tool
is a legacy meta-tool id — frontend tools register per-run natively now
(modules/engenty-copilot/ai/agents/engenty.copilot/tools.ts) — so any
desk/dynamic run of invoices.manager or offers.manager failed before the
model saw the first token. The remaining ids in both manifests are all
builtin (engenty_tools_search, engenty_tool_execute, memory_*) and
resolve.

Sweep of the other module manifests: tasks.assist, inbox.assist,
knowledge-base.manager/.answers, engenty-remote, engenty-coordinator, and
engenty.app-coder all carry resolvable ids. contacts.manager and
company-profile.manager do NOT — their manifests declare camelCase module
wrappers (createContact, loadCompanyProfile, …) that exist neither as
builtin tools nor as operation contracts, so both are broken on the
dynamic lane the same way; they need a time-tracking-style rewiring to
operation ids, which is a bigger change left out of this fix.

commits.message: wire agents and skills to operation contracts
commits.body:
Live testing on the agent desk surfaced that manifest agents (agent.json)
resolve toolIds against the AI registry, which for module functionality
carries ONLY operation contracts from core's /api/tools/contracts — the
defineModuleAi Mastra tool wrappers never cross the process boundary (the
capability seed ships agent_configs/skills/actions, never tools). Every
module tool id in the agent manifests failed with
agent_threads.unknownTool, and invoke_frontend_tool (copied from the
invoices/offers manifests) is a dead legacy id — frontend tools register
per-run natively now.

Both agent manifests now declare operation ids (time_tracking_entries_*,
rows_*, week_get, context_get, saved-report reads for the reporter) plus
tasks_list/projects_list for resolution, and the three skills teach the
operations with their snake_case wire shape instead of the unreachable
camelCase wrappers. This also retro-fixes the pre-existing time-tracking
skill, whose phantom log_time_entry reference is what pushed models to
improvise raw entries_create calls with manual "#21" titles.

Verified end to end against a live space: task + project resolution, date
math (gestern), linked project rows, manual-title fallback disclosed for
identifiers that resolve to nothing (now: ask first), week summary. The
wrappers in ai/tools stay: they serve the dynamicCapability channel and
its tests; whether that channel should survive is a separate decision.

commits.message: an approval is not a decision, and an answered one must say what it approved
commits.body:
Every tool approval rides the decision-artifact pipeline — the gate returns
a decision-shaped artifact tagged `tool-approval|<op>` — so the transcript
part is named `requestDecision` and every reader that looks at the tool name
alone called it a decision. Answering then replaced the artifact in `output`
with `{approved, operation_id}`, which no decision reader recognises: the row
kept "Decision needed", was still counted as UNANSWERED, and hid a raw
`approved: true` behind a chevron. Four of those stacked up in one chat with
nothing to say which operation the user had let through.

- `ag-ui/tool-approval.ts` reads both shapes (the gate's artifact and the
  resolution it is overwritten with), tolerating raw-JSON output because the
  reloaded thread hands it over unparsed.
- The transcript row now reads `Approved "tasks_list"` / `Denied "…"`, with
  `+N more` for a bulk pre-approval, and an OPEN card leads with the gate's
  own question instead of "Decision needed".
- An answered approval renders its own compact card (verdict + operations)
  rather than falling through to the generic tool row.
- `pendingInterruptFromTranscript` stops at an answered approval. It only
  ever recognised a decision's `choice_label`, so it walked past the answer
  to an OLDER row and could re-dock a card the user had already answered.

Ports 64a74354d ("an answered question must still show the question") from
feat/spaces, which never reached main: a natively-suspended chooser resumes
with a model-facing sentence, so its question survives only in the tool's
`args`. Same symptom, same rows — the transcript now leads with the question
and trails the answer, and the resolved card renders the body it dropped.
The upstream test that pinned an answered approval to "Decision needed" is
replaced by the approval rows above.

Verified live on main (engenty.localhost, German UI): the reported thread's
four "Decision needed" rows now read "Freigegeben · time_tracking_context_get
/ projects_list / tasks_list / projects_list_tasks", and an answered chooser
shows title, body and "ANTWORT Ja, prüfen".

commits.message: full AI face — 13 tools, 3 skills, tracker + reporter agents
commits.body:
The module registered 26 gateway operations but exposed only four of them as
agent tools (load/log/update/delete entry) behind a single skill, so anything
report-, row-, or calendar-shaped was reachable only through generic
`engenty_tools_search` discovery with no guidance attached.

Tools (9 new): summarize_time_entries (grouped hours — the report-shaped op,
with the full filter set including the `*_contains` pattern filters that
load_time_entries omits), move_time_entry, load_timesheet_week (the only tool
returning row ids), create_timesheet_row, delete_timesheet_row, and the four
calendar ones: load_calendar_sources, load_calendar_events,
get/set_calendar_sync_settings.

Skills (2 new): time-tracking-reporting covers summarizing plus the saved
reports and snapshots that exist only as operations; time-tracking-calendar-sync
keeps overlay (read, Google + Outlook) apart from push sync (write, Google
only) and encodes the traps — isolated per-calendar errors, per-calendar event
caps, background backfill, no dedupe between meetings and logged hours.

footers.value:
time-tracking.tracker (write surface, timekeeping) and
time-tracking.reporter (read-only on entries, saved reports). Role names rather
than `.manager` because the split is write-heavy vs read-only.

time_tracking_calendar_sync_run deliberately gets no tool: it runs as the
service principal over every enabled connection in the tenant, so it stays
behind engenty_tool_execute with a confirm-first rule in the skill.

Also fixes engenty.plugin.json declaring `capabilities.ai: false` while the
module has registered an AI face all along (metadata only, nothing gates on it).

commits.message: engenty mascot system, fluffy renderer and manage styleguide
commits.body:
Move the engenties out of auth-ui into ui-core, give them a procedural fur
renderer for hero surfaces, and catalogue the whole visual system on a new
/styleguide page in manage.

Engenties now live in packages/ui-core/src/components/engenty and are exported
from @engenty/ui-core; the two auth-ui import sites were rewritten and no shim
left behind. The cast grows from five kinds to ten — bean, pebble, sprout,
tower and wedge join the founding round/drop/dome/flame/oval. The new fills are
derived from existing brand tokens by rotating hue rather than hardcoded, so
they keep tracking the tenant theme; the brand mark still cycles only the
founding five.

FluffyEngenty renders large-format engenties as procedural shell fur in a
WebGL2 shader, with no mesh, texture or library. forms.ts describes each kind
as metaballs and is the bridge between the two renderers: the flat SVG draws
outlines, the shader needs a field. The field is a metaball *sum* — smooth-min
of distances creases where a small blob meets a large one and the coat parts
along the valley, and smooth-min of normalised fields lumps instead. Strand
coverage is antialiased against the pixel rather than the cell, and shell
sampling gaps are closed at the tips, so the coat stays smooth rather than
speckled. One shared GL context serves every instance, since browsers cap live
contexts per document and evict silently.

Also lifts the dock icons off a near-grey wash by boosting only chroma on their
brand tokens, and fixes --rose, which was spelled out rather than aliasing
--danger and so never picked up the dark-mode override its siblings did.

commits.message:
fix(core): always register the agent escalation policy, and clear the red typecheck

Two things, both about a gate or a check that was silently not running.

ENGENTY_AGENT_ESCALATION is deleted and the agent escalation policy now
registers unconditionally. The flag was written as opt-in "until apps/ai
forwards agent/goal ids"; apps/ai has forwarded them for a long time, and the
2026-08-03 audit (AUTH-03) found the policy that policy.ts names as THE gate
governing agent runs registered in no deployment at all. It was then defaulted
to true in the two compose files, which left the real problem in place: unset
means no agent gating, silently, so any other way of running the images -- k8s,
plain docker run, a fresh worktree, the public repo's own setup -- had the
control simply absent. A gate whose absent-default is fail-open is not a gate.
The config half of the switch (config.agentEscalationEnabled) was dead anyway:
read in server.ts, assigned nowhere. To let an agent do more, widen its role
grants -- that is scoped, auditable and per-tenant; disabling the control
globally is not. Removed from both compose files, the env manifest and the
generated .env.example files.

Also repairs the three packages that had been failing typecheck since before
v0.1.120, so four releases shipped over a red gate:

- tenant-settings, user-settings: the registerHttpRoute test mocks declared a
  narrower inline param than PluginHttpRoute. Parameters are contravariant, so
  a narrower param is not assignable to Pick<PluginServerApi, ...>; the return
  type was void rather than the declared receipt. Both now use the real types.
- team-chat: an interface gets no implicit index signature, so neither dispatch
  shape satisfied the Record<string, unknown> that QueueServiceLike.send takes.
  Spread at the call site -- the anonymous object type does get one. Type
  aliases would also fix it but collide with useConsistentTypeDefinitions.

Verified: turbo run typecheck --force --continue is 129/129 for the first time
since v0.1.120; 177 tests across 28 files pass; and with no flag set anywhere,
a Copilot contacts search still files a pending approval request and raises the
card in the browser.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): implement core approval retry mechanism for user consent

Added a new function `settleCoreApprovalAndRetry` to handle user consent for approval requests, allowing the system to utilize previously granted approvals without re-prompting the user. This change ensures that if a user has already approved an action, the system can retry the operation without asking for consent again, thus improving user experience and reducing unnecessary prompts. Updated related functions to integrate this new approval handling logic.

Also, added the `decideApproval` method to the `EngentyToolsClient` interface and implemented it in the `EngentyCoreClient` class to facilitate the approval decision process. Updated tests to cover the new functionality.

commits.message:
feat(inbox): lead with the mail, offer the conversation view only where it fits

The tabs are now Email first, Conversation second, and Email is the
default view — the mail is what a thread is; the AI rendering is the
opt-in.

The Conversation tab only appears when the thread actually is one. A
receipt or a CI notification has nobody to converse with, so it gets the
mail view alone. The digest's category wins when one exists (it saw the
whole body); otherwise the eager classifier's verdict on the latest
message decides, straight off the thread — no digest fetch needed. An
unclassified thread keeps the tab rather than losing the view until
classification catches up.

A stored 'optimized' preference falls back to the mail view on threads
that have no Conversation tab, so the selection can never point at a tab
that is not there.

refactor(inbox): two levels of chrome instead of three

The shell topbar, a module action bar and the tab strip stacked into
three rows of navigation. The action bar is gone; its contents split by
scope.

Entity actions (mark processed, archive) go back to the shell topbar via
usePageConfig, as on every other screen — and their presence is what
keeps that bar from collapsing itself when the module nav is pinned. The
topbar drops contentBlend for the default solid chrome.

Everything scoped to the detail pane moves onto the tab strip: the list

commits.message:
fix(copilot): render decision choosers live in full-page and KB chats

`requestDecision` suspends the run natively, so its chooser exists only in
the open interrupt — the tool call has no output. Two surfaces still read
the interrupt from the persisted thread metadata alone, which lags until a
refetch, so a fresh decision rendered as a generic spinning "Decision
needed" row with no way to answer it and a disabled composer. Reloading the
page fixed it, which was the tell.

- engenty-copilot chat panel: prefer the live `openInterruptFromStream`
  before the session metadata (the drawer already did this).
- KB hub chat: passed no interrupt props at all — wire the same three-way
  resolution plus `respond`, `pendingInterruptToolCallIds`,
  `optimisticInterruptResults` and `awaitingInterrupt`.
- KB Answers agent: declare `requestDecision` so the surface can ask. Tools
  resolve from agent.json, so the TS tool ids are kept in sync with it.

Verified live on both surfaces: chained decisions render without a reload,
and answering resumes the parked run in place.

commits.message:
perf(ai): stop rewriting the prompt cache prefix, and slim the always-on tool surface

The copilot's prompt was ~64% fixed overhead re-sent on every model call, and
the part that wasn't fixed sat in the worst possible place.

Cache prefix:
- The per-run runtime context (pathname, selection, list filters, row previews,
  workspace + module list) rode `instructions`, which Mastra folds into the
  run's SYSTEM PROMPT — the head of the provider's cacheable prefix. Every
  navigation or filter change therefore invalidated the ~8k of recalled history
  behind it. It now rides an input processor that inserts it directly before the
  current user turn, mirroring what the generate lane already did. Runs LAST, so
  the history limiter can never drop it.
- Tools are name-sorted before assembly. Insertion order was not stable: the
  frontend half arrives in whatever order the browser registered its hooks.

Tool surface (~2.8k/call, ~30% of the tool block):
- update_ui_guide + dismiss_ui_guide register only while a guide is open, via a
  new `enabled` option on useFrontendTool/useEngentyFrontendTool. update_ui_guide
  errors when no guide is open, so it was provably dead weight the rest of the
  time. The flag is the general seam for page-gated tools.
- artifact_create/_update/_get/_list/_store -> artifact_write / artifact_read.
  The verb is implied by the arguments; four of the five differed only in which
  two fields they carried.
- The five vault tools -> one `vault_files` with an `action` discriminator that
  dispatches to them, so key scoping and the delete gate stay defined once. The
  granular five remain registered for engenty.file-analyst.
- updateWorkingMemory dropped via `workingMemory.agentManaged: false`. The
  profile is still injected every run (that read path is a separate input
  processor gated on `enabled` alone) — it is simply no longer writable from
  chat, so memory_save owns durable facts.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): correct the token accounting, and show what the numbers are made of

Three defects, all in the same place: cached and reasoning tokens are SLICES of
input and output, and the two chat lanes disagreed about what "usage" meant.

- Cost double-charged every cache hit. computeUsageCost billed all input at the
  input rate AND the cached read on top; on a 75%-cached prompt that is most of
  the prompt charged twice. Each slice is now priced at its own rate and removed
  from its base. The same figures feed bumpPeriodTotals, so quota enforcement
  was inflated too.
- The composer headline summed input + output + cached + reasoning, reporting a
  98.3k thread as 172.1k. sumThreadUsageTokens is input + output; the popover
  shows cached/reasoning as indented sub-rows so they cannot be re-added.
- The streaming lanes metered `lastUsage`, but Mastra emits usage_update once
  per step carrying THAT step's usage — a five-step turn was billed as one call.
  The bridges now expose totalUsage (accumulated, for billing) alongside
  lastUsage (last step). Conversely the generate lane stored the step-summed
  totalUsage in prompt_tokens, which the context meter renders as window
  occupancy — overstating fill by roughly the step count. New nullable column
  ai.agent_run.context_prompt_tokens holds the last step's input; readers fall
  back to prompt_tokens, so old rows are unchanged.

And the drill-ins, because a number nobody can decompose is a number nobody
trusts:
- ThreadUsageDialog behind the thread-total rows: one row per metered run from
  ai.usage_event (new GET /ai/threads/:id/usage/events), split into fresh vs
  cached input, with the calls x prompt multiplier spelled out.
- The composer line has three states. A fresh thread reports a ZEROED summary,
  not null, so it rendered a naked "0"; it now shows the ring's empty track.
  While running it shows a spinning mark and a live "2m 31s - 2.4k tokens" —
  duration_ms only exists once a run has finished, and the token figure comes
  off the stream via a new engenty.usage.update CUSTOM event.

conversation-run.ts and resume-conversation-run.ts also carry their half of the
cache-prefix move from the previous commit — same files, one edit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): relay chat approvals to the decision request core filed

Work in progress from a separate session, committed as-is.

Chat approval wrote only an operation-id grant in thread metadata, which just
the AI-side pre-gate reads. When the card came from core's 202 — the
agent-escalation policy, a connections policy, any decision only core can make —
core knew nothing about the approval, re-gated the retry, and the run landed on
approvalUnavailableResult: the user approved and nothing ran. The decision is
now posted to core's own request, so evaluatePolicy finds a covering grant.

  new `enabled` option on useFrontendTool/useEngentyFrontendTool. update_ui_guide
  errors when no guide is open, so it was provably dead weight the rest of the
  time. The flag is the general seam for page-gated tools.
- artifact_create/_update/_get/_list/_store -> artifact_write / artifact_read.
  The verb is implied by the arguments; four of the five differed only in which

  dispatches to them, so key scoping and the delete gate stay defined once. The

  profile is still injected every run (that read path is a separate input
  processor gated on `enabled` alone) — it is simply no longer writable from
  chat, so memory_save owns durable facts.

the part that wasn't fixed sat in the worst possible place.

Cache prefix:
- The per-run runtime context (pathname, selection, list filters, row previews,
  workspace + module list) rode `instructions`, which Mastra folds into the
  run's SYSTEM PROMPT — the head of the provider's cacheable prefix. Every
  navigation or filter change therefore invalidated the ~8k of recalled history
  behind it. It now rides an input processor that inserts it directly before the
  current user turn, mirroring what the generate lane already did. Runs LAST, so
  the history limiter can never drop it.
- Tools are name-sorted before assembly. Insertion order was not stable: the
  frontend half arrives in whatever order the browser registered its hooks.

commits.body:

refetch, so a fresh decision rendered as a generic spinning "Decision

  resolve from agent.json, so the TS tool ids are kept in sync with it.

and answering resumes the parked run in place.
