commits.message: lead with the mail, offer the conversation view only where it fits
commits.body:
The tabs are now Email first, Conversation second, and Email is the
default view — the mail is what a thread is; the AI rendering is the
opt-in.

The Conversation tab only appears when the thread actually is one. A
receipt or a CI notification has nobody to converse with, so it gets the
mail view alone. The digest's category wins when one exists (it saw the
whole body); otherwise the eager classifier's verdict on the latest
message decides, straight off the thread — no digest fetch needed. An
unclassified thread keeps the tab rather than losing the view until
classification catches up.

A stored 'optimized' preference falls back to the mail view on threads
that have no Conversation tab, so the selection can never point at a tab
that is not there.

hours math as the editor, both now sharing working-hours-schedule.ts

destructive action belongs; the row keeps only the pencil.

commits.message:
fix: add typecheck coverage to 34 packages, fix pre-existing errors

tsup --dts (removed in 2ad377936) hid every type error in a package with no
typecheck script of its own — 36 packages had none. Adding `typecheck: tsc
--noEmit` to each surfaced ~110 pre-existing errors across
knowledge-base (72), contacts/offers/invoices/projects (29), and 7 smaller
packages (a2ui-catalog, live-cache, document-sources, tenant-settings,
user-settings, files-ui, engenty-coordinator). All fixed with real types —
no @ts-ignore, no as-any, no tsconfig loosening.

A handful of the errors were latent runtime bugs the missing typecheck had
been hiding, now fixed:
- kb article-edit could throw navigating before the article query resolved
- kb vector-search suggestions navigated with an undefined kb id
- kb graph dedupe used the wrong graphology addEdge overload, so the
  edge-key check never matched
- kb 'add in tree' category creation invalidated the wrong cache key
  (missing kbId)
- a Radix-only outside-press guard was dead code after the Base UI
  migration; reimplemented via onOpenChange's event reason
- engenty-coordinator's staff workspace mount was declared without
  enabled: true, making it inert on any non-zod-parsed config path

Also removed ~2200 lines of dead code the new checks exposed: an entire
unused commercial-editor/commercial-core engine subtree, two orphaned
team components, and an unreferenced ai-core runtime file.

Verified: every touched package's tsc --noEmit is green; full-repo test
run is 210/211 green (the one failure, ai-ui's composer-status-flap test,
is a 5s-timeout flake under load — passes in 6s isolated, and ai-ui has
zero changes in this commit).

modules/team and modules/team-hr are excluded from this commit: another
session has in-progress edits there as of this commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
perf(deploy): probe every 2s during container startup (start_interval)

The server is up in ~5s, but the first health probe fired only after
interval (10s), the node -e probe costs ~4s to boot, and one missed probe
pushed the first passing check to ~25-30s — all time where the container
runs but Traefik does not route to it. start_interval (Docker 25+; VPS runs
29.x) probes every 2s during start_period, cutting running-but-not-routed
to roughly server-boot + 2s + probe cost.

commits.message:
fix(time-tracking): show newly added rows in weeks with no entries

time_tracking_week_get received week_start but never passed it to
listRows, which derived the week from the fetched entries instead. An
empty week resolved to weekStart "", skipping the timesheet_rows query
entirely — so freshly added rows stayed invisible until the week already
had at least one time entry. Every add path (task / project / manual)
was affected.

listRows now takes the requested week as an explicit hint and only falls
back to deriving it from the entries.

Also fixes a broken relative import in gateway-methods/shared.ts that
made the module fail tsc.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(time-tracking): stop clipping the entry notes popover

The detail panel was absolutely positioned inside the cell, so the
timesheet scroller (overflow-x-auto, which clips vertically too) cut it
off for rows near the bottom of the table.

It now portals to <body> with fixed positioning measured off the cell,
flips above the cell when there is no room below, clamps horizontally,
and re-measures on scroll and resize. Tab-into-notes resolves the
textarea through a ref since it is no longer a DOM descendant.

The server is up in ~5s, but the first health probe fired only after
interval (10s), the node -e probe costs ~4s to boot, and one missed probe
pushed the first passing check to ~25-30s — all time where the container
runs but Traefik does not route to it. start_interval (Docker 25+; VPS runs
29.x) probes every 2s during start_period, cutting running-but-not-routed
to roughly server-boot + 2s + probe cost.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(deploy): probe / instead of /api/openapi.json in the edge healthcheck

/api/openapi.json 500s when any route schema contains a zod type the OpenAPI
generator cannot serialize (v0.1.117/118 shipped a z.custom that does exactly
that) — which turned a docs-endpoint bug into a full outage: the probe fails,
edge sits unhealthy, Traefik routes nothing. Probe / (UI index) instead: it
proves the server accepts and answers requests without depending on OpenAPI
document generation. The openapi 500 itself is fixed separately.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(kb): serialize the custom: sort-by schema for OpenAPI

The z.custom introduced in 2ad377936 cannot be serialized by
getOpenAPIDocument — /api/openapi.json 500'd in prod (v0.1.117/118), and with
the edge healthcheck probing that endpoint it became a full outage. Replace it
with a plain ZodString + startsWith check cast to the template-literal type:
identical runtime validation, a known zod type for the OpenAPI walker, and the
narrow inferred type stays.

Also:
- new regression test mounts the page-layout schema on an OpenAPIHono route
  and generates the document, so an unserializable schema fails in CI
- module-metadata-guardrails now enforces types -> ui/plugin.ts source (the
  internal-packages convention); dist .d.ts files no longer exist
- portless-proxy-check curl gets --max-time so a starved proxy fails fast
  with instructions instead of hanging dev:portless

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(deploy): prefer the SSH pre-pull path over the Coolify API

v0.1.117 proved the ordering wrong: the runner reached the Coolify API
(HTTP 200), so the deploy bypassed /opt/coolify-deploy.sh entirely and the
new pre-pull never ran — the images downloaded inside the outage window
again (~3.5 min of 503s, measured in the Coolify deployment log). The API
can only queue; only the SSH forced-command script pre-pulls while the old
stack still serves. So: SSH first, API as the explicit no-pre-pull fallback
for an unreachable host (v0.1.114 morning). The SSH branch now also demands
the QUEUED marker before trusting rc=0.

Takes effect from the NEXT tag — a tag's workflow is frozen at that tag.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
perf(deploy): pre-pull images on the VPS before queueing the deploy

Coolify's compose deploy removes the old containers first and only then lets
docker compose up pull, so every layer not already on the host downloads inside
the outage window — release deploys pulled 1-2 GB and turned the whole 3-4 min
Coolify window into downtime (v0.1.115/116), while config-only deploys stayed
at ~30s. The forced-command deploy script now docker-pulls the six app images
before queueing: the pull runs while the old stack still serves, the deploy's
own pull finds every layer local, and the outage returns to the
recreate+healthcheck floor. Failed pulls warn but never block — the deploy
then pulls whatever is missing, exactly as before.

Requires reinstall on the VPS (install -m 750 … /opt/coolify-deploy.sh) — done.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
perf(build): drop dts generation — internal packages read types from source

tsup --dts was ~99% of every package build (measured: ESM 485ms vs DTS 49s for
a 2 KB d.ts) and dependsOn ^build cascades one foundation-package edit into ~34
rebuilds — pnpm build took 20-30 min after any app-shell/ui-core change. The
internal-packages pattern removes the cost instead of caching around it:

- build/dev scripts lose --dts across all 80 tsup packages (esbuild only;
  a full cold build of all 83 tasks now takes ~36s)
- package.json types + exports.types point at the source entry; runtime
  exports stay on dist JS, so the prod images and jiti loading are unchanged
- module tsconfigs drop their NodeNext overrides and inherit bundler from
  tsconfig.base.json — they are tsup-bundled, and NodeNext programs reject the
  extensionless relative imports they now read from upstream source

Consumers type-checking source directly surfaced ~25 latent errors that
tsup --dts (which never type-checks) had hidden — 36 packages have no
typecheck script of their own. All fixed in this commit; notable ones:

- app-shell mobile-nav-sheet passed a nonexistent hideCloseButton prop, so
  the close button showed; now showCloseButton={false} as intended
- ui-core Slot read element.ref, removed in React 19 — now child.props.ref
- auth-ui password schema switched off z.preprocess (input type unknown broke
  react-hook-form resolver generics for every consumer)
- knowledge-base: InboxQueryParams import from the module that exports it,
  KbSettings chunking defaults added, slug threaded through the article
  nav-order helpers, custom:-sort zod schema keeps its template-literal type
- ambient shims (vite/client, node, css/untyped libs) now travel with the
  source files via triple-slash references

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
perf(deploy): stop serialising the whole stack behind every deploy

Prod 503s for the entire deploy. Three causes, all removable:

- The images' healthchecks use interval 30s / start_period 60s. Docker only
  marks a container healthy on the first PASSING check, so a container ready in
  seconds stayed "starting" for half a minute and Traefik would not route to it.
  Overridden to 5s/10s.

- core waited on engenty-ai with condition: service_healthy, putting ai's entire
  boot inside the outage — for a dependency it only proxies to at request time.
  Now service_started; /ai/* briefly 502s while ai finishes, everything else is

commits.message:
feat(core,ai): let the server lane sign ES256 for asymmetric projects

v0.1.113 minted the engenty_server JWT with HS256 only. That holds on local and
self-hosted stacks, which verify a shared symmetric secret — but prod's Supabase
Cloud project has completed the JWT-signing-keys migration: it publishes a JWKS
with one ES256 key and keeps the private half, so there is no secret to sign
with and PostgREST rejects HS256 outright ("No suitable key or wrong key type").
The boot preflight did its job and refused to start, and prod 503'd.

Set ENGENTY_SERVER_LANE_PRIVATE_KEY (PKCS8 PEM, or base64 of one so it survives
single-line env plumbing) plus ENGENTY_SERVER_LANE_KEY_ID to mint ES256 with a
key we hold and the project trusts; otherwise the symmetric secret is used and
local dev is unchanged. Half-configuring the pair now throws at boot instead of
degrading to HS256 and failing later with a message blaming the wrong thing —
and the preflight error names the algorithm it actually used, pointing at the
asymmetric migration when HS256 hits that exact PostgREST error.

Verified against a JWKS-verifying PostgREST, not just in unit tests: the real
factory's tokens are accepted (HTTP 200), the request runs as engenty_server
(a table anon cannot read returns rows for us and 401 without a token), and
each tenant's token still sees only its own rows.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(deploy): unpin prod and pass the server-lane signing key through

Reverts the v0.1.112 pin now that the lane can sign ES256 with a key the
project trusts (imported as a STANDBY key — it is advertised in the JWKS, so
tokens verify without rotating and Supabase Auth keeps signing user sessions
with its own key; confirmed against prod's PostgREST, HTTP 200).

Also plumbs ENGENTY_SERVER_LANE_PRIVATE_KEY / _KEY_ID into both composes.
Coolify env vars only reach a container if the compose references them, so
without this the release would have failed the preflight exactly as before.

While doing so: engenty-ai never received SUPABASE_ANON_KEY or
ENGENTY_SECURITY_JWT_SECRET in either compose, so its tenant lane (WP6) has
resolved to null in prod since it shipped — every apps/ai store has been on
the service client there. Added alongside.

tenant JWTs and hands out cached clients via the plugin SDK.

tenant's rows, cross-tenant writes are rejected, browser-lane semantics
unchanged.

commits.message:
fix: make the server lane usable end-to-end (subject, RPC grants, honest auth errors)

Live smoke testing on a running stack found three defects the harness missed.

1. Server-lane JWT subject was the synthetic string `server-lane:<tenant>`.
   17 pre-existing per-user policies across 6 tables read the subject as
   `(current_jwt() ->> 'sub')::uuid`, and were created without a role list, so
   they also applied to engenty_server. The cast threw at plan time and took
   whole tables down for the lane — every chat and agent run failed
   (`agent_threads.createFailed`) and no user setting could be saved. The
   subject is now the nil UUID, and 20260809250000 scopes those policies to
   `authenticated` so both guards hold independently.

2. ai.upsert_thread_with_owner / ai.merge_thread_metadata were ACL'd to
   service_role before the lane existed, so WP6's move to tenant-locked
   handles left them uncallable. Both are SECURITY INVOKER, so granting
   execute adds no authority — the caller's policies still gate every
   statement. Reads worked while creation failed, which is why it looked
   like a chat bug rather than a grant gap.

3. A failure to REACH the auth server was reported as 401 Unauthorized. A
   slow local Supabase container made every session look invalid and sent the
   investigation into permissions for an outage. AuthUnavailableError now
   separates "could not verify" from "rejected", the three resolvePrincipal
   call sites answer 503, and the previously silent catch logs its cause.

Harness/CI, so this class cannot recur silently:
  * the leak sweep hand-wrote claims WITHOUT `sub`, testing a shape
    production never sends — it now mirrors the real minted claims, and a
    query that fails for the lane is reported as a failure rather than
    "? rows visible".
  * coverage rule 4: no PUBLIC policy may cast the JWT subject to uuid.
  * coverage rule 5: no SECURITY INVOKER function may be callable by
    service_role but not by engenty_server.
  Both rules were negative-tested by injecting the regression.

Verified: chat creates threads and persists messages, project + client
creation works through the UI, 343-operation contract pass, 155-table sweep,
all four guards green, core typecheck clean.

commits.message:
fix: close the rest of the class — audit follow-ups from the live-smoke fixes

Swept the codebase for more instances of the three defect shapes found by
smoke testing. Four real ones, one of them in the checker written to prevent
the first.

CROSS-TENANT READ (the only new security hole):
  /api/queues and /api/queues/:name/messages read GLOBAL pgmq state through a
  service-role client but were gated by requireAuth, so any member of any
  tenant could enumerate the queues and peek message bodies — payloads that
  carry whichever tenant's data is enqueued. Verified as a plain member
  holding only module.tasks.read: 200 before, 403 after; superadmin still 200.
  Nothing in the product calls these routes; they are operator diagnostics.

THE NEW CHECKER WAS BLIND (rule 4, shipped an hour earlier):
  It matched the subject cast only as literal text, but our own module
  guidance tells authors to write `core.current_user_id()` — whose body holds
  the ::uuid cast. Following the documented advice made a policy invisible to
  the rule. It reported OK while EIGHT such policies were live on
  module_inbox.*, module_connections.*, module_apps.app_config and
  ai.thread_participant — all of which would have died with the lane exactly
  like ai.thread did. Rule 4 now derives the set of subject-casting helpers
  from pg_proc and follows the indirection; 20260809270000 scopes the eight,
  and refuses to touch any table lacking srv_tenant_isolation so it can never
  strand the lane.

THE 401-FOR-AN-OUTAGE FIX WAS INCOMPLETE:
  resolveRouteAuth (routes/authz.ts) had the same bare `catch { return null }`
  feeding requireAuth/requireSuperAdmin/requirePlatformSuperAdmin — roughly 18
  route modules, and unlike the case already fixed it logged nothing at all.
  auth-provider's own resolveTenantForSession had it too. Below both, the
  core-users DAL turned any PostgREST error on core.users into "user has no
  tenant" (-> 401 / 403 "not yet onboarded") and into "not an admin"
  (-> 403), computing security decisions from errors. All now raise
  AuthUnavailableError; the gates answer 503 and log the cause.

Also verified clean, so recorded rather than changed: no lane-readable table
has RLS disabled; no views exist in app schemas (so no security_invoker
bypass); every function referenced by a lane policy is executable; no
sequences; the other two entries on the supabase-imports legacy list
(dev-login, file-storage) are correctly gated.

One reported finding was a false positive and left alone: feature-flags-routes
shadows requireAuth with a local helper returning { tenantId }, so its
destructuring is correct — the typechecker caught my attempted "fix".

Verified: core typecheck clean, 728 core tests pass, all four guards green,
155-table sweep, 343-operation contract pass, the eight rescoped tables still
readable by the lane, project creation still 201.

commits.message:
fix: wire the boot preflight in, and make the leak sweep prove positive access

Two checks that could not fail. Both were written to guard the exact failure
mode that shipped last week, and neither would have caught it.

PREFLIGHT — defined, documented as the boot guard, never called.
assertServerLanePreflight() existed in both tenant-db.ts files with a header
promising it "fails loud at boot when the minted tokens don't verify against
PostgREST". Nothing invoked it. A deployment with a mismatched JWT secret, or
without migration 20260809200000, would boot green — health checks pass and
the DB guards stay green because they talk to psql, not PostgREST — while
every tenant-scoped query failed at runtime.

It now rides on the registry beside the lane it verifies, and startApiServer
awaits it before the port opens, behind a 10s timeout so a hung probe cannot
wedge startup. Policy is deliberately asymmetric: in production a configured
lane that does not verify REFUSES to start, because a silent boot there means
a wholly broken deployment and a crash loop is far easier to diagnose than
"up but nothing loads"; outside production it logs loudly and continues so a
half-configured worktree stays workable. An unconfigured lane is skipped — the
loader already warns about that case.

Verified all four paths against the live stack: healthy dev boots and logs OK;
broken secret in dev logs the failure and keeps serving; broken secret with
NODE_ENV=production refuses to start and never opens the port; healthy
production boots normally.

LEAK SWEEP — asserted only a negative, so denial looked like isolation.
The sweep checked that no foreign-tenant row was visible. A policy scoped to
the wrong role, or a using(false), hides EVERYTHING — which passes that test
perfectly while every read in the app returns empty. Isolation and total
denial were indistinguishable. It now also asserts the positive: every row
belonging to tenant A must be visible to the lane, compared against a
superuser count of the same table. Proved the new assertion can fail by
scoping core.tenant_settings' lane policy to the wrong role — caught as
"lane sees 0/1 of tenant A's OWN rows", where the old sweep reported green.

It also stops overstating itself. Tables holding no tenant-A row are counted
and listed as NOT PROVEN rather than folded into a reassuring total: on a
fresh database that is 144 of 155, and "0 foreign rows" from an empty table is
not evidence of anything. Today's run proves own-tenant access on 11. NULL
tenant_id now counts as foreign (`is distinct from`, not `<>`, which silently
dropped those rows from the comparison). The header states plainly what a
green run does not prove: the WITH CHECK probe still covers one representative
table, and SELECT is the only verb swept.

Runtime 21s for the doubled query count.

Verified: core typecheck clean, 728 core tests pass, all four guards green,
343-operation contract pass, dev-server smoke still passing.

commits.message:
test: make apps/ai store tests able to detect a lost tenant binding

normalizeDbSource accepts either a plain SupabaseClient or a
TenantScopedDbSource, and the plain-client branch returns
`forTenant: () => client` — it DISCARDS the tenantId. Every store test passed
a bare fake client, so all of them exercised that branch. The consequence is
that no test in this suite could detect a store asking for the wrong tenant,
asking for an empty tenant, or dropping the tenant handle entirely and running
on the service lane. They asserted on rows while the thing that actually
matters — the tenant binding — did not exist in the scenario under test. Same

commits.message:
fix(kb): stop offering knowledge-base creation to users who cannot do it

The KB hub empty state showed every user a primary "Create knowledge base"
button linking to /settings/knowledge-base. That route is a plugin route under
/settings/ outside PERSONAL_SETTINGS_PREFIXES, so AuthenticatedRoutes computes
adminOnly and renders <Navigate replace to={COPILOT_CHAT_ROOT}> for anyone who
is not a tenant admin. A member clicking it was silently teleported to the
copilot chat — no error, no explanation, nothing in the console. Reproduced
live with tenant_role=member. The settings gear in the KB header navigated to
the same place with the same result.

Modules could not do better, because the workspace context published to them
carried only { currentTenant, currentUserId } — there was no way to ask
whether the user may reach tenant-config surfaces, so the hub guessed and
guessed wrong.

Adds isTenantAdmin / isSuperAdmin to the workspace context and threads them
from apps/ui (which already computes both) through AppLayout into
WorkspaceProvider, plus a useCanAdministerTenant() convenience hook. The
context default is NOT admin, so a module rendered outside a provider hides
the affordance rather than dead-ending someone. This is a rendering hint only
— the route guard and the server-side capability checks remain the
enforcement points.

The KB hub now shows the button only to admins and tells everyone else to ask
an administrator (new hub.empty_no_permission string, en + de); the settings
gear is hidden for non-admins.

Not fixed here, same shape, worth a look: inbox → /settings/connections,
offers → /settings/pdf-templates, tasks and copilot → /settings/memory all
link members into admin-only routes.

commits.message: wire the boot preflight in, and make the leak sweep prove positive access
commits.body:
Two checks that could not fail. Both were written to guard the exact failure
mode that shipped last week, and neither would have caught it.

PREFLIGHT — defined, documented as the boot guard, never called.
assertServerLanePreflight() existed in both tenant-db.ts files with a header
promising it "fails loud at boot when the minted tokens don't verify against
PostgREST". Nothing invoked it. A deployment with a mismatched JWT secret, or
without migration 20260809200000, would boot green — health checks pass and
the DB guards stay green because they talk to psql, not PostgREST — while
every tenant-scoped query failed at runtime.

It now rides on the registry beside the lane it verifies, and startApiServer
awaits it before the port opens, behind a 10s timeout so a hung probe cannot
wedge startup. Policy is deliberately asymmetric: in production a configured
lane that does not verify REFUSES to start, because a silent boot there means
a wholly broken deployment and a crash loop is far easier to diagnose than
"up but nothing loads"; outside production it logs loudly and continues so a
half-configured worktree stays workable. An unconfigured lane is skipped — the
loader already warns about that case.

Verified all four paths against the live stack: healthy dev boots and logs OK;
broken secret in dev logs the failure and keeps serving; broken secret with
NODE_ENV=production refuses to start and never opens the port; healthy
production boots normally.

LEAK SWEEP — asserted only a negative, so denial looked like isolation.
The sweep checked that no foreign-tenant row was visible. A policy scoped to
the wrong role, or a using(false), hides EVERYTHING — which passes that test
perfectly while every read in the app returns empty. Isolation and total
denial were indistinguishable. It now also asserts the positive: every row
belonging to tenant A must be visible to the lane, compared against a
superuser count of the same table. Proved the new assertion can fail by
scoping core.tenant_settings' lane policy to the wrong role — caught as
"lane sees 0/1 of tenant A's OWN rows", where the old sweep reported green.

It also stops overstating itself. Tables holding no tenant-A row are counted
and listed as NOT PROVEN rather than folded into a reassuring total: on a
fresh database that is 144 of 155, and "0 foreign rows" from an empty table is
not evidence of anything. Today's run proves own-tenant access on 11. NULL
tenant_id now counts as foreign (`is distinct from`, not `<>`, which silently
dropped those rows from the comparison). The header states plainly what a
green run does not prove: the WITH CHECK probe still covers one representative
table, and SELECT is the only verb swept.

Runtime 21s for the doubled query count.

footers.value:
core typecheck clean, 728 core tests pass, all four guards green,
343-operation contract pass, dev-server smoke still passing.

commits.message: close the rest of the class — audit follow-ups from the live-smoke fixes
commits.body:
Swept the codebase for more instances of the three defect shapes found by
smoke testing. Four real ones, one of them in the checker written to prevent
the first.

CROSS-TENANT READ (the only new security hole):
  /api/queues and /api/queues/:name/messages read GLOBAL pgmq state through a
  service-role client but were gated by requireAuth, so any member of any
  tenant could enumerate the queues and peek message bodies — payloads that
  carry whichever tenant's data is enqueued. Verified as a plain member
  holding only module.tasks.read: 200 before, 403 after; superadmin still 200.
  Nothing in the product calls these routes; they are operator diagnostics.

THE NEW CHECKER WAS BLIND (rule 4, shipped an hour earlier):
  It matched the subject cast only as literal text, but our own module
  guidance tells authors to write `core.current_user_id()` — whose body holds
  the ::uuid cast. Following the documented advice made a policy invisible to
  the rule. It reported OK while EIGHT such policies were live on
  module_inbox.*, module_connections.*, module_apps.app_config and
  ai.thread_participant — all of which would have died with the lane exactly
  like ai.thread did. Rule 4 now derives the set of subject-casting helpers
  from pg_proc and follows the indirection; 20260809270000 scopes the eight,
  and refuses to touch any table lacking srv_tenant_isolation so it can never
  strand the lane.

THE 401-FOR-AN-OUTAGE FIX WAS INCOMPLETE:
  resolveRouteAuth (routes/authz.ts) had the same bare `catch { return null }`
  feeding requireAuth/requireSuperAdmin/requirePlatformSuperAdmin — roughly 18
  route modules, and unlike the case already fixed it logged nothing at all.
  auth-provider's own resolveTenantForSession had it too. Below both, the
  core-users DAL turned any PostgREST error on core.users into "user has no
  tenant" (-> 401 / 403 "not yet onboarded") and into "not an admin"
  (-> 403), computing security decisions from errors. All now raise
  AuthUnavailableError; the gates answer 503 and log the cause.

Also verified clean, so recorded rather than changed: no lane-readable table
has RLS disabled; no views exist in app schemas (so no security_invoker
bypass); every function referenced by a lane policy is executable; no
sequences; the other two entries on the supabase-imports legacy list
(dev-login, file-storage) are correctly gated.

One reported finding was a false positive and left alone: feature-flags-routes
shadows requireAuth with a local helper returning { tenantId }, so its
destructuring is correct — the typechecker caught my attempted "fix".

footers.value:
core typecheck clean, 728 core tests pass, all four guards green,
155-table sweep, 343-operation contract pass, the eight rescoped tables still
readable by the lane, project creation still 201.

commits.message: make the server lane usable end-to-end (subject, RPC grants, honest auth errors)
commits.body:
Live smoke testing on a running stack found three defects the harness missed.

1. Server-lane JWT subject was the synthetic string `server-lane:<tenant>`.
   17 pre-existing per-user policies across 6 tables read the subject as
   `(current_jwt() ->> 'sub')::uuid`, and were created without a role list, so
   they also applied to engenty_server. The cast threw at plan time and took
   whole tables down for the lane — every chat and agent run failed
   (`agent_threads.createFailed`) and no user setting could be saved. The
   subject is now the nil UUID, and 20260809250000 scopes those policies to
   `authenticated` so both guards hold independently.

2. ai.upsert_thread_with_owner / ai.merge_thread_metadata were ACL'd to
   service_role before the lane existed, so WP6's move to tenant-locked
   handles left them uncallable. Both are SECURITY INVOKER, so granting
   execute adds no authority — the caller's policies still gate every
   statement. Reads worked while creation failed, which is why it looked

commits.message:
fix(deploy): build the UI with the real version, not the cache sentinel

The layer-caching fix normalises the root package.json version to
0.0.0-cache in the `manifests` stage so the ~3.7 GB install layer stays
byte-identical across releases. `build` inherits that normalised manifest
from `deps` — and apps/ui/vite.config.ts reads exactly this file to bake
VITE_APP_VERSION into the bundle. The runtime stage restores the real
manifest, so `docker exec … grep version /app/package.json` reported
0.1.111 while the About dialog rendered "0.0.0-cache" to users. v0.1.110
and v0.1.111 both shipped that way.

Restore the real manifest in the build stage, below the cached install so
the caching win is untouched, and fail the build if the sentinel reaches
a bundle — it is invisible until someone opens the About dialog in prod.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(deploy): ship the docs site as a prebuilt image

/docs has returned 502 for every URL since the route was switched on:
ENGENTY_GATEWAY_DOCS_ENABLED=true points the gateway at engenty-docs:3000,
but the service sits behind the `docs` compose profile and Coolify has no
--profile flag, so it was silently skipped on every deploy. The gateway
flag alone is a dead proxy.

Build the image in CI like the other five rather than on the VPS — it is
a full monorepo install plus a Next build — and pull it by tag.

Two latent breaks surfaced building it for the first time; the image had
never actually been built:
- no patches/ in the deps stage, so the install died on the patched
  @mastra/core (the trap the other images document from v0.1.75);
- only the root node_modules in runtime, leaving `next` unresolvable —
  the container exited 254 on ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_EXEC_FIRST_FAIL.

Verified by building and running the image: /docs, /changelog and the
user-guide tree all serve 200.

Also route /changelog to docs — the docs nav links there and the page
lives outside its /docs tree, so it landed on the SPA — and document that
COMPOSE_PROFILES is the other half of enabling docs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): let Code Mode write behind the approval gate

Sandbox programs could only read. The wall was a SECOND fence in front of
core's authoritative gate, so removing it costs no authz: a write from a
sandbox program now needs a grant, exactly like a write from chat.

- engenty_tool_execute is exposed inside the sandbox with a `sandbox` option
  instead of `enforceReadOnly`. Reads run; a gated write without a grant
  returns `approval_required` and tells the model how to get one.
- New engenty_tools_preapprove: one card covers every write op a program
  will use, so a 200-row job asks once instead of 200 times. It drives the
  SAME gate cascade as execute — the interactive start lane gates under the
  "artifact" policy, not "suspend", which an earlier version got wrong.
- Delegated child runs inherit the parent's grants, so an approval given to
  the copilot is not re-asked by engenty.cli.

Approval cards: the artifact id is parsed the way the server encodes it
(first segment, decodeURIComponent) instead of being printed raw — a bulk
card used to show `%7B%22operation_ids%22...%7D`, and a secrets_reveal card
would have shown the secret's id. Bulk cards list every covered operation
and say "for this run"/"for this chat", since "once"/"always" promised the
wrong scope. Choice ids are unchanged; the resume route matches on them.

Suspend/park/resume durability:

- A parked run keeps its sandbox. Mastra's Sandbox._destroy() latches
  status="destroyed" (and returns early when the sandbox never started, so
  it does not even reach Docker), and the resume continues the SAME Session
  whose Workspace holds that instance — execute_typescript after an approval
  died with SandboxNotReadyError and no container ever existed. The park now
  owns the sandbox lifecycle like it owns the controller; teardown persists
  the workspace without destroying, and disposal happens on resume or TTL.
- requestDecision suspends natively instead of returning an artifact, so an
  answer resumes the run in place rather than re-running the turn.
- Suspended runs persist their transcript; `requires_action` runs used to
  write no thread_message rows, leaving history empty on every resume.
- Failed runs record why: an upstream provider failure (rate limit,
  content-policy block, timeout) left error_message NULL on the run row.

Client: RUN_ERROR releases the composer instead of leaving it stuck on
"Stop generation"; the AG-UI inspector resets per thread (it reads a
server-wide firehose, so a new chat showed the previous thread's events)
and gained a Clear button. Tool-search results and Code Mode outcomes are
budget-capped to keep tool schemas from dominating the prompt.

Verified live at https://engenty.localhost: preapprove -> one card ->
"approve for this chat" -> one program created 3 time entries; and
requestDecision -> approve -> execute_typescript ran in the resumed run
with the sandbox container coming up and being torn down after.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(projects): create many tasks in one approved call

An agent building a project plan had no batched write: manage_project_task
created exactly one task per call, so a 40-task plan meant 40 gated calls,
40 round-trips and 40 approval prompts. Watching that loop is what surfaced
it — the model read the whole project tree, returned it as an 88 KB Code Mode
result, then started creating tasks one at a time.

projects_create_tasks takes up to 100 tasks and reads project settings ONCE
for the batch instead of per task, which is most of the per-call cost.

Deliberately NOT transactional: createTask fans out to the tasks module per
row, so there is no single statement to wrap. A bad row is reported in
`failed` and the rest of the batch still lands — a partial batch beats losing
39 good rows to one invalid status. Risk level, capabilities and the approval
gate match the singular op exactly, so one approval covering the batch is the
same authorization, not a weaker one.

The tool description tells the model to use create_many rather than looping
create, since the loop is what costs an approval per item.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): rebuild the workspace when resuming from a snapshot

The parked lane reuses the original Session, which still carries the run's
Workspace and the sandbox instance attached to it. The snapshot lane assembles
a BRAND-NEW agent and passed it no workspace at all, so `ctx.workspace.sandbox`
was undefined for the continuation: after a server restart or a park TTL
expiry, resuming a suspended turn silently lost Code Mode and the workspace
file/skill tools, and the model reported them as unavailable mid-conversation.
Same class of gap the lane already fixed for frontend tools next to it.

The route now passes a `resolveWorkspace` thunk. It is lazy on purpose — the
parked fast path must never call it, or it would build a second sandbox
provider and run its syncIn over the staging dir the live one is using.

Nothing is parked on this lane, so the snapshot resume owns the sandbox
outright and tears it down in a `finally` — including the no-snapshot bail,
which is the easiest place to leak, since the workspace is already resolved by
the time we learn there is nothing to continue. A failed resolution is logged
and the resume continues: a degraded turn beats a stranded interrupt.

Rebuilding is safe because the container is keyed by lifecycle scope
(`engenty-session-<threadId>`), so a fresh instance reconnects to the same
container by label. Reusing a torn-down instance would not work at all —
Mastra latches status="destroyed" and ensureRunning() then throws
SandboxNotReadyError without reaching Docker.

Verified live: parked a run on a requestDecision card, restarted the AI
service to drop the park, answered the card. The resume took the snapshot lane
and built engenty-session-b309233c..., which was torn down when the run
finished. Both halves are mutation-checked by the new tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(time-tracking): refine the saved-reports UI

Follow-up polish on the reports sidebar, settings panel, grouped table and
print stylesheet.

Lint fixes so CI's changed-file check passes:

- Report deletion asks in-app via AlertDialog instead of window.confirm. The
  native dialog is unstyled, blocks the whole tab, and cannot be driven by
  tests. Mirrors the offers sidebar, and adds a `deleteConfirmDescription`
  string in both locales.
- The dimension drag handle states `role="button"` literally. dnd-kit's
  `attributes` spread already sets exactly that (its draggable default role IS
  "button"), but only a literal is visible to static a11y analysis, so the
  aria-label read as unsupported. It has to come after the spread — last wins —
  or TypeScript flags the duplicate.
- ProjectLookup is an interface, matching the codebase's type style.

Verified in the browser: the delete dialog renders with both locale strings,
Cancel closes it, and the saved report survives.

commits.message:
fix(ui-core): keep the doc-sidebar overlay sheet viewport-fixed

DocSidebarLayout passed `relative` into SheetContent's className so the
drag-resize handle had a containing block. SheetContent is `fixed`, and
cn() is tailwind-merge — it treats the two as conflicting position
utilities, so the caller's `relative` silently stripped `fixed`.

The overlay sheet then fell out of viewport positioning: left-aligned at
x=0, starting mid-page at y=300, 832px tall inside a 900px viewport and
overflowing the bottom. Every page using DocSidebarLayout below the
800px inline threshold was affected; it went unnoticed because overlay
mode only triggers on narrow viewports.

`position: fixed` already establishes a containing block for absolutely
positioned descendants, so the handle needs no help. Measured after the
fix: fixed, x=336 (right-aligned), y=0, full 900px height.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(time-tracking): rework report filters into searchable rows

The filter panel rendered five permanently-expanded checklists, each a
max-h-40 scroller over the full catalog. That does not survive hundreds
of projects, and it contradicted the data layer: an empty filter has
always meant "include everything", but the UI read as "curate a list"
and gave no signal that unchecked meant included.

Filters are now one row per dimension, always visible, defaulting to
"Alle". Values are picked in a searchable popover, never inline:

- Checkbox click toggles that item; label click solos it (select it,
  drop the rest). Solo is the common move at catalog scale, so it gets
  the larger hit area. The solo cues (underline + "nur") hang off their
  own hover zone so the checkbox never advertises them, and are
  hover-gated rather than data-selected because cmdk auto-selects the
  first item on open.
- Pattern filters (project name, client name, note) are evaluated
  server-side, so a saved report stays live as projects are added --
  an enumerated id list goes stale. project_name_contains also matches
  manual_project_title so manual entries are not silently dropped.
- Task filter gets a UI; task_ids already worked server-side.
- The phase filter no longer sits dead until a project is picked: with
  no project selected it loads phases across all projects.
- Grouping is capped at three dimensions, clamped on parse so a
  hand-edited URL or an older saved report cannot exceed it.

The sidebar toggle moves from the workspace topbar into the report
heading, per DocSidebarToggle's contract, and is renamed Einstellungen
-> Aufbau: this panel is not preferences beside the report, it is the
report's definition.

commits.message:
fix(ai): continue the run after a snapshot resume re-suspends

The crash-recovery resume lane (`resumeFromSnapshot`) answered a decision
card after a restart and then went silent: the run's events were only
RUN_STARTED, TOOL_CALL_RESULT, RUN_FINISHED, and nothing was written to
thread history. Two gaps, both the same class as the three this lane has
already been patched for — things the parked lane gets from its live
Session that a re-assembled agent does not.

The lane runs under `approvalPolicy: "suspend"`, so the first thing a
recovered continuation usually does is park AGAIN on a gated tool. Mastra
reports that with a `tool-call-suspended` chunk and ends the stream — no
`tool-call` chunk and no text for the newly suspended call. Nothing read
that chunk, so the resume looked like a run that finished with nothing to
say, and the caller cleared the open interrupt on a run that was in fact
waiting: the card vanished and the answer could never be delivered. It now
raises the next interrupt the same three ways the parked lane does. The
resume target stays the SAME run id, because Mastra resumed it in place
and wrote the new suspension back under that id.

The agent was also assembled without a memory instance (the parked lane's
comes from its AgentController), so the continuation recalled no history
and persisted nothing.

Pinned by a test that drives the real Mastra runtime with a second Agent
standing in for the restart — `resumeStream({untilIdle, toolCallId})` does
re-enter the agent loop, so the resume API was never the problem.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): fail loudly when a snapshot resume cannot finish

Two ways the crash-recovery lane reported SUCCESS for a run that had in
fact failed or was still waiting. Both matter more than the missing
answer, because the success path CLEARS the open interrupt — and that
metadata key is the only pointer back to the suspended run, so once it is
gone no reconciler, reload, or retry can reach the turn again.

`DurableAgUiConverter` has no case for Mastra's in-band `error` chunk, and
nothing inspected `finishReason` either (`readMastraStreamFailure` exists
for exactly that and had no callers). A gateway failure mid-continuation
therefore reached neither the client nor the run row: the thread flipped
to completed and the interrupt was deleted. Both signals are now read and
raised. The parked lane gets this from its session's `error` event.

The second is narrower and newer: when a re-suspend cannot be rendered as
an interrupt — a frontend tool this POST did not declare — Mastra still
holds the suspension, so falling through to RUN_FINISHED stranded it. The
parked lane's `finally` rescues that case via `suspensions.hasPending()`;
this lane has no live session to ask, so it raises instead.

commits.message:
fix(security): give tenantless join tables a real tenant boundary

Module DAL runs on a service-role client that bypasses RLS, so every
tenant boundary is application-level. Five join tables had none of their
own: their RLS policies reached through a parent to find the tenant, and
with RLS bypassed that join was the only thing separating tenants. Any
reader that skipped it turned a foreign id into an authoritative answer
— which is how the secrets reveal path came to grant cross-tenant access
via project_team.

Each table now carries tenant_id/scope_id backed by a composite foreign
key against (id, tenant_id, scope_id) on its parent, so a row that
disagrees with its own parent is unrepresentable and a parent changing
scope drags its children along:

  module_projects.project_team              20260809120000
  module_tasks.task_collaborators           20260809140000
  module_contacts.contact_roles             20260809141000
  module_kb.article_tags / faq_tags         20260809142000
  module_kb.kb_source_item_{sections,media,links}
                                            20260809143000

task_collaborators was the worst placed: three modules read it and two
keyed on user_id alone, which is global, so those reads returned task
ids from every tenant that user touched.

The kb tag joins needed a different recipe. They have TWO tenant-scoped
parents, so a column alone would not stop an article being tagged with
another tenant's tag — both composite FKs point at the same
(tenant_id, scope_id) pair, forcing owner and tag into one tenant. Those
two FKs must be DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED: two ON UPDATE CASCADE
constraints sharing a column pair otherwise deadlock, because moving an
article's scope cascades the join row onto a tag that has not moved yet.
Verified in psql across insert, cross-tenant insert, scope move and
cascade delete.

Two unbounded cross-tenant scans closed along the way, both of the shape
that produced the secrets leak — ids fetched across all tenants and only
narrowed by a later filter:
  - contacts listContactIdsByRole, .eq("role") with nothing else
  - knowledge-base article search by tag_id

Guard changes (scripts/check-foreign-schema-scope.mjs):
  - UNSCOPED_TABLES is now deliberately empty. task_collaborators was
    its last entry and did not survive scrutiny; wanting to add one is
    the signal a table needs a boundary instead.
  - Accepts an insert/upsert that sets tenant_id and scope_id in the
    payload — a write carries its tenant there, not in a filter.
  - BASELINE 5 -> 3; the project-tasks-bridge entries are fixed.

Also drops two tables the audit found dead — no readers, no rows, no FK
children, no views or functions: module_projects.portal_rate_limits
(20260809144000) and module_secrets.service_secrets (20260809145000).

All five tenant migrations are re-runnable: the child composite FK is
dropped first, since it depends on the parent unique index the migration
recreates.

commits.message:
feat(time-tracking): add free-text notes to a saved report

A saved report could carry a title and nothing else, so the reasoning
behind a report — what period it covers, what was excluded, who asked
for it — lived outside the tool. `notes` is edited inline under the
report heading and persists on the saved_reports row.

Nullable with no default: an absent note and an empty note mean the same
thing, so existing reports stay valid without a backfill.

Notes are deliberately NOT carried in the URL. Every other part of the
builder state round-trips through search params so a report is
shareable as a link, but prose would bloat every navigation, and the
saved report is the only meaningful source for it — an unsaved draft
simply starts empty. reportStateFromSavedFilters now takes the notes
alongside the title for the same reason.

Also persists the three *_contains predicates
(client_name_contains, project_name_contains, notes_contains) on
SavedTimeReportFilters. They were added to the filter row UI but not to
the saved shape, so reopening a saved report silently dropped them.

Printing renders the notes under the heading and hides the inline edit
affordance.

commits.message:
fix(security): scope the portal client lookup to the project's tenant

The portal resolved a project's client name by reading module_contacts by
id alone. The adapter from getDatabaseAdapter() is service-role and
bypasses RLS, and projects.client_id is plain text with no foreign key, so
nothing confined that read to the project's own tenant — and the portal
visitor is anonymous, so the result renders on a public page.

The read also named module_contacts.entities, which no longer exists: the
contacts migration replaced entities/people/contact_organisation with
module_contacts.contacts. So it has been erroring on every portal load and
falling through to the stored client_name. Point it at contacts and route
it through foreignSelect, which takes the tenant scope as a required
argument. Scope comes from the project row itself, as getPublicGeneralTasks
and createRequestTask already do here; single() becomes maybeSingle() so a
client_id with no in-tenant match is an ordinary miss rather than an error.

Where a project has a real client_id the portal now shows the contact's
display_name instead of the stored client_name string. That is what this
code always intended, but it is visible if the two have drifted apart.

Drops the matching BASELINE entry from the guardrail; the other two sites
it named were already fixed in 72454c190.

commits.message:
fix(ai): make the snapshot resume exclusive and rebuild its agent context

Two more members of the "a re-assembled agent has none of it" family, both
of which only misbehave AFTER a restart — which is precisely when nobody is
watching.

Mutual exclusion. `takeParkedSessionRun` claims the in-flight marker for
the parked lane, but on the snapshot lane it returns nothing, so that lane
had no mutual exclusion at all: two answers for one run executed
concurrently, each resolving AND destroying the single session-scoped
sandbox (the second continuation then hit SandboxNotReadyError, plus a
syncOut race over one staging dir). Both were also invisible to the
thread-load reconciler, which reads that same marker as proof an interrupt
is still live, so a concurrent load could clear an interrupt mid-resume.
`claimResumeInFlight` is a check-and-set the snapshot lane owns and
releases; the `finally` now releases only a claim this call actually made.

Agent context. The re-assembled agent was given no instruction overrides,
no per-run runtime instructions, and no model config — the parked lane
inherits all three from its live Session. The visible symptom is language:
`route_context` carries the user's UI language, so a German user's
post-restart continuation came back in English. Persona and skill overrides
vanished the same way, and the continuation could answer on a different
model than the first half of its own turn. Instructions ride
`instructionExtras.appendBodies`, which is where the controller's per-run
instructions land on the start lane; resolution is best-effort, since
degraded instructions beat a stranded interrupt.

Still missing on this lane and deliberately left out of scope: delegation
tools, which need child-workspace plumbing the resume input does not carry.

commits.message:
fix(ai): give the resume lanes the executor's post-run pass

Neither resume lane ran the teardown the START executor has always run, so
everything a resumed turn produced after the gate was invisible: the
transcript, the sub-agent Log, and the tokens.

The case that needs it most is the one Mastra memory can never cover. A
continuation ending on a SECOND suspend never reaches end-of-generation, so
memory flushes nothing at all — the whole continuation was lost, and the
next turn read an empty transcript and re-asked the question the user had
already answered. Multi-hop approvals (approve -> tool -> approve again)
are the common shape, not an exotic one. The pass therefore lives in
`finally`, where every exit path reaches it.

Metering was the same story from the other end: a gated turn does its cheap
half before the approval and its expensive half after, and only the first
half was ever billed. A failed resume also stored `error_message = NULL`,
which is exactly the field you go looking for afterwards.

`DurableAgUiConverter` gained the state this needs — transcript parts, a
`lastUsage` from the `finish` chunk, and resolved/suspended tracking — so
the snapshot lane can also answer a tool the model invents mid-continuation
instead of leaving its card spinning forever. A tool that SUSPENDED is
tracked apart from one that dangles: settling it would resolve the very
interrupt the run just raised.

`usageFromSession`/`recordSessionUsage` move to run-usage.ts rather than
being copied, so both executors meter through one implementation.

commits.message:
fix(ai): stop the native decision suspend from losing and duplicating its turn

`requestDecision` suspends the run instead of returning its artifact as a tool
result, which quietly invalidated two assumptions the surrounding code still
encoded.

"The artifact arrives as a tool RESULT" — `emitArtifactInterrupt` was the only
one of the three interrupt emitters not putting the card on the CUSTOM
`engenty.open_interrupt` side channel. It never needed to: the client could read
the artifact off the result. With no result and no event, the RUN_FINISHED
outcome (schema-stripped to an id and a title, no choices) was all that reached
the browser.

"An interrupted turn leaves NOTHING behind" — memory flushed only at
end-of-generation back when a decision ABORTED the run, so the executor wrote the
transcript itself as a safety net. A suspend keeps the turn inside Mastra, which
flushes on park; the safety net became a second copy of the same tool call, once
as `tool-invocation` and once as `dynamic-tool`. Both lanes now stand down on
parked paths. `native-suspend-memory-flush.test.ts` pins that against the real
runtime rather than assuming it.

Two more that fell out of the above:

- `resolveToolCallResultInHistory` only ever patched memory's shape and stopped
  at the first row, so an answered decision left its duplicate spinning. It now
  resolves both shapes and every row carrying the call, which also repairs
  threads that already hold doubles.
- The snapshot lane handed its converter over by RETURN VALUE, so a continuation
  that died mid-stream threw past the handover and the post-run pass silently did
  nothing — dropping the half-answer, the sub-agent log and the token count for
  exactly the failure it exists to salvage. It is handed over the moment it
  exists now.

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): route the decision card by tool name, not by tool output

The chooser was registered with `match: (ctx) => matchesDecisionArtifactOutput(
ctx.output)` — it decided whether to render from the tool call's OUTPUT. A
natively suspended `requestDecision` has no output, so the match failed and the
call fell through to the generic card: a spinning "Decision needed" row with no
way to answer it. The choices were on the wire the whole time; nothing was
listening, because the component that reads the open interrupt was never the one
being rendered.

Matching on tool name as well hands those calls to the card that knows how to
hydrate from the open interrupt. The output arm stays: tool-approval cards still
arrive as an artifact result under `engenty_tool_execute`.

Routing by name means the card now also sees answered and dangling decision
calls, which brings three consequences with it:

- No artifact resolves for those, and returning null erased the tool call from
  the turn entirely. They fall back to the normal transcript row.
- Every unanswered decision row would otherwise render whichever chooser is
  currently open — the same question several times, only one of which can be
  answered. The open interrupt now only hydrates the call it names.
- An open interrupt on this call counts as "waiting". `pendingInterruptToolCall-
  Ids` is populated from RUN_FINISHED, so after a reload it is empty and an
  unanswered card reported itself as "Decision submitted".

commits.message:
feat(ai): open the context meter's prompt number into a size breakdown

Developer mode turns the composer's "Prompt 29.9k" into a link; it opens a modal
splitting the prompt into system instructions, recalled history and tool
definitions, with tools listed heaviest first.

RECONSTRUCTED on request, not captured per run. Storing each run's assembled
prompt would duplicate the whole conversation every turn (~120KB for a 30k-token
prompt) for a read almost nobody performs, and would put a second copy of that
content under a different retention rule than the thread it came from. The cost
is that this describes the NEXT run rather than the last one, so it does not
match the meter's `prompt_tokens` — which is stated in the panel rather than
smoothed over, and is also what makes it useful: it moves as you prune.

`GET /ai/v1/threads/:id/prompt-preview` assembles the agent through the same
`resolveAgentForSessionMemory` a run uses, but deliberately WITHOUT a run id — a
run id is what makes that function write an `ai.agent_run` row and provision
workspaces and sandboxes, which a GET that only reads sizes has no business
causing. What that costs (workspace tools) goes out as a caveat rather than
quietly shrinking the total. Dev-only, 404 in production, same switch as the
AG-UI debug firehose.

Verified against the live dev thread, which caught the one bug that mattered:
tools arriving from `getToolsForExecution` are AI SDK CoreTools whose
`parameters` is the SDK's `Schema` wrapper, not a Zod type, so a Zod-only
conversion measured all 46 tools at zero and reported the prompt's HEAVIEST
section as weightless — 12k chars instead of 36.6k. Tool schemas turn out to be
59% of that thread's prompt, which is the whole answer the panel exists to give.
Unreadable schemas now report `schema_source: "none"` and name themselves in the
caveats instead of reading as cheap.

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): mark the seam where the inspector timeline reverses direction

The Application stream panel concatenates two lists that run in OPPOSITE
directions: messages oldest-first (they are a conversation) and raw events
newest-first (they are a live tail). Both orderings are right on their own, but
they sat in one unbroken list under one header, so the panel read as a thread
that had lost its ordering — or replayed itself.

A divider row now names the seam and states which way each half runs. Copying
the stream is unaffected: divider rows are filtered out before the transcript is
assembled oldest-first.

directions: messages oldest-first (they are a conversation) and raw events
newest-first (they are a live tail). Both orderings are right on their own, but
they sat in one unbroken list under one header, so the panel read as a thread
that had lost its ordering — or replayed itself.

A divider row now names the seam and states which way each half runs. Copying
the stream is unaffected: divider rows are filtered out before the transcript is
assembled oldest-first.

commits.message:
fix(ai): stop a snapshot resume re-persisting the user turn it is resuming

Answering a decision card wrote the user's original question to the thread a
SECOND time, so the model re-read it on every later turn and the chat showed it
twice on reload.

Mastra delivers user turns as SIGNAL messages, and the id of the signal MESSAGE
is not stable across runs. The start run persisted the row under one id; the
snapshot resume — which rebuilds the turn from Mastra's own workflow state rather
than from our rows — re-saved the same turn under another. Keyed only on
`message.id`, the second save matched nothing and inserted a duplicate.

The turn's durable identity is the signal id, which survives both paths and was
already being persisted in row metadata; both copies in the thread that surfaced
this carry the same one. A user row now matches on it when the message id does
not. Role-gated, because folding a user turn onto an assistant row would
overwrite the model's answer with the question.

Found by reading the AG-UI inspector's timeline top-down, which is what the
preceding ordering fix was about.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(copilot): stop navigate from reporting success for routes that do not exist

`engenty_tools_modules`, the runtime-context preamble and the navigation-paths
prompt all reported a module's base URL as `/mdl/<pluginId>` — synthesized from
the plugin id, never read from the router. Over half the modules register no
such route (`commercial-settings` has only `/mdl/commercial-settings/settings`),
so navigating there fell through to the `path="*"` catch-all, which redirects to
the copilot chat root with `replace`: the user was bounced back to the chat they
started from and even the URL evidence was overwritten. `navigate` returned
`{ok:true}` regardless, so the agent then said it had opened the page.

Route paths are declared in each module's client-side `ui/plugin.ts` and never
reach a server, so the check has to live in the browser. `navigate` now resolves
against the live contribution list: a prefix owning exactly one static page goes
there and reports where it landed, anything else throws listing the routes that
exist. Scoped to `/mdl/*`, the only prefix that list is complete for — the host
declares ~25 routes inline that never appear in it.

Hoists `UiContributionsProvider` above `shellUiHost` in App.tsx; the copilot
mounts beside `AuthenticatedRoutes`, so the table was out of its reach.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(ai-ui): show usage on every copilot surface and stop the flap opening empty

The usage meter takes `threadId` from its host and renders nothing without one.
`panelContentProps` never set it, so it was mounted but inert on the sidebar,
drawer and modal; the compact launcher never passed it either. Only the bottom
dock and full-page chat, which wire `activeThreadId` directly, ever showed it.

The status flap is gated on the interrupt element being non-null, but
`CopilotOpenInterruptBanner` returns null for interrupts it has no card for
(frontend-tool suspends, artifacts with no choices) — so the flap slid open
around nothing. Gated on `hasRenderableOpenInterrupt` instead.

Also compacts the meter to `89.2k / 3.7M · 4s`; the dropped "run"/"total" labels
move to the button title and stay spelled out in the popover.

commits.message:
feat(commercial-settings): collection-scoped write operations for the AI catalog

The module registered exactly one operation, `commercial_settings_get`, so the
copilot could read commercial defaults but never change them — the write path
existed as `repo.set()` and `PATCH /api/commercial-settings`, it was just never
exposed as an operation. Asked to add disciplines, the copilot clicked the form
instead and saved nothing.

Adds one write per collection (disciplines, units, tax_rates,
expense_categories, tax_deduction_rules) plus `commercial_settings_defaults_set`
for the scalars, rather than a single whole-settings write. Each collection has
its own JSON column, and a whole-object write is how a caller that only cares
about disciplines erases the tax rates: `set()` built every column on every call
and wrote null for anything absent. It only ever ran from the UI, which GETs the
whole object and PATCHes it back whole, so it stayed latent — the first partial
caller would have lost data, and an AI tool is exactly that caller.

`set()` now writes only the fields it was given; absent leaves a column alone,
explicit null clears it. Tax rate validation moves onto the array schema so the
scoped operation validates identically to a full settings write. Approval is
required for the money-bearing collections (tax rates, expense deductibility,
deduction rules, currency) but not for catalog data.

Verified against the running stack: writing only disciplines left the tenant's
4 tax rates, 19 expense categories, currency and locales intact.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(pdf-templates): full template lifecycle in the AI catalog, plus authoring skills

`pdf_templates_get` was the module's only operation, and it needs an id — with
no list operation there was no way to reach one, so the AI could neither
discover nor change the templates that offers and invoices are printed from.

Adds list, create, update, delete and preview. `pdf_templates_preview` is the
important one: it renders markup against sample or record data without saving,
so markup can be checked before it overwrites a live template. Writes are
approval-gated; preview stays open, or the check-before-you-write loop would
need an approval per attempt.

Two skills carry the authoring knowledge. The engine fails quietly in ways that
only surface on a client's PDF — an unknown element silently degrades to
<View>, a missing style name is ignored, and <Text> drops child elements — so
the reference documents those failure modes and the workflow skill makes
preview-before-write the rule.

Fixes a bug the update operation would otherwise have inherited: `.partial()`
does not strip zod defaults, so a name-only patch arrived carrying
`is_default: false` and `schema_version: 1`. updateTemplate guards on
`!== undefined`, so the guard never fired — renaming a template cleared its
default flag. types.ts already documented the trap for `document_template`; it
just was not applied to these two fields.

Verified against the running stack: all six operations resolve in the catalog,
list and get return 200, and preview renders Liquid against real sample data.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(commercial-settings): keep the settings page in sync with out-of-band writes

The copilot's commercial_settings_*_set operations wrote correctly, but the page
kept showing the values it was mounted with. Two independent reasons, both
needed fixing:

The module had no live binding, so nothing invalidated the
`["commercial-settings"]` query root when the row changed — every other module
with a settings surface declares one. Adds it, with the realtime migration the
signal needs (authenticated SELECT, replica identity full, publication
membership) and `agentToolIds` for the agent-write fast path, which invalidates
the moment a copilot tool call resolves instead of waiting for the round trip.

That alone changed nothing visible: the form seeded from the query exactly once
per mount behind an `initialSyncedRef` and ignored every later result, so a
refetch could not reach the inputs. It now re-adopts server state whenever the
payload differs from the snapshot it currently mirrors — unless the user has
unsaved edits, which win, because adopting mid-typing would delete what they
are writing.

Verified live: with the page open, a write through the operation surfaced in the
inputs without a reload, and a pending local edit survived a concurrent external
write untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
docs(user): document every module and the cross-cutting agent operations

The user guide had four pages and a line saying module guides were coming. It
never said what the copilot can actually do, so the only way to find out was to
ask it and see.

Adds two sections. **Modules** covers the thirteen modules with a UI — offers,
invoices, commercial settings, company profile, PDF templates, projects, tasks,
time tracking, contacts, team, inbox, team chat, knowledge base — each
explaining what the module is for and listing its agent operations. **Agent
operations** covers what is not tied to one module: workspace search,
connections and the connected services behind them, memory, secrets, apps,
remote channels and the browser bridge.

All 359 operations are listed, each marked as a read or a write, with the
approval-gated ones called out where the consequence is real (issuing an
invoice, changing a tax rate, deleting a template). The operation names come
from the live catalog and every one was checked back against the source; the
reads/writes split and the "agents write through operations, not by clicking
your forms" rule are stated once in the section index and referenced from there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(dev): raise the open-file limit before starting the dev stack

`pnpm dev:portless` died in a storm of "EMFILE: too many open files, watch" from
the docs webpack watcher. macOS hands GUI-launched terminals a 256-descriptor
soft limit (`launchctl limit maxfiles`), which a Next webpack compile of the
docs app exhausts in seconds.

The hard limit is unlimited, so the soft limit raises without sudo. Clamped to
the hard limit where one exists, silent when the shell already has headroom,
and a warning rather than a failure if the raise is refused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(dev): raise the open-file limit for `pnpm dev` too

`dev:portless` got the EMFILE fix; the port-based `pnpm dev` ran Turbo straight
from package.json, where there is nowhere to raise a ulimit, so it still died on
a 256-descriptor terminal.

Moves the raise into a sourceable helper both entry points share, and gives
`pnpm dev` a one-line script whose only job is to raise the limit and then
`exec` the same Turbo invocation — exec, so signal handling and exit codes are
unchanged from running it inline. Extra arguments pass through.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message: raise the open-file limit before starting the dev stack
commits.body:
`pnpm dev:portless` died in a storm of "EMFILE: too many open files, watch" from
the docs webpack watcher. macOS hands GUI-launched terminals a 256-descriptor
soft limit (`launchctl limit maxfiles`), which a Next webpack compile of the
docs app exhausts in seconds.

The hard limit is unlimited, so the soft limit raises without sudo. Clamped to
the hard limit where one exists, silent when the shell already has headroom,
and a warning rather than a failure if the raise is refused.

commits.message: document every module and the cross-cutting agent operations
commits.body:
The user guide had four pages and a line saying module guides were coming. It
never said what the copilot can actually do, so the only way to find out was to
ask it and see.

Adds two sections. **Modules** covers the thirteen modules with a UI — offers,
invoices, commercial settings, company profile, PDF templates, projects, tasks,
time tracking, contacts, team, inbox, team chat, knowledge base — each
explaining what the module is for and listing its agent operations. **Agent
operations** covers what is not tied to one module: workspace search,
connections and the connected services behind them, memory, secrets, apps,
remote channels and the browser bridge.

All 359 operations are listed, each marked as a read or a write, with the
approval-gated ones called out where the consequence is real (issuing an
invoice, changing a tax rate, deleting a template). The operation names come
from the live catalog and every one was checked back against the source; the
reads/writes split and the "agents write through operations, not by clicking
your forms" rule are stated once in the section index and referenced from there.

commits.message: keep the settings page in sync with out-of-band writes
commits.body:
The copilot's commercial_settings_*_set operations wrote correctly, but the page
kept showing the values it was mounted with. Two independent reasons, both
needed fixing:

The module had no live binding, so nothing invalidated the
`["commercial-settings"]` query root when the row changed — every other module
with a settings surface declares one. Adds it, with the realtime migration the
signal needs (authenticated SELECT, replica identity full, publication
membership) and `agentToolIds` for the agent-write fast path, which invalidates
the moment a copilot tool call resolves instead of waiting for the round trip.

That alone changed nothing visible: the form seeded from the query exactly once
per mount behind an `initialSyncedRef` and ignored every later result, so a
refetch could not reach the inputs. It now re-adopts server state whenever the
payload differs from the snapshot it currently mirrors — unless the user has
unsaved edits, which win, because adopting mid-typing would delete what they
are writing.

Verified live: with the page open, a write through the operation surfaced in the
inputs without a reload, and a pending local edit survived a concurrent external
write untouched.

commits.message: full template lifecycle in the AI catalog, plus authoring skills
commits.body:
`pdf_templates_get` was the module's only operation, and it needs an id — with
no list operation there was no way to reach one, so the AI could neither
discover nor change the templates that offers and invoices are printed from.

Adds list, create, update, delete and preview. `pdf_templates_preview` is the
important one: it renders markup against sample or record data without saving,
so markup can be checked before it overwrites a live template. Writes are
approval-gated; preview stays open, or the check-before-you-write loop would
need an approval per attempt.

Two skills carry the authoring knowledge. The engine fails quietly in ways that
only surface on a client's PDF — an unknown element silently degrades to
<View>, a missing style name is ignored, and <Text> drops child elements — so
the reference documents those failure modes and the workflow skill makes
preview-before-write the rule.

Fixes a bug the update operation would otherwise have inherited: `.partial()`
does not strip zod defaults, so a name-only patch arrived carrying
`is_default: false` and `schema_version: 1`. updateTemplate guards on
`!== undefined`, so the guard never fired — renaming a template cleared its
default flag. types.ts already documented the trap for `document_template`; it
just was not applied to these two fields.

Verified against the running stack: all six operations resolve in the catalog,
list and get return 200, and preview renders Liquid against real sample data.

commits.message: collection-scoped write operations for the AI catalog
commits.body:
The module registered exactly one operation, `commercial_settings_get`, so the
copilot could read commercial defaults but never change them — the write path
existed as `repo.set()` and `PATCH /api/commercial-settings`, it was just never
exposed as an operation. Asked to add disciplines, the copilot clicked the form
instead and saved nothing.

Adds one write per collection (disciplines, units, tax_rates,
expense_categories, tax_deduction_rules) plus `commercial_settings_defaults_set`
for the scalars, rather than a single whole-settings write. Each collection has
its own JSON column, and a whole-object write is how a caller that only cares
about disciplines erases the tax rates: `set()` built every column on every call
and wrote null for anything absent. It only ever ran from the UI, which GETs the
whole object and PATCHes it back whole, so it stayed latent — the first partial
caller would have lost data, and an AI tool is exactly that caller.

`set()` now writes only the fields it was given; absent leaves a column alone,
explicit null clears it. Tax rate validation moves onto the array schema so the
scoped operation validates identically to a full settings write. Approval is
required for the money-bearing collections (tax rates, expense deductibility,
deduction rules, currency) but not for catalog data.

Verified against the running stack: writing only disciplines left the tenant's
4 tax rates, 19 expense categories, currency and locales intact.

commits.message: show usage on every copilot surface and stop the flap opening empty
commits.body:
The usage meter takes `threadId` from its host and renders nothing without one.
`panelContentProps` never set it, so it was mounted but inert on the sidebar,
drawer and modal; the compact launcher never passed it either. Only the bottom
dock and full-page chat, which wire `activeThreadId` directly, ever showed it.

The status flap is gated on the interrupt element being non-null, but
`CopilotOpenInterruptBanner` returns null for interrupts it has no card for
(frontend-tool suspends, artifacts with no choices) — so the flap slid open
around nothing. Gated on `hasRenderableOpenInterrupt` instead.

Also compacts the meter to `89.2k / 3.7M · 4s`; the dropped "run"/"total" labels
move to the button title and stay spelled out in the popover.

commits.message: stop navigate from reporting success for routes that do not exist
commits.body:
`engenty_tools_modules`, the runtime-context preamble and the navigation-paths
prompt all reported a module's base URL as `/mdl/<pluginId>` — synthesized from
the plugin id, never read from the router. Over half the modules register no
such route (`commercial-settings` has only `/mdl/commercial-settings/settings`),
so navigating there fell through to the `path="*"` catch-all, which redirects to
the copilot chat root with `replace`: the user was bounced back to the chat they
started from and even the URL evidence was overwritten. `navigate` returned
`{ok:true}` regardless, so the agent then said it had opened the page.

Route paths are declared in each module's client-side `ui/plugin.ts` and never
reach a server, so the check has to live in the browser. `navigate` now resolves
against the live contribution list: a prefix owning exactly one static page goes
there and reports where it landed, anything else throws listing the routes that
exist. Scoped to `/mdl/*`, the only prefix that list is complete for — the host
declares ~25 routes inline that never appear in it.

Hoists `UiContributionsProvider` above `shellUiHost` in App.tsx; the copilot
mounts beside `AuthenticatedRoutes`, so the table was out of its reach.
